Alemanha planeja dobrar sua capacidade de data centers
11 de outubro de 2026
O futuro digital na Alemanhaestá tomando forma na cidade de Dietzenbach. Google, EdgeConnex e Maincubes – duas empresas de tecnologia americanas e uma alemã – reservaram terrenos para a construção de centros de dados (data centers) nessa pequena cidade próxima a Frankfurt.
Dietzenbach é um polo logístico nas proximidades do aeroporto da metrópole financeira e tem cerca de 35 mil habitantes. A região de Frankfurt é um dos locais mais atraentes do mundo para operadores de computação em nuvem.
À medida que a demanda por capacidade computacional continua crescendo, mais centros de dados estão sendo planejados no local.
Consumo de eletricidade e água
No entanto, a notícia sobre os planos para um quarto megacentro de dados encontrou resistência entre os moradores.
As dezenas de milhares de computadores instalados num data center precisam de um enorme fornecimento de energia para funcionar ininterruptamente.
Esses equipamentos geram grandes quantidades de calor e necessitam de sistemas de refrigeração, que, por sua vez, consomem enormes volumes de água.
As pessoas entrevistadas pela DW em Dietzenbach demonstraram preocupação com o aumento das contas de água e energia, além de possíveis elevações da temperatura local.
"Queremos saber duas coisas: quais são os benefícios para a comunidade local aqui em Dietzenbach? E quais são os impactos ambientais?", afirmou o morador Wilhelm Sauer, apontando para as quatro imponentes chaminés que se erguem do centro de dados da EdgeConnex.
Ele e outros ativistas locais acreditam que o impacto dos centros de dados sobre os recursos da região talvez não seja compensado pelo número relativamente baixo de novos empregos anunciados.
Já o prefeito de Dietzenbach, Dieter Lang, do Partido Social-Democrata (SPD), de centro-esquerda, mostra-se otimista. Segundo ele, cerca de cem empregos de alta qualificação deverão chegar à cidade por meio do centro de dados da Google. Ele também disse esperar benefícios para as finanças municipais por meio de impostos.
Mas a pesquisadora Tara Merk, do projeto Community Data Centers no Instituto Weizenbaum, é cética. Ela acredita que a Alemanha provavelmente arrecadará pouco com centros de dados operados por empresas americanas "porque os lucros podem ser tributados em outros lugares".
Em especial as grandes empresas de tecnologia, diz ela, não vão pagar seus impostos em Dietzenbach.
Falta de informação sobre data centers
Em agosto de 2026, o governo alemão lançou um cadastro nacional de centros de dados que lista consumo de energia e de água e medidas de eficiência energética dos centros já em operação.
No entanto, a lista inclui apenas cerca de 300 instalações, muito menos que os aproximadamente 2 mil centros de dados que, segundo o próprio governo, operam no país.
"Algumas empresas informam seus projetos menores, mas não os grandes", disse Werner Neumann, membro da diretoria da organização ambientalista Bund.

artigo.texto: Virginia Tops AI Data Center Readiness Ranking as Smaller Markets Advance TRG DataCenters’ August 2026 ranking places Virginia in the lead, while states with abundant power, low-carbon electricity, and favorable water conditions gain ground. Power supply and water availability could help states outside established data center hubs compete for AI infrastructure investment, according to a new survey of US states from TRG DataCenters. The report, published in August 2026, compares 24 states using measures of infrastructure scale and environmental exposure and points to a more geographically diverse market as AI demand expands. Virginia topped the August ranking of states positioned for AI data center growth, but the findings also suggest smaller markets can compete by offering a favorable combination of electricity supply, lower-carbon generation, and water availability. “When planning infrastructure for the long term, that balance between scale and resource efficiency matters as much as raw megawatts,” Chris Hinkle, CEO of TRG DataCenters, told Data Center Knowledge. TRG’s analysis considered mapped large-scale AI data center sites, power capacity, electricity use, estimated annual carbon emissions, and the proportion of mapped facilities in areas of high water stress. Capacity figures reflect the AI infrastructure included in TRG’s dataset and do not represent each state’s total data center market. Virginia’s Lead Comes with Water Constraints Virginia received a readiness score of 100, followed by Ohio at 88.2, Tennessee at 83.7, Georgia at 81.8, and Texas at 80.8. TRG’s dataset mapped seven large AI sites in Virginia totaling 1,085 MW of capacity, while Ohio and Tennessee showed higher mapped capacities – 1,410 MW in Ohio and 1,373 MW in Tennessee. Virginia’s advantage reflects performance across several measures, including lower estimated grid carbon intensity serving the mapped facilities. Hinkle said Ohio’s mapped AI capacity was around 30% greater, but the grid serving Virginia’s facilities had roughly one-third lower carbon intensity than Ohio’s. “As a result, the AI facilities in our dataset are associated with around 2.3 million tons of CO2 emissions annually, compared with roughly 4.5 million tons in Ohio and 4.3 million in Tennessee,” he said. Water – or lack thereof – is a complicating factor. About one-third of Virginia’s mapped data centers are located in areas of high water stress, compared with none in Ohio and just 7% in Tennessee. “One factor Virginia will need to continue managing as the market expands is site selection around water availability,” Hinkle said. Those differences make the ranking a starting point for evaluating markets rather than evidence that development conditions are uniform within a state. Smaller Markets Offer Competing Advantages South Carolina placed sixth with a score of 80.5, just behind Texas, despite having only one large AI site and 142 MW of capacity in the study. “What surprised us most was South Carolina,” Hinkle said. “It has just one large AI data center site and around 142 MW of capacity, yet it finished almost level with Texas in our overall readiness ranking, despite Texas having 13 large sites.” He attributed that performance partly to the state’s nuclear-heavy electricity supply and the absence of mapped facilities in areas of high water stress. Hinkle also pointed to New York, Iowa, and Mississippi. New York combined relatively limited large-scale AI capacity with one of the lowest-carbon grids in the dataset, while Mississippi already supported more than 500 MW of AI capacity. “States that can combine reliable power with a relatively low-carbon electricity mix and favorable water conditions could become increasingly attractive as demand expands,” he said. Texas Faces a Siting Challenge Texas had the largest number of AI sites in the study – 13, with a combined capacity of 1,301 MW. However, 58.8% of those facilities were located in areas of high water stress. Hinkle said he expects those conditions to influence cooling choices and project locations. “That is likely to encourage more sophisticated siting and infrastructure strategies rather than simply slowing development,” he said. “We could see greater use of approaches such as closed-loop or air-based cooling, recycled water, and locations where local water conditions are more favorable.” TRG notes that the water-stress measure describes facility locations and does not establish actual water consumption or the impact of individual cooling systems. Developers still need to assess those conditions at the project level. From Readiness to Deliverable Infrastructure Statewide advantages must also translate into infrastructure that developers can use. A relatively small share of statewide electricity use does not, by itself, establish that a particular site has power available for expansion. “Grid connections, transmission capacity, fiber connectivity, build-ready sites, and long-term power availability can all influence where major projects ultimately land,” Hinkle said. For emerging markets, those requirements determine whether attractive resource conditions can support projects at scale. For established hubs, the requirements shape where additional development can proceed. “The result could be a more geographically diverse AI infrastructure market as developers match projects with the locations best equipped to support them.”

artigo.texto: Speed Bumps Slow Asia-Pacific’s Data Center Gold Rush Firmus and PLDT pulled data center IPOs this week while governments pressed pause on development in the latest hurdles to Asia’s data center boom. Asia-Pacific's hectic data center rollout has hit a series of speed bumps. The most dramatic by far was the collapse Friday of Australian-based Firmus’ planned AU$7.1 billion (US$4.97 billion) IPO, which had been expected to be the biggest ASX debut since Telstra’s 1997 IPO. Firmus, a neocloud company whose shareholders include Blackstone, Jane Street and Nvidia, withdrew its ASX listing application Friday and said it would seek up to $3 billion through private fund-raising, the Financial Times has reported. It had struggled to win market support at its target price of around AU$11 ($7.67), but even after it offered to cut the price, investors did not have the appetite. Trading in Maas Group, one of Firmus' shareholders, was halted Friday after the stock dropped 27% in two days. Maas Group has a 3.2% stake in the company as well as outstanding contracts with Firmus worth AU$727 million ($507 million). Two days earlier, Firmus had been dumped by CDC Data Centers from their joint AI infrastructure project in Australia after CDC had become troubled by Firmus’ southeast Asian expansion, which had not been a part of the original partnership. PLDT delays IPO to 2027 Firmus' wasn't the only IPO to go south this week. Philippine telco PLDT put its data center REIT listing on hold until 2027, blaming the decision on higher interest rates. The REIT, Vitro, was expected to generate as much as 24.2 billion Philippine pesos (US$385.1 million) on the Manila bourse. PLDT said in an exchange filing it had decided to delay the IPO until 2027 due to "current market conditions and rising interest rates." But it said it was committed to the IPO as an important part of its asset monetization and deleveraging plans. The Philippines' central bank last month hiked interest rates by 25 basis points and is widely expected to announce two more rate rises by the year's end. Southeast Asian governments have also been forced to press pause on the AI boom. Last week, Indonesia's West Java province halted a 640MW project by Singapore–based BDX, claiming it had not received key approvals, including an environmental assessment. A month ago, Thailand suspended 166 data center projects – of which 49 were under construction and 117 awaited approval – to allow government committees to write new industry rules that would set standards and maximize the economic benefit to Thailand. In Malaysia, the center of Asia's data center boom, officials are anxious about soaring the new digital infrastructure's power consumption. Electricity demand growth has gone from 1.5%-2% annually to nearly 10% due to data centers, Siti Safinah Salleh, head of the Malaysian Energy Commission, is reported to have said. Salleh warned that recovering energy costs from data center operators is difficult because many are on short-term contracts and have refused to make long-term commitments. artigo.texto: How to Secure Data Centers During the Construction Phase Before operations begin, layered defenses at the site and in the supply chain help prevent theft, vandalism, counterfeit gear, and covert endpoints. As data center build-outs accelerate, most conversations about physical security focus on operational facilities, with threats ranging from mundane events, such as break-ins, to novel threats like drone attacks. Yet the period of greatest exposure is often earlier: during construction. Sites are porous, contractor populations are large and fluid, and high-value materials and preinstalled equipment can be targeted or tampered with. Protecting the build phase should be a core pillar of any data center’s broader physical security strategy. Construction-Phase Risks to Data Centers Physical intrusions during construction come in many forms: Material theft. Theft of construction materials is common on open or lightly controlled construction sites. Copper, cabling, generators, and networking gear are all attractive targets, leading to financial losses and construction delays. Vandalism and sabotage. In some markets, community opposition to data center expansion can increase the likelihood of on-site disruption or damage. Deployment of spy devices. More covertly, malicious actors may attempt to plant devices – such as rogue wireless access points, small network switches, or hidden sensors – during construction to enable remote backdoor access once the facility is operational. Supply chain tampering. Risks also extend into supply chains: tampering with shipments, swapping components, or introducing counterfeit or compromised gear can create backdoors or degrade reliability before the facility ever goes live. Aerial reconnaissance or nuisance activity. Hobbyist drones can expose site layouts and procedures or create safety hazards. Practical Strategies to Secure Data Center Construction Sites While the overarching goal is simple – prevent unauthorized access to construction sites and their supply chains – executing this amid complex projects and large contractor populations is challenging. The following layered controls help reduce risk while maintaining construction speed. Establish a strong perimeter and active monitoring. Build robust physical barriers, ensure all ingress/egress routes are controlled, and funnel all foot and vehicle traffic through staffed gates. Pair this with temporary but professional-grade surveillance cameras covering the perimeter, material laydown yards, and sensitive areas; lighting designed with Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design principles; and motion or thermal sensors where feasible. Verify and control who enters the construction site. Vet contractors and delivery personnel before granting access, consistent with local laws and company policy. Require visible badges and use zoned access so workers can enter only the areas relevant to their tasks. This is no guarantee that bad actors won’t find their way in, but it’s one way to reduce risk. Grant access in phases. Bringing contractors on-site in smaller groups (e.g., having electricians complete their work before allowing HVAC workers to begin) reduces crowding and makes anomalous activity more visible. The trade-off is that this may slow construction by reducing the amount of work contractors can perform in parallel. Rope off construction areas. In addition to establishing a strong perimeter around the data center site, roping off or caging high-value storage (e.g., copper, cabling, generators, and networking equipment) provides another layer of defense against theft and sabotage. Harden the supply chain and track custody. Vet vendors for chain-of-custody controls, tamper-evident packaging, and secure transit practices. Upon receipt, record serial numbers and MAC addresses of networked devices, use barcodes or RFID to track movement, and keep sensitive equipment in controlled cages until deployment. Prepare for drone threats. Use drone detection where appropriate for visibility into potential aerial activity. Many forms of active drone interdiction are illegal, so coordinate with local authorities and legal teams, emphasizing deterrence, detection, and evidence capture rather than unlawful countermeasures. Validate what’s installed before commissioning. Another way to detect supply chain abuse is to compare installed assets against purchase orders and approved bills of materials. Conduct technical sweeps for unauthorized wireless signals or unexpected network endpoints to identify situations where someone installed a device that isn’t supposed to be included. Balancing Speed and Security Complete eradication of construction-phase physical security risks isn’t realistic, just as fully preventing cyberattacks isn’t. However, a multilayered defense strategy based on practices like those described above goes a long way toward reducing the likelihood and impact of intrusions, while improving your chances of detecting and remediating those that do occur.

A disposição de data centers para pagar por energia está muito alta e os projetos conseguem manter bons retornos financeiros mesmo quando as negociações na Europa chegam aos 200 euros por megawatt-hora (MWh), segundo cálculos do banco de investimentos SB1 Markets.
“Essa demanda é real”, disse o vice-presidente do SB1 Markets, Alexander Askling, em participação no evento Green Power Sweden, em Estocolmo, esta semana.
Askling apontou que o consumo de energia por esses projetos pode elevar a demanda elétrica apenas na Suécia em 25% nos próximos anos.
A Aurora Energy Research estima que o consumo adicional no país devido ao aumento do processamento de dados chegará a 10 terawatt-hora até 2030.
“Mas se eu apresentar um cenário semelhante para a Finlândia ou a Noruega, essa tendência está ainda mais acentuada”, disse o chefe de pesquisa para países nórdicos e bálticos da Aurora, Alexander Esser, durante o evento.
Investimento bilionário do Google
Até o momento, um dos países da região que tem sido mais bem sucedido na atração desses investimentos é a Finlândia.
Em setembro, o Google anunciou que o país nórdico será o destino do maior investimento individual da empresa na Europa, com 13 bilhões de euros para a construção de quatro data centers e infraestruturas relacionadas entre 2027 e 2028.
Em paralelo, o Google assinou um contrato de compra de energia (PPA, na sigla em inglês) com a finlandesa Fortum para aquisição de metade da capacidade de geração da usina nuclear de Loviisa.
O acordo tem duração de 22 anos e vai permitir a extensão da vida útil da usina nuclear até o fim da licença de operação em 2050.
Segundo a Fortum, a planta é responsável por 10% de todo o suprimento de energia finlandês e, sem esse contrato, precisaria ter a vida útil encerrada em 2030.
As companhias também assinaram um memorando de entendimento para desenvolver novos projetos de geração nuclear, renováveis, soluções de flexibilidade e serviços de gestão do portfólio de energia.
Parte do acordo envolve o desenvolvimento de um projeto de 94 megawatts (MW) para armazenamento de energia em baterias, que ficará adjacente a um dos data centers do Google no país.
“O próximo passo é explorar como nuclear, renováveis, flexibilidade, como baterias e hidrelétricas reversíveis, além de tecnologias digitais, podem trabalhar juntar para atender à crescente demanda por energia de uma forma competitiva e sustentável”, disse em nota o CEO da Fortum, Markus Rauramo.
Concorrência com eletrificação é desafio
O alto crescimento na demanda para processamento de dados é um desafio em um continente que também busca ampliar a eletrificação em diversas áreas para reduzir o uso de combustíveis fósseis.
A meta atual da União Europeia é eletrificar 47% de todo o consumo energético até 2040

artigo.texto: [Photo: MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND CLIMATE CHANGE/ FACEBOOK] Fiji has launched a five-year $5.2 million plan aimed at preparing the country to enter international carbon markets by 2030. The Five-Year Costed Carbon Market Plan was launched yesterday during the opening of the Pacific Pre-COP31 in Nadi. The plan sets out the regulatory, technical and institutional systems Fiji needs before its first international carbon trade under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. It focuses on sectors including energy, transport, agriculture, waste and forestry, with strong emphasis on forests, mangroves, wetlands and other nature-based solutions. Minister for Rural, Maritime Development and Disaster Risk Management Mosese Bulitavu says carbon markets must deliver benefits beyond the trading of carbon. “For Fiji, carbon markets must be about more than trading carbon. They must deliver real climate action, unlock new and sustainable sources of climate finance, and ensure that the benefits reach our communities and resource owners.” The plan places communities and resource owners at the centre, with provisions for fair benefit-sharing, social and environmental safeguards and Free, Prior and Informed Consent. Fiji will also establish a Fijian Transactional Registry and a National Carbon Market Inter-Agency Technical Working Group to manage and track carbon market activities. The Government will use the plan to engage development partners, donors and potential carbon buyers to secure the finance and technical support needed for implementation. Conservation International says the plan could help Fiji attract high-integrity carbon finance while protecting ecosystems and supporting resilient livelihoods.

A empresa russa de tecnologia e inteligência artificial Yandex informou na madrugada deste domingo (11) que um ataque com drones danificou suas instalações e provocou o fechamento completo de seu centro de dados na região de Vladimir, na Rússia.
Segundo a companhia, ninguém ficou ferido, mas alguns de seus serviços estão indisponíveis para os usuários.
Este é o terceiro grande centro de dados da empresa a ficar fora de operação nos últimos dias.
Na sexta-feira (9), a Yandex informou que outro de seus centros de dados, localizado na região de Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou, havia sido atingido por drones ucranianos. O ataque danificou parcialmente as instalações e comprometeu seu funcionamento.
Um dia antes, um ataque ucraniano havia paralisado o centro de dados da empresa em Sasovo, a sudeste de Moscou. O local abriga dois dos três supercomputadores usados no desenvolvimento do modelo de inteligência artificial da companhia.
Yandex: a "Google da Rússia"
A Yandex é uma das principais empresas russas de tecnologia e tem participação importante no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial no país. Por sua atuação em serviços digitais, como buscas na internet, é frequentemente chamada de “Google da Rússia”.
Centros de dados são instalações que abrigam servidores e outros equipamentos responsáveis por armazenar e processar informações e manter serviços digitais em funcionamento.

A expansão acelerada da Inteligência Artificial está criando um desafio que vai muito além de processadores, GPUs e capacidade computacional. À medida que novas aplicações aumentam a demanda por processamento, a infraestrutura elétrica dos Data Centers passa a ocupar posição estratégica na expansão do mercado.
No Futurecom 2026, Marco Aurélio Munhoz, líder Telecom e Datacenter da Megmeet, pontuou que o desafio não está apenas em disponibilizar energia, mas em garantir que ela seja entregue de forma confiável, eficiente e sustentável.
“Não está em entregar a energia, mas é importante saber como essa energia está sendo entregue”, afirmou durante palestra sobre a infraestrutura necessária para sustentar a evolução da Inteligência Artificial (IA) na arena Future Talks.
A questão ganha dimensão diante do crescimento projetado para o consumo dos data centers. O consumo desses ambientes chegaria a cerca de 485 TWh em 2025 e poderia praticamente dobrar até 2030, impulsionado principalmente pela IA, de acordo com Dados apresentados da Agência Internacional de Energia.
De servidores a megawatts por rack
A transformação não ocorre apenas na escala dos Data Centers. A própria arquitetura interna desses ambientes está mudando.
Munhoz destacou que, anteriormente, racks operavam com demandas de energia na faixa de 10 kWh a 15 kWh e passam a enfrentar uma multiplicação significativa da potência necessária. A projeção apresentada é de que a demanda possa chegar a 1 MW por rack em determinadas aplicações de IA.
A mudança altera as premissas de engenharia e infraestrutura dos Data Centers. Mais potência significa também novos desafios para distribuição elétrica, barramentos, cabeamento, refrigeração e investimentos.
“Estamos mudando a escala da física internamente no data center”, resumiu Munhoz.
O ponto é relevante para um mercado no qual a capacidade de expansão computacional pode deixar de ser determinada apenas pela disponibilidade de servidores e passar a depender também da capacidade de conexão e fornecimento de energia.
Eficiência passa a ser parte da capacidade computacional
A discussão sobre eficiência energética deixa de ser apenas ambiental ou operacional e passa a ter impacto direto sobre a capacidade de processamento que um Data Center consegue entregar.
Uma das arquiteturas em desenvolvimento, segundo o executivo, é o uso de 800 VDC, que busca trabalhar com tensão mais elevada e corrente menor na distribuição de energia. De acordo com os dados apresentados, estudos associados à Nvidia apontam potencial de redução de aproximadamente 45% na utilização de cobre e ganho de 5% em eficiência energética.
A lógica é reduzir perdas ao longo do processo de conversão e distribuição. Em instalações de grande escala, mesmo pequenos ganhos percentuais podem representar volumes relevantes de energia que deixam de ser dissipados e, consequentemente, menor pressão sobre sistemas de refrigeração.

artigo.texto: JANESVILLE – This week, The Gazette is taking a closer look at three questions we originally wrote for a public forum we hosted Sept. 30 on the GM/JATCO ballot referendum that's set for the Nov. 3 election ballot. The referendum asks Janesville residents to respond “Yes” or “No” to a question that asks if they'd want voters to have the authority to decide whether to approve any development project worth more than $450 million at the GM/JATCO site. The Gazette didn’t get to all the questions we’d hoped to ask at our forum, so we posed three unasked questions to the public — and to panelists who attended the forum. We received several responses, and we plan to examine them this week in a three-part series, with each story focusing on one question and the range of views it drew from some of those who responded. The first question: Q: The Janesville City Council has approved a 12-month, citywide moratorium on all data center developments, which it says would allow the city more time to research and craft policy and guardrails tied to data centers. Should voters take that moratorium into consideration when deciding on the GM/JATCO site referendum in the Nov. 3 election? Why or Why not? Mandy Witt is a local commercial property realtor and one of the six panelists at our forum. She opposes the referendum because she says if it passes, it could bring unpredictability to decisions usually made based on local planning and economic development policies — structures developers are accustomed to working with. In her response to this question, Witt said she thinks a residents’ vote on projects bigger than $450 million at the GM site could deter developers. She thinks voters should pay attention to the moratorium’s intent, which she believes is to give the City of Janesville extra time to research data centers and develop standards and local protections for the projects. Witt points out a contrast between the two measures: The referendum would apply to a variety of large-scale projects at the GM/JATCO site, not just data centers, while the city moratorium only applies to data centers only. “I am voting “No” (on the referendum) because I want clear requirements, early communication, and a predictable approval process,” Witt said. “The moratorium provides an opportunity to develop data center rules. The referendum adds a separate voter approval requirement without establishing those rules or a timetable for that vote.” Cathy Erdman fronts SNOW Janesville, a grassroots group that advocates for south-side Janesville residents and businesses, and one of the six panelists at our forum. She was another forum panelist. Erdman supports a “Yes” vote on the referendum, which would give voters authority over whether to approve large-scale projects at the GM/JATCO site. She says she’s more interested in what a citywide data center moratorium eventually accomplishes than the city's stated intentions going into the moratorium. In her response, Erdman said she believes it’s impossible to separate data centers from the conversation on the GM/JATCO referendum – despite the city’s recent passage of a data center moratorium. Erdman points out the city’s nearly more than year-long rewrite of the city’s zoning code has rolled out during the period in which the city was considering a proposal by Viridian Partners. During that time, Erdman notes, planners have not written standards for data centers that would require impact studies, setback requirements or neighbor notification rules. She points out a zoning reboot with fewer data center rules than she thinks is appropriate could get approved before the city drafts and OKs companion ordinances tied to the moratorium. Meanwhile, Erdman said, a new data center proposal should come after the moratorium ends. Now, there’s no clarity on what new rules the moratorium will produce. She thinks that’s why voters should weigh both the moratorium and the possibility of data centers when they vote on the referendum. “Despite the presence of a moratorium, future data center projects at GM/Jatco remain a possibility, and that should be a part of a voter’s decision-making process,” Erdman said. “Voters should be asking 'What happens when the moratorium expires, and who should have the final say on any exceptionally large development project at the publicly-owned GM/Jatco site, including data centers?'" Elaine Strassburg is a Janesville resident who responded to The Gazette’s request for local reader feedback on our questions on the referendum. Strassburg opposes the referendum. In her response, she says she thinks residents should separate the city’s data center moratorium from their consideration of the GM/JATCO site referendum, in part because Strassburg takes a more measured stance on data centers. “I’m hopeful the strong feelings against data centers will motivate the industry to innovate because unless we put a lid on AI, and I doubt that will happen, we will need data centers,” Strassburg said. The city of Janesville cut short a due-dillegence process at the GM/JATCO site with data center developer Viridian Partners earlier this year after the company failed in six months to show any concerted plans on how it might pursue a data center project. Strassburg believes public pressure against against Viridian Partners’ proposal is what led the city to in turn enact a data center moratorium. She believes public pressure against data centers provides reason enough for the city to use the moratorium period to craft data center protections that respond to residents’ concerns. “Interested citizens had sufficient influence on city government to ensure there will be no data center anywhere in Janesville until environmental issues such as water and electrical usage, and noise levels of current data centers, are cared for to the satisfaction of Janesville citizens,” she said. artigo.texto: Mercado global de equipamentos de teste Ethernet: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Previsão do Mercado de Equipamentos de Teste Ethernet até 2035: Crescimento Impulsionado por 800GbE e Data Centers de IA Resumo De acordo com o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de equipamentos de teste Ethernet, o mercado entra em 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de equipamentos de teste Ethernet entra em uma fase decisiva à medida que a infraestrutura de rede avança para 800GbE e as primeiras implantações de 1.6TbE, impulsionadas por cargas de trabalho de IA, expansão da nuvem e backhaul 5G-Advanced. Os equipamentos de teste Ethernet abrangem instrumentos e sistemas especializados que verificam, analisam e validam o desempenho, a conformidade e a funcionalidade de redes e dispositivos baseados em Ethernet ao longo de todo o ciclo de vida, da pesquisa e desenvolvimento à fabricação, chegando à implantação em campo e à manutenção. O mercado é definido por um conjunto diversificado de produtos, incluindo analisadores de rede, analisadores de protocolo, testadores de cabos, testadores de taxa de erro de bit, emuladores de rede, equipamentos de teste óptico, testadores de campo portáteis e equipamentos de laboratório de bancada. A demanda concentra-se na implantação de redes de telecomunicações, testes de infraestrutura de data centers, manutenção de redes corporativas, validação de Ethernet industrial, testes de Ethernet automotiva, sistemas aeroespaciais e de defesa, garantia de qualidade na fabricação e pesquisa e desenvolvimento. Com o crescimento do tráfego de dados e a evolução dos padrões Ethernet, a necessidade de ferramentas de validação precisas e de alta velocidade torna-se ainda mais crítica. O período de previsão de 2026 a 2035 será moldado pela comercialização da Ethernet de maior velocidade, pelo amadurecimento das operações de rede orientadas por IA e pela exigência de arquiteturas de data center energeticamente eficientes. Este relatório oferece uma visão baseada em dados sobre tamanho de mercado, estrutura, principais tendências, vetores de demanda, restrições de oferta e dinâmica competitiva para fabricantes, distribuidores, investidores e consultores. O cenário-base para o mercado de equipamentos de teste Ethernet de 2026 a 2035 prevê expansão sustentada, com taxa de crescimento anual composta de 6,2% e índice de mercado atingindo 182 em 2035 (2025=100). Essa perspectiva é sustentada pela aceleração da implantação de 800GbE e pela adoção inicial de 1.6TbE em data centers de hiperescala, que exigem soluções de teste avançadas para integridade de sinal, conformidade de protocolo e interoperabilidade. As operadoras de telecomunicações continuarão investindo em 5G-Advanced e backhaul pré-6G, impulsionando a demanda por testadores de campo portáteis e equipamentos de teste óptico. A manutenção de redes corporativas continuará sendo uma fonte estável de receita à medida que as organizações migram para Ethernet de maior velocidade para suportar aplicações intensivas em largura de banda. A validação de Ethernet industrial e os testes de Ethernet automotiva representam áreas de crescimento emergentes, impulsionadas pela manufatura inteligente e pelo desenvolvimento de veículos autônomos. O mercado também se beneficiará da crescente complexidade das arquiteturas de rede, incluindo redes desagregadas e abertas, que exigem testes e monitoramento abrangentes. No entanto, restrições como o alto custo dos equipamentos, a escassez de técnicos qualificados e os longos ciclos de substituição de equipamentos de teste legados podem moderar o crescimento. O cenário competitivo deverá registrar consolidação contínua e uma transição para soluções de teste definidas por software, que oferecem escalabilidade e automação. Geograficamente, a Ásia-Pacífico liderará o consumo, seguida pela América do Norte e Europa, enquanto a América Latina e o Oriente Médio e África apresentam oportunidades ainda não exploradas. No geral, o mercado está preparado para um crescimento robusto, com inovação tecnológica e transformação digital como principais viabilizadores. artigo.texto: Virginia Tops AI Data Center Readiness Ranking as Smaller Markets Advance TRG DataCenters’ August 2026 ranking places Virginia in the lead, while states with abundant power, low-carbon electricity, and favorable water conditions gain ground. Power supply and water availability could help states outside established data center hubs compete for AI infrastructure investment, according to a new survey of US states from TRG DataCenters. The report, published in August 2026, compares 24 states using measures of infrastructure scale and environmental exposure and points to a more geographically diverse market as AI demand expands. Virginia topped the August ranking of states positioned for AI data center growth, but the findings also suggest smaller markets can compete by offering a favorable combination of electricity supply, lower-carbon generation, and water availability. “When planning infrastructure for the long term, that balance between scale and resource efficiency matters as much as raw megawatts,” Chris Hinkle, CEO of TRG DataCenters, told Data Center Knowledge. TRG’s analysis considered mapped large-scale AI data center sites, power capacity, electricity use, estimated annual carbon emissions, and the proportion of mapped facilities in areas of high water stress. Capacity figures reflect the AI infrastructure included in TRG’s dataset and do not represent each state’s total data center market. Virginia’s Lead Comes with Water Constraints Virginia received a readiness score of 100, followed by Ohio at 88.2, Tennessee at 83.7, Georgia at 81.8, and Texas at 80.8. TRG’s dataset mapped seven large AI sites in Virginia totaling 1,085 MW of capacity, while Ohio and Tennessee showed higher mapped capacities – 1,410 MW in Ohio and 1,373 MW in Tennessee. Virginia’s advantage reflects performance across several measures, including lower estimated grid carbon intensity serving the mapped facilities. Hinkle said Ohio’s mapped AI capacity was around 30% greater, but the grid serving Virginia’s facilities had roughly one-third lower carbon intensity than Ohio’s. “As a result, the AI facilities in our dataset are associated with around 2.3 million tons of CO2 emissions annually, compared with roughly 4.5 million tons in Ohio and 4.3 million in Tennessee,” he said. Water – or lack thereof – is a complicating factor. About one-third of Virginia’s mapped data centers are located in areas of high water stress, compared with none in Ohio and just 7% in Tennessee. “One factor Virginia will need to continue managing as the market expands is site selection around water availability,” Hinkle said. Those differences make the ranking a starting point for evaluating markets rather than evidence that development conditions are uniform within a state. Smaller Markets Offer Competing Advantages South Carolina placed sixth with a score of 80.5, just behind Texas, despite having only one large AI site and 142 MW of capacity in the study. “What surprised us most was South Carolina,” Hinkle said. “It has just one large AI data center site and around 142 MW of capacity, yet it finished almost level with Texas in our overall readiness ranking, despite Texas having 13 large sites.” He attributed that performance partly to the state’s nuclear-heavy electricity supply and the absence of mapped facilities in areas of high water stress. Hinkle also pointed to New York, Iowa, and Mississippi. New York combined relatively limited large-scale AI capacity with one of the lowest-carbon grids in the dataset, while Mississippi already supported more than 500 MW of AI capacity. “States that can combine reliable power with a relatively low-carbon electricity mix and favorable water conditions could become increasingly attractive as demand expands,” he said. Texas Faces a Siting Challenge Texas had the largest number of AI sites in the study – 13, with a combined capacity of 1,301 MW. However, 58.8% of those facilities were located in areas of high water stress. Hinkle said he expects those conditions to influence cooling choices and project locations. “That is likely to encourage more sophisticated siting and infrastructure strategies rather than simply slowing development,” he said. “We could see greater use of approaches such as closed-loop or air-based cooling, recycled water, and locations where local water conditions are more favorable.” TRG notes that the water-stress measure describes facility locations and does not establish actual water consumption or the impact of individual cooling systems. Developers still need to assess those conditions at the project level. From Readiness to Deliverable Infrastructure Statewide advantages must also translate into infrastructure that developers can use. A relatively small share of statewide electricity use does not, by itself, establish that a particular site has power available for expansion. “Grid connections, transmission capacity, fiber connectivity, build-ready sites, and long-term power availability can all influence where major projects ultimately land,” Hinkle said. For emerging markets, those requirements determine whether attractive resource conditions can support projects at scale. For established hubs, the requirements shape where additional development can proceed. “The result could be a more geographically diverse AI infrastructure market as developers match projects with the locations best equipped to support them.”

artigo.texto: Maryland regulators denied financial credits for a controversial battery storage project proposed for Harford County, but the decision does not necessarily stop the project from moving forward. The 500-megawatt Oystercatcher Energy Storage System is proposed near BGE's Conastone substation in White Hall. Harford County has opposed the project and has been involved in the Public Service Commission proceedings surrounding the proposal. According to the PSC decision provided to WMAR-2 News, regulators denied the project's application for Energy Storage Capacity Credits, citing concerns about whether the project would be cost-effective and provide enough benefit to ratepayers. The decision does not prevent developers from continuing the project's separate approval process. Oystercatcher could also seek the financial credits again during the state's next round of applications after Jan. 1. Regulators also called for continued engagement with local stakeholders in Harford County if the project moves forward. WMAR-2 News previously reported on opposition to the proposed facility, particularly over its location near Deer Creek. Residents have raised concerns about lithium-ion battery fires and potential impacts to the air and nearby water. Supporters of battery storage have argued that the technology could help support Maryland's electric grid as demand grows and other sources of electricity generation are retired. Harford County created a workgroup involving county agencies, fire companies, health officials, community organizations and residents to examine battery energy storage projects proposed in the county. The county says it has also explored legal action over environmental and public-safety concerns. The Oystercatcher project would connect to BGE's Conastone substation near Norrisville Road and Deer Creek. County materials describe the proposed facility as capable of storing 500 megawatts of energy. This is a developing story, so check back with WMAR2News.com for updates. artigo.texto: Behind-the-Meter Power Offers Control, Flexibility and Speed for the AI Age Key Highlights - AI is driving data centers to rethink their relationship with power. - BESS helps data centers manage volatile AI compute loads and grid constraints. - UPS, BESS and on-site generation create a coordinated energy stack. - Virtual power plants can turn backup assets into strategic grid resources. - Energy-as-a-Service can reduce upfront costs for behind-the-meter infrastructure. For the last decade, the data center industry has been a quiet engine of the digital economy, but today, the explosive rise of AI is exacerbating power sourcing issues that must be solved to keep building at the speed of innovation. Electric Power Research Institute projects that data centers could consume as much as 17% of U.S. electricity by 2030, more than triple their current 4-5% share. This massive spike in demand is clashing directly with a severely constrained power grid. At the end of 2025, more than 2,060 GW of new generation and storage capacity was represented by projects actively seeking interconnection to the U.S. grid. In turn, data center operators are fundamentally rethinking their relationship with power, shifting from passive grid consumers to active, localized energy producers. Grid capacity is no longer the ceiling. Instead, the next chapter of digital infrastructure will be written behind the meter. Behind-the-meter (BTM) refers to energy assets located on the customer side of the utility connection, including battery systems, microgrids, generators, fuel cells, and distributed energy resources that can operate independently of grid constraints. The Role of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) While every data center developer face grid constraints, the industry’s two dominant business models are adopting distinctly different strategies to bypass the power bottleneck. Hyperscale Operators Hyperscale operators (tech giants like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft) utilize their massive balance sheets to secure gigawatt-scale capacity directly. Rather than acting as passive grid customers, hyperscalers are taking direct, active control of their energy supply chains. They negotiate custom, state-level tariffs directly with utilities, co-locate facilities next to large nuclear or baseload assets, and sign massive off-site Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). Increasingly, hyperscalers are also deploying large-scale, on-site Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to bypass grid delays and accelerate their projects, or turning to behind-the-meter natural gas generation to provide additional power on-site. Colocation Providers In contrast, colocation providers lease space, power, and cooling to third-party tenants. Colos operate on a highly competitive, faster-to-market model where speed-to-revenue is the primary metric. Colocation facilities are geographically constrained, as their facilities must be located close to business hubs to minimize latency rather than simply next to remote power plants. Consequently, data center and colocation developers are increasingly integrating on-site, behind-the-meter energy solutions. In highly congested markets, BTM generation and battery storage can provide a path to power while developers wait for grid interconnection. In Virginia, for example, LS Power is pursuing a 300 MW data center project designed to receive power directly from its adjacent natural gas-fired Doswell power plant, creating a behind-the-meter supply arrangement that can help accelerate access to power. The New Coordinated Energy Stack: UPS + BESS + Generators Historically, a data center’s power architecture was passive, consisting of an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) to bridge 5-to-15 minutes of downtime and backup diesel generators to handle prolonged outages. AI has shattered this legacy design. Although many enterprise deployments still operate below 20 kW per rack, next-generation AI clusters are increasingly exceeding 100 kW per rack, with some designs targeting significantly higher densities. Furthermore, AI training runs create highly volatile, synchronized compute loads, causing electricity draw to spike and drop in massive, sub-second waves. To protect both sensitive computing equipment and the local grid from these fluctuations, operators are deploying a layered, grid-interactive energy stack: - UPS (Instant Protection): Positioned in series with the servers, the traditional UPS remains essential for providing millisecond-fast power conditioning and preventing data loss during transient voltage sags. - BESS (On-site Shock Absorber & Optimizer): Connected in parallel at the facility level, BESS acts as a real-time shock absorber. It smooths out volatile AI compute spikes, stores cost-effective off-peak power for use during peak hours, and participates in grid-balancing services. - On-site Generation (Long-Term Firm Power): Customer-sited generation, including natural gas microturbines, provides the ultimate firm baseload capacity, insulating the facility from grid failures for days or weeks. By layering these technologies, operators can stop treating their power systems like a pricey “insurance policy” that sits idle, and start using them as a smart, money-saving asset. By discharging on-site batteries during peak demand periods — a strategy known as peak shaving — operators can reduce the peak loads used to calculate demand charges, potentially lowering electricity costs significantly. Turning Backup Assets into Strategic Grid Partners Historically, backup diesel generators sat untouched, accumulating maintenance costs unless a blackout occurred. Today, utilities and data center operators are establishing mutually beneficial partnerships. artigo.texto: Prime Minister Narendra Modi has recently inaugurated two projects in Tamil Nadu. These projects are expected to support renewable energy integration ports and address growing demand for Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) projects in Tamil Nadu. One of the projects involves the development of port infrastructure across the country to help the shipping sector reach new heights. Tamil Nadu is expected to play an important role in this initiative. The central government has recently taken a significant decision In this direction with approximately Rs. 17,000 crore investment. The VOC Port in Thoothukudi is being developed into a mega container port and green energy hub. Once completed, the port will be able to accommodate even the ultra-large container vessels. This development is expected to help transform Tamil Nadu into a global hub for industry and transportation. BESS Project in Tamil Nadu Prime Minister Narendra Modi also laid the foundation stone for the 250 MW/500 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, on October 11, 2026. According to the tender, awarded to NLC India Renewables Limited (NIRL), a subsidiary of NLC India Limited (NLCIL), last year, it would develop this project across Ottapidaram, Anuppankulam, and Kayathar. The systems are designed to support two full charging and discharging cycles daily, enabling them to manage peak power demand and improve energy availability during critical load periods. It will follow a Build-Own-Operate (BOO) model under which the company will receive financial assistance under the State component of the Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme. Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) will procure the energy storage services from NIRL for a period of 12 years through a Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA). About NLC India's 250 MW/500 MWh BESS Project The 500 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project was originally awarded to NLC India Renewables Limited (NIRL), a subsidiary of NLC India Limited (NLCIL), following a tender issued by Tamil Nadu Green Energy Corporation Limited (TNGECL) in June 2025. It is the first large-scale energy storage initiative for NLCIL. The project involves the development of three standalone BESS units with a combined capacity of 250 MW/500 MWh. These units will be installed at three substations in Tamil Nadu—Ottapidaram, Anuppankulam, and Kayathar—each operating at 400/230/110 kV. The systems are designed to support two full charging and discharging cycles daily, enabling them to manage peak power demand and improve energy availability during critical load periods. The project will follow the Build-Own-Operate (BOO) model and was awarded through a tariff-based competitive bidding process. It will receive financial assistance under the state component of the Viability Gap Funding (VGF) scheme. As part of the agreement, Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) will procure energy storage services from NIRL for 12 years under a Battery Energy Storage Purchase Agreement (BESPA). This long-term arrangement is expected to provide reliable support for Tamil Nadu's grid infrastructure and energy requirements.

artigo.texto: Mercado global de coletores de calha parabólica: Tamanho, Tendências e Previsão até 2035 - Relatório completo em PDF · pacote de dados Excel · documento Word · apresentação executiva - Entrega por e-mail 24/7, inclusive fins de semana e feriados - Copiar e colar habilitado · formato pronto para impressão - Rodadas ilimitadas de esclarecimentos após a entrega Mercado global de coletores de calha parabólica deve se expandir até 2035, impulsionado pela demanda por armazenamento de energia térmica Resumo Segundo o mais recente relatório da IndexBox sobre o mercado global de Coletores de Calha Parabólica, o mercado inicia 2026 com fundamentos de demanda mais amplos, comportamento de compra mais disciplinado e uma arquitetura de oferta mais diversificada regionalmente. O mercado global de coletores de calha parabólica (PTC, na sigla em inglês) entra em uma fase de renovada importância estratégica, à medida que os sistemas de energia priorizam capacidade renovável despachável. Diferentemente dos sistemas fotovoltaicos, os coletores de calha parabólica integram armazenamento de energia térmica de custo competitivo, o que permite gerar eletricidade ou fornecer calor industrial além das horas de luz solar. Este relatório analisa o mercado de 2026 a 2035, abrangendo conjuntos completos de coletores, espelhos, tubos receptores, estruturas de suporte e sistemas de rastreamento. A análise identifica as usinas CSP de escala utilitária como o principal uso final, enquanto o calor de processo industrial, o aquecimento distrital, a dessalinização e a recuperação avançada de petróleo oferecem caminhos de diversificação. O cenário competitivo reúne empresas de engenharia consolidadas e fabricantes especializados de componentes. A dinâmica regional é moldada pela qualidade do recurso solar, pelo apoio de políticas públicas e pelas capacidades de fabricação locais. O cenário-base da previsão pressupõe continuidade moderada das políticas, queda dos custos tecnológicos e reconhecimento crescente do valor do armazenamento de longa duração. Os principais riscos incluem a concorrência de sistemas fotovoltaicos com baterias, atrasos no licenciamento e concentração da cadeia de suprimentos. O relatório oferece uma perspectiva baseada em dados para fabricantes, empreiteiras EPC, investidores e formuladores de políticas que atuam nesse mercado em evolução. O cenário-base para o mercado de coletores de calha parabólica de 2026 a 2035 prevê uma expansão moderada, porém constante, com taxa de crescimento anual composta de 4,2% em termos reais. Essa perspectiva se ancora na proposta de valor singular dos coletores de calha parabólica: a capacidade de armazenar energia térmica em escala, oferecendo eletricidade e calor despacháveis que complementam as fontes renováveis variáveis. O crescimento da demanda não repetirá o boom impulsionado por subsídios da década de 2010; será movido, isso sim, por projetos integrados de energia, configurações híbridas e mandatos de descarbonização industrial. As usinas CSP de escala utilitária continuarão sendo o maior segmento, mas sua participação diminuirá gradualmente à medida que as aplicações de calor de processo industrial e aquecimento distrital ganharem tração. Avanços tecnológicos, como receptores de maior temperatura e sistemas avançados de sais fundidos, aumentarão a eficiência e reduzirão o custo nivelado. Restrições na cadeia de suprimentos de componentes especializados, como tubos receptores evacuados, podem moderar o crescimento em determinados anos. Geograficamente, Oriente Médio e África, junto com a Ásia-Pacífico, responderão pela maior parte das novas adições de capacidade, apoiadas por planos nacionais de diversificação energética. América do Norte e Europa terão implantação seletiva, muitas vezes vinculada a projetos de pesquisa ou híbridos. O índice de mercado, com 2025 como ano-base em 100, deve alcançar 151 até 2035, refletindo o crescimento acumulado. Esse cenário-base pressupõe ausência de reversões políticas relevantes e queda gradual dos custos de capital, em linha com as curvas de aprendizado históricas. Vetores e Restrições da Demanda Principais Vetores de Demanda - Crescimento da demanda por energia renovável despachável, impulsionado por requisitos de estabilidade da rede e pela integração de geração solar e eólica variável. - Adoção crescente de soluções de calor de processo industrial, à medida que os fabricantes buscam descarbonizar a produção de vapor em alta temperatura. - Políticas e incentivos governamentais de apoio à implantação de energia solar concentrada, incluindo leilões e créditos fiscais em regiões de cinturão solar. - Redução de custos na integração do armazenamento de energia térmica, ampliando a competitividade econômica dos sistemas de calha parabólica. - Expansão de projetos híbridos solar-gás e solar-dessalinização, sobretudo no Oriente Médio e no Norte da África. - Foco crescente no armazenamento de energia de longa duração para viabilizar o fornecimento renovável ininterrupto. Possíveis Restrições ao Crescimento - Concorrência intensa de sistemas fotovoltaicos com armazenamento em baterias, que registraram rápida queda de custos e prazos de implantação mais curtos. - Altos custos de capital iniciais e longos prazos de desenvolvimento das usinas CSP de escala utilitária, o que desestimula parte dos investidores. - Disponibilidade limitada de componentes especializados, como tubos receptores evacuados, criando gargalos na cadeia de suprimentos. - Incerteza regulatória e mecanismos de apoio inconsistentes em mercados-chave, afetando os pipelines de projetos. - Consumo de água para resfriamento nas usinas CSP convencionais, uma restrição em regiões áridas com escassez hídrica. artigo.texto: Previsão do Preço das Ações da Oracle: Atrasos nos Data Centers de IA Exacerbam a Pressão da Dívida, Quais Riscos a ORCL Enfrenta? A expansão da infraestrutura de IA da Oracle enfrenta gargalos no fornecimento de energia, atrasando a receita de computação em nuvem e concentrando necessidades de financiamento para 2028. Projetos em Wisconsin e no Novo México sofrem com atrasos e custos operacionais elevados. Esse cenário impacta a monetização do backlog de RPO, elevando o CDS para 261 pontos-base em 8 de outubro e pressionando os custos de captação. No aspecto técnico, a ação é negociada a US$ 141,40, abaixo das médias móveis, mantendo viés de baixa no curto prazo com suporte crítico em US$ 136. TradingKey - A expansão da infraestrutura de IA da Oracle (ORCL) enfrenta um novo teste. À medida que múltiplos projetos de grandes data centers enfrentam gargalos no fornecimento de energia, a receita de computação em nuvem que a empresa esperava monetizar rapidamente pode ter seu reconhecimento adiado, enquanto os custos de financiamento inicial e as pressões de amortização da dívida não desaparecerão em decorrência disso. O Morgan Stanley destacou em sua análise de crédito mais recente que os atrasos nos data centers podem desacelerar o ritmo de reconhecimento de receita e a recuperação de caixa da Oracle, além de concentrar parte de suas necessidades de financiamento por volta de 2028. Se os cronogramas dos projetos se desviarem significativamente dos planos originais, a empresa poderá precisar comprometer mais capital no curto prazo para concluir a construção das instalações e a implantação dos equipamentos, complicando ainda mais a gestão de caixa. O fornecimento de energia é atualmente um dos principais obstáculos para o avanço dos projetos. O projeto de data center Lighthouse da Oracle, em Wisconsin, foi impactado pelo ritmo de aprovação de energia. O Morgan Stanley prevê que a data real de entrega do fornecimento de energia do projeto pode ser adiada para meados de 2028, mais tarde do que a expectativa anterior do segundo semestre de 2027. O projeto Jupiter, no Novo México, também enfrenta problemas de suprimento de energia. A Oracle está avaliando uma solução alternativa de transporte de gás natural comprimido por caminhões, mas o custo desse método pode ser várias vezes superior ao do transporte por gasoduto, aumentando a carga operacional subsequente do projeto. Os atrasos nos projetos podem afetar a monetização do grande backlog de contratos da Oracle. A empresa possui atualmente cerca de US$ 638 bilhões em obrigações de desempenho remanescentes (RPO), o que representa receitas contratadas que ainda não foram reconhecidas. Enquanto isso, os mercados de crédito têm mostrado sinais que merecem atenção. Em 8 de outubro, o credit default swap (CDS) de cinco anos da Oracle fechou em 261 pontos-base, atingindo uma máxima histórica. O aumento nos preços dos CDS significa que o mercado está pagando custos mais elevados para se proteger contra potenciais riscos de crédito da empresa. Além disso, os preços dos títulos de longo prazo da Oracle estão sob pressão, e seus custos de financiamento enfrentam pressão de alta. Embora a empresa ainda mantenha uma classificação de crédito de grau de investimento, os investidores estão avaliando de forma mais cautelosa se seus investimentos em IA podem gerar receita conforme o esperado, bem como o impacto dos intensos gastos de capital no seu balanço patrimonial. Análise Técnica do Preço da Ação da Oracle Fonte: TradingView No gráfico diário, as ações da Oracle avançaram 4,21% na última sessão, fechando a US$ 141,40, mas permanecem ligeiramente abaixo de sua média móvel de 20 dias, de US$ 142,07, e da média móvel de 60 dias, de US$ 141,80. As duas médias móveis convergiram significativamente, indicando que as forças compradoras e vendedoras estão atingindo o equilíbrio; se a média móvel de 20 dias cruzar abaixo da média móvel de 60 dias, será formado um sinal de baixa, o que pode pressionar ainda mais o sentimento do mercado. Desde que disparou para cerca de US$ 168 no início de setembro, a ORCL continuou a formar topos de repique mais baixos, e sua estrutura de baixa no curto prazo ainda não se reverteu totalmente. Atualmente, a faixa de US$ 142–US$ 145 forma a primeira zona de resistência; somente se o preço da ação se mantiver firmemente acima de US$ 145 com um volume elevado é que terá a oportunidade de desafiar a faixa de US$ 150–US$ 152, com um alvo potencial de US$ 158–US$ 160 após um rompimento. No lado de baixa, a atenção deve se voltar primeiramente para a zona de suporte de US$ 136–US$ 138. Se o preço da ação cair abaixo de US$ 136, poderá retestar a faixa de US$ 130–US$ 133; uma vez perdida essa região, o alvo de baixa apontará para US$ 125 e, em circunstâncias extremas, um reteste da mínima de julho, de US$ 116–US$ 120, não pode ser descartado. O RSI está atualmente em 48,18. Embora esteja acima da linha de sinal suavizada de 45,34, indicando uma recuperação de momento no curto prazo, ele ainda não ultrapassou os 50 pontos, o que temporariamente é insuficiente para confirmar uma reversão de tendência. O volume também não se expandiu significativamente, sugerindo que a confiança dos compradores permanece limitada. Este conteúdo foi traduzido por IA e revisado por humanos. artigo.texto: Swatara Township approves community benefits plan for data center projects DAUPHIN COUNTY, Pa. (WHP) — Swatara Township's Board of Commissioners approved community benefits agreements for a pair of proposed data centers last week. The agreements include $84.15 million in contributions associated with Highlands West and $36.15 million associated with Highlands East, according to the board. Highlands West is expected to be built over Dauphin Highlands Golf Course at 650 South Harrisburg Street. Highlands East would be at 4951 Highland Street, according to preliminary plans from the developers. READ MORE | Dauphin County golf course will turn into data center after $45.6M sale The total of $120.3 million in contributions will be split between the following initiatives, the board said. - $38 million to build a joint police and fire headquarters and emergency operations center - $27 million in restricted long-term funding for roads, public works equipment, snow removal, facilities, parks, technology, capital reserves and debt and service stabilization. - $24 million for a second public safety facility, which would include a fire station, police substation, EMS support and a backup emergency operations center - $12 million to fund career firefighter positions, recruitment and retention, firefighter pension funding, and future police, public works and code enforcement staffing - $8 million for fire apparatus replacement - $4 million for operating-cost stabilization, including residential trash collection, assistance for seniors, veterans and residents in hardship, fee stabilization and taxpayer-impact mitigation - $3 million for a municipal training facility for fire, police and EMS training, emergency-response exercises and emergency-management preparedness - $3 million to replace patrol vehicles, make technology and communications upgrades and for equipment for criticial infrastructure protection. - $1 million for scholarships for township residents and training programs to support data center workforce readiness - $300,000 for solicitor, engineer and consulting fees The contributions will be paid in installments based on development milestones, the township said.

artigo.texto: Três novas usinas fotovoltaicas e um grande sistema de baterias reduzem a dependência do diesel e protegem o fornecimento de energia no arquipélago africano. Em ilhas isoladas no meio do oceano, produzir eletricidade queimando combustível importado custa caro e gera apagões constantes. A chegada da energia solar associada a baterias transforma a estabilidade elétrica do arquipélago das Comores. Por que redes elétricas em ilhas sofrem tanto para manter a luz acesa? Você já reparou na luz piscando em casa quando um aparelho pesado é ligado? Em pequenas ilhas, qualquer variação repentina no sol faz com que a usina solar perca potência instantaneamente, desequilibrando toda a cidade. Isso acontece porque redes isoladas não contam com a força mecânica de grandes hidrelétricas para absorver choques. O projeto resolve esse gargalo utilizando inversores solares inteligentes grid-forming, que reagem em milissegundos para manter a voltagem constante sem derrubar o sistema. Quais são os números e a capacidade técnica do novo parque solar? Para substituir os motores a combustível e garantir energia limpa contínua, a engenharia do projeto integrou módulos fotovoltaicos de alto rendimento a um moderno centro de armazenamento químico. Capacidade total de geração solar: atinge 20 MW de potência instalada dividida em três usinas fotovoltaicas distribuídas estrategicamente pelas ilhas. - Armazenamento elétrico BESS: banco de baterias de íon-lítio com capacidade de 16 MWh para suporte e regulação de frequência. - Investimento internacional: montante aproximado de 23 milhões de dólares financiado pelo Abu Dhabi Fund for Development. - Empresa executora: desenvolvimento técnico e montagem estrutural realizados pela multinacional Masdar. - Redução de emissões: substituição direta de milhões de litros de óleo diesel queimados anualmente em geradores térmicos. Como o sistema de baterias e painéis funciona no dia a dia? Durante o dia, quando o sol brilha forte, os painéis suprem o consumo das cidades e direcionam o excesso de energia para carregar as baterias. Se uma nuvem densa passa sobre a usina, a bateria injeta carga na rede em frações de segundo. Essa troca automática impede que a frequência da eletricidade caia, garantindo que eletrodomésticos, hospitais e comércios continuem funcionando perfeitamente sem necessidade de acionar geradores poluentes de emergência. Onde ver como a tecnologia solar é aplicada em ilhas e países vulneráveis? Projetos de engenharia solar desenvolvidos para regiões insulares exigem planejamento rigoroso sobre como armazenar e distribuir energia em ambientes isolados do continente. Entender a infraestrutura montada por empresas especializadas ajuda a visualizar os desafios práticos de levar energia estável e limpa a comunidades distantes. Projetar usinas desse porte exige o cumprimento de diretrizes rigorosas da Comissão Eletrotécnica Internacional. A norma IEC 62933 define as regras de segurança e operação para sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias de grande escala. Já os módulos solares e inversores seguem os padrões da IEC 61724, garantindo resiliência contra corrosão salina provocada pela maresia e suporte às elevadas temperaturas das ilhas tropicais. Quando é necessário consultar um especialista em energia renovável? artigo.texto: Peugeot has revived the RCZ nameplate with the RCZ Vision concept car, showcasing the brand’s new design language for a coupé based on the STLA One platform, featuring a solid-state battery and a 1,000-volt electrical architecture. The RCZ Vision concept’s powertrain is claimed to output 500 hp and deliver up to 600 km of range with a claimed energy consumption figure of 11.5 kWh per 100 km, and its solid-state battery is said to to be able to be recharged from 10-80% in just 10 minutes, according to Peugeot. The RCZ Vision concept is Peugeot’s first expression of its “Feline Future” direction that will inform the design of future Peugeot models. According to Autocar, the RCZ Vision concept measures 4.65 m long, 1.35 m tall and 1.94 m wide, while its rolling stock is a set of forged aluminium wheels measuring 21 inches and 22 inches in diameter front and rear, respectively. Its cabin is designed to be a true four-seater, rather than the 2+2 configuration of its discontinued production namesake, and the RCZ Vision concept aims to accommodate two adults comfortably in the second row. The double-bubble roof of the previous RCZ has been rethought to optimise rear-seat headroom, while adding light to the cabin. Further maximising interior space is the RCZ Vision’s battery, which measures just 110 mm thick in order to retain a low floor and low-profile silhouette. Practicality and usability were priorities for the design team when designing the new RCZ Vision, as to maximise the likelihood of the car being adapted to production, said Peugeot design director Matthias Hossann. “This was an important part of my brief. I asked my team to make it look quite realistic in terms of proportion and size, in order to make this car more approachable. It’s not just designing a UFO or something which is highly futuristic,” Hossann told the publication. Inside, the cabin of the RCZ Vision concept is installed with the Hypersquare steering “wheel” that first featured on the Polygon concept, and the rectangular steering “wheel” will feature in the next-generation e-208. Displays in the RCZ Vision concept are transparent displays rather than traditional screens, which Peugeot says enables the driver to configure the information displayed, and the central display can even be completely switched off, where the transparent screen offers cleaner aesthetic. This setup of transparent displays complements the Hypersquare “wheel”, which offers access to main functions via the four rings close to hand, and therefore does not require the driver to move their hands from the steering control, says Peugeot. The RCZ Vision concept also serves to showcase the French manufacturer’s “X-by-wire” technologies including steer-by-wire, which means that it does not have a physical connection between the steering and the steered wheels. Peugeot says that steer-by-wire enables the use of variable ratio steering, such as to offer much quicker input at low vehicle speeds and reduced ratios for more stable steering when the vehicle is travelling at higher speeds. Also taking the by-wire approach is the braking system in the RCZ Vision, and the system is said to offer more precise braking modulation and seamless integration of regenerative braking. For ADAS, the RCZ Vision gets “Level 2++” automation, according to Peugeot.

artigo.texto: APsystems to Showcase Advanced C&I Energy Storage Solutions at Smart Energy Forum 2026 PRAGUE, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- October 14–15, 2026, APsystems will present its latest solar and energy storage solutions at Smart Energy Forum (SEF) 2026, held on October 14-15 at PVA EXPO PRAHA in Letňany, Prague. Visitors are invited to meet the APsystems team at Booth 1-10 and discover a comprehensive portfolio of solutions spanning commercial & industrial energy storage, residential storage, DIY energy storage, and microinverter technologies. As Europe's energy landscape continues to evolve, the integration of solar generation, energy storage, and intelligent energy management is becoming increasingly important. Commercial and industrial customers are seeking energy storage solutions that deliver exceptional safety, long-term reliability, and operational flexibility. These market demands are at the heart of the technologies APsystems will present in Prague. Advanced Liquid-Cooled C&I Energy Storage in Focus Taking center stage at the APsystems booth will be the APstorage 261L and APstorage 2000L, two all-in-one liquid-cooled energy storage systems designed to meet the needs of demanding commercial and industrial projects. The APstorage 261L is a robust industrial-grade solution engineered for challenging environments. It features a four-layer fire protection architecture, IP65-rated battery packs, and a C4/C5 anti-corrosion cabinet for enhanced durability. The system has successfully passed the rigorous UL 9540A fire propagation test, further validating its industry-leading safety performance. Its all-in-one design supports up to ten units in parallel, providing up to 2 MWh of storage capacity, while its compact 1.3 m² footprint and factory pre-assembled configuration can reduce on-site installation time by more than 40%. For larger-scale applications, the APstorage 2000L delivers utility-grade performance with system availability exceeding 99%. Its cluster-level independent management architecture ensures continued operation even in the event of a PCS failure. Equipped with advanced grid-forming capabilities, the system supports black-start functionality and reliable performance in both weak-grid and off-grid environments. It also maintains full-rated output at ambient temperatures of up to 50°C, making it suitable for a wide range of operating conditions. Residential Storage, DIY Solutions and Microinverters In addition to its C&I portfolio, APsystems will showcase the ELT-12 three-phase AC-coupled residential energy storage solution, paired with the APbattery 51.2V / 10.24 kWh battery system. The company will also feature the APB-U-16L, its latest high-capacity 16 kWh battery, providing homeowners with even greater flexibility when designing residential storage systems. Visitors will also have the opportunity to discover Lake-6, a single-phase plug-in AC-coupled energy storage system featuring an integrated 6 kWh battery and 2,500 W charging and discharging power. Designed for simplicity and ease of installation, Lake-6 makes DIY and residential energy storage more accessible than ever. Completing the lineup is the QT2D, APsystems' proven three-phase microinverter solution. Offering module-level monitoring and control, the QT2D combines high efficiency, safety, and intelligent energy management, making it an excellent choice for both residential and commercial solar installations. Meet APsystems in Prague Throughout SEF 2026, APsystems product specialists and sales representatives will be on hand to demonstrate the company's latest technologies, answer technical questions, and discuss project opportunities and potential partnerships. Visitors can also take part in interactive games and activities at the booth for a chance to win exclusive APsystems giveaways while exploring the full range of solutions on display. Visit APsystems at Booth 1-10, PVA EXPO PRAHA, Prague, on October 14-15, 2026. For more information, please visit APsystems to Showcase Advanced C&I Energy Storage Solutions at Smart Energy Forum 2026 - APsystems EMEA

artigo.texto: BYD is studying whether to manufacture lithium batteries in Argentina, Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said on Thursday after meeting Stella Li, the Chinese electric vehicle maker’s executive vice-president. According to Quirno, the company was looking at “investment opportunities in Argentina linked to the lithium value chain, particularly in the production of batteries and energy storage systems”. He did not say how much BYD might spend or where the factory could go. The minister tied the talks to Argentinian President Javier Milei’s economic agenda, saying Argentina was positioning itself “as a platform for projects aimed at both the domestic market and exports”. Quirno credited the government’s policies with promoting investment and mining in the country. BYD has sold only imported cars in Argentina since it opened for business in October last year, and it has not announced production plans in the country. It sold 10,000 vehicles in August, including a Dolphin Mini in Rosario, and now has 21 dealerships, most of them in Buenos Aires. The company’s local subsidiary, BYD Auto Argentina SAU, registered with the Justice Ministry in August last year with a corporate purpose that already included making vehicles, batteries and auto parts, the South China Morning Post reported at the time. Christian Kimelman, who runs the Argentine operation, said a car factory was not on the table for now. “It is not in the plans, but anyone who knows the Argentine industry knows that, to lead the sector in the current context, you need to have some kind of vision in that direction,” he told Bloomberg Linea earlier this year. Kimelman said most of BYD’s supply for Argentina and Mexico would come from its factory in Camacari, in the Brazilian state of Bahia. The plant opened in October last year with capacity for 150,000 vehicles a year, and in March Li said it had orders for 50,000 cars from each country. Cars made in Brazil can enter Argentina largely duty-free under the automotive agreement between the two Mercosur members. Vehicles from outside the bloc pay a 35 per cent tariff, except for a quota of 50,000 units that Chinese brands have dominated. BYD has also kept shipping cars from China on its own vessels, and in January the BYD Changzhou unloaded more than 5,000 vehicles at the port of Zarate. The company registered 9,266 cars in Argentina in the first half of the year, according to the importers’ chamber. A lithium venture in Argentina would follow BYD’s failed attempt in Chile, where it had planned a US$290 million cathode plant in Antofagasta. The factory was meant to make 50,000 tonnes a year of lithium iron phosphate cathode material, using lithium from SQM at a preferential price. But BYD and Tsingshan, the other Chinese company Chile’s development agency, Corfo, picked for the scheme, both pulled out in May last year. At that time, Corfo blamed the collapse in lithium prices. -- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST
