artigo.texto: Solid-state batteries are really coming. From winning by scale to leaping to defining industry standards. On the eve of this year's National Day, seven government departments including the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the National Development and Reform Commission unveiled an ambitious industrial plan. On September 28, 2026, the seven departments jointly issued the "15th Five-Year Plan for the Development of the New-Type Battery Industry" (MIIT Joint Regulation No. 220 [2026]). This is the first national-level special plan in China's battery sector, and it has for the first time included all-solid-state batteries in the national timetable — by 2030, all-solid-state batteries will initially achieve large-scale application. The document also sets two more rigid indicators: the cycle life of long-life lithium batteries will reach 15,000 times, and the product defect rate of leading enterprises will drop to PPB level (parts per billion). The authorities have clearly marked the future direction of China's power battery industry in the most direct way. Liquid batteries are still the absolute main force at present, while all-solid-state batteries have not yet crossed the mass production threshold. The gap between them is temporarily filled by hybrid solid-liquid batteries. This type of transitional product in the eyes of many people has been gradually mass-produced and launched on the market since the end of last year. ▲ The current market performance of the MG4 is quite good, partly due to pricing factors, but the bonus brought by its semi-solid-state battery also plays a role. SAIC Motor once planned to launch the IM L6 Lightyear version in 2024, which was the first to be equipped with the Lightyear semi-solid-state battery developed by SAIC Qingtao, but this model was later aborted. Until the end of last year, the new generation MG4 was equipped with the second-generation semi-solid-state battery for the first time and launched on the market in batches, bringing this technology to the 100,000-yuan vehicle market. NIO's 150kWh battery pack (cells supplied by Welan New Energy, 360Wh/kg) has been put into operation on the market in June 2024. ▲ NIO's 150kWh battery pack can also be described as "long-awaited by the public before its arrival". But the real bottleneck lies in all-solid-state products. Toyota has postponed the mass production time of its first solid-state battery vehicle to 2028, and Nissan has set the time in fiscal year 2028. Most of the solid-state battery mass production news in the past two years actually refers to hybrid solid-liquid products that still contain electrolyte. However, there is no lack of progress: at least since the beginning of this year, the market cost of sulfide solid electrolytes has dropped from the previous 20 million yuan per ton to less than 1 million yuan per ton. Pilot production lines have been put into operation intensively, and 60Ah-class all-solid-state cells have started to roll off the production line. The last remaining stretch of road determines who will stay at the table in the next decade. 01 The last three barriers, and the solid-liquid batteries that have taken the lead Liquid electrolyte is like water, which can seep into every gap of the electrode, while solid-state batteries are solid-to-solid contact, and the interface impedance accounts for 60~80% of the total impedance. During charging and discharging, the electrode expands and shrinks repeatedly, the contact surface cracks and fits again, accompanied by microcracks, side reactions and lithium dendrites. The data of small laboratory samples is excellent, but problems break out intensively once scaled up to vehicle-grade cells. This is a typical scaling effect, not a problem of unadjusted formula. The core difficulty of mass production lies in how to break through three barriers — The first barrier is the interface: high voltage on the cathode side will oxidize and decompose the electrolyte, and lithium metal on the anode side will drive the reduction of the electrolyte, and high-resistance layers are continuously generated on both sides; The second is lithium dendrite: sulfide is relatively soft, lithium still precipitates along grain boundaries and micro-pores, and maintaining contact often requires 50~150MPa external pressure. Excessively high pressure will induce dendrite penetration, while insufficient pressure will lead to contact failure; The third lies in cost and manufacturing: sulfide will generate highly toxic hydrogen sulfide once it meets water and oxygen. The dew point of the production line must be lower than -40℃ or even -70℃. The equipment investment per GWh is 2~3 times that of the liquid production line. Even under the most optimistic estimation, the cost of all-solid-state cells in the initial mass production period will be more than 2 yuan/Wh, or even more than 3 yuan, while the cost of lithium iron phosphate cells has been reduced to less than 0.5 yuan/Wh. Of course, from the perspective of mass production and vehicle loading as soon as possible, the real key bottleneck at present is the first barrier mentioned above, that is, the interface impedance problem. Liquid electrolyte has good fluidity and can fully infiltrate the electrode surface. For the semi-solid/solid-liquid batteries that have been mass-produced and installed on vehicles at present, even if the solid electrolyte interface film breaks after the cell is violently shaken, the remaining small amount of electrolyte can seep in and re-form the interface film. However, the solid system has no fluidity, and defects on the interface film will accumulate to form a locally over-thick and uneven component structure, and once the contact is lost, it will be lost permanently. The actual state of solid electrolyte is more like a pressed powder cake. The porosity of the cold-pressed sulfide sheet is as high as 25~28%, which looks dense but is actually a pile of particles. artigo.texto: Unwilling to pay the "CATL tax" any longer, Li Auto, Xiaomi and Leapmotor start to develop and produce batteries on their own. On October 9, Li Xiang, founder and CEO of Li Auto, warmed up for the 2026 Li Auto i6 on Weibo. Among the six major upgrades, the most notable one is the self-developed ultra-fast charging large battery with 96 kWh capacity and a CLTC range of 780 km. The battery replacement adjustment targets Li Auto's best-selling model. Li Auto delivered more than 120,000 units of the i6 in the first half of this year, contributing over 50% of its total sales. The latest announcement from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology shows that the manufacturers of the two battery assemblies for the 2026 Li Auto i6 are both Shandong Li Auto Battery Co., Ltd., with cell suppliers being Sunwoda and CALB. For the 2025 i6, the battery suppliers were CATL and Sunwoda. This shift means CATL has withdrawn from Li Auto's main selling model. Li Auto is far from the only new energy vehicle enterprise that has replaced CATL's batteries, chosen to cooperate with other manufacturers or develop batteries independently. On September 4, Xiaomi released its Longjia Battery, announcing strategic cooperation with CALB and Sunwoda Power, which will be equipped on all models of the Pengcheng series. On September 16, Leapmotor announced at its Huzhou Technology Day that it has achieved 100% independent R&D of battery cells. Shortly after, He Xiaopeng, Chairman of Xpeng Motors, stated at the G9L launch event: "Starting from this year, Xpeng will develop and produce all its batteries on its own." Jointly defining batteries with second-tier battery manufacturers, independently developing and producing battery cells, or only manufacturing battery packs. Despite different paths, leading new car-making forces have collectively written "independent R&D" into their strategies. In the past, except for BYD which operates a fully self-contained system, almost all automakers' battery budgets flowed to CATL. The phrase "equipped with CATL batteries" used to be a major selling point at press conferences. Today, however, "de-CATL" has become the most consistent collective action taken by automakers this year. Automakers and CATL: The Competition for Consumers Has Arrived In mid-September, the official website and App of Li Auto i6 stopped accepting online orders. An offline store salesperson revealed to Tech Planet that the available units that can still be delivered are basically the versions equipped with Sunwoda batteries. During the National Day holiday, a salesperson of Li Auto i6 said that the CATL battery version is basically unavailable for purchase. However, he also told Tech Planet that the most frequently asked question from customers entering the store during the National Day period is "Is the new version's battery still made by CATL?" Automakers have chosen to develop batteries independently or replace suppliers, but consumers' perception has not changed for the time being. In the past few years, the advertising slogan "When buying an EV, choose CATL" has appeared more and more frequently on TV, stadiums, elevators and mobile phone screens. This repeated anchoring of consumer psychology has turned a component brand hidden under the car chassis into the "default option" for Chinese consumers when purchasing electric vehicles. On September 17, Nielsen IQ released the *2026 Global New Energy Vehicle Consumer Research Report*, pointing out that power batteries have become a key decision-making factor for consumers when selecting and purchasing vehicles. The most obvious reflection of consumers' trust in CATL is a conclusion that 40% of Chinese respondents said they will not choose a vehicle that is not equipped with CATL batteries. Specifically, 37.1% of Chinese consumers stated directly that they will give up buying their favorite model if it does not use CATL batteries. The votes cast by consumers are finally reflected in CATL's financial statements. Data from SNE Research shows that in the first seven months of this year, CATL's global power battery usage increased by 26.6% year-on-year, and its share rose from 38% in the same period of the previous year to 39.9%. In the first half of 2026, its net profit reached 43.284 billion yuan, which is more than the total net profit of 15 mainstream listed domestic vehicle enterprises combined. When it comes to specific car purchase decisions, this perception is influencing consumers' choices. Many consumers started to look at other brands after learning that Li Auto i6 had a facelift; a consumer who planned to replace his existing vehicle said that the safety of a battery requires long-term verification by the owner, and he "does not want to be a guinea pig". However, some consumers said that replacing CATL's batteries is not unacceptable, and the key factor is the price. "If Li Auto offers a sincere price, we may consider it." Consumers' obsession does not come out of nowhere. CATL's total installed capacity in 2025 was 464.7 GWh, with a global market share of about 39%. It has profound accumulation in technology, production capacity and brand, and is the preferred supplier for most high-end models. As for CALB, the new battery supplier for Li Auto i6, although it is the fastest-growing dark horse in recent years, its global installed capacity in 2025 was about 44.4 GWh, with a market share of about 5.3%, which is far behind CATL. Automakers' Battery Calculation: From Cost Reduction to Discourse Power Struggle Although it is difficult to change consumers' perception in the short term, by giving up the CATL brand, automakers aim at two things: reducing costs and gaining greater discourse power. After all, up to now, the battery is still the largest single cost item of the whole vehicle, a "heart-level" component, and the core variable that defines the differentiation of the whole vehicle at the technical level. artigo.texto: Key credit data to be recorded on blockchain; Korea Exchange to handle early trading Credits classified by host-country transfer approval; developing nations to join governance The South Korean government plans to formally launch the Global Verified Carbon Market, or GVCM, next year. Key information on carbon credits — which represent greenhouse gas reduction outcomes — will be recorded on a blockchain, and the government is also reviewing the possibility of issuing the credits as digital assets. Credits will be classified based on whether the host country of an overseas reduction project has granted transfer approval, broadening their use from voluntary corporate carbon-reduction activities to regulatory compliance. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il unveiled the detailed GVCM implementation plan at the 274th Council of Ministers on External Economic Affairs at the Government Complex Seoul on Monday. The government aims to secure participating countries this year and move into full operation next year, including establishing a credit issuance body and advancing individual projects. The GVCM is a framework designed to boost the credibility of international carbon markets and invigorate the trading of verified emission reductions. To reflect its intent to cover both voluntary and compliance markets, the government is renaming the initiative from "Global Voluntary Carbon Market" to "Global Verified Carbon Market." Central to the plan is how carbon credits are recorded and issued. Key data — including the project operator, the country and region where the project is located, a unique identification number, the emission reduction methodology, and the volume of reductions — will be stored on a blockchain. Full records will be kept in a conventional database, with the blockchain serving to verify the integrity of core information. In the early stage, credits will be issued through conventional electronic means and traded on a Korean voluntary carbon market exchange to be built by Korea Exchange. The plan draws on Korea Exchange's experience operating an emissions trading platform to build trust among market participants. The government will later consider issuing credits in parallel as digital assets, taking into account credit issuance and trading volumes, the legislative progress of a basic digital assets law, and market confidence in digital assets. Under the existing exchange framework, round-the-clock trading and participation by individuals and foreign investors are constrained by operating hours, eligible participant rules, and foreign exchange regulations. However, the government said it will take into account each participating country's position, given that digital asset legislation varies across nations. Credits will be divided into two categories: "GVCM A," which has received transfer approval from the host country, and "GVCM NA," which has not. Approved credits are intended for use in regulatory compliance — such as meeting a country's nationally determined contribution under the Paris Agreement or satisfying requirements under CORSIA, the international aviation carbon offsetting and reduction scheme — as well as for ESG activities. Non-approved credits will be directed toward ESG activities that contribute to the host country's own emission reduction goals. Credits in the non-approved category can be converted to approved status if the host country subsequently grants corresponding adjustment approval. The government is also reviewing whether GVCM credits could be used under South Korea's domestic emissions trading scheme and greenhouse gas target management system. Doing so would require meeting conditions related to credit credibility, corresponding adjustments under the Paris Agreement, and eligibility criteria for domestic project operators. Consultations with relevant agencies will also be pursued to enable use under CORSIA. The issuance body will consist of a board of directors, a technical oversight committee and a secretariat. The board, in which member countries participate, will set policy direction; the technical oversight committee will decide whether to issue credits; and the secretariat will handle issuance and management. Developing countries, where most emission reduction projects take place, will be able to join the board and recommend expert committee members, ensuring their views are reflected in operations. The government will work with related ministries and the Global Green Growth Institute to secure participating countries and identify reduction projects that combine developing-country development needs with South Korean technology. Examples cited include nature-based projects such as mangrove forest restoration, agricultural waste management, methane capture and energy efficiency improvements. The government will also discuss converting emission reductions generated through World Bank and Green Climate Fund projects into GVCM credits. It plans to pursue the signing of letters of intent at this year's 31st UN Climate Change Conference of the Parties, and to finalize participating countries, establish the issuance body, and flesh out the project structure next year. fact0514@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: South Korea to Fully Launch GVCM International Carbon Market Next Year, Review Digital-Asset Credit Issuance Summary - The government said it will begin full operations of the international carbon market GVCM next year and issue credits divided into 'GVCM A' and 'GVCM NA'. - The government said it plans to record key information, including project operators and emissions reductions, on the blockchain and build a trading market using the Korea Exchange (KRX). - The government said it will also discuss issuing carbon credits in digital-asset form in the future and converting project results from the World Bank (WB) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) into GVCM credits. Forecast Trend Report by Period South Korea plans to fully launch its international carbon market next year and is also reviewing a plan to issue carbon credits in digital-asset form. The government discussed detailed measures for the Global Voluntary Carbon Mechanism, or GVCM, at a ministerial meeting on external economic affairs on Oct. 12, Seoul Economic Daily reported. GVCM is a market for trading greenhouse-gas reduction credits. Credits will be issued as either "GVCM A" or "GVCM NA," depending on whether the host country approves the project. Approved credits can be used to meet national greenhouse-gas reduction targets, or NDCs, and to comply with international aviation rules. Unapproved credits would be used for companies' voluntary environmental activities. To bolster trust in trading, the government plans to record key information such as project operators and emissions reductions on a blockchain. It also plans to build a trading market using the Korea Exchange, or KRX, and is reviewing the future issuance of carbon credits in digital-asset form. The government plans to secure countries interested in participating this year and set up an issuing body next year to flesh out the project. It will also discuss converting emissions-reduction results generated by World Bank and Green Climate Fund projects into GVCM credits. artigo.texto: Report Overview In 2025, the Global AI Data Center GPU Market was valued at USD 7.4 billion. The market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 18.5% during 2026–2035, reaching approximately USD 40.4 billion by 2035. North America dominated the global market in 2025, accounting for more than 37.7% of the total market share and generating approximately USD 2.8 billion in revenue. The data center build-out for AI drives this growth. The IEA reported that global data center power use will roughly double from 415 TWh in 2024 to about 945 TWh by 2030. That equals just under 3% of all power used in the world. The IEA also expects power use in accelerated servers, which run mostly on GPUs, to grow 30% each year. Power use in regular servers will grow only 9% each year. Accelerated servers will cover almost half of the net rise in data center power demand. Each new AI facility needs dense GPU clusters, so higher power demand points straight to higher GPU spending. A regular data center draws 10 to 25 MW. A large AI facility can draw more than 100 MW. North America region hosts the biggest cloud and AI model builders. The IEA found that the United States and China together will make up nearly 80% of global data center power growth to 2030. Berkeley Lab, part of the US Department of Energy, projects that AI data centers will drive more than 40% of US power demand growth through 2030. Key Takeaways - The Global AI Data Center GPU Market reached USD 7.4 billion in 2025 and will reach USD 40.4 billion by 2035. grow at a CAGR of 18.5% from 2026 to 2035. - Graphics Processing Units lead the Product Type segment with a 24.3% share. - Inference leads the Function segment with a 71.2% share. - Cloud leads the Deployment Mode segment with a 62.3% share and is also the fastest-growing sub-segment. - Information Technology and Telecom leads the End User Industry segment with a 33.9% share. - North America leads with a 37.7% share and USD 2.8 billion in revenue. By Product Type Graphics Processing Units dominate with 24.3% due to mature software support across AI workloads. Accelerator Cards are growing fastest as buyers want more speed for each watt and each rack. NVIDIA posted record quarterly Data Center revenue of $62.3 billion in the fourth quarter, up 75% from a year earlier. Cloud firms and large companies add plug-in cards to their current servers to raise output without building new halls. Fast links between chips also push this shift. NVIDIA’s Data Center networking revenue jumped 142% as NVLink connections spread across GB200 and GB300 systems. These links let many cards work as one large engine. Server makers now design around dense card setups, which keeps demand for accelerator cards rising quickly. By Function Inference dominates with 71.2% due to daily use of live AI apps. Inference holds the largest share because every chatbot reply, search answer, and code suggestion runs on inference chips. Microsoft says its AI business passed $37 billion in annual revenue run rate, up 123%. Each new user adds steady, round-the-clock compute load. Training is growing faster as model builders race to release larger and smarter models. The IEA projects that electricity use in accelerated servers will grow 30% per year, against only 9% for regular servers. Training runs drive much of that power demand because they keep thousands of chips busy for weeks at a time. By Deployment Mode Cloud dominates with 62.3% due to hyperscaler spending on rented GPU capacity. Cloud leads because most firms prefer to rent GPU power rather than buy costly hardware. Microsoft’s fiscal 2026 capital spending reached about $115.95 billion, up 79.6%. In one quarter, roughly two-thirds of its $31.9 billion capex went to short-lived assets, mainly GPUs and CPUs. Cloud is also the fastest-growing mode, because buyers can scale up in hours instead of waiting months for chips. Microsoft Cloud revenue hit $54.5 billion in one quarter, up 29%. Pay-as-you-go pricing lets startups and mid-sized firms test AI without high upfront costs. The spending plans stay large. Microsoft expects to invest roughly $190 billion in calendar 2026, including about $25 billion linked to higher component prices. On-premises setups still serve banks and defence users with strict data rules. Even so, cloud keeps winning new workloads because of its speed and flexibility. By End User Industry Information Technology and Telecom dominates with 33.9% due to large data centre and network ownership. IT and telecom firms lead because they own and run most of the world’s data centres. The IEA puts data centre power use at about 415 terawatt hours in 2024, roughly 1.5% of global electricity. That demand has grown 12% a year over the past five years, mostly driven by tech and telecom operators. Healthcare and life sciences are growing fastest as hospitals and drug makers put AI into daily work. The US FDA list covers 1,357 AI-enabled medical devices cleared or approved through December 2025. Imaging, drug discovery, and genomics all need heavy GPU compute to train and run their models. Large funding moves add to this demand. NVIDIA announced commitments worth $1 billion to build US capacity for research in fields including healthcare. As more medical tools reach approval, hospitals and research groups will keep buying GPU capacity. artigo.texto: Chinese battery makers are losing some of their biggest competitive advantages in the US as rising freight costs and import tariffs erode their price edge. Energy storage system (ESS) battery prices in North America were 20% higher than factory prices in China in September and also exceeded prices in Europe. With US import duties of up to 40.9% adding to the cost, Chinese cells are becoming less attractive to American buyers. South Korean battery makers with local production facilities are positioned to gain market share. According to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence's Q3 2026 Battery Cell Price Review, released on October 9, the CIF North America price of Chinese 314-ampere-hour (Ah) lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells reached $61.99 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in September. That was $10.37, or 20.1%, above the ex-works (EXW) China price of $51.62 per kWh. The CIF Europe price for the same cells was $59.18 per kWh, $2.81 below the North American price. CIF prices include the cost of the goods, insurance and freight to the destination, but exclude US import tariffs. The price relationship between North America and Europe reversed in September. In July, the North American price was $64.99 per kWh, below Europe's $67.11. Prices declined in both regions in August, but diverged the following month. North American prices rose 3.3% month on month in September, while European prices fell 4.8%. Rising freight costs were a key factor in the reversal. Higher shipping costs on routes from China to the US have weakened the price advantage of Chinese cells by the time they reach North American customers. US import duties pose an additional challenge. Applying a tariff rate of up to 40.9% to the North American arrival price of $61.99 per kWh would raise the cost to approximately $87 per kWh. That is nearly 70% above the $51.62 per kWh factory price in China. Even if Chinese manufacturers cut their cell prices, US buyers could still face higher procurement costs. For a 1-gigawatt-hour (GWh) ESS project, every $10-per-kWh increase in battery prices adds $10 million to procurement costs. This shift could benefit South Korean battery makers with manufacturing facilities in North America. LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On are converting or using local production capacity to manufacture LFP batteries for ESS applications as electric vehicle (EV) demand weakens. LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI are expanding their US ESS LFP battery production capacity, with annual capacity expected to exceed 50 GWh by the end of 2026 and in the second half of 2028, respectively. They are also supplying complete, containerized ESS solutions developed in-house to renewable energy engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) companies and ESS system integrators (SIs). Their customer base is expanding to include global hyperscalers operating artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. Chinese battery makers' price competitiveness in the US could weaken further. China ended export tax rebates for battery products and introduced a 2% consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries effective September 1, narrowing manufacturers' room to cut prices. These changes could also put pressure on Chinese suppliers' competitiveness in Europe. Major Chinese battery makers have already begun raising prices. Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. (CATL), EVE Energy and REPT BATTERO raised prices for EV and ESS batteries starting in July. ESS system integrators also increased product prices by 5% to 30%. In September, CATL raised prices for its 280Ah ESS cells by 1.1% and its 314Ah cells by 2.0%.

artigo.texto: Mixing Two Unsuitable Solvents Nearly Triples Lithium-Metal Battery Life [Reading Science] UNIST, KAIST Maintain 80% Capacity After 150 High-Voltage Charge-Discharge Cycles Identify "Cooperative Solvation" Principle That Weakens Lithium-Ion Binding Mixing two solvents considered unsuitable for lithium-metal batteries instead nearly tripled battery life. When used separately, the solvents bound lithium ions so strongly that they interfered with charging and discharging. But when combined, they became more likely to release the lithium ions. A South Korean research team has extended the life of next-generation batteries using an approach that overturns conventional wisdom about electrolyte design. Performance comparison of lithium metal batteries using a cooperative solvation electrolyte. Their charge-discharge cycle life was approximately three times longer than that of batteries with conventional electrolytes, and lithium was found to deposit evenly on the anode surface. Gas generation and electrolyte consumption were also greatly reduced, improving battery stability. Provided by the research team. View original image Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) said on October 12 that a joint research team led by Professor Song Hyeon-gon of its Department of Energy and Chemical Engineering and Professor Seo Donghwa of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) had developed an electrolyte that extends the charge-discharge life of lithium-metal batteries by about three times. The findings were published in the international journal ACS Nano on August 11. Unlike the widely used lithium-ion batteries, lithium-metal batteries use lithium metal instead of graphite as the anode. They have attracted attention as next-generation, high-capacity batteries because they can store more electrical energy at the same weight. However, lithium metal reacts unnecessarily with the electrolyte during charging and discharging, causing capacity to decline rapidly. This problem becomes more severe when batteries are charged at high voltages to store more energy. A reversal for two unsuitable solvents...reducing lithium loss The research team mixed two solvents, ethylene carbonate (EC) and sulfolane (SL), in a 3:7 ratio, then added a lithium salt and a small amount of an additive to create a new electrolyte. Both solvents were considered difficult to use in lithium-metal batteries because they bind strongly to lithium ions. During charging, lithium ions must shed the surrounding solvent molecules and deposit as metal on the anode surface. But when solvents hold the lithium ions tightly, this process does not proceed smoothly. Lithium then deposits unevenly, and side reactions with the electrolyte reduce battery capacity. When the team mixed the two solvents, the results were contrary to expectations. As the solvent molecules attracted one another, their hold on the lithium ions actually weakened. This allowed the lithium ions to shed the solvent molecules more easily and deposit evenly on the anode surface. The team named this effect "cooperative solvation." Solvation is the process in which solvent molecules surround lithium ions. The term describes how two types of solvents influence one another to regulate their bonds with lithium ions. Experiments confirmed the performance improvement. The developed electrolyte recorded an initial Coulombic efficiency of 98.24% and an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.35%. Coulombic efficiency indicates how much of the lithium deposited during charging can be recovered during discharging. A higher value means less lithium is consumed during charge-discharge cycles. Three times longer life even with high-voltage charging...further validation needed for commercialization The research team tested the developed electrolyte in batteries with high-nickel cathodes and compared their performance. When charged to 4.5 V at 25°C, the batteries retained about 80% of their initial capacity even after approximately 150 charge-discharge cycles. By contrast, batteries using a conventional carbonate-based electrolyte fell below 80% of their initial capacity after about 50 cycles. Under the same conditions, the charge-discharge life was therefore about three times longer. The team also confirmed reductions in gas generation caused by electrolyte decomposition and in the dissolution of nickel from the cathode. UNIST researchers (from left): Professor Song Hyungon and researcher Hong Jingi. Photo courtesy of UNIST. View original image The study is significant because it improved battery performance using combinations of commonly used solvents, without relying on expensive fluorinated solvents or highly concentrated lithium salts. However, 150 charge-discharge cycles remain limited for applications in electric vehicles or energy storage systems (ESS). Further validation is needed to determine whether the performance can be maintained during long-term use, across a range of temperatures, and under fast-charging conditions. First author and researcher Hong Jin-gi said, "Mixing two solvents with strong bonding forces to weaken their bonds with lithium ions is a new design principle that overturns conventional wisdom about electrolyte design." He added, "It could also be used to improve electrolyte performance in commercial lithium-ion batteries, in addition to lithium-metal batteries." artigo.texto: Cut Carbon Overseas, Sell as Credits... Government Moves to Establish 'Global High-Integrity Carbon Market' The government plans to establish the Global High-Integrity Carbon Market (GVCM), an international market where greenhouse gas reductions achieved in developing countries are issued as carbon credits and traded internationally. The initiative aims to build a foundation for international carbon trading that will enhance the credibility of emissions reductions and allow Korean companies to use credits earned by participating in overseas reduction projects for regulatory compliance and environmental, social and governance (ESG) management. On the 12th, the government discussed detailed plans for the GVCM at a meeting of foreign economic ministers held at the Government Complex Seoul, chaired by Lee Hyungil, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy. The GVCM is an international carbon market being developed to address credibility issues raised in existing international carbon markets. The government plans to build a framework covering everything from identifying and supporting emissions reduction projects to issuing and trading credits and establishing cooperation among countries, with the aim of increasing the market's credibility. The international carbon credit market is projected to grow to $7 billion-$35 billion by 2030 and $45 billion-$250 billion by 2050. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyung-il speaks at the inaugural Emergency Economic Headquarters Meeting and Ministerial Meeting on Economic Affairs at Government Complex Seoul in Jongno-gu, Seoul, on Oct. 1, 2026. Photo by Cho Yongjun. View original image Credits Classified by Host-Country Approval...Usable for ESG and Regulatory Compliance The GVCM's core feature is to classify credits according to whether the country hosting an emissions reduction project authorizes their transfer. Credits approved for transfer by the host country will be classified as "GVCM A," while those without approval will be classified as "GVCM NA." GVCM A credits are intended for use in meeting the investing country's national greenhouse gas reduction target and for regulatory compliance, including under the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). They may also be used for corporate ESG activities. GVCM NA credits are intended for corporate ESG activities, and may be converted to GVCM A if the host country subsequently approves the corresponding adjustment. Approval from the host country is required to use emissions reductions achieved overseas for domestic or international regulatory compliance. When emissions reductions are transferred to the investing country, they may be counted toward the reduction targets of the investing and purchasing countries. Without approval, however, the reductions are in principle counted toward the host country's national reduction target. The government plans to specify in the operating rules an obligation for participating countries to make efforts to approve credit transfers. The scope of credit use will also be expanded beyond voluntary markets to include compliance markets. The government will consider linking the credits with the domestic emissions trading system and the greenhouse gas target management system, assessing whether they meet requirements for credit credibility, corresponding adjustments under the Paris Agreement, and business participation under domestic laws and regulations. Overseas, it will consult with relevant agencies to enable the credits to be used for regulatory compliance, including under CORSIA. Blockchain technology will also be introduced to ensure credit credibility. Key information, including the project operator, the country or region where the project is carried out, a unique identification number, the reduction methodology, and the volume of reductions, will be recorded on the blockchain, while the complete dataset will be stored in a conventional database. The aim is to prevent double counting of emissions reductions and greenwashing during trading, while improving the security of records. Initially, credits will be issued through conventional electronic processes. The government plans to use the Korea Exchange as the trading platform. It believes the Korea Exchange can help secure the confidence of market participants, given its experience operating an emissions trading exchange since 2015. However, constraints related to operating hours, eligible trading participants, and foreign exchange regulations limit the possibility of 24-hour trading and participation by individuals and foreign investors. The government has therefore left open the possibility of issuing digital assets alongside the existing system in the future. Issuing Body to Include Developing Countries...Identifying Overseas Emissions Reduction Projects The GVCM's governing body will consist of a board, a technical supervisory committee, and a secretariat. The board, made up of member countries, will set policy direction and oversee the technical supervisory committee. The technical supervisory committee will decide whether to issue credits, and experts nominated by developing countries will be able to participate so that the needs and policy positions of host countries are reflected. The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), an international organization, will temporarily serve as the secretariat, and the government plans to establish a separate secretariat after the GVCM's official launch. artigo.texto: Redata torna Brasil mais competitivo para atrair data centers, diz diretor da Brasscom AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 9 de outubro de 2026 Em setembro, o Plenário do Senado aprovou o projeto que institui o Redata, Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center, que prevê a suspensão de tributos federais para empresas do setor que cumpram critérios ambientais, sociais e econômicos estipulados pelo governo. Dois dias depois da aprovação, Câmara e Senado aprovaram o Projeto de Lei Complementar, que flexibiliza regras fiscais para viabilizar a concessão dos incentivos previstos no regime. Os dois textos ainda precisam da sanção presidencial para entrar em vigor, enquanto seguem aguardados pelas empresas e entidades do segmento. Isso porque, com a sua aprovação, as regras de atuação do setor, nas esferas jurídicas, competitivas e tributárias, ficarão mais claras, o que deve refletir em mais segurança e tranquilidade para quem quer operar no País. Para Sergio Sgobbi, Diretor de Relações Institucionais e Governamentais da Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais do Brasil (Brasscom), a aprovação torna o Brasil mais atrativo para investidores e empresas do setor, especialmente em tempos de um ambiente global altamente competitivo. “O Redata contribui justamente para aumentar a competitividade nesse processo”, afirma. Confira, a seguir, a entrevista completa. Engrenagens do Crescimento — Depois de quase um ano de tramitação, com a medida provisória caducando e o projeto de lei parado no Senado, qual foi o momento mais crítico para a aprovação do Redata na avaliação da Brasscom? Sergio Sgobbi — O momento mais crítico ocorreu justamente quando houve a caducidade da medida provisória sem a conversão imediata em lei, ampliando a incerteza regulatória em torno do tema. Para um setor intensivo em capital e com ciclos longos de investimento, a previsibilidade é um elemento importante na tomada de decisão. O principal risco naquele momento era o adiamento de projetos e a perda de competitividade do Brasil frente a outros mercados que também disputam investimentos em infraestrutura digital. Alguns investimentos foram para outras geografias, mas o Congresso Nacional, a tempo, tomou a decisão correta pela aprovação do PL. Engrenagens do Crescimento — A Brasscom, junto com outras entidades, pediu ajustes no Projeto de Lei Complementar (PLP) para viabilizar os incentivos ainda em 2026. Pode explicar qual foi o ajuste e dizer o que estava em jogo se essa costura não tivesse funcionado? Sergio Sgobbi — O objetivo do ajuste foi garantir a previsão de renúncia fiscal para que os incentivos pudessem produzir efeitos ainda em 2026, compatibilizando o regime com as regras fiscais vigentes. Sem a solução legislativa, não haveria como o presidente sancionar a lei, ou seja, o PLP aprovado deu contornos legais ao orçamento da União para que a política pública do Redata possa acontecer em 2026. Engrenagens do Crescimento — Na votação da Câmara, o Redata quase ficou de fora do relatório do PLP e só voltou por emenda de plenário. Como o setor reagiu a esse momento de incerteza e o que isso revela sobre a prioridade que o tema tem no Congresso? Sergio Sgobbi — O setor acompanhou com atenção esse processo e intensificou o diálogo institucional para demonstrar a relevância estratégica do estabelecimento dessa política pública. O episódio mostrou que existe reconhecimento crescente da importância do tema, mas também evidencia que a agenda ainda precisa disputar espaço com outras prioridades legislativas. A aprovação posterior demonstrou a capacidade de articulação entre governo, Congresso e setor produtivo em torno de uma agenda considerada estratégica para o País. Engrenagens do Crescimento — O texto final trocou a exigência de energia limpa por baixa emissão, permitindo que gás natural e fontes nucleares supram data centers, além das fontes eólica e solar. Como a Brasscom avalia essa mudança — foi decisiva para destravar investimentos represados? Sergio Sgobbi — A Brasscom entende que o mais importante é garantir uma expansão sustentável da infraestrutura digital, conciliando segurança energética, competitividade e compromisso ambiental. A adoção do conceito de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão amplia as opções tecnológicas disponíveis e oferece maior flexibilidade para o desenvolvimento dos projetos, sem afastar os objetivos de sustentabilidade previstos no regime. Engrenagens do Crescimento — Que tipos de empresas associadas à Brasscom estavam com decisões de investimento “em compasso de espera” à espera do Redata e quais eram os negócios estimados? Qual é a expectativa de quando esses projetos devem sair do papel? Sergio Sgobbi — A Brasscom não trabalha com uma estimativa consolidada de investimentos efetivamente represados. O que observamos é que operadores de data centers, provedores de infraestrutura digital, empresas de nuvem e investidores analisam continuamente diferentes mercados para alocação de capital. Em um ambiente global altamente competitivo, a previsibilidade regulatória e tributária influencia o ritmo de tomada de decisão. O Redata contribui justamente para aumentar a competitividade do Brasil nesse processo. Engrenagens do Crescimento — As estimativas de mercado falam em algo entre R$ 60 bilhões e R$ 100 bilhões em novos investimentos em data centers nos próximos quatro anos. Esse número parece realista para a Brasscom e o que precisa acontecer para que ele se confirme? Sergio Sgobbi — As projeções divulgadas pelo mercado refletem fundamentos estruturais que permanecem presentes: crescimento da inteligência artificial, expansão dos serviços em nuvem, aumento da demanda por processamento de dados e vantagens competitivas do Brasil em energia e conectividade. O potencial de investimento continua existindo. Para que ele se concretize plenamente, é importante ampliar a previsibilidade regulatória, fortalecer a c

artigo.texto: Data centers have divided America. The ire of everyday citizens continues to increase against a backdrop of enthusiastic and deep-pocketed Wall Street investors betting artificial intelligence is the economic engine of the future. And as data centers that power the answers for Google's Gemini, Meta's Muse, Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's ChatGPT spread across the U.S. landscape, the financial firms are attempting to pitch investors on AI infrastructure as part of a real estate allocation that can diversify a portfolio. For the most part, the funds from alternative investment companies promising investors a piece of the physical infrastructure powering the AI economy remain the province of institutional investors like pension funds. But the trend has to a limited degree also dipped into the retail investor market. Alternative investments giant Blackstone has been at the forefront, creating the Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust, a newly formed real estate investment trust, or REIT, that trades on the NYSE, earlier this year. "We saw this as an opportunity to capture the whole market of stabilized data centers and build a home in the public market where we think it belongs," CEO Nick Pell said in a CNBC "Squawk on the Street" interview in May. While many new data center projects across the U.S. remain subject to shifts in public and political opinion — and various moratoriums including in the states of New York and Texas — the Blackstone REIT is primarily focusing on data centers in already mature markets such as Northern Virginia and Dallas, where sprawling data centers have had a significant presence that predates the AI boom. "It is the lowest risk way to play," Pell said, adding that Blackstone can then hand-select data centers to offer investors from what it says is a $300 billion market. The company sold 87.5 million shares at $20 apiece in its mid-May debut. But the fund is down roughly 16% since then, with shares closing under $17 on Thursday. Blackstone declined to offer further comment. Equinix and Digital Realty Trust, data center developers that trade as REITs, have fared well longer-term, though their shares have stalled in the period since the BXDC launch. The REIT sector has performed better this year than it typically does during periods of rising rates and higher bond yields, a situation in which the real estate sector is typically volatile due to the increased cost of lending and investors finding sectors of the stock market associated with income-generating assets less attractive. But most of the gains came earlier in the year before the bond market stress intensified, with many REIT investments selling off since August. Pell described the opportunity on the company's most recent earnings call as "massive, with a total addressable market for our business expected to eclipse $1 trillion over the next several years." Data centers are an increasingly big part of construction spending nationally. In fact, construction spending across the U.S. has been propped up by AI construction while many other sectors' construction spending has been on the decline. Blackstone is not alone among alternative investment firms offering up data centers as investment opportunities. Blue Owl, which already runs a private digital infrastructure fund for sophisticated investors, is reportedly considering the launch of a public REIT with a value as high as $6.5 billion which will roll up existing data center investments into the new fund. The company says it owns over 130 data centers in 32 global markets representing over $18 billion in assets. By contrast, Blackstone's BXDC has not yet deployed any capital into investments. Blue Owl declined to comment to CNBC, but Blue Owl's co-CEO Marc Lipschultz made the case for the sector in a recent LinkedIn post, calling data centers one of the strongest long-term investment opportunities in decades and citing an attractive, lower risk-return profile. "These projects have delivered consistent results with reduced credit risk. Contracts are structured with protections that make us whole even if a tenant exits early," Lipschultz said. While not a REIT, real estate asset management giant Brookfield Asset Management listing its data center services provider, Csquare, as a stand-alone trading vehicle on the NYSE in July. Its shares have declined close to 16% since debuting. But the investment case is running into a headwind that was less intense when Blackstone launched its fund: a fast-growing political backlash. National polling from Gallup found 70% of Americans oppose a data center being built in their area, and that opposition is bipartisan — a New York Times/Siena poll this fall found roughly two-thirds opposed regardless of party. New York became the first state to pass a moratorium on new hyperscale data center approvals in July, and Texas followed in August, with Gov. Greg Abbott — who called the state the AI "epicenter" just a year earlier — ordering a halt on new approvals after already having called for a grid-connection audit in August. For investors, the risk isn't just whether a data center gets built, but whether local and state politics slow down or derail projects already baked into a fund's return assumptions. Oracle's stock fell 4% in late September after the company sent a force majeure notice tied to Project Jupiter, a New Mexico data center campus and part of the broader Stargate AI buildout developed by Blue Owl. Oracle is seeking to delay payment on the project if it isn't operational by 2028, citing a mix of regulatory hurdles and local opposition. But it says the project remains on track. These risks are global as well for investors that own and finance projects around the world. An Nvidia and Blackstone-backed Australian data center company just pulled its planned IPO due to underwhelming investor interest. artigo.texto: Nearly 4 million abandoned US oil wells could become underground batteries, with geothermal heat boosting storage output by 9.5% Abandoned oil wells may hold a second life as underground energy storage — and a Penn State study suggests trapped geothermal heat could make the whole system 9.5% more efficient. Renewable energy is growing fast — but the grid still goes dark when the wind dies and the sun sets. Solving that problem has sent engineers searching for new ways to store power at scale, from massive battery farms to pumped-water reservoirs. The answer, according to a new Penn State study, may already be in the ground. Across the United States, nearly 4 million depleted oil and gas wells sit largely forgotten — rusting relics of the fossil fuel era. Researchers now believe that infrastructure could be repurposed into something the clean energy transition urgently needs. Regions built around oil and gas extraction — western Pennsylvania, parts of Texas, Appalachia — face real economic disruption as fossil fuel production declines. A grid problem hiding in plain sight Renewable energy’s central weakness isn’t generation — it’s timing. Solar panels produce power at noon; demand peaks at dinner. Wind turbines spin through the night when most of the grid is asleep. That mismatch between supply and demand is one of the biggest structural challenges of the clean energy transition. Energy storage is the obvious fix, but storing electricity at grid scale is harder than it sounds. Battery farms help — they’re just expensive and limited in capacity. Pumped-water reservoirs work well where geography cooperates, which isn’t everywhere. Compressed-air energy storage, or CAES, offers another path. During periods of low demand, excess electricity compresses air and pushes it underground. When demand rises, that pressurized air drives turbines to generate power. It’s a proven approach in principle, but building the infrastructure needed to make CAES commercially viable has kept most projects on the drawing board rather than in the ground. What Penn State researchers discovered The Penn State team, led by Arash Dahi Taleghani — a professor of petroleum and natural gas engineering — proposed a way to change that equation. Their study, published in the Journal of Energy Storage, describes a geothermal-assisted CAES system built around depleted oil and gas wells. The key insight is thermodynamic. Deep underground, rock formations retain significant natural heat, and when compressed air is stored in those hot environments, its temperature rises. Higher temperature means higher pressure, and higher pressure means more energy stored in the same space. Using numerical modeling and simulation, the researchers quantified the effect: placing CAES systems in abandoned wells significantly increased air temperature, boosting efficiency by 9.5% over conventional CAES. “Without taking advantage of the geothermal setup, you could not get enough encouraging numbers,” Taleghani said. That efficiency gain, combined with cost savings from reusing existing wells, is what makes the economics potentially viable. Nearly 4 million wells — already in the ground The scale of America’s abandoned well problem becomes, in this context, an unexpected asset. The Environmental Protection Agency estimates approximately 3.9 million depleted oil and gas wells across the United States. Most sit idle — already drilled, already cased, already connected to the surface. Reusing those wells eliminates one of CAES’s biggest cost barriers. For an industry weighing whether a project pencils out, that upfront savings could tip the calculation. Pennsylvania illustrates both the opportunity and the urgency. State regulators estimate hundreds of thousands of orphaned and abandoned wells within its borders alone. Many are improperly plugged or structurally compromised, and when that happens, they can leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas — into the atmosphere and groundwater alike. Two problems, one solution Sealing a leaking well and converting it into an energy storage asset aren’t competing goals. They’re the same action. “If we use existing wells, we are basically hitting two birds with one stone,” Taleghani said. “First, we are sealing these wells. That stops any potential leaks. And then if we are repurposing these wells for energy storage, we are still using the infrastructure that is in place in these communities.” The social dimension matters too. Regions built around oil and gas extraction — western Pennsylvania, parts of Texas, Appalachia — face real economic disruption as fossil fuel production declines. Repurposing existing infrastructure could preserve technical jobs and keep communities tied to the energy sector rather than left behind by it. This research is part of Penn State’s Repurposing Center for Energy Transition, known as ReCET, and was funded by the U.S. Department of Energy. What comes next The 9.5% efficiency figure comes from modeling and simulation — no real-world pilot has been built and tested yet. The gap between a promising simulation and a functioning commercial system is significant, and worth being clear-eyed about. Challenges remain across several dimensions. Regulatory frameworks for underground energy storage in repurposed wells don’t fully exist. Each candidate well would need structural integrity assessments before it could be safely pressurized, and scaling the concept to a network capable of meaningfully supporting the grid is a separate engineering problem entirely. But if those hurdles can be cleared, the potential payoff is substantial. A validated system could simultaneously accelerate clean energy storage deployment and begin cleaning up nearly four million sources of legacy pollution — the kind of practical convergence that tends to attract serious investment. You can learn more about this discovery here: Penn State. “Reusing old oil and gas wells may offer green energy storage solution.” ScienceDaily

artigo.texto: The handwritten warning was left at an Amazon data center construction site in suburban Virginia: A dozen pipe bombs scattered throughout the building would explode in the next half hour. Officers rushed to the scene as workers dropped their tools and fled. Bomb-sniffing dogs prowled every corner of the site. That April 22 message in the city of Manassas, authorities soon confirmed, was an empty threat – the latest in a string this year that has rattled the state and communities across the nation. As thousands of new data centers have been built to fuel the booming artificial intelligence industry, escalating public resentment against both the energy-sucking infrastructure and AI itself is roiling small towns and suburban communities from coast to coast, a CNN investigation has found. Police have been called into action to investigate dozens of threats to data centers, from bomb claims etched on bathroom walls to online incitements to “use bullets on city council members” to suggestions that protesters should “unalive” pro-development officials, according to a CNN review of more than 100 police reports filed since last year. Aside from rare cases like an Indianapolis council member whose home was sprayed with gunfire, those threats have rarely led to actual violence – but they’ve eaten up hundreds of hours of police time, alarmed workers and inflamed communities already on edge over the projects. That rising outrage has also inspired a growing police crackdown, including federal agencies tracking data center protests and local cops questioning vocal activists, and even filing criminal charges against critics that have later fallen apart in court. The police records as a whole paint a vivid picture of a national backlash against the rise of data centers and AI reaching a boiling point at a moment when the debate has become a key issue threading party lines ahead of the midterm elections. They also show growing concern among law enforcement agencies about extremist groups at opposite ends of the political spectrum hopping on the anti-data-center bandwagon. “Anti-technology extremist narratives appeal to a broad array of ideological movements – including anarchists, environmental extremists, and white supremacists – creating a common target between otherwise opposing movements,” Colorado state officials warned in an April bulletin for police agencies. A similar California memo warned in June of “a broad range of threat actors… mobilized by AI-related grievances.” Still, some people who have been charged with making threatening comments insist they’re not extremists and do not actually wish violence upon anyone. Rather, they say they were driven to take dramatic action by rising electricity bills, environmental worries or fears of AI. “I’m not really political,” Anthony Hinojosa, an Illinois man arrested in February over an alleged data center threat, told an investigator who interrogated him, according to police recordings. “I feel like we don’t have a vote.” But elected officials say the reports show how the battle over data centers and AI is entering dangerous territory, where they’re fearing for their lives just for doing their jobs. Minneapolis council member Michael Rainville was left pleading in an August letter to his constituents for a more peaceful dialogue over the issue. “Please stop the threats against me and my family,” he wrote. ‘Terroristic threats’ In early February, police in Troy, Illinois fielded multiple calls about ominous statements on a community Facebook page. At the time, the city had been debating whether to clear the way for a roughly 200-acre data center that backers said could create hundreds of jobs. Like similar proposals around America, the once-anodyne pitch had become hugely contentious. Views of data centers have soured significantly this year. Nearly nine in 10 Americans say they’re more concerned than excited about the rise of these facilities, a CNN poll conducted by SSRS found in September. Amid that debate, Troy officials confronted a tirade on Facebook: “My hypothesis is no one would want to be shot at so just start shooting the people involved and it’ll never be built,” Hinojosa, a 33-year-old lawn-care businessman, commented beneath a post about the proposed data center. When a user asked if he was really suggesting violence, Hinojosa responded, “for sure,” screenshots of his posts show. Later that day, officers knocked on his door. “You’re being placed under arrest for making terroristic threats,” an officer said. “I think people are taking things out of context,” Hinojosa told the authorities. He said he had been upset about the proposed data center’s potential strain on electricity and water supply, but he insisted he would not hurt anyone and his words had been misconstrued. “Over a misunderstanding you are literally going to ruin my life,” he said. “It just feels like the mayor of Troy and the city council, they’re just not really listening to the public.” Hinojosa, who described himself in police recordings as a moderate Republican, now faces felony charges for intimidation and harassment through electronic communication. He has pleaded not guilty. His lawyer declined comment, citing an upcoming trial. Hinojosa’s case is one of about 70 among the police reports CNN reviewed that include allegations of threats, intimidation or planned attacks – a collection showing a striking range of anger at AI infrastructure that at times has spilled into serious claims of potential violence. artigo.texto: With electricity demand projected to double by 2045, finding ways to generate and store more reliable, around-the-clock power is more important than ever. As California hits all-time highs in renewable energy generation, batteries are becoming the key to making sure that power doesn't go to waste. SCE has one of the largest battery energy storage portfolios in the nation, with enough capacity to power about 6.6 million homes for four hours. But even as battery storage becomes more common across California, many people have never heard of it or are unfamiliar with how it works — leading to some common misconceptions. Let’s separate facts from fiction and bust seven common battery storage myths. Myth: Battery storage works only with solar energy. Fact: Battery storage usage is not limited to storing solar energy. Batteries can store electricity from the grid when supply is available and deliver it later when customers need it most. Myth: Battery storage is new and experimental. Fact: Battery storage is an established technology that continues to evolve. SCE began operating the Tehachapi Energy Storage Project in 2014, which was one of the first large-scale battery storage systems in North America. Since then, the technology has grown and advanced, improving performance and reliability. Myth: Battery facilities are built and left unattended. Fact: While SCE’s battery storage facilities are not typically staffed on-site full time, they are remotely operated and monitored 24/7. Operators continuously track facility performance and coordinate with crews when maintenance or on-site support is needed. Myth: Battery storage facilities and data centers are the same thing. Fact: They may look similar from the outside, but they serve entirely different purposes. A data center is a warehouse full of powerful computers that store data and process the digital services people use every day. A battery storage facility stores electricity and delivers it to the grid when it is needed most. SCE has one of the largest battery energy storage portfolios in the nation, with enough capacity to power about 6.6 million homes for four hours. Myth: Battery storage is being built mainly to power data centers. Fact: Battery energy storage systems are designed to support the entire grid, and data centers are only one part of growing electricity demand. Battery storage helps keep energy reliable and resilient as electricity demand grows across homes, businesses and communities. Myth: Battery storage facilities are not safe. Fact: Battery storage facilities are designed, constructed, tested and operated under extensive engineering and emergency-response requirements. The facilities are monitored and maintained with safety as the top priority. Myth: Batteries only benefit people who own one. Fact: Batteries help keep power reliable year-round. Customer-owned batteries can provide backup power whenever needed, while grid-scale batteries can support entire communities during periods of high demand. Triple-digit heat drove SCE’s energy demand to an all-time high in September, yet the power kept flowing without a Flex Alert or rotating outages. This is a direct testament to the benefits of battery storage. For more on SCE’s clean energy efforts, visit edison.com/cleanenergy.

artigo.texto: Lithium Metal Battery Lifespan Extended Threefold — South Korean Researchers Overturn Electrolyte Design Convention South Korean researchers have developed an electrolyte technology that extends battery lifespan by nearly threefold by blending two commercial solvents previously deemed unsuitable for lithium metal batteries due to their strong lithium-ion binding properties. The approach resolves the rapid capacity degradation that occurs during high-voltage charging without relying on expensive specialty solvents or high-concentration salts. Professor Song Hyun-kon of the Department of Energy and Chemical Engineering at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) and Professor Seo Dong-hwa of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) announced the findings on the 12th. The research was published in the August 11 issue of ACS Nano, an international journal in the nanoscience field. Unlike commercial lithium-ion batteries that use graphite anodes, lithium metal batteries employ lithium metal as the anode, theoretically enabling nearly double the capacity. They have been regarded as a key technology for extending electric vehicle driving range and increasing the capacity of energy storage systems (ESS). However, lithium metal undergoes unwanted side reactions with the electrolyte during charge-discharge cycles, sharply reducing lifespan — a problem that worsens under high-voltage charging conditions. 'Cooperative Solvation' Overturns Conventional Design Principles The research team focused on ethylene carbonate (EC) and sulfolane (SL). Both solvents had been excluded from lithium metal battery design because of their strong binding affinity for lithium ions. During charging, lithium ions must shed surrounding solvent molecules and deposit as metal on the anode surface. When solvents bind lithium ions too tightly, this process is impeded, causing uneven lithium deposition and capacity loss through side reactions with the electrolyte. The team inverted the conventional approach by mixing the two solvents at a 3:7 weight ratio and adding a lithium salt along with a small amount of electrode protective film stabilizing additive. The result defied expectations. Strong intermolecular forces — including hydrogen bonding between EC's hydrogen atoms and SL's oxygen atoms — emerged between the solvents, paradoxically weakening each solvent's individual binding affinity for lithium ions. The team characterized this phenomenon, in which the two solvents mutually influence each other to modulate lithium-ion binding and anion interfacial accessibility, as "cooperative solvation." Hong Jin-ki, the first author of the study, explained: "Mixing two strongly binding solvents to actually weaken their interaction with lithium ions represents a new design principle that overturns conventional electrolyte design wisdom. Beyond lithium metal batteries, this approach could be applied to enhance electrolyte performance in commercial lithium-ion batteries as well." Performance Validated Under High-Voltage Conditions Performance verification results were confirmed quantitatively. The new electrolyte achieved an initial Coulombic efficiency of 98.24% and an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.35%. Coulombic efficiency measures how much of the lithium deposited during charging can be recovered during discharge — higher values indicate less lithium is consumed during charge-discharge cycles. When applied to a high-nickel (NCM811) cathode battery and tested at 25°C with charging up to 4.5V, the battery retained approximately 80% of its initial capacity after 150 charge-discharge cycles. Compared with the conventional carbonate-based electrolyte, which fell below 80% capacity after roughly 50 cycles, the new electrolyte extended cycle life by approximately threefold under the same capacity retention standard. Note: Coulombic efficiency figures for the conventional electrolyte were not disclosed by the research team. Gas generation from electrolyte decomposition and nickel dissolution from the cathode material were also suppressed. This indicates that the major factors accelerating battery degradation under high-voltage charging conditions were simultaneously controlled. Professor Song Hyun-kon stated: "We improved electrolyte performance using commercial solvents without relying on expensive fluorinated solvents or high-concentration salts. We expect this will help extend the operational life of high-capacity lithium metal batteries for ESS and electric vehicle applications." Additional Validation Needed for Commercialization The study is significant in that it improved battery performance using only combinations of low-cost, commercially available solvents. However, 150 charge-discharge cycles remains a limited benchmark for real-world EV or ESS applications, as EV batteries typically require cycle lives in the thousands. Further validation is needed to confirm performance retention under long-term use, diverse temperature conditions, and fast-charging environments. The research team expects the technology can be extended beyond lithium metal batteries to high-voltage lithium-ion batteries and various next-generation battery systems, including sodium-ion and potassium-ion batteries. The research was supported by the Korea Evaluation Institute of Industrial Technology (KEIT) under South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, and the National Research Council of Science & Technology (NST).

artigo.texto: China's Solid-State Battery Stock Frenzy Cools as Companies Rush to Clarify They Have No Such Business Shidai Wanheng (600241.SS), which had locked in the daily limit-up for five consecutive trading sessions, issued an urgent announcement after market close on October 9, explicitly stating that the company's products are not involved in solid-state batteries. The clarification directly targets the core concept driving this round of market speculation—yet the company had issued risk warnings in the prior three trading days without making any mention of its solid-state battery business status. According to Shidai Wanheng's announcement, the company's lithium battery products are small-power cylindrical ternary lithium batteries primarily used in small electric tools, with the 1865 and 1450 models as its mainstay products. Its nickel-metal hydride (NiMH) battery products are mainly applied in personal care, consumer goods, and electric tools. The company's existing main products and production lines remain unchanged, and its fundamental production and operations have not undergone material changes, with production currently organized on an order-by-order basis. Zizhu High-tech, which had also hit the daily limit-up for four consecutive sessions, issued a clarification announcement the same day. The company stated that as of now, its aluminum-plastic film products for lithium batteries and solid-state battery-related business remain in an early stage of exploration and R&D, and there is considerable uncertainty over when these products can achieve commercialization and contribute stable, scalable revenue. This round of solid-state battery concept speculation was ignited by the release of a heavyweight industrial policy on September 28. Seven agencies—including China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Transport, the Ministry of Commerce, the State Administration for Market Regulation, the National Energy Administration, and the National Railway Administration—jointly issued the 15th Five-Year Plan for New Battery Industry Development. This is China's first national-level special plan for the battery sector, explicitly setting targets for initial scaled application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030, long-life lithium batteries achieving 15,000 charge cycles, and leading enterprises reaching PPB-level defect rates, while continuing to build out lithium battery standards systems and advancing standards development in key areas such as all-solid-state batteries and sodium batteries. The plan also, for the first time, elevates new batteries from a "component" positioning to "the foundational layer of multi-domain electrification and the new energy system," meaning the battery industry's service boundaries will expand significantly from new energy vehicles to emerging pillar sectors including energy storage, the low-altitude economy, and intelligent robotics. Catalyzed by the policy, China's A-share battery supply chain rallied against an overall weak market on October 9. More than 4,100 stocks fell across the market that day, with 13 hitting limit-down, yet the solid-liquid battery index surged 3.80% to lead all sectors, the lithium cathode index rose 3.65%, the power battery index gained 3.29%, and the solid-state battery index climbed 2.50%. At the individual stock level, China's Keheng Co. hit the 20% limit-up, Fengyuan Chemical rose 10% to notch a second consecutive limit-up, Tinci Materials gained 10%, and Guibao Science & Technology soared 14.71%. Heavyweight leaders also performed strongly: CATL (300750.SZ) surged as much as 4.85% intraday with turnover exceeding 9.1 billion yuan (approximately $1.4 billion); Ganfeng Lithium (002460.SZ) rose 4.23%, EVE Energy (300014.SZ) gained 2.91%, and BYD (002594.SZ) advanced 2.50%.
