artigo.texto: South Korea to Launch International Carbon Market Next Year with Blockchain-Based Credit Issuance South Korea will fully launch an international carbon market next year for trading overseas greenhouse gas reduction credits. The plan involves issuing reduction credits as carbon credits, trading them on the Korea Exchange, and enabling their use for corporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) activities as well as national emissions reduction target compliance. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il presided over a meeting of economy-related ministers at the Government Complex Seoul on the 12th, where the government finalized the "Detailed Implementation Plan for the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM)." The GVCM is a market for issuing and trading carbon credits generated from overseas greenhouse gas reduction projects. The government has now specified the operational framework based on the roadmap announced in December last year. The core of this plan lies in ensuring credit credibility and activating trading. The government has decided to apply blockchain technology to data management. A dual-track approach will be adopted: core information such as project operators, reduction volumes, unique identification numbers, and reduction methodologies will be recorded on the blockchain, while remaining data will be stored in conventional databases. The intent is to apply the technology selectively to core information rather than uploading all data to the blockchain, thereby securing both management efficiency and stability. Credits will initially be issued in standard electronic form and traded on South Korea's voluntary carbon market exchange. Going forward, the government plans to consider parallel issuance in digital asset form, taking into account issuance and trading volumes, the status of digital asset legislation, and market confidence. The market's name has also been changed from "Global Voluntary Carbon Market" to "Global Verified Carbon Market." The change reflects the intent to encompass regulatory markets as well, based on the judgment that the previous name could give the impression that credits were only usable in voluntary markets. Credits are divided into two categories depending on whether the host country grants transfer authorization. "GVCM A" credits, which have received authorization, can be used for both regulatory compliance—such as fulfilling investor countries' Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) or the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA)—and ESG activities. "GVCM NA" credits, which have not received authorization, are limited to corporate voluntary environmental activities. However, GVCM NA credits can be converted to GVCM A status if the host country subsequently grants corresponding adjustment approval. The government is also reviewing options to link the GVCM with South Korea's domestic emissions trading scheme or greenhouse gas target management system, provided that credibility requirements, corresponding adjustments under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, and domestic legal participation conditions are met. The issuing body will consist of a board of directors, a technical oversight committee, and a secretariat. The board, composed of member countries, will determine policy direction and oversee the technical oversight committee. The technical oversight committee will decide on technical matters such as credit issuance, with expert members recommended by developing countries able to participate in issuance decisions. The secretariat will handle issuance, management, and registry operations. The Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI) is currently serving as interim secretariat, with a separate secretariat to be established upon official launch. The government is also prioritizing participation from developing countries. Governance has been designed so that developing countries can reflect their needs in operational processes and gain experience in carbon market operations. The approach respects participating countries' sovereignty when establishing operational regulations, emissions baseline setting, and sustainable development guidelines. Project sectors will be identified based on participating countries' development needs and South Korea's technological competitiveness. Examples include nature-based solutions such as mangrove forest restoration, agricultural waste treatment, methane capture, and energy efficiency improvements. The government is also in discussions with international organizations including the World Bank (WB) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) to convert reduction volumes generated from existing reduction projects into GVCM credits. International carbon markets are gaining attention as a means to achieve national greenhouse gas reduction targets. This comes as major Paris Agreement parties anticipate difficulty in meeting their 2030 NDCs through domestic reduction efforts alone. However, the lack of standardized international market criteria has led to ongoing controversy over credit credibility and actual reduction effectiveness. The government has taken note of the international carbon market's growth potential. According to MSCI projections, the carbon credit market is expected to grow to $7 billion–$35 billion by 2030 and $45 billion–$250 billion by 2050. The government's assessment is that, as the boundary between voluntary and regulatory carbon markets weakens internationally, credits usable in both markets must be developed. The government plans to collaborate with GGGI to leverage networks such as the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (IPEF) and the Asia-Pacific Carbon Market Roundtable (APCMR) to secure participating countries. At the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) next month, the government will pursue signing letters of intent with countries wishing to participate, and will promote the GVCM to domestic and international stakeholders through

artigo.texto: SERES expands CATL in-plant capacity layout and ramps up overseas charging infrastructure SERES Group and CATL signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement in Chongqing on October 10, under which the two sides will advance construction of the second phase of the battery pack "plant-within-a-plant" at SERES' super factory, and extend cooperation to supercharging, battery swapping, battery services, and overseas markets. The AITO brand will continue to equip all models with CATL batteries over the long term, while AIVA plans to adopt a battery-swap model and become a key brand for SERES' overseas business expansion. Under the agreement, CATL will continue to increase investment in Chongqing, and SERES and CATL will strengthen local industrial synergy, deepening cooperation in areas including battery safety, supply chain coordination, and global ecosystem collaboration. The two sides will also jointly promote AITO's entry into Europe, the Middle East, and Central Asia, and explore a battery service system covering the full vehicle lifecycle. One of the core projects under this cooperation is the battery pack production line located inside SERES' super factory. CATL's first-phase project began production on June 30, 2025, comprising two CTP 2.0 high-end battery pack production lines primarily supplying localized power battery systems for flagship models such as the AITO M9 and M8. This marked CATL's first adoption of the "plant-within-a-plant" model and its first production base in Chongqing. The second-phase project is planned for annual capacity of 10–12 GWh; once completed, combined first- and second-phase annual capacity will exceed 20 GWh. The "plant-within-a-plant" model places battery pack manufacturing directly inside the vehicle production base. Battery cells are integrated into vehicle-ready battery packs, which then enter the vehicle assembly process nearby, helping to shorten transport distances and improve coordination efficiency among battery pack supply, vehicle production scheduling, and delivery. The two sides can also coordinate on the same production site for model refreshes, battery specification adjustments, and changes in vehicle production capacity. Although the production line is located inside SERES' factory, battery pack manufacturing remains CATL's responsibility. This means SERES is bringing the supply link even closer to the vehicle production site while continuing to leverage the manufacturing capabilities of a specialized battery company. Unlike full in-house development and manufacturing, this arrangement separates the production location from the manufacturing entity, reflecting the automaker's trade-offs across different stages of the battery business. Note: The above capacity figures are planned data; cumulative delivery figures were disclosed by CATL and relevant partners. AITO is the primary focus of the existing cooperation between the two sides. The brand, jointly launched by SERES and Huawei in 2021, has equipped all models with CATL batteries since its inception, with cumulative deliveries exceeding 1.2 million units. When the first-phase production line began operations in June 2025, its installed base exceeded 700,000 vehicles. As the installed base grows, the battery supply relationship no longer covers only new-vehicle assembly but will also extend to diagnostics, maintenance, and technical support during vehicle use. This agreement brings supercharging networks and battery services into the scope of cooperation, signaling that both sides are extending their partnership from the manufacturing end to after-sales and charging infrastructure. Overseas business adds a new application scenario to the relationship. SERES and CATL jointly participate in building the AIVA brand. Saidou Technology, which owns AIVA, was formerly Chongqing Landian Technology under SERES. After completing a capital increase of approximately 6.671 billion yuan (approximately $996.8 million) in 2026, Chongqing local state-owned capital became the largest shareholder, with SERES as the second-largest shareholder and CATL holding approximately 9.89% through its subsidiary Wending Investment. The AIVA brand was unveiled in June 2026 and, under current plans, will adopt a battery-swap model, positioned as one of SERES' main brands for overseas expansion. According to earlier reporting by LatePost, its first production model, the ME7, is planned to debut within 2026, with pre-orders expected to open in early 2027. The battery-swap model requires alignment among vehicle products, battery specifications, swap facilities, and operational services. After vehicles enter a new market, in addition to sales channels, there must be synchronized arrangements for battery turnover, maintenance, swap station construction, and ongoing operations. Since launching its battery-swap service brand EVOGO in 2022, CATL has been advancing battery swapping as large-scale infrastructure from the end of 2024, introducing standardized "Choco-SEB" swappable battery blocks. As of the end of June 2026, CATL had built 2,000 Choco-SEB swap stations covering 31 provinces and 180 cities in China, and was jointly building a "super-swap shared network" with multiple automakers including Changan, Chery, GAC, and SERES. AIVA plans to connect to this existing public battery-swap network. CATL's participation in AIVA's battery-swap and overseas business means its cooperation scope will extend further from battery manufacturing to charging infrastructure and service systems. SERES places AIVA in an important position for overseas expansion, while CATL provides support in battery supply, battery-swap technology coordination, and market infrastructure. For both sides, whether overseas business can advance smoothly depends not only on vehicle sales but also on whether local charging networks can be built in sync with product launches. artigo.texto: Seres Deepens Partnership with CATL as AITO Cumulative Deliveries Surpass 1.2 Million Units Chinese new energy vehicle manufacturer Seres (09927.HK) announced the signing of a long-term strategic cooperation deepening agreement with battery giant CATL (03750.HK), with both parties further consolidating their strategic partnership in areas including battery safety, supply chain coordination, and global ecosystem cooperation. Following the announcement, Seres' share price rose more than 4% in early trading on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Under the agreement, Seres' AITO brand has been equipped exclusively with CATL batteries across its entire lineup since the brand's inception, with cumulative deliveries surpassing 1.2 million units to date. Building on this milestone, AITO will continue to use CATL batteries across all models on a long-term basis, with cooperation spanning core areas including the expansion of "plant-within-a-plant" production capacity, the construction of a supercharging energy replenishment ecosystem, and the acceleration of global expansion. The signing ceremony was held in Chongqing on October 10, attended by Seres Group Chairman Zhang Xinghai and CATL Chairman Robin Zeng. Cooperation Focuses on Three Key Areas The deepening agreement clarifies both parties' continued commitment to the Chongqing production base. The Phase II "plant-within-a-plant" project for premium battery packs at Seres' super factory will be accelerated, while both parties will also deepen cooperation in supercharging, battery swapping, and battery services, jointly exploring innovative pathways for new energy vehicle energy replenishment ecosystems. On the global expansion front, both parties will work together to expand into overseas markets. The agreement also specifies that CATL will continue to increase investment in Chongqing, supporting the city's efforts to build a trillion-yuan premium intelligent connected new energy vehicle industrial cluster. Capital Market Reaction Seres' share price rose more than 4% in early trading on the first trading day following the announcement, with gains narrowing to 2.84% at HK$34.74 (approximately $4.4) as of press time, with trading volume of HK$13.6042 million (approximately $1.7 million). Market observers noted that the deepening cooperation between Seres and CATL helps stabilize the AITO brand's battery supply chain, particularly in premium battery pack capacity expansion. The "plant-within-a-plant" model effectively shortens supply chain distances and reduces logistics costs, which carries positive implications for Seres' gross margin improvement. Industry Background Seres and CATL have a long-standing cooperative relationship. The AITO brand, jointly developed by Seres and Huawei as a premium intelligent electric vehicle brand, has used CATL batteries across its entire lineup since launch, with both parties establishing deep ties at the battery technology and supply chain levels. The timing of this agreement coincides with intensifying competition in China's new energy vehicle market. As competitors such as BYD and Xiaomi continue to expand market share, battery supply stability and cost control have become critical competitive factors for automakers. Seres' decision to deepen its strategic cooperation with CATL at this juncture is being interpreted by the market as an important move to secure supply chain safety and enhance long-term competitiveness. Chongqing, as Seres' key production hub, has been actively promoting the development of the intelligent connected new energy vehicle industry in recent years. CATL's continued investment in Chongqing also aligns with the local government's policy objective of building a trillion-yuan industrial cluster.

artigo.texto: Bilhões de dólares foram investidos em centros de dados. De acordo com o relatório "Asia Pacific Data Centre Investment Landscape 2026" da Cushman & Wakefield, o valor total dos ativos de data centers operacionais na região Ásia-Pacífico (APAC) deverá ultrapassar US$ 950 bilhões até 2030. Para acomodar o crescente número de projetos, a APAC precisará de mais de US$ 280 bilhões em novos investimentos. Ainda há um espaço significativo para crescimento, visto que a região da Ásia-Pacífico representa mais de 60% da população mundial , mas atualmente possui apenas cerca de 22% da capacidade total global de data centers. A capacidade da região deverá aumentar 2,7 vezes até 2030. Atualmente, 26.455 MW de capacidade estão em desenvolvimento, em comparação com 15.135 MW em operação. A maior parte do capital permanece concentrada nos grandes mercados de data centers. Aproximadamente 77% da demanda total de investimentos na região da Ásia-Pacífico até 2030, equivalente a US$ 215 bilhões, deverá ser destinada ao Japão, Malásia , Austrália, Índia e Indonésia. Nessa onda de investimentos, o Vietnã ainda não está entre os líderes em termos de escala, mas é cada vez mais reconhecido como um destino promissor no cenário regional de infraestrutura digital. De acordo com a Cushman & Wakefield, o Vietnã atualmente apresenta a maior escassez de data centers na região da Ásia-Pacífico, com aproximadamente 1,4 milhão de pessoas por MW de capacidade operacional. Enquanto isso, a demanda por serviços digitais e computação em nuvem continua a crescer rapidamente. O custo de construção de um centro de dados no Vietnã varia atualmente de US$ 5,7 milhões a US$ 8,7 milhões por MW, com uma média de cerca de US$ 7,2 milhões por MW. O Vietnã também ocupa o segundo lugar na região da Ásia-Pacífico em termos de retorno sobre o investimento. O mercado analisado pela Cushman & Wakefield é dominado principalmente pelos dois "motores" de Hanói e Cidade de Ho Chi Minh, com aproximadamente 73 MW de capacidade operacional atual e mais 137 MW projetados para serem fornecidos até 2030. A diferença entre a capacidade existente e a demanda futura está começando a atrair projetos de grande escala. Will Tran, Diretor de Negócios Industriais e de Escritórios no Vietnã da JLL, observa que o mercado está entrando em uma nova fase, onde os motores de crescimento vêm cada vez mais de indústrias de alta tecnologia, em vez de indústrias tradicionais com uso intensivo de mão de obra. No Norte, as indústrias de eletrônica, equipamentos elétricos, alta tecnologia e engenharia de precisão continuam em expansão. Enquanto isso, o Sul atrai crescente interesse em áreas de alta tecnologia, pesquisa e desenvolvimento, produtos farmacêuticos, centros de dados e logística moderna. Espera-se que os centros de dados, em particular, se tornem uma nova força motriz, à medida que a inteligência artificial (IA), a computação em nuvem e a economia digital aumentam a demanda por infraestrutura de dados. Esse segmento também possui requisitos específicos em relação à energia, infraestrutura técnica e conectividade, abrindo assim outra via para o desenvolvimento de imóveis industriais no Vietnã. De fato, essas oportunidades começam a se refletir na escala dos fluxos de capital para a cidade de Ho Chi Minh. Recentemente, o Comitê Popular da cidade de Ho Chi Minh decidiu arrendar quase 4,5 hectares no Parque de Alta Tecnologia de Ho Chi Minh (bairro de Tang Nhon Phu) para a Starmason Joint Stock Company, a fim de desenvolver um complexo de data center de grande porte. O projeto tem um investimento total de 480,2 milhões de dólares, construído em fases, com capacidade de computação de até 90 MW. Ainda no Parque de Alta Tecnologia da Cidade de Ho Chi Minh, a Evolution DC VN HCMC Joint Stock Company arrendou mais de 49.500 m² de terreno para investir em um centro de dados com um capital total de 508,7 milhões de dólares, implementado por um consórcio de três investidores de Singapura : Hathor, Frontier e Evolution. Fluxos de capital ainda maiores estão sendo direcionados para diversos projetos em andamento ou propostos. O complexo de data center e IA do campus SGI-HCM, no Parque Industrial Tan Phu Trung, investido pela Kinh Bac Urban Development Corporation (KBC) em colaboração com a Accelerated Infrastructure Capital (AIC) e o VietinBank , tem um investimento total projetado de aproximadamente US$ 2,1 bilhões. Um novo megacentro de dados para IA foi proposto pela G42, Microsoft, FPT, Viet Thai e VinaCapital, com um investimento total de aproximadamente US$ 2 bilhões. Os investidores continuam a refinar o plano e a pesquisar possíveis locais para a implantação. É necessária uma nova geração de infraestrutura industrial. De centros de dados de escala relativamente pequena, o mercado agora testemunha o surgimento de complexos que abrangem dezenas de megawatts, com investimentos que variam de centenas de milhões a bilhões de dólares, e profundamente integrados à IA. Essa mudança de escala impõe uma demanda diferente ao setor imobiliário industrial: a infraestrutura deve ser preparada adequadamente para acomodar esse influxo de capital. Diferentemente das fábricas convencionais, os centros de dados exigem um fornecimento de eletricidade muito grande e contínuo. Os sistemas de backup, as telecomunicações e a conectividade de dados também devem atender a altos padrões de estabilidade. É nesse ponto que os centros de dados criam novas exigências para o setor imobiliário industrial. O Sr. Nguyen Tuan Anh, Vice-Diretor Geral do Grupo KN Holdings, afirmou que, embora anteriormente um terreno limpo fosse uma vantagem competitiva crucial, atrair projetos de alta tecnologia exige agora que os desenvolvedores de parques industriais preparem infraestrutura especializada para cada setor. artigo.texto: Regarding “Data centers are hot. We should use Lake Michigan to cool them” (Oct. 6): I think the idea of cooling coils under Lake Michigan for data centers has merit. Of course, a thorough environmental assessment would need to be done prior to moving forward. And with one reservation, the idea of data centers occupying former industrial sites in Chicago is also attractive. But what about the impact regarding electrical usage? Does Chicago have the capacity to support possibly multiple data centers? What impact would there be on residents’ electric bills if this were to go forward? While this is good news, there are still a few hurdles to get over before the city leaps forward. — Tom Canning, Homer Glen Cooling proposal’s flaws Regarding Joe Holberg’s op-ed, his mayoral candidacy, math knowledge and business ownership are impressive. But should he be promoting vast, expensive projects such as coolant loops “miles, perhaps tens or hundreds of miles, long and coiled far offshore at or near the bottom” of Lake Michigan to cool data centers? Holberg addresses the concern that this cooling loop plan for data centers might “cook the lake.” He writes that “setting a sealed coffee thermos in a swimming pool” wouldn’t change the pool’s temperature. He misunderstands heat exchange parameters with that inelegant comparison — a sealed, insulated thermos is not comparable to a metallic coil. He states without evidence that “we likely could not even marginally increase the temperature or create an environmentally noticeable impact.” Tell that to the fish. Taking his inexact idea of heat exchange even further, hot data centers “should have windows.” As every Chicago resident without air conditioning knows, opening windows does not satisfy the need to cool, and it would only add to atmospheric heat. He must know the heat has to go somewhere, as he quixotically writes “climate change increases the overall temperature throughout the year.” While seeming to minimize or disregard the impact of data centers on humans and the environment, Holberg spends several paragraphs addressing the saving of money. Normally, when I read commentary supporting the building of these projects, there seems to be an unbalanced emphasis on money, including arguments for creating jobs and adding to local tax bases. Does money have an overriding importance? What is the effect to our neighborhoods and communities, to our noise and pollution levels, to our air and water quality? Midway, Holberg proposes “a water and environmental study before a single pipe goes in, with the results and data published where anyone can read it.” Perhaps he should have opened with that. — Patrick Comer, Clarendon Hills More study is needed Joe Holberg’s op-ed contains sufficient information to earn further review and consideration. I was initially concerned about a few of the points, including that miles of coil in Lake Michigan would “not even marginally increase the temperature” of the lake. He saves himself by suggesting a study. Opening and closing windows to take advantage of Chicago weather vicissitudes seems simplistic, so it, too, needs deep study. More information about Toronto and Cornell University is intriguing and ought to provide a few clues. Although touting Cornell University’s prowess is gutsy, if not a welcome “first step”-like program. — Terrance W. Gainer, Wheaton Who committed these crimes? Regarding the story “Aldermen advance $261M police misconduct settlement” (Oct. 6): There is a proposed settlement to resolve 16 lawsuits filed against the city of Chicago by people who claim that they were victims of police misconduct by a former Chicago detective and that they were convicted of crimes they did not commit. Dozens of men have been issued certificates of innocence. Important questions come to mind: If the plaintiffs did not commit these crimes, who did commit the crimes? Have these investigations been reopened? Has anyone new been charged with or convicted of the crimes in question? Don’t the victims and their families deserve fresh investigations to identify the real perpetrators? — John Mulvey, Chicago Helping Chicago’s seniors Why do millions of budgeted 2026 funds go unspent while low-income seniors continue to struggle to access help for critical home repairs and modifications? A group of Chicago community organizations — including Housing Opportunities and Maintenance for the Elderly (H.O.M.E.), Access Living, North Branch Works, Mothers Opposed to Violence Everywhere (M.O.V.E.), Illinois Anti-Foreclosure Coalition, Light Up Lawndale, Rebuilding Together Metro Chicago and Northside Community Resources — sent a letter on Sept. 1 to Mayor Brandon Johnson and housing leaders in his administration and in the City Council calling for an explanation. We are still waiting. Approximately $6.3 million in unspent 2025 funds associated with the city’s Home Repair Program is being carried over into the next budget. At the same time, approximately $28 million in federal Community Development Block Grant funding is identified for administrative costs, including about $20.8 million carried over from 2025 and a new allocation of $7.3 million. This is not just about looking at numbers in a budget. This represents a disconnect between available resources and the urgent needs of Chicago’s most vulnerable residents. In 2025, the city folded the Small Accessible Repairs for Seniors (SARFS) program into a general Home Repair Program. SARFS provided safety and accessibility repairs to many senior households yearly. artigo.texto: NBC’s comedy show “Saturday Night Live” mocked “Shark Tank” investor Kevin O’Leary and his plans to build the massive Stratos data center in Utah — with a fake O’Leary calling it “the most evil name of all time.” “All I want is to buy up 40,000 acres of God’s untouched splendor and replace it with a very loud computer that steals your job,” actor James Austin Johnson said Saturday night from the show’s “Weekend Update” desk, wearing a bald cap to impersonate O’Leary, aka “Mr. Wonderful.” “Is it going to take up precious water? Absolutely. Is it going to provide a necessary service? Who’s to say?” Johnson’s O’Leary continued in a calm voice echoing the real O’Leary’s cadence. “But on the flip side, it’s going to make me a tremendous amount of money, and I think that’s great.” Anchor Colin Jost then noted that most Americans don’t want data centers near them, and Johnson’s O’Leary agreed, saying, “that’s why I’m building one in Utah.” He held up a map of Utah, with the Stratos site in Box Elder County ringed with a red target zone, which he said would be the area affected by noise and water pollution. “You have to understand — I don’t live there,” he said. Jost countered that other people do live there. “You’re missing the point,” the fake O’Leary replied. “That’s not real to me. … Those are Sims.” Johnson’s O’Leary then referenced one of the real O’Leary’s “Shark Tank” failures: “When I missed out on Scrub Daddy, I learned a very valuable lesson, which is I’m going to destroy the world.” Jost asked about the defamation lawsuit O’Leary is facing from activists protesting the Stratos project. The fake O’Leary noted that “yes, I made the mildly inflammatory claim that every single person in Utah who opposes me is a paid Communist super-agent from China. Was I wrong? Perhaps. But just because they’re not doesn’t mean they aren’t.” Last month, the real O’Leary’s lawyers filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that no “reasonable viewer” would have taken his claims that China funded his opposition as fact. Johnson’s O’Leary concluded the three-minute skit with another observation based on the real O’Leary’s “Shark Tank” experience: “When I missed out on Bombas socks, I could have gotten mad. But instead I made a decision: I’m going to make the future go away. And we’re doing just that in Utah.” Utahns by an overwhelming margin, 76%, don’t want more data centers built in the state, according to a survey released this month by Utah State University’s Community and Natural Resources Institute.

artigo.texto: Words by Oliver Milman photographs by michael hauptman Our world is already beset by a climate crisis, galloping biodiversity loss, and a plague of plastic that has reached nearly every waterway and mountaintop. It may be unfortunate timing, then, that another—and perhaps final—environmental frontier is now rapidly coming into view: space. A slew of industrial projects designed for Earth’s orbit or other celestial bodies are currently underway. Some, like mining the moon for helium or reflecting sunlight back to Earth after dark with giant mirrors, remain out-there aspirations that may never materialize. Others are moving more quickly. Some of the world’s wealthiest people are determined that even if they cannot yet colonize other planets, they will soon be able to encircle our own with fleets of space-based data centers. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin has applied to the Federal Communications Commission to launch 51,600 data centers, while Elon Musk’s SpaceX has even grander ambitions—a constellation of 1 million facilities, with testing set to begin next year. Google on October 1 launched Project Suncatcher, its orbital data center initiative exploring how to power AI in space, into low Earth orbit. The prospect of banishing data centers to space may appeal to people on Earth who abhor their explosive growth and decry their ravenous use of energy and water. In the United States, the issue has become so politically toxic that living next to a data center polls even worse than residing beside a nuclear plant. Musk has said space-based data centers will prove “ridiculously better” than their terrestrial counterparts. “Elon (Musk) and others in the industry are like, ‘Let’s take the data centers that no one likes in your backyard—it seems like there’s a lot of consensus on that—and put them into space where they won’t bother anyone,’” Jared Isaacman, administrator of NASA, said in August on the Pod Force One podcast. Isaacman has said separately that while countries like China escalate their space ambitions, the U.S. can win the “space race for sure, but the AI race, too.” The potential environmental payoff is substantial. The Department of Energy projects that data centers could account for as much as 12% of U.S. electricity demand by 2028, driven largely by the growth of AI. A large terrestrial data center can require around 100 megawatts of power and around 200,000 gallons of water a day for cooling, according to the Government Accountability Office. Moving some of that computing into orbit could, in theory, reduce the need for new power infrastructure, freshwater, and land on Earth. In sun-synchronous orbit, satellites could also receive near-continuous sunlight, allowing them to generate solar power without the nighttime interruptions affecting solar farms on the ground. Space could also shift one of the most resource-intensive parts of computing: cooling. Rather than consuming freshwater to carry away heat, an orbital data center would use large radiators to release that heat into space, though cooling in a vacuum remains technically difficult. For proponents, the appeal is that networks of solar-powered satellites could eventually take on some of the computing now driving the construction of energy- and water-intensive facilities on Earth. Whether that produces a net environmental benefit depends on what it takes to manufacture, launch, maintain, and ultimately dispose of them. But some experts are more wary. “Many issues occur with data centers in space that wouldn’t happen on Earth,” said Daniel Capper, a professor of philosophy at the Metropolitan State University of Denver and a proponent of space environmentalism. Even if the daunting cost and logistics of launching data centers into orbit can be overcome, adding 1 million large structures to low Earth orbit raises uncomfortable questions about energy, debris, and what happens when those structures eventually fall back to Earth. “A land-based data center can’t fall on your head. If one falls in this way, upon a city or in the ocean causing a tsunami, we are in big trouble.” Space-based data centers would be roughly the size of a tennis court, with only a fraction of the area housing computing equipment. The rest would be devoted to shielding the hardware from radiation, dispersing heat, and generating power. Should large, 5-gigawatt data centers make it into orbit, the solar arrays required to power them would also be sprawling—measuring more than six square miles, according to Starcloud, a company developing space-based data centers. All of that would require hundreds of rocket launches, generating additional emissions while adding large satellites to a band of space already cluttered with human-made debris. Around 30,000 pieces of tracked debris currently hurtle through orbit at roughly 10 times the speed of a bullet, posing a threat to satellites and other infrastructure we depend on for everyday functions such as GPS. “We have already entered a period of unstable debris growth in low Earth orbit; the amount of stuff in orbit will continue to grow even without human intervention,” said Cole Donovan, an advocate for the Stand Up for Science group who previously worked for the U.S. government on a new “air traffic control” system for various space actors. Satellites are equipped with automated collision-avoidance systems, but adding another million large objects could increase the risk of Kessler syndrome, a theoretical chain reaction in which collisions create more debris, which in turn triggers further collisions until parts of orbit become impossible for new missions. “We are already at the beginning of Kessler syndrome; if it gets extreme we will have to remain grounded,” said Capper. artigo.texto: Peugeot is looking to bring back the spirit of its iconic RCZ coupe with the Peugeot RCZ Vision, a futuristic electric sports car concept that combines French design, advanced battery technology and a renewed focus on driving pleasure. Positioned as a successor to the original Peugeot RCZ, produced between 2009 and 2015, the RCZ Vision previews the brand’s vision for high-performance electric mobility. It introduces Peugeot’s new “Feline Future” design language while showcasing technologies intended to shape the company’s next generation of vehicles. The concept’s headline specifications include 500 horsepower, up to 600 km (373 miles) of range and a targeted energy consumption of 11.5 kWh/100 km. It also features a solid-state battery developed with Factorial Energy and a 1,000-volt electrical architecture designed to deliver exceptionally fast charging. Peugeot has not presented the RCZ Vision as a conventional production-car launch. Instead, it serves as a design and technology manifesto, offering a glimpse of what future Peugeot models could look like. Peugeot RCZ Vision Revives an Iconic Coupe The original Peugeot RCZ became one of the French automaker’s most distinctive modern models thanks to its sculpted bodywork, low roofline and characteristic double-bubble roof design. Although production ended in 2015, the coupe has since developed a following among enthusiasts and collectors. The RCZ Vision revisits that heritage with a more futuristic interpretation. Its proportions combine a low, wide stance with muscular bodywork, a compact-looking glass cabin and flowing surfaces intended to improve aerodynamic efficiency. The concept also introduces Peugeot’s “Feline Future” design philosophy, built around five principles: freedom, courage, elegance, inner force and instinct. Together, these ideas aim to create a car that looks powerful without appearing unnecessarily aggressive. At the front, ultra-slim lighting elements reinterpret Peugeot’s signature three-claw light design. An illuminated emblem, a distinctive RCZ graphic and intricately detailed air intakes give the concept a dramatic appearance. The rear continues the same minimalist approach, with integrated three-claw lighting and an active spoiler that remains hidden when the car is stationary and deploys while driving to improve aerodynamic performance. Peugeot has also retained the original RCZ’s distinctive double-bubble styling, reinterpreting it with slimmer, seemingly floating roof arches. The glass-bubble concept extends across much of the vehicle, creating a light and futuristic silhouette. 500 HP and Up to 373 Miles of Electric Range Beyond its styling, the Peugeot RCZ Vision showcases an ambitious electric powertrain concept. Peugeot targets 500 horsepower and a driving range of up to 600 km, equivalent to approximately 373 miles. The company also cites energy consumption of 11.5 kWh/100 km on the WLTP combined cycle, although the figure is marked as subject to confirmation. If achieved in practice, that combination would make the RCZ Vision an especially efficient proposition for a high-performance electric sports coupe. Its final range and consumption would, however, depend on the production specification, driving conditions and other factors. The concept is based on an architecture derived from Stellantis’ STLA One platform concept, designed to accommodate next-generation technologies and different battery solutions. A key highlight is the solid-state battery developed in collaboration with Factorial Energy. Solid-state batteries are attracting interest across the automotive industry because their potential advantages include higher energy density, reduced packaging requirements and improved charging performance. In the RCZ Vision, the battery is paired with a 1,000-volt electrical architecture. Peugeot targets a charging time of just 10 minutes to increase the battery’s state of charge from 10% to 80%. These figures describe the concept’s intended capabilities rather than verified performance from a production vehicle. Nevertheless, they illustrate Peugeot’s ambition to combine sports-car performance with more efficient energy use and shorter charging stops. Hypersquare Steering and Brake-by-Wire Technology The RCZ Vision is also a showcase for Peugeot’s next-generation driving technology, particularly its Hypersquare steering control and electronic vehicle-control systems. Hypersquare replaces the conventional round steering wheel with a distinctive rectangular control featuring four circular openings. The layout places key functions within easy reach, allowing the driver to keep their hands on the steering control. Combined with steer-by-wire technology, Hypersquare eliminates the traditional mechanical connection between the steering control and the front wheels. Instead, electronic systems manage steering inputs and adjust the steering ratio according to vehicle speed. At low speeds, the system is designed to make parking and tight manoeuvres easier by reducing the amount of steering input required. At higher speeds, the steering response is adjusted to provide greater stability and smoother control. The concept also introduces brake-by-wire technology, replacing the conventional hydraulic connection between the brake pedal and braking system with electronic control. Peugeot says this approach can improve braking precision and integrate regenerative braking more effectively, helping recover energy during deceleration. The RCZ Vision additionally previews Level 2++ automated-driving capabilities, including a hands-free function available on demand in city and highway environments. The precise operating conditions and availability of these features have not been detailed for a production vehicle. Importantly, Peugeot says the production version of Hypersquare will also feature in the next-generation Peugeot E-208, indicating that at least part of the technology is intended to extend beyond the concept itself. artigo.texto: Baterias já são mais baratas que turbinas a gás de data centers Relatório da Wood Mackenzie mostra que baterias de 4 horas custam menos que turbinas a gás em todos os 43 mercados analisados. A tendência deve se acelerar. Existe um consenso quase universal de que a inteligência artificial vai consumir quantidades absurdas de energia nos próximos anos. O debate, até agora, girava em torno de qual fonte supriria essa demanda. Um novo relatório da consultoria Wood Mackenzie traz uma resposta que pode surpreender: baterias de armazenamento já são mais baratas que as turbinas a gás usadas por boa parte dos data centers no mundo. A conclusão vale para todos os continentes e cada um dos 43 mercados analisados pela consultoria. Baterias com duração de quatro horas custam menos que turbinas de ciclo aberto a gás natural. E a tendência é de divergência crescente: o custo da eletricidade armazenada em baterias deve continuar caindo, enquanto o da geração a gás tende a encarecer nas próximas décadas. Por que as turbinas a gás ficaram tão caras A explicação passa diretamente pela corrida da IA. Desenvolvedores de data centers voltados para inteligência artificial têm comprado qualquer modelo de turbina disponível no mercado, pressionando preços para cima. O efeito é mais agudo nas turbinas de ciclo aberto, que são mais simples de fabricar, porém menos eficientes e mais caras de operar. Essas turbinas costumam ser usadas por concessionárias como plantas de pico, acionadas em momentos de alta demanda. Quando o preço desses equipamentos sobe, o custo repassa para toda a cadeia elétrica. Mesmo sendo mais simples, turbinas de ciclo aberto agora levam de dois a quatro anos para serem entregues. As de ciclo fechado, mais eficientes, têm filas que se estendem até o início da década de 2030. O resultado: os preços de novas usinas a gás natural dispararam em praticamente todas as categorias. Como mostramos em nossa cobertura sobre infraestrutura tecnológica, a demanda por energia dos data centers já pressiona tarifas elétricas nos Estados Unidos e em outros mercados. Solar é a energia nova mais barata do mundo O relatório da Wood Mackenzie traz outro dado relevante: a energia solar já é a forma mais barata de nova geração em todos os mercados analisados. Inclusive na América do Norte, apesar das tarifas de importação e restrições comerciais que pressionam o setor. Nos Estados Unidos, projetos solares em escala de concessionária (utility-scale) estão relativamente protegidos no curto prazo. Cerca de 168 gigawatts em capacidade se beneficiam de cláusulas de proteção (safe-harbor provisions) que mantêm créditos fiscais para projetos já iniciados ou concluídos antes do fim de 2027. Na prática, isso significa que boa parte da expansão solar americana já contratada não será afetada pelas oscilações regulatórias atuais. Quem acompanha o impacto de políticas energéticas nos mercados financeiros sabe que essa previsibilidade regulatória é decisiva para a alocação de capital em infraestrutura. O mapa global da transição energética em data centers Os números regionais reforçam a tese de que a transição é estrutural, não conjuntural. No Oriente Médio e na África, baterias de quatro horas devem ser 33% mais baratas que turbinas de pico a gás até 2035, deslocando a geração a gás por questões puramente econômicas em cada mercado da região. Na China, os custos de armazenamento de energia são 55% inferiores aos dos países vizinhos. Isso dá à indústria chinesa uma vantagem competitiva significativa na corrida pela infraestrutura de IA, um ponto que frequentemente escapa ao debate focado apenas em chips e modelos de linguagem. “Essa mudança econômica é decisiva e está se ampliando”, afirmou Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, analista principal da Wood Mackenzie, no comunicado que acompanha o relatório. O que isso significa para a infraestrutura de IA A consequência prática é profunda. Até agora, grande parte dos projetos de data centers para IA vinham sendo planejados com geração a gás como pilar energético. Empresas como Microsoft, Google e Amazon fecharam contratos bilionários envolvendo usinas nucleares e a gás para garantir fornecimento estável. Com baterias mais baratas e tempos de entrega menores que os das turbinas, a equação muda. Baterias de quatro horas não substituem geração de base, é verdade. Elas são ideais para cobrir picos de demanda, exatamente o papel que as turbinas de ciclo aberto desempenham. Nessa função específica, a competição já está decidida em termos de custo. Para investidores que acompanham o setor de tecnologia e infraestrutura digital, o sinal é claro: os próximos data centers provavelmente terão mais baterias e painéis solares do que turbinas a gás. Isso altera a dinâmica de investimento em toda a cadeia, dos fabricantes de células de lítio às concessionárias de energia. O gás natural perde espaço, mas não desaparece É importante contextualizar. O relatório da Wood Mackenzie não decreta o fim do gás natural na geração elétrica. Turbinas de ciclo fechado, mais eficientes e capazes de operar como geração de base, seguem relevantes. O que muda é a lógica das plantas de pico: onde antes se instalava uma turbina simples para cobrir momentos de alta demanda, agora faz mais sentido econômico instalar baterias. No mercado americano, a demanda por gás natural deve se estreitar na próxima década, segundo a consultoria. Não por regulação ambiental, mas por economia pura. Quando a alternativa limpa é também a mais barata, a transição deixa de depender de subsídios ou vontade política. O dado mais revelador do relatório talvez seja esse: a virada não é projetada para o futuro. Ela já aconteceu. Em todos os 43 mercados analisados, sem exceção, armazenar energia em baterias custa menos que gerar com turbinas a gás de ciclo aberto. A pergunta agora é a velocidade com que o mercado de data centers vai absorver essa realidade. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Rentabilidade

artigo.texto: I will show you firsthand how cold minus 30 degrees is. Yi er san (one, two, three). On the 8th in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China, at BYD headquarters' "ultra-low-temperature ultra-fast charging room." When an employee threw 90-degree hot water into the air, a white mist spread in an instant. Frost settled on the silver car inside, and icicles hung from the front bumper. As the door opened and I stepped in, the chill crept up my legs. When an ultra-fast charger was connected to the Z9 GT, an electric vehicle made by BYD's premium brand Denza, the state of charge climbed about 1 percentage point every five seconds. It reached 97% in nine minutes. Even in the bitter cold of minus 30 degrees, the charging gauge rose without hesitation. BYD, which started in 1995 as a battery maker for mobile phones, has grown into a leading company in the global electric vehicle market in just over 30 years. The technology that delivers fast charging speeds even in extreme cold is one facet that shows BYD's competitiveness. We visited BYD's headquarters to find out the secret. ◇97% charge in nine minutes even at minus 30 degrees… maximum output 1,500 kW BYD's secret to achieving fast charging speeds even in extreme cold lies in its second-generation Blade Battery and ultra-fast "flash charging" technology unveiled in Mar. The charger used in this demonstration supports up to 1,500 kW of output per connector. The company said it drastically cut charging time by combining a battery that can accept a surge of power with a high-output charger. BYD's goal is to reduce EV charging times to be close to the fueling time of internal combustion engine cars. There is also a reason why charging stops at 97% instead of 100%. Chair Wang previously said they leave about 3% spare capacity to maintain regenerative braking. Regenerative braking converts the energy generated when a vehicle slows down into electricity and stores it in the battery. If the battery is fully charged, the function can be limited because there is no room to store the recovered power. BYD is also accelerating the expansion of charging infrastructure. A BYD official said, "We have installed 10,000 ultra-fast charging stations across China and plan to expand to 20,000 by the end of this year." The strategy is not only to cut charging time but also to solve the shortage of charging stations. ◇Floats on water and runs on three wheels… technology that breaks car conventions Opposite the freezer, a miniature production line replicating the car manufacturing process was set up. It showed multiple robot arms moving body parts and welding them through the process until a car was completed. A BYD official explained, "A car is produced every 51 seconds." Deeper in the pavilion, technologies that break conventional wisdom about cars drew attention. The U8, an SUV from BYD's top-tier brand Yangwang, is equipped with an emergency buoyancy feature that allows it to float on water for a certain period if it falls in. The company said it can drive each of the four wheels independently, allowing limited steering and movement even on water. They also showcased technology that moves the vehicle on the remaining three wheels even if one wheel lifts off the ground. The technology is applied to models such as the Bao 8 from BYD's off-road brand Fangchengbao. Technology that rotates or parks the vehicle in tight spaces by controlling the wheels individually was also on display. Technology that rotates or parks the vehicle in tight spaces by controlling the movement of each wheel individually was also introduced. Behind BYD's ability to develop a wide range of technologies is a business structure that produces key components in-house. It develops and manufactures not only batteries but also power semiconductors, motors, and electronic control units on its own. A BYD official said, "We source more than 80% of vehicle parts ourselves, excluding tires and glass," and added, "Our strength is that we can quickly apply new technologies to actual vehicles and production lines." ◇Packed with 1,260 patent certificates… invests 14 trillion won a year in R&D A space that symbolically shows BYD's technological edge was in the center of the pavilion. It was a wall filled with 1,260 patent certificates. Patent certificates issued in countries around the world, including Korea, hung densely. In the middle was a phrase that read, "Technology is king, innovation is fundamental (技術為王 創新為本)." Founder Chair Wang Chuanfu has emphasized a business structure that develops technology in-house and manufactures key components independently. According to BYD, cumulative patent applications amount to 71,000. A company official said, "If you lay out all the patent certificates, they could fill 12 soccer fields." Spending on research and development (R&D) is also massive. BYD posted 804 billion yuan in sales last year. Of that, 7.89%, or 63.4 billion yuan (about 14 trillion won), went into R&D. The share of research and development investment relative to sales far exceeds the roughly 3% at Hyundai Motor and Kia. As price competition intensifies in China's electric vehicle market and tariff and regulatory barriers rise overseas, BYD is seeking a breakthrough by leaning on its technological edge. The company directly secures core technologies from batteries to car production and quickly commercializes them. The charging gauge that climbed rapidly in a minus-30-degree freezer was a scene that showed the technological competitiveness BYD has built over just over 30 years.

artigo.texto: Japan's electric vehicle field is about to get a new entrant. Suzuki is debuting its first battery-powered mini car, the e-Sky, which is expected to be the category's lowest-priced model — thanks in part to lithium iron phosphate packs likely coming from rival BYD's battery division. Here's what to know According to Electrek, which cited Nikkei Asia, Suzuki will launch the e-Sky on Nov. 16 in Japan with a price of about 2.12 million yen, or $13,387. At that level, it would cost less than both BYD's 2.145 million yen ($13,546) Racco and Nissan's 2.4 million yen ($15,463) Sakura. Suzuki lists the e-Sky with a range of up to 310 kilometers (193 miles) and says its 97 watt-hour per kilometer AC energy consumption rating is "class-leading." The e-Sky rides on a kei EV platform developed specifically for it and uses Suzuki's own electric drive system. More background Subsidy details for the e-Sky are pending. Should it qualify for the same 568,000 yen ($3,587) offered for the commercial kei-class e-Every, the resulting price would move much closer to the 1.53 million yen ($9,663) Spacia, Suzuki's top-selling gas-powered kei car, according to Electrek. Chinese automaker BYD is also invested in mini-car development, saying it has the first kei EV to exceed 300 kilometers (186 miles) of range. The company's Racco 200 uses a 22.4 kilowatt-hour LFP battery and is rated for 210 kilometers (130 miles), while the Racco 300 Plus and Premium has an increased capacity of 35.84 kWh and a range of as much as 320 kilometers (199 miles). What can be done? For drivers considering buying an electric vehicle, the e-Sky could open the door at a low price point. Charging strategy affects long-term EV savings, too. Charging an EV at home often costs half as much as using public chargers, but basic Level 1 charging tends to be slow. Qmerit provides free, instant installation estimates for faster Level 2 home charger installations. Where can I learn more? Other developments provide a fuller picture around Suzuki's budget-minded kei EV push and its use of BYD battery tech. • At BYD, battery cost cuts could make entry-level EVs even cheaper. • BYD's next-gen Blade battery is poised to lift range while lowering pack prices. • In Japan, Enechange is offering unlimited monthly charging for less than $20. • Nissan's N7 sedan pairs stunning driving range with an affordable price. • Kia's EV3 brings more affordable pricing to a feature-packed electric SUV. artigo.texto: - Aito will continue using CATL batteries across its lineup, with total annual capacity set to exceed 20 GWh after a joint project is completed. - The companies will also collaborate on supercharging networks and battery services, and jointly pursue markets in Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia. CATL (HKEX: 3750) has signed a long-term strategic cooperation agreement with Seres (HKEX: 9927) to expand battery production capacity for the automaker's Aito brand and extend their partnership into charging services and overseas markets. The companies signed the agreement on Saturday in Chongqing, where Seres is headquartered. Aito will continue using CATL batteries across its lineup over the long term, reinforcing their existing supply relationship. Aito has used CATL batteries in all its models since the brand's inception, and cumulative deliveries have surpassed 1.2 million vehicles, the Chinese battery giant said in a statement. Capacity expansion is a key part of the agreement. The companies will accelerate construction of the second phase of their "plant-in-plant" project at the Seres plant, with planned annual capacity of 10 to 12 GWh. Once the second phase is completed, combined annual capacity across both phases will exceed 20 GWh. CATL said the companies aim to improve supply chain resilience and competitiveness by concentrating production at the site. The expansion builds on their model of producing batteries within an auto assembly plant, integrating battery system production with Aito vehicle manufacturing at the same site. On June 30, 2025, CATL began operating 2 CTP (cell-to-pack) 2.0 battery pack production lines at the Seres plant, providing a local supply of battery systems for Aito vehicles. The project marked CATL's first production base in Chongqing and its first use of the "plant-in-plant" model. The latest agreement will expand that manufacturing footprint. Beyond capacity expansion, the companies will collaborate on supercharging networks and battery services to build a service system covering the full battery lifecycle. They will also jointly pursue overseas markets including Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia, according to CATL's statement. The announcement did not disclose the agreement's duration or when the second phase would begin operations. It provided no details on the models or implementation plans involved in the overseas cooperation. Seres also recently renewed its Aito partnership with Huawei, another key partner. The companies signed a new 5-year cooperation agreement in Shenzhen on September 30 to jointly develop the Aito business. Under arrangements announced on October 1, Huawei and Seres will jointly establish a dedicated Aito team and continue developing brand-specific operations to strengthen the brand and improve customer service. For CATL, the agreement further cements its long-term supply relationship with Aito. The company remains the world's largest EV battery supplier. CATL's global EV battery installations reached 333.0 GWh in the first 8 months of this year, up 25.2% from a year earlier, giving it a 39.4% market share, according to data released on October 2 by South Korean market researcher SNE Research.

artigo.texto: Key points: The solid-state battery investment clock has five stages: in the concept stage, watch cash, R&D, and the main business; in the pilot stage, watch equipment tenders, delivery, and yield; in the verification stage, watch lithium sulfide supply and demand (830 mt to 8,000 mt); in the mass production stage, watch costs (400-500 million to 200-300 million yuan/GWh), where involution risk is highest; in the endgame stage, watch patents and share (500 GWh, 400 billion yuan). Keep a close eye on tenders, lithium sulfide, and yield. SMM recently reviewed the future of solid-state batteries and compiled it into a ten-year series. Using the current development of the lithium battery industry as a reference, especially the intertwined love-hate relationship between the LFP and ternary routes, an epic chapter has unfolded over the years. In the long river of conventional liquid lithium batteries, solid-liquid hybrid and all-solid-state batteries will take the stage, outlining a new generation of high-specific-energy battery world. The ten-year series will be divided into nine parts: introduction, westward movement, industry chain structure, industry-wide involution, Cinderella moment, ternary becoming great again, patent shadow war, investment clock, and conclusion. Introduction: Dreams will surely shine into reality: Why we need to re-understand the industrial logic of solid-state batteries - the gap between ideal and reality, and the result is that dreams shine into reality Part 1: Will it replicate the westward movement of liquid batteries: The logic of concentration in the west - will solid-state batteries replicate the "westward movement" of liquid lithium batteries? Part 2: A good opportunity to reverse the distorted power structure of the industry chain: Industry chain power structure - upstream windfall profits, midstream under pressure, downstream delayed payments? Part 3: Warning of PV-style industry-wide involution: Will solid-state batteries enter PV-style industry-wide involution? artigo.texto: BYD Explores 1,500kW Ultra-Fast EV Charging for Pakistan Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer BYD is in talks to introduce its cutting-edge 1,500kW ultra-fast charging technology in Pakistan. These discussions are ongoing with Mega Motor Company, a local automotive player, as BYD assesses the viability of deploying this advanced charging system within the country’s evolving infrastructure. Next-Generation Charging Technology BYD’s new charging platform integrates the second-generation Blade Battery with its FLASH Charging technology, capable of delivering up to 1,500kW through a single connector. This allows compatible EVs to recharge from 10% to 70% battery capacity in just five minutes, and reach up to 97% in nine minutes under optimal conditions. Even in cold climates of -30°C, the system can charge a vehicle from 20% to 97% within 12 minutes. However, these ultra-fast charging speeds are limited to vehicles designed specifically for BYD’s new battery and charging system. Existing BYD models available in Pakistan may not achieve such rapid recharge rates, as actual performance depends on a vehicle’s battery design and maximum supported charging power. Strategic Growth and Local Production In addition to technology deployment, BYD is planning to expand its footprint in Pakistan through a local assembly facility scheduled to commence operations in the latter half of 2026. The plant is expected to produce approximately 25,000 vehicles annually, with scalable capacity to double production as demand grows. BYD Vice President Liu Xueliang emphasized that the availability of local infrastructure and stakeholder feedback will shape the decision to launch the ultra-fast charging network. “The rollout depends largely on local readiness and future vehicle plans,” Liu noted, signaling a cautious but optimistic approach. Significance for Pakistan’s EV Market As Pakistan gradually embraces electric mobility, the introduction of high-capacity charging stations could alleviate major obstacles such as long charging times and limited infrastructure. These improvements may accelerate EV adoption by providing more convenience for consumers and encouraging investment in the sector. By exploring this technology and establishing local manufacturing, BYD is positioning itself as a leading player in Pakistan’s burgeoning EV landscape, which could contribute to cleaner transportation and reduced reliance on fossil fuels. While no official timeline has been confirmed for either the ultra-fast charger rollout or vehicle production start, these developments mark a potential turning point in Pakistan’s electric vehicle ecosystem.

artigo.texto: Electronics distributor Richardson Electronics (NASDAQ:RELL) announced better-than-expected revenue in calendar Q3 2026 (fiscal Q1 2027), with sales up 18.9% year on year to $64.92 million. Its non-GAAP profit of $0.27 per share was significantly above analysts' consensus estimates. Is now the time to buy RELL? Find out in our full research report (it's free). Richardson Electronics (RELL) Q3 CY2026 Highlights: - Revenue: $64.92 million vs analyst estimates of $58.99 million (18.9% year-on-year growth, 10.1% beat) - Adjusted EPS: $0.27 vs analyst estimates of $0.09 (significant beat) - Operating Margin: 7.9%, up from 1.8% in the same quarter last year - Backlog: $184.4 million at quarter end, up 36.9% year on year - Market Capitalization: $297.5 million StockStory's Take Richardson Electronics delivered results ahead of Wall Street expectations in Q3, with management crediting robust demand for its engineered power and energy storage solutions as key drivers. CEO Ed Richardson highlighted strong adoption in semiconductor wafer fabrication, RF and microwave components, and green energy systems, as well as continued expansion into global markets. The company's focus on broadening its customer base and enhancing engineering capabilities contributed to operating margin gains and improved cash generation. Management also noted that favorable product mix and a one-time tariff refund supported gross margin improvement this quarter. Looking forward, management sees accelerating opportunities in energy storage and power management solutions, as customers across industrial, infrastructure, and defense sectors seek greater reliability and cost efficiency. COO Wendy Diddell emphasized that converting backlog and inventory into revenue remains a top priority, pointing to a growing pipeline of engineered projects, especially in battery energy storage. Management also referenced ongoing investments in U.S.-based manufacturing and AI-enabled business processes, expecting these to improve execution and position the company for further double-digit growth. CFO Bob Ben cautioned that tariff refund benefits may not recur at the same level next quarter, but the underlying demand trends remain strong. Key Insights from Management's Remarks Management attributed the quarter's strong performance to healthy demand across its core markets, new product rollouts, and disciplined cost management, while noting that favorable product mix and a tariff refund provided additional support to margins. - Semiconductor demand momentum: The Power and Microwave Technologies (PMT) group saw continued strength in semiconductor wafer fabrication and RF/microwave products, with customer optimism extending well into next year. - Growth in wind and energy storage: Green Energy Solutions (GES) benefited from increased adoption of Pitch Energy Modules for wind turbines and a $2 million order for battery energy storage systems (BESS), reflecting momentum in both domestic and international markets. - Expanding international footprint: Management highlighted new orders and product rollouts in Europe, Asia, and South America, including partnerships with top wind turbine operators and expansion into new turbine platforms. - One-time tariff refund impact: Gross margin improvement was partly driven by a one-time IEEPA tariff refund, which management does not expect to repeat at the same scale in future quarters. - Operational discipline and backlog: The company maintained flat inventory levels while growing backlog, with management focused on converting backlog into revenue and cash through disciplined execution and targeted investments in manufacturing and engineering resources.

artigo.texto: For luxury electric cars, longer range often comes with a familiar compromise: a bigger battery adds weight. Solid-state technology could help ease that trade-off by storing more energy without requiring a heavier pack. BYD’s upcoming Yangwang executive sedan brings that possibility into the ultra-luxury conversation. Spotted testing in China, the roughly 5.5-meter (about 18 feet) vehicle combines coach doors and imposing proportions with reports that it could carry solid-state batteries. BYD has not confirmed that specification. While its appearance draws comparisons with the Rolls-Royce Phantom, the battery question connects it to a broader development effort. BMW and Mercedes-Benz are already using electric sedans to investigate how advanced cells perform beyond the laboratory. What changes inside the battery? The difference begins with the electrolyte, which allows lithium ions to move between electrodes during charging and discharging. Conventional lithium-ion cells typically use a liquid electrolyte. All-solid-state designs replace that liquid with a solid material. This change can support electrode materials such as lithium metal, potentially increasing the energy stored for a given battery weight. For an electric car, that could mean longer range without simply adding more battery mass. Mercedes-Benz identifies higher energy density as a key benefit of its solid-state development work. More from Transportation See All Safety is another potential advantage. According to the US Department of Energy, solid electrolytes are less prone to leakage when damaged, although a complete battery’s performance still depends on its materials and construction. None of these possibilities establishes the Yangwang sedan’s range or charging speed. Those figures require confirmed specifications and testing. How Yangwang supports BYD’s luxury push Yangwang occupies the highest tier of BYD’s lineup, above Denza, and showcases technologies such as the company’s quad-motor e4 platform. The upcoming sedan extends that role into the executive segment. Its long wheelbase, boxy profile and coach doors introduce styling associated with established luxury flagships, giving BYD’s technological ambitions a more traditional exterior. Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing described it as “the culmination of three years of meticulous development by Yangwang, featuring the brand’s signature design language, and is an ultra-luxury executive sedan.” The combination suggests a strategy built around luxury design and technological differentiation. A solid-state battery could strengthen that positioning, but its inclusion remains unconfirmed. What road tests actually demonstrate BMW announced in May 2025 that an i7 prototype near Munich was testing Solid Power’s all-solid-state cells. Engineers are examining cell expansion, pressure control and temperature management, with BMW acknowledging that further development is needed for a competitive complete battery system. Mercedes-Benz demonstrated another step in August 2025. An EQS prototype fitted with Factorial lithium-metal solid-state cells traveled 1,205 kilometers (748.8 miles) without recharging. Mercedes reported 25 percent more usable battery energy with comparable pack size and weight. These were development results, rather than specifications for a car available to buyers. Such tests show progress while revealing the engineering work still involved. For BYD, the next step is confirmation of what powers its flagship, followed by evidence that the battery can deliver alongside the luxury experience.

artigo.texto: Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centers Finnish authorities have ordered work to stop at two planned Google data centre sites following concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest. The projects in Muhos and Kajaani are part of Google‘s €13 billion investment in Finland, announced less than a month ago as its largest single investment in Europe. Finland’s Supervisory Agency said work at one site had been carried out without a mandatory environmental impact assessment. Preparatorywork included removing trees and topsoil, building roads and storage areas, and altering ditches. Google acknowledged it had “fallen short” of its own standards and said it would follow the authorities’ guidance. The company behind the projects has been ordered to explain how it intends to proceed, with officials warning that enforcement action could follow if requirements are not met. artigo.texto: Cleveland City Council is preparing to extend the city’s moratorium on data centers for another three months. Council Member Brian Kazy said he plans to introduce legislation on Monday to continue the pause. Passed this summer, the moratorium was meant to give City Hall time to draw up regulations for the centers, which have become central to the artificial intelligence boom. Kazy, the chair of council’s Utilities Committee, convened a trio of public meetings on the topic. Council members also toured two local data centers, he said. He took away from the hearings that most people oppose the “hyperscale” centers that require large amounts of energy to power AI. He drew a distinction between those centers and small and medium-sized facilities that form part of the infrastructure of the internet. Now the city needs 90 more days “to assure that we get this thing right,” Kazy told Weekly Chatter. Democrats try to rock the southwest suburbs Strongsville is a Republican stalwart in strongly Democratic Cuyahoga County. But Democrats hope to unseat the suburb’s longtime County Council representative this fall. Council Member Mike Gallagher faces a Democratic opponent for the first time since 2010, when he originally won his seat with 59% of the vote. Democrats have already flipped the other two GOP seats on the 11-member council. Democratic challenger Courtney Scheff, an attorney and former prosecutor, has the support of County Executive Chris Ronayne, who has accused Gallagher of trying to “thwart progress.” A critic of the administration, Gallagher has embraced Ronayne’s opposition. Despite Ronayne’s support, Scheff told Weekly Chatter that she “absolutely” could serve as a check on the Democratic executive. Asked about the county’s budget troubles, she suggested consolidating programs and holding down department spending. Scheff said she wouldn’t have voted for a new building department the county created last year, for instance. Both candidates emphasized their ability to reach across the aisle. The Republican-leaning district reaches beyond Strongsville to include North Royalton, Berea, Olmsted Falls and Olmsted Township. President Donald Trump won the district by about 5 percentage points in 2024. Can a down-ballot Democrat win there? Scheff argued that, nationwide, voters are tiring of Trump and the GOP-controlled Congress. “Whether that translates into the district, I don’t know,” she said. “But I believe it will. I think that people are kind of fed up with the same old thing over and over again.” Rainbow Terrace family goes to court The estate of Cordale Sheffield, the man who died from burns he received in last year’s explosion and fire at Rainbow Terrace, has brought a wrongful death lawsuit over the blast. Sheffield’s estate is suing Enbridge Gas, the owner of the apartment building and others. Attorneys for the estate focused on a gas line at the site, writing that it was decades old. The suit also cites a finding by the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio that, after the blast, Enbridge removed pipes in such a way that they “could not be leak tested.” An investigation by the City of Cleveland pointed to a gas leak as the likely fuel for the explosion but said the ultimate cause was “undetermined.” A spokesperson for Enbridge declined to comment on the suit but wrote in an email, “Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragic event, particularly the Sheffield family.”
