artigo.texto: A senior Iranian official says Tehran finds the latest U.S. response to a proposal to end the war “insufficient” and warns of attacks on regional data centers and cables if fighting intensifies again. Meanwhile, Israel’s former attorney general took the witness stand in corruption cases against Benjamin Netanyahu, as the political future of the country’s longest-serving prime minister hangs in the balance with elections weeks away. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here. Iran says latest US response is ‘insufficient’ The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States “insufficient” as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along. The comments by Mohsen Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander, were carried by Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency. Rezaei added that Iran is no longer responding to the U.S. and said Washington must clarify certain issues, without giving details. He said the U.S. has accepted some of the seven conditions but others remain unclear. Iran’s delegation to the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders last month proposed a sped-up agreement that echoed the memorandum of understanding that collapsed days after the U.S. and Iran signed it in June. The new proposal was rejected, but the two sides have remained in contact via mediation. Rezaei also threatened “cables, data centers, AI facilities and other sites in the region” if intense fighting breaks out again. Meanwhile, the Guard’s navy warned that any ship on the strait that turns off navigation and identification systems would be “identified as hostile,” according to an IRNA report. Attacks on ships transiting the strait have increased since Iran’s proposal was rejected. One attack was reported Sunday. Former legal adviser testifies in Netanyahu corruption case Israel’s former attorney general took the witness stand in Netanyahu’s long-running corruption trial. Avichai Mandelblit indicted the prime minister seven years ago for fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. The charges were the first-ever against a sitting Israeli prime minister. Netanyahu was in the courtroom to hear Mandelblit testify. The prime minister handpicked Mandelblit, his former Cabinet secretary, for the attorney general job. His tenure ended in 2022. Netanyahu has been accused of offering or exchanging favors with wealthy associates and media moguls for political gain. He denies any wrongdoing. Saudi Arabia on alert as Houthis warn of new strikes A projectile struck the same passenger terminal at the Riyadh international airport that was hit on Saturday. The airport had been closed after Saturday’s attack, which killed 12 people, but Saudi authorities reported injuries in the latest attack. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed responsibility for both attacks on King Khalid International Airport, which has been targeted every day since Wednesday. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis’ military spokesperson, urged “everyone to take our warnings seriously” about the risks of flying in Saudi airspace. The attacks have marked a major escalation in the war between the Houthis and the kingdom, and complicated efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war. Gaza residents return to rubble as strikes continue Residents in central Gaza returned home to assess the damage caused by Israeli strikes after they had been warned to evacuate the day before. Bassam Abed said at least 10 residences housing some 300 families were reduced to rubble, and families were not given enough time to flee. “Women slept outdoors. We did not take clothes,” Abed said. Israel’s military said it had targeted militant infrastructure, including a rocket launch site and a command center used by Hamas militants to attack soldiers. One year after Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire deal, Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes. Netanyahu wants probe into ‘NAZA’ documentary Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked the attorney general and head of the Shin Bet security service to investigate people who participated in the new documentary “NAZA,” in which Israeli military insiders describe what they say was the reckless killing of civilians in Gaza. Netanyahu said the film, which debuted at the Venice Film Festival to a record 25-minute standing ovation, tells “a false, misleading and biased story that slanders the State of Israel” and its military. The documentary has angered and unsettled Israelis, whose view of the war in Gaza differs sharply from that of much of the world, where criticism of Israel’s actions in the Palestinian territory has grown. Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power in the Oct. 27 election, in which security is a major issue. Lebanese army says retired officer killed by Israeli shelling Lebanon’s army said it had recovered the body of a retired army officer who was killed by Israeli artillery fire while checking on his property in the southern town of Yater. It said Ali Abdul Hassan Sweidan was “directly targeted by a hostile Israeli tank” and called it “a flagrant violation of existing understandings.” An Israeli military spokesperson said they were not aware of the incident. Israel has occupied a large swath of southern Lebanon since the outbreak of its latest war with the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah in March.

artigo.texto: Drones ucranianos derrubam centro de dados do "Google da Rússia". Um ataque com drones desativou o grande centro de dados da Yandex em Vladimir, na Rússia, na manhã de 11 de outubro (horário local), interrompendo mais de 80 serviços. Segundo a mídia russa, o centro de dados da Yandex em Vladimir teve que interromper temporariamente suas operações, causando ampla interrupção em mais de 80 serviços, incluindo plataformas digitais e ferramentas de IA. Este é o terceiro ataque à infraestrutura de servidores da Yandex em quatro dias. Anteriormente, os alvos estavam localizados nas regiões de Ryazan e Kaluga. Especificamente, em 8 de outubro, drones ucranianos atacaram um centro de dados da Yandex em Sasovo (Ryazan), causando um incêndio e forçando seu desligamento completo, desativando a infraestrutura de servidores usada pela Russian Railways (RZhD), pela rede MegaFon e por diversas agências de notícias. No dia seguinte, 9 de outubro, drones atacaram outro centro da Yandex em Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou. A Yandex confirmou que vários módulos de hardware foram desativados. Você também pode gostar O Centro de Vladimir foi projetado para acomodar até 2.880 racks de servidores, representando um dos principais centros de processamento da Yandex. Após as explosões, a Yandex confirmou que as operações em seu centro de dados em Vladimir foram temporariamente suspensas. O incidente afetou diversos aplicativos para o consumidor, incluindo a assistente de voz Alice, o Yandex Music, a ferramenta de videoconferência Telemost e o Yandex Smart Home. Os sistemas empresariais hospedados na Yandex Cloud também sofreram interrupções nos serviços de computação, armazenamento e gerenciamento de banco de dados, incluindo Compute Cloud, Object Storage, Managed Kubernetes, PostgreSQL e ClickHouse. Além disso, ferramentas e interfaces de programação de IA, como a API YandexGPT, SpeechKit e Vision OCR, também foram afetadas. A interrupção se estendeu além dos aplicativos principais da Yandex e afetou plataformas de comércio de terceiros na Rússia e em países vizinhos. Usuários relataram falhas de conexão ao acessar aplicativos de bancos, transporte por aplicativo e varejo. Segundo o prefeito Vladimir, ataques com drones danificaram subestações locais, derrubando a rede elétrica da cidade. Na manhã do mesmo dia, aproximadamente 80% do fornecimento de energia elétrica nas áreas afetadas já havia sido restabelecido. Você também pode gostar O Ministério da Defesa russo anunciou que seus sistemas de defesa aérea interceptaram 479 drones ucranianos em 16 regiões, incluindo Vladimir, Belgorod, Bryansk, Kursk e Rostov. Especialistas militares ucranianos observam que o bloqueio sistemático de centros de dados e redes de comunicação corporativas interromperia a logística, a governança corporativa e prejudicaria as capacidades de comando digital da Rússia.

artigo.texto: Projects related to energy transition, green infrastructure development, green transportation, waste treatment, circular economy , and emission reduction activities often require large capital investments and long payback periods, while potentially involving technological and policy risks. Therefore, the challenge is not just how much capital is needed, but also where that capital comes from, with what terms and costs, and how the risks are distributed. Bank credit remains crucial, but it cannot alone meet the long-term capital needs. Along with credit, it is necessary to expand capital markets, green finance, climate finance, private capital, and risk-sharing mechanisms. But opening new channels of capital only solves half the problem. The harder part is determining what value a green project creates, where the risks lie, and to what extent that value can be converted into cash flow. This is where the carbon market becomes crucial. Carbon pricing creates an economic signal: emissions have a cost, while emission reductions can create value. For businesses, this signal can shift the balance between continuing to use high-emission technologies and investing in energy, fuel, or raw material-saving technologies. For projects that meet the credit mechanism, the resulting emission reductions can even become a source of revenue. However, carbon value only truly matters to investment decisions when businesses and investors have reason to believe that this value is clear, stable, and can be converted into monetary value. The gap between “potential emission reduction” and a tradable asset is therefore vast. Potential does not equate to tangible value. The creation of carbon value requires methodology, baseline data, and a measurement-reporting-verification (MRV) system, along with mechanisms for issuance, trading, and payment. Without one link, environmental value is not sufficiently solid to become a financial asset. Singapore's experience shows that a carbon market cannot be created solely through an exchange. The country combines price signals via carbon taxes with credit quality standards, international cooperation, and a financial services ecosystem. Policies create demand, standards build trust, and the financial system connects carbon value with capital flows. The lesson for Vietnam, therefore, is not just about building a place to buy and sell carbon credits, but about creating the necessary infrastructure for a market to form a reliable value. In Vietnam, this gap is evident in data and valuation, as emissions data remains fragmented, lacking sufficiently long data series and reliable benchmarks. Banks and investors struggle to reach a consensus on forecasting cash flows and pricing risks. Furthermore, the costs of due diligence, verification, and disclosure can also become a barrier for businesses. And especially, when information is not standardized, the "green label" alone is insufficient to build financial confidence. This also explains why green credit and carbon markets must be viewed within the same value chain. Capital needs arise very early, right from the project preparation stage, equipment procurement, technology investment, and production organization. Meanwhile, carbon revenue typically only emerges after emission reduction results are measured, verified, credits are issued, or sales contracts are formed. This gap creates a financial void that credit, bridge financing, guarantees, cash flow management, and combined financial mechanisms can fill. From a banking perspective, the appropriate approach is not to treat carbon credits as a guaranteed source of repayment from the outset. It's necessary to distinguish between cash flow from core business operations and carbon revenue. Core cash flow forms the foundation for repayment; carbon revenue is an additional layer and should only be recognized to the extent of certainty. Carbon value can impact the financial plan through three channels: reducing production costs through low-emission investments; reducing the need to purchase additional quotas for compliant businesses; or generating revenue from transferring emission reduction results or carbon credits. These three channels need to be quantified separately to avoid double counting or overestimating the potential for generating cash. On the capital market side, the requirements are similar. Carbon prices can only be passed on to the cost of capital when investors have sufficient information to assess risk. This requires verifiable data, consistent verification standards, clear disclosure, and post-audit mechanisms. When a project's emissions, emission reduction results, rights to carbon value, and projected cash flows are clearly defined, banks can better assess creditworthiness, and investors have a basis for valuing the asset. Therefore, unlocking green capital is not just about "getting more capital," but about creating a chain of links from emission reduction to data, from data to carbon value, and then to credit and capital markets. When this chain is transparent and reliable, the carbon market truly becomes a financial tool for green transition, instead of just a place to buy and sell credits. The ultimate measure lies not in the number of green labels or the scale of transactions, but in the actual emissions reduced, the number of projects funded, and the ability for the cost of capital to accurately reflect the quality, risk, and value of each project. The workshop focused on discussing the linkages between credit policy, carbon markets, and capital markets, thereby seeking solutions to unlock financial resources for the green transition process. artigo.texto: Ucrânios lançaram drones que derrubaram dois dos cinco data centers da Yandex, a gigante russa de tecnologia, deixando seu chatbot de IA e vários serviços online fora do ar. O que foram os ataques de drones ucranianos nos data centers da Yandex? Nos dias 8 e 9 de outubro de 2026, unidades não tripuladas de ataque – os FP‑1 da empresa ucraniana Firepoint – atingiram instalações de processamento de dados nos estados de Sasovo e Kaluga, ambos na Rússia. O primeiro ataque visou o data center de Sasovo, onde estavam instalados dois dos três supercomputadores que treinam o modelo de linguagem YandexGPT. Já o segundo golpe foi direcionado ao maior data center da Yandex, localizado em Kaluga, considerado a principal infraestrutura de cálculo da companhia. Como os ataques afetaram os serviços de IA e outros produtos da Yandex? Com a destruição parcial das máquinas de alto desempenho, a Yandex perdeu parte da capacidade de treinamento e inferência do seu chatbot baseado em IA. Embora a empresa não tenha confirmado a extensão exata da queda, relatos de usuários russos apontam falhas ao acessar plataformas de mídia, aplicativos bancários e serviços de transporte ferroviário. A interrupção demonstra a dependência crítica da Yandex em poucos centros de processamento para manter seu ecossistema digital. Qual foi a resposta do governo ucraniano e da empresa Firepoint? O presidente ucraniano Volodymyr Zelenskyy, em postagem oficial na rede X, afirmou que os ataques foram uma “resposta simétrica” aos bombardeios russos contra infraestruturas ucranianas. Ele destacou que a estratégia ucraniana tem sido “alta precisão”, indicando que os alvos foram escolhidos para minimizar danos colaterais. Por sua vez, a Firepoint divulgou que seus drones FP‑1 foram empregados nas duas missões, reforçando a capacidade de ataque de longo alcance da Ucrânia. Quais serviços russos sofreram interrupções? Conforme a publicação independente Meduza, usuários russos relataram problemas de acesso a: - Plataforma de streaming de vídeo Ivi; - Serviço bancário digital T‑Bank; - Site da empresa estatal Russian Railways. Esses serviços são parte do portfólio de consumo massivo da Yandex, o que ampliou o impacto dos ataques ao cotidiano de milhões de usuários. O que isso indica sobre a guerra cibernética e física entre Ucrânia e Rússia? Os ataques mostram uma convergência crescente entre operações cibernéticas e ofensivas tradicionais. Enquanto a Rússia tem usado drones para atingir infraestruturas críticas ucranianas – como redes de telecomunicações – a Ucrânia responde com a mesma tecnologia, mas focada em alvos de alto valor estratégico, como data centers que sustentam a inteligência artificial russa. Essa “guerra de duas frentes” eleva o risco de interrupções globais em serviços digitais que dependem de servidores concentrados em regiões de conflito. O que vem depois? Para a Yandex, a prioridade será restaurar a capacidade de processamento e garantir a continuidade dos serviços essenciais. A empresa ainda não informou planos de migração de carga ou reforço de segurança física nos demais data centers. No cenário geopolítico, espera‑se que a Ucrânia continue a empregar drones de ataque como ferramenta de pressão, enquanto a Rússia pode intensificar suas defesas anti‑drone para proteger infraestruturas críticas. Observadores de tecnologia alertam que, se a tendência se mantiver, outras empresas de grande porte – tanto na Rússia quanto em países vizinhos – precisarão rever seus planos de contingência e diversificar a localização de seus centros de dados.

artigo.texto: Rapid City to hold open house on proposed data center rules RAPID CITY, S.D. (KOTA) - Rapid City residents will have a chance to weigh in on proposed rules for data centers during a public open house on Oct. 14. The city’s Community Development Department will host the event Wednesday from 5 to 7:30 p.m. at City Hall in the Council Chambers and Circle of Friends Community Room. City staff will explain the proposed ordinance and collect public feedback. The proposal would expand rules adopted in December 2024, which defined data centers and allowed them in light and heavy industrial districts. New standards would address issues including setbacks from residential areas, power, water and sewer use, noise and vibration. The Planning Commission reviewed the proposal Sept. 10 but postponed further discussion until its Nov. 5 meeting to allow more time for revisions and public input. Residents are encouraged to attend the open house and share their thoughts before the proposal returns to the Planning Commission. See a spelling or grammatical error in our story? artigo.texto: BYD to Bring Ultra-Fast EV Charging Technology to Pakistan Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD is in talks with its local partner, Mega Motor Company (MMC), to introduce its next-generation ultra-fast EV charging technology in Pakistan. The move could make electric vehicles more convenient for local consumers and support the wider adoption of new energy vehicles in the country. Liu Xueliang, Vice President of BYD and General Manager of its Asia Pacific Auto Sales Division, confirmed the discussions in an interview with Business Recorder. He said the company is exploring how to bring the technology to Pakistan in cooperation with MMC. According to Liu, the introduction of the new charging system will depend on infrastructure readiness, consultations with relevant stakeholders, and the company’s future product plans. BYD to Bring Ultra-Fast EV Charging Technology to Pakistan BYD’s Mega Flash Charging technology uses the company’s second-generation Blade Battery. The system aims to significantly reduce the time required to charge an electric vehicle, making EVs more practical for everyday use. Faster charging could help address one of the major concerns among potential electric vehicle buyers: the time needed to recharge a battery during long journeys or daily travel. Liu said the technology could help accelerate the adoption of new energy vehicles by making charging more convenient for consumers. The new system is designed for next-generation vehicles equipped with BYD’s latest battery platform. However, existing BYD vehicles will also be compatible with the charging infrastructure, although they may not achieve the same charging speeds as newer models. Despite the potential benefits, BYD has not announced a launch date for the technology in Pakistan. Its introduction will depend on the development of suitable charging infrastructure and further discussions with local partners. BYD’s Local Manufacturing Plant Nears Launch Alongside its charging technology plans, BYD is preparing to launch its manufacturing facility in Pakistan. Liu said the project is approaching its planned launch in the second half of 2026. The facility will be BYD’s sixth manufacturing plant outside China and will initially have an annual production capacity of 25,000 vehicles. The company could expand this capacity to 50,000 units per year, depending on future requirements. The manufacturing project is expected to create more than 1,100 jobs and support the development of Pakistan’s automotive industry. It could also contribute to sustainable industrial growth by increasing local vehicle production. According to Liu, the project is expected to help avoid an estimated 165,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions by 2034. BYD has not yet shared all the details of the manufacturing facility, but the company plans to provide further information as the project progresses. See Also: Chery Master Offers PKR 1.29 Million Upfront Savings on Tiggo 8 Super Hybrid AWD What It Means for Pakistan’s EV Market The potential introduction of ultra-fast charging technology could be an important development for Pakistan’s electric vehicle market. Shorter charging times could make EVs more attractive to consumers who are concerned about charging convenience and long-distance travel. However, the benefits will depend on the availability of compatible charging stations, reliable electricity supplies, and supporting infrastructure across major cities and highways. BYD’s planned manufacturing facility could also strengthen its position in Pakistan by supporting local production and creating employment opportunities. For now, the ultra-fast charging system remains under discussion. If BYD and MMC move forward with the plan, Pakistan could eventually gain access to faster EV charging technology as the country’s electric mobility sector continues to develop. artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – The buildings that house thousands of computer servers powering cloud computing and artificial intelligence have increasingly caught heat over environmental and energy concerns. Another common criticism is that state and local governments offer data centers sweetheart deals to attract them, including tax breaks and other incentives, potentially leaving ordinary residents to shoulder some of the costs associated with their development. But the National Taxpayers Union has released a pair of studies in a series arguing that at least two common state tax policies treat data centers less favorably than other industries. Most states allow a tangible personal property tax on data centers, a tax the group contends is not only antiquated and generally harmful but disproportionately disadvantages data centers. The NTU also calls the tax an “international anomaly,” noting that “only seven of the 38 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries tax tangible personal property at all, and among them, only Japan imposes them as broadly as the U.S.” A tangible personal property tax is a tax exacted on property “that can be moved or touched, such as business equipment, machinery, inventory and furniture,” as defined by the Tax Foundation. It’s paid annually and, like real estate property taxes, is calculated based on the assessed value of the property. For example, in some states, residents pay an annual property tax on their vehicles, often referred to as a car tax, based on the vehicle’s assessed value and the applicable tax rate. Data centers can pay tangible personal property taxes on their servers, networking equipment and other computer hardware, depending on state and local tax laws. Only, like with the car tax, the assessed value can be inaccurate. “Suppose the government thinks, ‘Well, your car is only two years old. It’s this make and model. You pay this much tax.’ But then you say, ‘Well, wait a minute! I drive this thing into the ground, and I’ve had to replace part of the suspension on it. It’s not in as good of shape as you think,’” NTU President Pete Sepp told The Center Square. Similarly, the assessed value of technology used in data centers can differ drastically from its market value — to the point that NTU argues state tangible personal property tax laws actually “discriminate against technology.” “The complex depreciation schedules required to value property are designed around manufacturing machinery that often performs at the same level after a decade or more of use,” NTU writes. “Applying the same standards to companies like data centers can significantly overvalue equipment like computer servers, which are often obsolete after three years.” And those depreciation schedules can also vary widely by state. In Florida, a three-year-old server is valued at 56% of its original cost according to its TPP tax law, while a handful of states would value that same server at 40% of its original cost. To avoid “discriminating” against technology-heavy industries like data centers, NTU recommends that states refrain from introducing new tangible personal property taxes but also avoid replacing existing ones with higher taxes elsewhere. And Sepp recommends going a step further. “State lawmakers should reform personal property laws so they’re uniform, neutral, simple and stable,” Sepp said in a statement. “Data centers are the manufacturing plants of the information age, and our laws should reflect that reality with equal treatment.” NTU also examined sales-and-use-tax exemptions in the first report of its series, addressing a more widely debated tax policy that has recently drawn criticism for its application to data centers. Thirty-three states offer a conditional form of the exemption to data centers (two offer it by right), but between May and August, eight states took steps to suspend or eliminate the exemptions “or benefit programs” for data centers, according to an analysis by S&P Global Market Intelligence. In the two states that offer sales-and-use-tax exemptions to data centers without having to meet special investment or employment requirements, the exemptions allow data centers to purchase computer servers, networking equipment and other hardware without paying applicable state and local sales taxes. Such exemptions are often perceived as unique to the industry, but that is a misconception, according to NTU Senior Fellow Jared Walczak, and “betrays a misunderstanding of how sales taxes are supposed to work.” There is a general consensus in tax policy that sales taxes should apply to final consumption rather than the inputs used to produce goods and services so as to avoid tax pyramiding, which occurs when a good or service is taxed multiple times at different stages of the production and supply chain, inflating the final consumer price. For example, if a data center pays sales tax on its computer servers, it may pass that expense along to businesses that use its computing services. Those businesses may then pass the added cost along to their customers through higher prices, which are taxed again when consumers make purchases. “No state’s perfect on exempting business inputs, but there are a few bright lines that basically all states adhere to,” Walczak told The Center Square. “They don't tax raw materials, and they almost always exempt machinery and equipment.” The vast majority of states offer sales tax exemptions for machinery and equipment used in manufacturing, while exemptions are also available for equipment used in industries such as agriculture, mining and energy production. “The problem is, where do data centers fit in that? Are they manufacturing? You know, what are they?” Walczak said. “A lot of states didn’t have a ready-made category for that.” Many states created similar exemptions years ago for data centers through incentive programs to help attract data centers, but unlike in manufacturing, in 33 states, data centers’ equipment

artigo.texto: Kiev tem realizado ofensivas contra alvos da infraestrutura russa, como instalações de energia, refinarias e portos A André de Sena, com informações da Reuters Fumaça em centro de dados da Yandex em Sasovo, na Rússia | Redes Sociais via Reuters Um ataque ucraniano realizado nesta sexta-feira (9) deixou parcialmente inoperante um centro de dados mantido pela empresa russa Yandex na região de Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou. Um dia antes, uma instalação semelhante, mantida pela mesma companhia, já havia sido atingida em Sasovo, na região de Ryazan. 🤳 Notícias em primeira mão: baixe nosso aplicativo gratuito e leve o jornalismo do SBT News com você, onde estiver! Clique aqui A Yandex tem um papel importante no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial e já chegou a ser chamada de "Google da Rússia". A fabricante uraniana de armas Firepoint informou que na ofensiva dessa sexta-feira (9) foram utilizados drones de ataque unidirecionais FP-1 produzidos pela empresa. De acordo com a companhia, a estrutura atingida é o maior centro de dados da Yandex e teve vários de seus módulos colocados completamente fora de operação. Acompanhe o SBT News nas TVs por assinatura Claro (586), Vivo (576), Sky (580) e Oi (175), via streaming pelo +SBT,Site e YouTube, além dos canais nas Smart TVs Samsung, LG e Roku. Já o ataque de quinta-feira (8) desativou o centro de dados da Yandex em Sasovo, onde estão instalados dois dos três supercomputadores usados para desenvolver seu modelo de IA. A empresa informou que está avaliando os danos e não foi capaz de confirmar se o equipamento poderá ser restaurado, mas disse que apesar do cerne de suas operações ter sido prejudicado, está tentando manter seus serviços em funcionamento. “Os centros de dados são o coração de ferro da Yandex. Sua operação é fundamental para os serviços que se tornaram parte do dia a dia das pessoas. Milhões de usuários verificam o trânsito e planejam rotas, ouvem música, assistem a filmes, fazem pedidos de mantimentos e obtêm respostas para suas perguntas”, diz um comunicado divulgado pela empresa. “Nossa tecnologia ajuda centenas de milhares de empresas a administrar seus negócios. Elas a utilizam para receber pedidos, atender clientes e trabalhar com parceiros”, afirmou a empresa, que também alegou que havia fechado um acordo com outros provedores de nuvem para permitir que os clientes do Yandex Cloud transferissem rapidamente seus dados e serviços. A ofensiva contra a Yandex é uma resposta de Kiev aos ataques de Moscou contra centros de dados ucranianos. Os dois países também miram outros alvos de infraestrutura, como instalações de energia, refinarias, portos, navios que transportam petróleo e grãos, além de depósitos que fazem parte da logística de sites de comércio eletrônico. Apelo ucraniano aos EUA Os ataques russos não apenas danificam a infraestrutura ucraniana, mas também matam civis. De acordo com o presidente da Ucrânia, Volodymyr Zelensky, ofensivas feitas por Moscou entre quarta e quinta-feira, deixaram 78 pessoas mortas e 215 feridas. A situação levou o líder ucraniano a acusar os Estados Unidos de não estarem dispostos a ajudar Kiev. Ele também fez um apelo para que Washington amplie o acesso da Ucrânia ao serviço de internet via satélite da SpaceX, a Starlink. "Abram o Starlink para a Ucrânia. Vocês o abriram quando responderam ao Irã... Eu disse abertamente: deem-nos o Starlink, ajudem-nos a defender nosso espaço aéreo e a dominá-lo. E então Putin se sentará à mesa de negociações", disse. Além disso, o ucraniano criticou declarações recentes do secretário de Estado americano, Marco Rubio, dadas durante sua visita a Portugal. Ele afirmou que a atualmente a guerra se encontra em um impasse. "Não se pode, por um lado, negociar com os russos sobre projetos econômicos futuros e, por outro, dizer que nos encontramos em uma espécie de impasse diplomático", argumentou Zelensky. Altos funcionários russos e americanos, incluindo o enviado especial dos Estados Unidos, Jared Kushner, tiveram conversas sobre a possibilidade de trazer um investidor americano para os gasodutos Nord Stream, que forneciam gás russo para a Alemanha antes do conflito entre Moscou e Kiev ter início. Zelensky disse que negociadores ucranianos estarão nos Estados Unidos nessa sexta e no sábado para conversar com autoridades americanas, na tentativa de convencer o presidente americano, Donald Trump, a aumentar a pressão sobre Moscou. Ele também afirmou que esperava que os parceiros europeus de Kiev se juntassem às negociações com Washington. artigo.texto: Four-Hour Battery Storage Now Cheaper Than Gas Turbines: Report Lower battery costs, gas turbine shortages, and fuel volatility aid storage October 12, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights Four-hour battery energy storage systems, utility-scale energy storage systems that are designed to discharge at their full rated capacity for approximately four hours, now cost less than open-cycle gas turbines across 43 markets, according to Wood Mackenzie’s latest global report on levelized cost of electricity (LCOE). This shift is driven by technological advancements and evolving market dynamics. Single-axis tracking solar is the lowest-cost new power generation option in 43 of the 48 markets analyzed. Wood Mackenzie attributed the shift to declining battery costs, gas turbine shortages, and volatile fuel prices. North America U.S. solar costs face pressure from tariffs, antidumping and countervailing duties, and Section 232 import restrictions. Utility-scale solar is partly insulated by 168 GW of safe-harbored capacity, although module prices are projected to rise 5% annually through 2030. Residential and commercial solar projects face greater cost pressures, with module prices expected to increase 6% in 2027 and 14% in 2028. Onshore wind’s LCOE is projected to decline 16% by 2060, driven by lower capital and operating costs, despite policy uncertainty and potential tariff impacts. Tax credits are expected to support battery storage economics despite foreign entity of concern restrictions and supply chain constraints. Storage costs could rise after investment tax credits phase out in 2038. Technological advances and domestic manufacturing expansion are projected to reduce storage LCOE by 10% by 2060. Growing data center demand is likely to constrain gas generation equipment supply through the late 2030s, keeping capital costs elevated. Latin America Single-axis tracking solar so far remains Latin America’s lowest-cost power generation technology in 2026. Its average costs are projected to decline 38% by 2060. Brazil, Chile, and Mexico benefit from strong solar resources and high capacity factors. Onshore wind’s average LCOE is projected to fall nearly 21%, from $73/MWh to $58/MWh by 2030, supported by the expansion of Chinese manufacturers and larger turbines. Grid-scale battery storage is expanding through renewable energy-linked mandates and standalone procurement. Its LCOE is projected to decline 42% by 2060. Offshore wind costs are expected to approach parity with combined-cycle gas turbines, before firming, in the early 2040s. Asia Pacific Utility-scale solar remains the most cost-competitive power source in Asia Pacific, although costs differ substantially across markets. In 2026, solar generation costs in the region’s most expensive market are over 200% higher than in the cheapest. The gap is expected to widen to 250% by 2030, despite declining costs across all markets. Onshore wind costs vary more than sixfold across the region. Greater penetration of Chinese turbine manufacturers and the adoption of higher-capacity turbines are expected to narrow the cost gap with coal in South and Southeast Asia. China has the world’s lowest grid-scale storage costs, more than 55% lower than the rest of Asia Pacific’s average of $134/MWh. Chinese equipment supply is expected to reduce the regional average to $92/MWh by 2036. Japan, Australia, and the Philippines face higher costs due to import duties, installation expenses, and domestic manufacturing policies. Offshore wind costs outside China are expected to decline significantly from the early 2030s. Europe Solar remains Europe’s cheapest power generation technology. The LCOE for fixed-tilt systems is projected to decline 22% by 2060, despite a 14% increase in capital expenditure (CAPEX) in 2026 due to higher module prices. Onshore wind CAPEX is expected to decline 2.5% annually through 2030 as manufacturers benefit from improved financial stability and growing demand. Higher capacity factors are expected to bring its LCOE to $60/MWh by 2060. Battery storage turnkey CAPEX rose 2%, the first increase in three years, as cell prices rebounded 10% from 2025 lows amid stronger demand and higher lithium prices. CAPEX is projected to decline 12% by 2031, although rising lithium prices could slow subsequent reductions. Europe has the highest fossil fuel generation costs among the regions analyzed, with carbon costs expected to exceed fuel costs by 2030. Offshore wind costs are projected to decline from the 2030s as supply chains stabilize and turbine prices fall. Middle East and Africa The Middle East and Africa have the lowest regional LCOE for single-axis tracking solar, at $37/MWh in 2026. Costs are projected to decline to $24/MWh by 2035, while solar LCOE in Saudi Arabia and the UAE could fall below $20/MWh by 2033. Onshore wind costs are declining as Chinese turbines become more competitive. Egypt and Morocco have low wind generation costs, supported by capacity factors of 40% to 45%. Four-hour battery storage costs in the region are estimated at $120/MWh in 2026 and are projected to decline 33% to $80/MWh by 2035. Battery storage is more cost-competitive than open-cycle gas turbines across the region’s gas markets, supporting the integration of solar and wind and reducing reliance on gas-fired peaking capacity. According to Wood Mackenzie, renewable energy LCOE across major markets, including single-axis tracking solar in the Middle East and Africa, recorded the lowest regional LCOE of $37/MWh as of November 2025, driven by technological advances, supply chain stabilization, and improved module efficiencies. Battery storage project costs hit an all-time low in 2025, even as other renewables rose, according to BloombergNEF’s LCOE 2026 report.

artigo.texto: NEW PALTZ – Nearly 150 labor, civic and economic development leaders from a cross section of industries convened at the SUNY New Paltz campus on Thursday to learn more about battery energy storage systems (BESS). The first ever Hudson Valley Energy Storage Summit took place just as a proposed battery storage facility slated for a site just over a mile away remains hanging in the balance. Doreen Harris, President and CEO of the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA), says the demand for electricity in New York is the reason we need increased battery energy storage. “As the state’s energy authority, I’m here to say that systems are valuable irrespective of the composition of our electric grid,” said Harris. “They’re valuable from the perspective of reliability. They’re valuable from the perspective of reducing cost to consumers and critical as part of an energy system that we’re increasingly relying on for our economic growth as a state.” In 2024, the New York Public Service Commission raised the state’s energy storage target to 6,000 megawatts by 2030. Harris says that, to date, New York has installed more than 500 megawatts of storage capacity with an additional 2 gigawatts under development. The summit reinforced the notion that energy storage strengthens grid reliability, stabilizes costs, supports good-paying union jobs, and advances regional economic and climate goals. “When a company is deciding whether to expand here or somewhere else, one of the first questions they ask is about power. Can they count on it, and what is it going to cost,” said Mike Oates, President and CEO of the Hudson Valley Economic Development Corporation. “Battery storage helps make the grid our employers already rely on more dependable, and that kind of certainty is what keeps investment flowing into the region. From where I sit, this is critical infrastructure the Hudson Valley should be saying yes to.” Opponents to battery storage facilities raise concerns about fire safety, toxic emissions, the environmental impact and land use. Last month, the Ulster County Legislature put the brakes on a resolution to have the county act as the lead agency for the construction of a proposed battery energy storage system on Paradies Lane New Paltz. Harris admits that energy storage carries risks like many other energy facilities but says those risks must be managed. “Governor Hochul has set a very high bar for storage siting. We have some of the most robust energy safety codes in the nation. Others are following us,” said Harris. “We have a high standard for technology, for siting, for safety and, ultimately, anyone across the state should know that New York is leading the way on battery energy storge safety, and that we have brought the industry to a point where they can feel confident that the technologies we’re installing are to the highest standards.” In 2023, after fire incidents at energy storage facilities in Jefferson, Orange and Suffolk counties, the Governor created a nation-leading inter-agency fire safety working group. John D’Alessandro is Secretary of the Firefighters Association of New York State and attended the summit to learn more about battery energy storage facilities. “I understand some of the concerns that communities have with storage systems. Unfortunately, a lot of those concerns are generated by misinformation or the lack of information,” said D’Alessandro. “There certainly have been issues with some of these facilities, but they are few and far between. That’s why we, as first responders, have to be ready when the few and far between happens. It’s really not different from a chemical plant or a manufacturing facility, many of which are all around the state, including the Hudson Valley. There just has to be a constant dialogue between the developer and the community where the project will happen.” “There are clearly still remaining questions and concerns that we should be thinking about in order to move us forward, while having safeguards,” said New York State Assemblywoman Didi Barrett. (D, Hudson) “We also need the confidence from our communities to protect people’s lives, their lifestyle, their property value, all these things that communities care about. The Hudson Valley with its wide-open spaces is bucolic, and it’s easy to target our area. We have to protect it.” The state’s energy storage goals are projected to reduce New York’s electric system costs by nearly $2 billion by 2050.

artigo.texto: A PNAST fechou a primeira Temporada de Acesso em 7 de outubro com 367 pedidos e mais de 20 GW na fila. A conta de quem paga, o que muda para quem quer conectar uma usina e as datas do próximo ciclo. A PNAST deu o primeiro resultado prático nesta semana. O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) fez na terça-feira (6) o primeiro processo competitivo da política. Entregou 228 MW da rede básica de transmissão a três data centers em São Paulo, segundo o balanço divulgado pelo ONS e pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia. Sete projetos disputaram, somando 451 MW de demanda habilitada. Quase metade do que foi pedido ficou sem conexão na rede básica: 223 MW. O Decreto nº 12.772, de 5 de dezembro de 2025, é o texto que criou a PNAST e define as regras. O que é a PNAST, em português claro? Até o decreto, quem queria ligar uma usina ou uma fábrica grande à rede entrava numa fila por ordem de chegada. Agora o acesso permanente acontece em Temporadas de Acesso, janelas em que todos os interessados registram o pedido e o ONS analisa tudo junto. - Energia renovável perde ritmo no Brasil com cortes de geração e incerteza para investidores - Áustria teve 43.300 tickets em 10 minutos para disputar R$ 215 milhões de subsídio solar que paga R$ 838 por kWp, enquanto no Brasil painel novo já paga 60% do Fio B - Usina solar de Indiana instalou 20 mil painéis por dia com 1.800 operários em 18 meses e está prestes a operar - Agricultor de Illinois tem 10 torres eólicas na fazenda e recebe cerca de R$ 600 mil por ano, mas no Nordeste os relatos vão de R$ 600 a R$ 2 mil por mês por torre Onde o pedido total passa do que a rede básica aguenta, a vaga vai a leilão. O decreto manda fazer “processos competitivos dos pontos de conexão onde a demanda registrada superar a capacidade disponível”. A política vale para geradores e consumidores que queiram usar a rede básica, conforme a página da PNAST no ONS. Ficam de fora as distribuidoras de energia. Quanto custou a vaga e quem ganha com isso? Os lances médios ficaram na ordem de R$ 800 por kW. A informação é da associação das transmissoras, a Abrate, em nota divulgada ao Canal Solar. A conta, feita aqui: 228 MW são 228 mil kW. Multiplicados por R$ 800, dão cerca de R$ 182 milhões. É uma estimativa, porque o valor é uma média aproximada e o ONS não informou, nas fontes que li, o total arrecadado. O caminho do dinheiro está no decreto. As receitas dos processos competitivos “serão revertidas para a modicidade tarifária”, ou seja, para segurar a tarifa de energia. A regra detalhada fica com a Aneel, a agência reguladora. Quanto isso pesa na conta de luz de casa, nenhuma fonte calculou. Quem levou a capacidade? Duas das vencedoras, a Pahlavan One e a Pahlavan Three, são ligadas à norte-americana CloudHQ, que desenvolve um campus em Paulínia (SP), de acordo com a Eixos. A terceira é a Digital DC Brasil, que opera com a marca NextStream. A disputa foi só em São Paulo, em quatro pontos de conexão da rede básica. Nenhuma das usinas solares e eólicas do país aparece entre os vencedores desse primeiro leilão, pelas fontes que li. Os data centers levaram tudo. Onde entram as usinas solares e eólicas? As usinas solares e eólicas estão na mesma fila de pedidos da Temporada de Acesso. A temporada registrou 367 empreendimentos de geração e consumo, somando mais de 20 GW em solicitações, espalhados por 64 barramentos do Sistema Interligado Nacional. Somando a fase de transição, o ONS analisou mais de 43 GW. Desses, cerca de 30,7 GW foram viabilizados ou habilitados. As fontes não separam quanto desse total é solar, eólica ou carga, e essa divisão ficou sem resposta. A Abrate liga a política à expansão das usinas solares e eólicas e da geração distribuída. Liga também à chegada de grandes cargas, como data centers e hidrogênio verde. É a mesma rede para todos, e a Temporada de Acesso é o novo caminho para as usinas solares e eólicas e para os data centers. O que muda para quem quer conectar uma usina? Pelo decreto, três mudanças pesam para o dono de uma usina, solar ou eólica: - O pedido deixa de valer por data de chegada. O interessado precisa entrar na janela da Temporada de Acesso, com dados do projeto. - Onde há mais pedido que vaga, o ponto de conexão vira disputa, com lance. - O ONS passa a abrir duas temporadas por ano a partir de 2027, segundo o decreto, e avisa o cronograma com 90 dias de antecedência. Resta uma dúvida que o decreto não resolve sozinho: o preço da vaga. A nota técnica de metodologia só sai em 4 de dezembro, segundo o calendário publicado pelo ONS. A regra do lance depende dela. Quando abre a próxima Temporada de Acesso? O ONS publicou em 7 de outubro o calendário da primeira Temporada de Acesso de 2027, de acordo com o Times Brasil. O próprio ONS avisa que as datas ainda podem mudar. A novidade para quem já ganhou leilão de energia é a rota própria. Esses projetos são habilitados um mês antes da conta da vaga na rede básica. Nada garante, porém, que a capacidade seja suficiente em cada ponto. O que o gerador deve fazer agora? O cadastro abre em janeiro, mas o trabalho vem antes. Para a Temporada de Acesso de 2027, estudos, dados técnicos e a estratégia de uso da rede precisam estar prontos antes de 4 de janeiro, observa o Times Brasil. O diretor-geral do ONS, Marcio Rea, afirmou na cerimônia de encerramento que o primeiro ciclo mostrou a efetividade do novo modelo. A avaliação é do próprio operador. Quem pode medir é o investidor, quando a regra do lance sair.

artigo.texto: AI introduces unprecedented challenges in data centers; not just in power, but in cooling, latency, deployment speed and geography. These challenges carry through all data center areas, or “subsystems,” to varying degrees. These different subsystems often require tailored solutions in an AI data center, removing them from any semblance of a typical “uniform” design. Setting a foundation for a successful AI implementation requires a cable infrastructure partner with the capacity, agility and resources to deliver high-performance cabling systems designed for real-world data center environments. It also requires an understanding of how AI implementation interacts with each subsystem in the data center, and what the people responsible for maintaining those subsystems can expect. There are four key subsystems: the Entry Point, Front End, DC Interconnect and Back End Subsystems. Entry point The Entry-Point subsystem is traditionally part of the data center gray space, supporting infrastructure by connecting the cable coming from outside the data hall to the cable within it. Moreover, the entry point is where those fibers are separated and directed to different areas of the facility. Increasing density demands from AI applications are driving increases of high fiber count cables coming into the Entry Point, and increasing power and cooling demands have further limited available gray space in the data center. This can cause complications for space utilization, cable management and labor, resulting in speed of deployment being the most critical issue related to the entry point. So how can data center operators mitigate this issue? Rapid and versatile installation is key; innovative splicing enclosures, splicing and interconnect trays and consideration of pre-terminated solutions can be vital. These solutions unlock a modular approach to infrastructure, allowing for rapid and easy upgrades as needs evolve and require much less time to install overall. Front end The Front-End subsystem is typically in the white space, where the computing occurs inside the data center, and is the layer that handles traffic between users, internal resources and external networks. Of the four subsystems, the Front End is least impacted by the addition of AI, buoyed above the waves that hit other subsystems by its established infrastructure. The Front-End Subsystem’s foundation has only received minor updates over the last five years. However, local code compliance is almost always a concern when expansions occur on the frontend, especially when those expansions are in other geographic locations. Global solutions can alleviate this concern, allowing you to utilize the same infrastructure across locations where local codes differ slightly. Data center interconnect The DC Interconnect subsystem is part of the data center’s gray space, or areas that provide critical support for computing, and often consists of multiple high strand count fiber cables running between facilities that connect pods across the network. Somewhat ironically, AI struggles with the capability that the DC Interconnect subsystem was designed to deliver: connection over distance. An AI cluster on the back end is treated as a single system, housed in one location that then must spread itself over the rest of the facility. As the size of AI clusters increases, expansion of the data center interconnect system also grows exponentially to ensure that communication between facilities at maximum throughput. However, the data center interconnect system is notoriously difficult to expand, demanding time and labor to add or replace cabling. Leaders can mitigate this issue by deploying infrastructure that can handle the higher densities AI requires, while also being built for rapid deployment. Leviton’s 1728-strand MMC trunks, which are part of the STRATA™ family of Hyperscale and AI data center solutions, allow for a much higher density footprint than traditional alternatives. Moreover, Leviton’s trunks are designed to be installed quickly and easily – a huge boon when recabling a traditionally labor-intensive subsystem. Back end Finally, there’s the Back End; the subsystem that houses the AI cluster, and where AI implementation really changes the subsystem’s status quo. As the density of the system increases to accommodate the AI cluster, cable management and power become critical. The substantial power demands of AI technologies require data center operators to find ways to do more with their established power infrastructure. The challenge of managing the increased density is one that data center operators are familiar with; doing more with less. This is where Very-Small-Form-Factor (VSFF) connectors, like MMC, come in. VSFF connectors meet the need for higher density at connect points, while taking up less space than their MPO alternatives. This enables operators to scale fiber capacity without proportionally increasing rack space, as demonstrated by solutions such as Leviton's STRATA™ family, which supports up to 3,456 fibers per rack unit using a 16-fiber MMC connector. As for maximizing the potential of established power infrastructure, utilizing power more efficiently in the data center often boils down to cooling. Immersion cooling is an emergent technology wherein servers are submersed in non-electrically conductive, thermally conductive fluids, offering almost-instantaneous heat dispersion for high-density networks. The success of immersion cooling depends not only on thermal performance but also on ensuring network infrastructure can operate reliably in submerged environments. Solutions such as Leviton TORRENT™ are designed to address this challenge by maintaining signal integrity and resisting degradation in dielectric cooling fluids. artigo.texto: Fox stays positive on data centers even as public backlash grows The News Despite increasingly critical media coverage of AI and the spread of data centers across the US, one news network has been painting a more positive picture. More than half of the references to data centers on Fox News over the last two years would have left viewers with a favorable impression, compared to less than 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW, according to a new Semafor analysis of mentions of data centers on each network. The mentions were pulled from closed captions preserved by the Internet Archive, which keeps a digital, searchable library of recorded TV news. A pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI scored each reference on its content, with the network's name removed. Mentions of data centers have, predictably, shot up across all three networks in recent months as political backlash against AI swells and the data centers themselves have become a salient issue ahead of the midterms. But Fox's opinion and morning shows, including, , and leaned on the promise of AI, economic investment and the race with China, skewing Fox's coverage more favorably, the analysis showed. The network's news shows were more measured. In an Aug. 23 monologue that at one point featured a chyron reading "The case for data centers," Fox host Brian Kilmeade acknowledged "real concerns," but argued that "saying no to data centers nationwide also means saying no to the tax dollars that can flow into a community. … If Americans don't build the infrastructure to meet the demand, somebody else will." On CNN and MS NOW, the criticism focused as much on the facilities' political toxicity as on harms like power bills or water use, casting them as unpopular with voters and a liability for politicians who back them heading into the midterms. Data centers "are driving up energy costs, sucking up water supplies, wiping out rather than creating jobs," MS NOW's Katy Tur said in May. "Politicians beware." Polling shows that across demographic groups, Americans hold increasingly negative views of data centers: More than half of Americans say data centers are mostly bad for the environment, Pew Research Center found last month, compared with 39% in January. Fox News did not comment for this story. Max's view The pro-data center programming on Fox News comes as the right tries to define its positions in an AI-fueled, post-Donald Trump future. Fox's favorable data center coverage mirrors Trump's position on their growth and the need for AI companies to help fuel the US economy. "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," Trump wrote on Truth Social in August. "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame." But anger about data centers and the rapid advancement of AI represents a faultline within the MAGA coalition that swept Trump back into office. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., have questioned some data centers in their states, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott seems to have flipped from supporting data centers to looking to slow their growth in his state amid a tougher-than-expected reelection campaign. Some on the right I have talked to in the last several months worry that Fox News, which Trump watches religiously, and other pro-data center voices are encouraging the president to take positions that are broadly unpopular with his rural and suburban base. "The Big Tech oligarchs, the guys driving AI, did a terrible job," Steve Bannon, a staunchly anti-AI Trump ally, told the Daily Signal in September. "They came in to try to muscle local communities, and particularly since President Trump's strongest base is in exurban and rural communities, that's where they were really the ugliest, and they haven't made their case, and they particularly haven't made their case at the local level about the economics of this, and the energy of this, and the water of this, and the manifestation of what these things are going to be used for." Room for Disagreement Not all of Fox's data center coverage has been rosy; its tenor grew slightly less favorable in 2026 compared to last year. "It's taxing our system way too much on water, agriculture land, or electricity. We're gonna implode," the Texas agriculture commissioner said in an interview on a weekend Fox show in August. "We just can't do it. There's not enough.

artigo.texto: Dez anos após criação do CORSIA, setor aéreo cobra governos por regras globais mais fortes para reduzir emissões IATA defende fortalecimento do mecanismo internacional de compensação de carbono e critica possível expansão do sistema europeu de comércio de emissões Dez anos depois da criação do primeiro mecanismo climático global voltado especificamente à aviação internacional, a indústria aérea quer que os governos reforcem o arcabouço internacional para reduzir as emissões do setor. O apelo foi feito nesta terça-feira (6), em Genebra, pela Associação Internacional do Transporte Aéreo (IATA), que marcou o aniversário do CORSIA, sigla em inglês para Esquema de Compensação e Redução de Carbono para a Aviação Internacional. Aprovado em 2016 pela Assembleia da Organização da Aviação Civil Internacional (OACI), o CORSIA foi concebido como um mecanismo de mercado para enfrentar o crescimento das emissões da aviação internacional. Segundo a IATA, mais de 130 países já participam do programa e a expectativa é que, até o fim de 2026, ele tenha contribuído para a redução de aproximadamente 200 milhões de toneladas de CO₂. A partir de 2027, a estimativa da associação é que o mecanismo alcance cerca de 85% das emissões globais da aviação internacional. Ao longo de sua implementação, o programa poderá ainda mobilizar até US$ 120 bilhões em financiamento climático, destinados a projetos de redução de emissões e remoção de carbono. Para a IATA, os números reforçam a necessidade de preservar o CORSIA como principal mecanismo internacional para a descarbonização da aviação. “Como o primeiro acordo climático global para todo o setor de aviação, o CORSIA demonstra o melhor da colaboração internacional: uma solução global para um desafio global”, afirmou Marie Owens Thomsen, vice-presidente sênior de sustentabilidade e economista-chefe da IATA. A IATA representa mais de 370 companhias aéreas, responsáveis por aproximadamente 85% do tráfego aéreo global. Disputa com a política climática europeia O aniversário do CORSIA ocorre em meio a uma discussão particularmente sensível para as companhias aéreas: a revisão do Sistema de Comércio de Licenças de Emissão da União Europeia (EU ETS). A União Europeia avalia ampliar o alcance do mecanismo para voos com destinos de até 5.000 quilômetros do bloco, tomando Frankfurt como referência geográfica. Também está em discussão a criação de um mecanismo que permitiria estabelecer sistemas considerados comparáveis de precificação de carbono com países terceiros. Em nota, a IATA afirmou ser contrária à expansão extraterritorial do EU ETS e afirma que a medida poderia criar uma sobreposição entre regras regionais e o mecanismo internacional estabelecido pela OACI. Para Thomas Reynaert, vice-presidente sênior de assuntos externos da IATA, a revisão europeia deveria fortalecer o CORSIA, e não estimular a criação de sistemas paralelos. Segundo a associação, a ampliação proposta poderia elevar em 40% os custos de conformidade relacionados ao EU ETS, chegando a € 280 bilhões entre 2027 e 2040. A entidade também afirma que ainda não há uma avaliação de impacto que permita dimensionar adequadamente os efeitos da expansão sobre países terceiros, conectividade aérea e competitividade do setor. Combustível sustentável no centro da transição A crítica da indústria aérea não significa, segundo a IATA, oposição à precificação de carbono. A associação defende que os recursos arrecadados com mecanismos climáticos sejam direcionados principalmente para tecnologias capazes de reduzir as emissões da aviação. Entre as prioridades está o Combustível Sustentável de Aviação (SAF), considerado uma das principais alternativas disponíveis hoje para reduzir a pegada de carbono dos voos sem depender de uma renovação imediata de toda a frota. A IATA quer que a União Europeia amplie o apoio à produção de SAF já nos próximos anos, sem esperar 2029, e elimine restrições geográficas e outras condições que, na avaliação da entidade, poderiam limitar a oferta do combustível sustentável. A associação também defende que as receitas provenientes do EU ETS geradas pela aviação sejam destinadas exclusivamente ao desenvolvimento de SAF, infraestrutura aeroportuária e novas tecnologias. O pedido ocorre em um contexto em que a descarbonização da aviação enfrenta um dos seus principais obstáculos, que é a disponibilidade e o custo de combustíveis de menor emissão. Aviões elétricos e movidos a hidrogênio ainda não estão disponíveis em escala comercial para substituir aeronaves de grande porte em rotas de longa distância, tornando o SAF uma peça central da estratégia de transição do setor. Ao completar uma década, o CORSIA também expõe a dificuldade de conciliar uma atividade essencialmente internacional com regulações ambientais que podem ser adotadas de forma regional. Para a IATA, a existência de diferentes sistemas de precificação de carbono pode elevar custos, gerar conflitos regulatórios e dificultar a criação de condições equivalentes de competição entre companhias aéreas. A entidade defende, portanto, a implementação uniforme do CORSIA e a rejeição de mecanismos que possam funcionar como alternativas regionais ao sistema da OACI. O debate europeu, porém, representa uma questão mais ampla para a política climática: até que ponto mecanismos regionais podem acelerar a redução das emissões sem fragmentar as regras internacionais? Para o setor aéreo, a resposta passa por combinar um mercado global de carbono com investimentos maciços em combustíveis sustentáveis, infraestrutura e novas tecnologias. “Em um mundo cada vez mais marcado pela fragmentação, isso é um lembrete poderoso do que pode ser alcançado quando os Estados trabalham juntos”, afirmou Marie Owens Thomsen.

artigo.texto: AI data centers got the "Weekend Update" treatment on "Saturday Night Live" this week. Comedian James Austin Johnson portrayed "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary on the sketch comedy show, during which he addressed the dispute over the real O'Leary's proposed data center in Utah, known as the Stratos Project. "It's very simple. All I want is to buy up 40,000 acres of God's untouched splendor and replace it with a very loud computer that steals your job," Johnson's O'Leary said. "Is it going to take up precious water? Absolutely. Is it going to provide a necessary service? Who's to say? But on the flip side, it's going to make me a tremendous amount of money, and I think that's great." The "SNL" version of O'Leary said he understood that some Americans were concerned about data centers near their homes. (An actual May Gallup poll found that over half of American surveyors opposed constructing AI data centers in their local area.) "These things are terrible and shouldn't be anywhere. That's why I'm building one in Utah," he said. Data centers are a contentious issue in the United States. Leading tech companies rely on AI data centers to power their systems and products. Supporters say they'll create new jobs, bolster the economy, and help the US defeat China in the race to control the global AI market. Residents in the places where they are being built, however, are often much less excited about them. The Utah project, backed by O'Leary Digital, has drawn criticism from many local residents over concerns that the data center could strain local resources and worsen the environment. Some residents are also upset over what they consider a lack of transparency from O'Leary and local leaders. Critics of the Stratos Project have staged protests, created petitions, and taken legal action to stop its construction. O'Leary scaled back the data center's size from about 40,000 to just over 20,000 acres after public pushback. He has said he remains undeterred, though. "There are bumps in the road. There's litigation. There's misinformation. There's propaganda. You name it. But if you know what you're doing is right, you make it, you get there," O'Leary told Business Insider in June. "Persevere." During a May interview on Fox News, O'Leary said said some critics of the project have ties to the Chinese Communist Party, a claim he later walked back. A Utah advocacy group that has publicly opposed the project filed a defamation lawsuit against Fox News and O'Leary in July. On "Saturday Night Live," Johnson's O'Leary acknowledged the incident. "I made the mildly inflammatory claim that every single person in Utah who opposes me is a paid communist super agent from China. Was I wrong? Perhaps. But just because they're not, doesn't mean they aren't," he said. He added, "I'm going to make the future go away. And we're doing just that in Utah."

artigo.texto: Battery Storage Beats Gas Peakers. Is Canada Backing the Wrong Horse? October 10, 2026 | Markham on Energy According to a new report from consulting giant Wood Mackenzie, battery storage is now cheaper than gas peaker plants in almost every market. Analysts are hailing the milestone as a seminal moment for the electrification of the global economy – or, as we like to call it, the energy transition. Granted, this is an important moment. But it’s also just one data point in a process of technological change that will end many decades in the future. And, in that change, there is a critical lesson for Canada at this point in our country’s economic evolution. I’ve been writing about technological change for four decades. My model is based on the transition from horses and steam to tractors and modern industrial farming from 1900 to 1950. In that process are all the components of most technology adoptions. The slow initial development of the technology (1900 to 1920, when the first modern “small tractors” appeared in the market). The adoption inflection point (1920, with the introduction of the Fordson, cheap and built on automotive manufacturing). The mid- to late-1920s, when ancillary machines (the combined harvester-thresher, the three-point hitch, rubber tires) became available. Then, from 1930 to 1950, the now-superior economics of mechanical agriculture displaced horses from every field in North America. The story over the past 75 years has been about ever-improving technology and changing farm economics. But the war between the technologies – animals and steam versus the internal combustion engine – was fought in the first half of the 20th century. Pegging the date for the start of the modern technology competition – combustion vs electrotech, molecules vs electrons – is inexact, but let’s choose 2010. Comparatively speaking, then, we’re 16 years into a 50-year transition. In 2060, we’ll look back on that process and the triumph of electric over combustion will appear inevitable. Just as the triumph of the tractor seems inevitable from today’s vantage. That’s why the Wood Mackenzie analysis is interesting, but not cause for popping the champagne. The triumph of battery storage is one data point among many in a long, complex process. A decade from now we might have enough data to declare electrons the victory, just not quite yet. But one thing we can say for certain: if present trends hold, electrons will win. And that any country that wants to have an advanced, prosperous economy in 2060 has to bet on the tractor, not the horse. This is the lesson for Canada. Four-Hour Batteries Are Beating Gas Peakers on Cost Gas peaker plants fire up when electricity demand surges, supplying power for those relatively short periods when the grid needs extra help. Batteries that can deliver electricity for four hours increasingly compete for that job. Wood Mackenzie now finds their lifetime cost per unit of electricity is lower than that of open-cycle gas turbines in all 43 markets where it compared the technologies. The competitive gap is widening: turbine shortages and volatile fuel prices push up gas costs, while expanding battery manufacturing pushes storage costs down. The significance extends beyond batteries taking business from gas plants. Storage makes solar and wind more useful by saving electricity for when customers need it. Cheaper batteries therefore expand the market for other electric technologies, just as better implements expanded what farmers could accomplish with a tractor. This is the technological convergence at the heart of our theory of change: advances in one technology create opportunities for others, strengthening the economics of the emerging system. The Same Competition, Different Regional Advantages China shows what manufacturing scale can accomplish: its grid-scale storage costs are more than 55 per cent below the average for the rest of Asia Pacific, according to Wood Mackenzie. In the Middle East and Africa, abundant sunshine makes the combination of solar and batteries especially attractive. Four-hour storage already undercuts gas peaking across the region’s modelled gas markets, and WoodMac forecasts its cost will fall another 33 per cent by 2035. Different regional advantages are pushing the competition in the same direction. Across the rest of Asia Pacific, China’s manufacturing strength is helping drive storage costs lower. Wood Mackenzie expects competitive Chinese supply to help bring the regional average, excluding China, down from US$134 per megawatt-hour to US$92 by 2036. Japan, Australia, and the Philippines are expected to remain more expensive because of import duties, installation costs, and domestic manufacturing policies. The broader significance is that China’s investment in scaling electric technologies is changing the economics of energy well beyond its borders. North America illustrates how messy that competition can become. Tax credits help battery storage compete, while trade restrictions and supply-chain constraints push in the opposite direction. Meanwhile, data-centre demand is straining gas-generation supply chains, keeping capital costs elevated and strengthening the investment case for renewables and storage, according to WoodMac. The technologies compete within markets shaped by government decisions, industrial capacity, and changing demand. The direction of technological change can be clear even while the path remains uneven. Another lesson for Canada: whether 4-hour batteries are more competitive than gas peakers in Canada is the wrong question. The right one is the effect on electrification promoted by falling battery storage costs in the Global South where Canada hopes to sell Alberta oil and British Columbia LNG. More EVs mean falling demand for gasoline and diesel. More heat pumps and grid-storage batteries mean less demand for gas. artigo.texto: Seres Group has signed a long-term strategic agreement with Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) in Chongqing, securing CATL battery supply for every AITO model in its line-up. Concluded on 10 October 2026, the pact also enlarges their shared battery production and adds joint work on supercharging, battery services and overseas markets. AITO, the premium brand Seres develops with Huawei, has used CATL packs in every model since launch, with deliveries now past 1.2 million vehicles. Extending that arrangement across the full range gives Seres supply certainty and hands CATL a customer with proven volume. Production is the most concrete strand. The partners will fast-track phase two of their plant-in-plant facility inside the Seres Super Factory, adding 10 to 12 GW/h a year for a combined total above 20 GW/h. Building batteries inside the vehicle plant is meant to sharpen cost competitiveness, and the expansion also supports Chongqing’s drive to build a cluster of intelligent connected electric vehicle makers. Beyond the factory, the companies plan supercharging networks and battery services that follow a car through its whole life. They will also seek buyers together in the Middle East, Central Asia and Europe, a spread that gives AITO growth options outside the EU, where China-built electric cars face extra import duties. artigo.texto: COLOMBO, Sri Lanka, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sungrow, a globally leading supplier of PV inverters and energy storage systems, announced the successful commissioning and commercial operation launch of WKV Hydro Technics (Pvt) Ltd's 10 MW/40 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Galle, Sri Lanka on September 10, 2026. WKV Group, a subsidiary of Khen Energy Limited, deployed Sungrow's PowerTitan 2.0 solution, enhancing grid flexibility and delivering fast‑response energy storage capacity to support renewable energy integration. Sri Lanka is expanding renewable generation, with the country's long-term power plan targeting 70% of electricity generation from renewable energy sources by 2030, led by solar and wind. As the share of variable renewable generation grows, the power system requires more flexible resources that can respond quickly to fluctuations in supply and changing demand patterns. Electricity demand typically reaches its daily peak at around 7 p.m, placing additional pressure on the grid during the evening. Against this backdrop, Sri Lanka's power-sector planning has identified utility-scale battery energy storage as an important grid-support technology for maintaining system reliability and enabling greater renewable energy integration. PowerTitan 2.0 Designed for Local Project Requirements - End-to-end intelligent management: The system integrates station-level control with intelligent battery management, continuously tracking battery status and optimizing operation to support system stability and long-term performance. - Full-stack pre-commissioning capability: PowerTitan 2.0 integrates the battery system and PCS into an all-in-one AC-DC block, with key components pre-assembled before delivery. This simplifies on-site installation and commissioning, contributing to a 50% reduction in grid-connection time. - Built for a challenging coastal environment: Located approximately 500 meters from the sea, the project operates in a hot, humid and corrosive environment. PowerTitan 2.0 is designed to withstand challenging environmental conditions, supporting reliable long-term operation. The system is designed for an operational life of at least 15 years. The project strengthens the grid's peak-shaving and frequency-regulation capabilities, providing fast and flexible support as electricity demand and renewable generation fluctuate. By storing electricity when supply is available and dispatching it when needed, the BESS can help improve system efficiency, enhance supply reliability and create greater flexibility to integrate renewable energy.
