artigo.texto: Wood Mackenzie: Four-Hour Battery Storage Beats Gas Peaking on Cost Across 43 modeled markets, four-hour battery storage costs less than open-cycle gas turbines. Wood Mackenzie details cost trajectories for solar, wind and storage by region. Wood Mackenzie says its latest global report on levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) shows four-hour battery storage is cheaper than open-cycle gas turbines in all 43 markets where both technologies were modeled. According to the firm, gas turbine shortages and fuel volatility are raising peaking costs, while expanding battery manufacturing is pushing storage costs down. On the financing side, Lydian Energy and Infranity closed a $300 million credit facility for energy storage. The report covers Europe, North America, Latin America, Asia Pacific, the Middle East and Africa. Middle East, Africa and China lead on costs In the Middle East and Africa, utility-scale solar already stands at an LCOE of $37/MWh. The cost of four-hour storage is forecast to fall a further 33% to $80/MWh by 2035, which would place it ahead of gas peaking in every gas market in the region. China remains the global benchmark, with storage costs more than 55% below the Asia Pacific average excluding China. "This economic shift is decisive and widening," said Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie. He said gas turbine shortages and rising fuel volatility are driving up peaking costs, while expanding battery manufacturing continues to push storage costs down. He noted that a similar transformation has already reshaped baseload economics. Company Wood Mackenzie: company profile Solar dominates baseload generation According to the report, single-axis tracker solar is the lowest-cost new-build technology in 43 of the 48 modeled markets, with onshore wind leading in five. In Saudi Arabia and the UAE, the most competitive markets, solar LCOE is on track to fall below $20/MWh by 2033. In Latin America, solar PV with single-axis tracking remains the lowest-cost generation technology in 2026, with average costs expected to fall 38% by 2060. Brazil, Chile and Mexico hold a structural advantage tied to their solar resources and high capacity factors. The regional average onshore wind LCOE is expected to fall nearly 21% by 2030, from $73/MWh to $58/MWh, as Chinese manufacturers intensify price competition and larger turbines lift yields. Grid-scale storage LCOE is forecast to fall 42% by 2060, and offshore wind would approach combined-cycle gas turbine parity only in the early 2040s. Asia Pacific: sharp regional gaps In Asia Pacific, utility-scale solar remains the most cost-competitive source, but regional disparities are stark. In 2026, solar generation in the highest-cost market is more than 200% more expensive than in the lowest, a gap expected to widen to 250% by 2030. Onshore wind costs range more than six times between the cheapest and most costly markets in the region. China posts a benchmark grid-scale storage LCOE more than 55% below the rest of Asia Pacific average of $134/MWh. That average is expected to fall to $92/MWh by 2036, but Japan, Australia and the Philippines would remain at a premium because of import duties, elevated installation costs and domestic manufacturing policies. Outside China, offshore wind costs remain under near-term pressure, with declines expected from the early 2030s. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 % Europe: battery capex turns upward In Europe, solar PV remains the cheapest power technology, with fixed-tilt LCOE forecast to fall 22% by 2060, despite a 14% capex increase in 2026 driven by higher module costs. Onshore wind capex is declining at an average annual rate of 2.5% through the rest of the decade, after which rising capacity factors become the main LCOE driver, with costs of $60/MWh by 2060. Battery storage turnkey capex rose about 2%, the first increase in three years, as cell prices rebounded around 10% from their 2025 low on stronger demand and higher lithium prices. Capex is forecast to fall 12% by 2031, before the pace moderates, with lithium prices expected to roughly double in 2029.

artigo.texto: Neoextrativismo: quem lucra e quem sofre com a expansão acelerada dos data centers de Inteligência Artificial A popularização global de ferramentas como ChatGPT, Claude e Perplexity conecta os interesses de mineradoras aos de grandes complexos de processamento de dados, levando pouco em conta as consequências socioambientais e econômicas dessa exploração A expansão acelerada dos data centers para suportar a inteligência artificial impulsiona um neoextrativismo global predatório. Embora as big techs concentrem os lucros, os países fornecedores de minerais raros, água e energia arcam com severos impactos socioambientais, violações trabalhistas e poluição. A alta demanda energética, a geração massiva de lixo eletrônico e a falta de transparência nas cadeias exigem urgente responsabilização corporativa e governança socioambiental rigorosa. Mesmo que seja para fazer uma pergunta, criar uma imagem, gerar um vídeo de poucos segundos ou editar um texto, consultar um chatbot de IA na nuvem aciona servidores cujo funcionamento depende permanentemente de muitos recursos físicos: espaço, eletricidade, sistemas de resfriamento e, principalmente, minerais e metais raros, necessários para a fabricação dos servidores, redes, unidades de processamento, sensores e cabeamentos dos data centers que hospedam o serviço.. A popularização de ferramentas como ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini e Perplexity no dia a dia das pessoas alimenta o crescimento acelerado dessa infraestrutura, que para funcionar conecta os interesses dos proprietários de minas e refinadoras às necessidades de grandes complexos de processamento de dados. Essa expansão abre uma nova fronteira extrativa: os benefícios econômicos gerados pela nova tecnologia circulam por cadeias globais, mas grande parte dos custos socioambientais dessa exploração são arcados pelos países que fornecem a matéria prima, como poucas contrapartidas. Uma governança mais justa do desenvolvimento e do uso global da Inteligência Artificial exige, portanto, identificar e responsabilizar claramente quem controla e, por isso, quem deve responder pelos impactos provocados por essa nova tecnologia. Escala industrial Comumente associado à ideia simplificada de "nuvem", na verdade o funcionamento dos data centers que oferecem serviços e operam modelos de IA é caro e danoso ao ambiente. Atualmente, existem cerca de 12 mil data centers no planeta, entre unidades operacionais e projetos, dos quais cerca de 1.360 são considerados de hiperescala. No estado de Louisiana, nos EUA, por exemplo, a Meta constrói um complexo que abrigará o Hyperion, serviço global destinado ao treinamento de desenvolvedores de sistemas de IA. O projeto prevê uma área construída de cerca de 930 mil metros quadrados, e investimentos anunciados superiores a US$ 50 bilhões. A cadeia começa nas minas e se amplia com a energia Servidores, chips e redes necessários ao funcionamento de data centers de IA, grandes ou pequenos, exigem a utilização de cobre, silício, gálio, germânio, tântalo, terras raras, prata, ouro e metais do grupo da platina. Alguns desses materiais precisam atingir elevada pureza para uso eletrônico. Baterias e sistemas de fornecimento de energia ampliam essa dependência. Fabricar aparelhos com forte presença de componentes eletrônicos pode mobilizar entre 50 e 350 vezes o peso desses aparelhos em matérias-primas. A Agência Internacional de Energia estima que os data centers de IA existentes no mundo consumiram cerca de 485 terawatts (o equivalente a 485 trilhões de watts) por hora, só em 2025. E projeta um consumo de 950 terawatts por hora em 2030, considerando todo o setor. Empresas anunciam que grande parte dessa demanda deverá ser atendida por projetos de energia renovável. Embora as fontes solar e eólica sejam centrais para a descarbonização, seus equipamentos, as redes elétricas e os sistemas de armazenamento também exigem grandes quantidades de minerais. Um exemplo dessa infraestrutura é o parque solar Orion Solar Belt, no Texas, que reúne mais de 1,3 milhão de módulos fotovoltaicos de 700 watts cada. O empreendimento tem o Google como cliente âncora e fornece eletricidade à rede que abastece os data centers da empresa. Uma comparação hipotética ilustra a escala: para gerar os 950 terawatts por hora previstos para 2030 apenas com módulos solares de 700 watts, serão necessários cerca de 775 milhões de painéis. Os módulos solares podem operar por 25 a 35 anos, mas alguns equipamentos de data centers precisam ser substituídos em intervalos muito mais curtos, de poucos anos, e isso é outro grande problema. Um estudo de 2024 projetou o acúmulo de 1,2 milhão a 5 milhões de toneladas de resíduos eletrônicos pela IA generativa entre 2020 e 2030. Sem reutilização ou recuperação adequadas, perdem-se metais e aumentam os passivos ambientais para toda a sociedade. Os custos econômicos e sociais nos territórios produtores Além disso, fornecer minerais não assegura aos países de onde são extraídos nenhum controle sobre as tecnologias de maior valor agregado geradas para o desenvolvimento da IA. Como no século XVI, a tendência é que os ganhos com a comercialização do serviço concentrem-se nas empresas, enquanto as comunidades das regiões produtoras enfrentam poluição, riscos ocupacionais e disputas pela terra e pela água- esta última elemento fundamental para a operação a longo prazo de grandes data centers. Nesta complexidade, empregos, tributos e royalties precisariam ser acompanhados de proteção trabalhista, fiscalização e de serviços públicos. Nossas pesquisas bibliográficas e documentais reuniram evidências dessas desigualdades. As cadeias estudadas abastecem diferentes setores, incluindo eletrônica, baterias e sistemas de energia utilizados pelos data centers. Segundo estimativas do Serviço Geológico dos Estados Unidos, a República Democrática do Congo respondeu por cerca de 73% da produção mundial de cobalto em 2025. artigo.texto: Energy Construction Enerven to Build 400-MW Australian Battery Storage Project Scope includes civil works, 275-kV substation and transmission connection for Queensland energy storage facility ENR AT-A-GLANCE 5 Things to Know COLLAPSE ↑ Atmos Renewables selected Enerven to build balance-of-plant works for the four-hour Teebar battery energy storage project in Queensland, Australia. Enerven's scope includes design, procurement, construction and commissioning of the battery facility, a 275/33-kV substation and about 980 ft of 275-kV overhead transmission line connecting Teebar to Powerlink Queensland's network. Site mobilization is expected in October, with representatives from Atmos, Enerven, Valo and Powerlink scheduled to mark the start of construction Oct. 20. Commercial operation is targeted for late 2028. Atmos reached financial close on Teebar with support from Australia's Capacity Investment Scheme, which provides long-term revenue support for renewable generation and dispatchable energy projects. Atmos estimates peak construction employment at 100 to 150 workers, while public commitments tied to the federal program call for about $105.4 million in Australian and New Zealand procurement before commercial operation. Atmos Renewables selected Enerven Oct. 9 to build balance-of-plant works for its 400-MW Teebar battery energy storage project in the Australian state of Queensland, with site mobilization expected this month. The contractor's scope includes design, procurement, construction and commissioning of the 1,600-MWh battery facility, a 275/33-kV substation and approximately 980 ft of 275-kV overhead transmission line connecting the project to Powerlink Queensland's transmission network. Enerven will also perform site preparation, local road upgrades, bulk earthworks, drainage, internal roads and foundation construction. "It is important to Atmos to work with reputable and trusted delivery partners, and Enerven is well positioned to lead the safe and successful construction of the Teebar BESS," Atmos Renewables CEO Nigel Baker said in a statement. Commercial operation is targeted for late 2028. The four-hour battery project is planned next to Powerlink's existing Teebar Creek substation in Queensland's Fraser Coast region, about 37 miles west of Maryborough and roughly 150 miles north of Brisbane. Enerven's appointment follows approximately nine months of early contractor involvement with Atmos, battery supplier Valo and Powerlink to develop the project's design and delivery approach. The preconstruction work included site studies, detailed engineering, management plans and permitting support. When Atmos announced the arrangement in December 2025, it expected construction to begin in the third quarter of 2026. Looking for quick answers on construction and engineering topics? Try Ask ENR, our new smart AI search tool. Ask ENR → "Teebar is our first major project in Queensland and the start of a new partnership with Atmos Renewables," Enerven CEO Richard Amato said in a statement. Enerven's previous Australian battery work includes projects at Eraring, Torrens Island and Liddell. Battery System and Financing Valo will supply Teebar's battery storage technology. The company is a joint venture of Wärtsilä and RCT Solutions, combining battery hardware, software, engineering and system integration. The 400-MW Teebar battery energy storage project is planned near Maryborough in Queensland, Australia, about 150 miles north of Brisbane. Enerven will build the facility’s balance-of-plant works and grid connection. Map by ENR Australian technology publication ChannelLife reported Oct. 9 that Teebar will use Valo's GridSolve Quantum2 storage system and GEMS software and has secured Generator Performance Standards approval for grid-forming operation in Australia's National Electricity Market. Valo's contract also includes a long-term service agreement covering performance guarantees, maintenance, remote operational support, software updates and performance monitoring. Atmos reached financial close on Teebar Oct. 2. The project is supported through the Australian government's Capacity Investment Scheme, which provides long-term revenue support for renewable generation and dispatchable energy projects. Atmos will retain ownership during construction and operate the facility after completion. "The CIS provides important long-term revenue support, but an award is only one step," Baker said in a statement announcing the financial close. "Projects still need to secure financing, grid access, wider commercial arrangements and a credible delivery pathway." Atmos is backed by Igneo Infrastructure Partners, which also invests in U.S. renewable energy construction. In June, Igneo invested in U.S. developer Pathway Power, which has more than 1 GW of projects expected to begin construction in 2026 and 2027. Public commitments associated with the federal program call for approximately $105.4 million in Australian and New Zealand procurement before commercial operation, including about $796,000 in locally procured steel. Atmos estimates peak construction employment at 100 to 150 workers. Total project contract values have not been disclosed because of commercial sensitivities. Representatives from Atmos, Enerven, Valo and Powerlink are scheduled to gather at the Teebar site Oct. 20 for a ceremony marking the start of construction.

artigo.texto: Battery Manufacturing and Recycling Could Go Green With This ‘Glue’ Published Date Story by: Topics covered: Share This: Article Content Key Takeaways - A new battery binder — the glue that holds together a battery’s internal parts — could make lithium-ion batteries more environmentally friendly and easier to recycle without sacrificing performance. - The binder is fluorine free and dissolves in water, so it cuts down on toxic ingredients, energy use and waste in both battery manufacturing and recycling. - Batteries made with the new binder performed just as well as conventional lithium-ion batteries. A new battery binder — the glue that holds together a battery’s internal parts — could make lithium-ion batteries more environmentally friendly and easier to recycle without sacrificing performance. By creating a binder that is fluorine free and dissolves in water, engineers at the University of California San Diego showed that they can simplify both battery manufacturing and recycling by cutting down on toxic ingredients, energy use and waste. Batteries made with the new binder performed just as well as conventional lithium-ion batteries. The advance, published on Oct. 9 in Nature Communications, was a collaboration between the lab of Zheng Chen, professor in the Aiiso Yufeng Li Family Department of Chemical and Nano Engineering at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering, and John Muldoon at Toyota Research Institute of North America. The binder is the glue-like material that gets mixed with electrode powders to form solid layers, which are then stuck to thin metal foils inside the battery. These layers are stacked and rolled to create a battery. Although the binder makes up a small fraction of a battery's weight, it has a big impact on how the battery is manufactured and recycled. Lithium-ion batteries typically use a fluorine-containing binder because it produces strongly adhesive, uniform electrodes that remain stable throughout numerous charging and discharging cycles. That enables batteries to perform better and last longer. “But that same stability also makes batteries much harder to recycle,” said Chen, whose Sustainable Materials and Energy Lab at UC San Diego specializes in developing efficient and environmentally friendly methods to recover and restore materials from spent lithium-ion batteries. The Problem With Fluorine in Binders A fluorine-containing binder must be dissolved in a toxic solvent before it can be mixed with the electrode powders. After the electrodes are coated, large drying ovens are used to evaporate the solvent. Extra steps are then needed to recover and purify the solvent so it can be reused. “Those extra steps significantly increase the cost and energy use — as well as the environmental impact — of battery manufacturing,” said study first author Jiao Lin, a postdoctoral researcher in Chen’s lab. Fluorine-containing binders also complicate the battery recycling process. These binders leave behind stubborn residues that need high heat or corrosive chemicals to be removed. That, in turn, creates hazardous waste, as well as fluorine-containing byproducts that contaminate the recovered battery materials and make them harder to reuse in new batteries. No More Fluorine or Toxic Solvents To solve both problems, Chen’s team created a binder that contains no fluorine and can be processed using a nontoxic solvent: water. While other water-soluble binders already exist, they lack the strength and durability needed for high-performance batteries, Chen explained. The new binder is made from two inexpensive and widely used polymers. Polyacrylic acid helps the mixture spread evenly during manufacturing and provides flexibility. Meanwhile, carboxymethyl cellulose, a plant-derived material commonly used in foods and paper products, provides strength and stickiness. The polymers were first dissolved in water. Then, researchers added citric acid, the naturally occurring acid found in citrus fruits, to chemically link the polymers together. The result is a tightly connected network held together by various types of chemical bonds that reinforce one another. That gives this binder the strength, flexibility, stability and adhesion needed to rival conventional fluorine-containing binders. Making and Recycling Batteries With the New Binder Batteries built with the new fluorine-free binder delivered the same initial performance as conventional lithium-ion batteries. They even maintained their capacity longer after hundreds to thousands of charge cycles. The binder was also compatible with different types of electrodes, including lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathodes, nickel-rich cathodes, graphite anodes and silicon anodes. The new binder could also simplify battery recycling. Instead of using harsh chemicals and high temperatures to remove it, as is done with fluorine-containing binders, the researchers simply disassembled the battery and soaked the electrodes in water. This dissolved the binder and allowed the electrode coatings to cleanly separate from the metal foil sheets without leaving behind residues. The recovered electrode materials were then regenerated using direct recycling processes and used to build new batteries. These recycled batteries performed just as well as ones built from electrode materials that were recovered from batteries made with conventional fluorine-containing binder. Next steps include scaling up production of the binder for commercial manufacturing. The researchers are now working on optimizing the binder for different battery chemistries to improve their performance. Chen and his team plan to commercialize the binder through collaboration with industry partners. Full study: “Fluorine-free polymer binder enables circular manufacturing and recycling of lithium-ion batteries” This research was supported by an ECS Toyota Young Investigator Fellowship. artigo.texto: Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) has published results in all three waves of the Global Battery Alliance (GBA) battery passport pilot, a record the Chinese battery maker says no rival has matched. The latest round covered cell producers with nearly 80% of global capacity, ahead of a full certification scheme due in early 2027. The pilot is building a shared method to track, measure and verify the environmental, social and governance (ESG) record of a battery over its life. CATL’s entry this year reported ESG data for every stage of supply, from mining and refining through materials, cells and packs. That breadth matters as passports move from trial to obligation. EU rules will require digital passports for electric vehicle batteries from February 2027, giving suppliers with verified upstream data an edge with European automakers. CATL joined at the GBA’s first proof of concept in January 2023, and in the second wave sought separate passports for its Shenxing and cell-to-pack batteries, with results checked by an independent auditor. It also says its core operations are carbon neutral and targets a carbon-neutral value chain by 2035. In a statement, Dennis Pan, Head of Sustainable Development at CATL, said: “The GBA Battery Passport pilot program provides an effective methodology for the industry to monitor, quantify and demonstrate ESG performance across the battery value chain. It helps the industry better prepare for future sustainability risks and challenges.” Source: CATL

artigo.texto: A Yandex é a maior empresa de tecnologia da Rússia, oferecendo serviços como busca, transporte por aplicativo, comércio eletrônico, computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial (IA). Sua plataforma Yandex Cloud – especializada em poder computacional, armazenamento de dados e ferramentas de IA – é atualmente utilizada por mais de um terço das maiores empresas da Rússia. O ataque de 11 de outubro teve como alvo uma instalação da Yandex na região de Vladimir, a cerca de 180 km a nordeste de Moscou. Essa instalação também abriga o Galushkin, um dos três supercomputadores da empresa usados para o desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial. A Yandex anunciou no Telegram que o ataque danificou a infraestrutura do data center e forçou seu desligamento. “A infraestrutura do centro de dados da Yandex em Vladimir foi danificada por um ataque de drone, e as operações no local foram completamente suspensas. Vários serviços da Yandex estão atualmente inacessíveis aos usuários”, afirmou a empresa. Não houve relatos de vítimas no ataque mencionado. As equipes de resgate e os engenheiros da Yandex trabalharam para avaliar os danos e restabelecer o serviço. A empresa também recomendou que os clientes de serviços em nuvem ativem seus planos de contingência para responder a incidentes semelhantes. Segundo relatos da mídia, o ataque forçou a Yandex Cloud a entrar em modo de emergência; a interrupção do serviço afetou bancos, plataformas de comércio eletrônico, serviços de entrega, aplicativos de varejo, farmácias, academias e o site do Aeroporto Pulkovo em São Petersburgo. Em uma atualização posterior, o Yandex afirmou que o acesso a alguns de seus serviços – incluindo a assistente virtual de IA Alice, Busca, Mapas, Táxi e E-mail – estava sendo gradualmente restaurado. Este é o terceiro ataque contra instalações da Yandex em quatro dias. Anteriormente, o centro de dados da Yandex em Sasovo, região de Ryazan, foi severamente danificado em um ataque na noite de 7 de outubro, forçando seu desligamento. Outra instalação na região de Kaluga, a cerca de 150 km a sudoeste de Moscou, também foi danificada em um ataque com drone em 9 de outubro.

artigo.texto: The government is building an international carbon market that companies can use not only to trade voluntary greenhouse gas reduction credits but also to meet regulatory requirements, including national emissions targets. To that end, it will split the credit issuance system into two categories and begin full-scale operation of the Global Verified Carbon Market (GVCM) next year. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyoung-il discussed the detailed implementation plan for the GVCM at a ministerial meeting on international economic affairs on the 12th. The GVCM is designed to spur trading in greenhouse gas reduction credits, whose credibility has been questioned because of a lack of internationally standardized criteria. The government fleshed out the operating framework based on a roadmap announced in December last year. Credits will first be divided into two types depending on whether the host country of a project has approved their transfer. Credits approved for transfer, designated "GVCM A," can be used to meet an investing country's nationally determined contribution (NDC) or to comply with regulations in the international aviation sector. Credits without such approval, designated "GVCM NA," will be used for companies' voluntary environmental activities. Their scope of use can be expanded if the host country grants approval later. The government will also review linking the credits to the domestic emissions trading scheme and the greenhouse gas target management system if certain conditions are met. In line with that shift, the market's previous name, the Global Voluntary Carbon Market, has been changed, with "Voluntary" replaced by "Verified." To improve the credibility of transactions, key information such as project operators and reduction volumes will be recorded on a blockchain. The government plans to build the trading platform using the Korea Exchange (KRX) and to consider issuing credits in the form of digital assets in the future. The government will secure participating countries this year and form an issuing body next year to flesh out the project. It will also discuss converting credits generated by greenhouse gas reduction projects of the World Bank (WB) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) into GVCM credits. The meeting also reaffirmed existing plans, including the creation of a 3 trillion won ($2.1 billion) overseas construction fund, follow-up negotiations on the South Korea-China free trade agreement (FTA), and an industrial complex in India dedicated to Korean companies. Lee said exports have maintained solid momentum, noting that the current account posted a surplus of $46.11 billion in August. He cited trade issues with the U.S., supply chain instability and the possibility of adjustments in artificial intelligence (AI) investment as external risks. "The government will respond to external uncertainties without wavering as one economic team and create new growth opportunities," Lee said.

artigo.texto: For many years, the price of both solid state drives (SSDs) and hard drives (HDDs) were decreasing in price. About a year ago, I bought a 5TB HDD for backing up my desktop and paid $130 through Amazon. Today, that same drive is $230. People throughout the tech industry have seen the doubling of pricing across the board when it comes to computer storage. And, like so many things in the world today, you can blame AI. While so many are protesting the creation of massive data centers around the country with worries over higher electricity bills and environmental concerns, a slightly more niche issue has emerged thanks to AI’s need for computing power. Hard drives, for portable external ones to replacements for your PC, are going way up in price as data center companies swallow up as much storage as they can get their hands on. The surge in demand has rippled across the technology industry and hit the hard drive market particularly severely, which is ironic considering speculation over the last decade was that the need for hardware like this would slowly disappear with a shift into the cloud. But, data centers have rapidly changed the math when it comes to storage. And hard drive prices aren’t alone. Since early 2025, the price of RAM, once a fairly inexpensive upgrade that has been declining in price for decades, is now through the roof. What cost less than $100 in some cases to upgrade in early 2025 now runs three to four times that, what the industry has dubbed RAMageddon. Some of this might feel like much ado about nothing in the grander scheme of AI’s potential risks to the world and humanity itself, but if you need to make what used to be a pretty easy and cheap upgrade to your computer or storage, suddenly like gas, eggs and virtually everything else, you are going to pay more. And, there really is no clear sign that things will slow down, No doubt manufacturers will begin to stabilize pricing as they produce more tech, but no one would blame them if they didn’t. AI’s rise is still a huge gamble and many people in the technology world have predicted that data centers may eventually be replaced by smaller and cheaper tech options. For now, it just means more money out of your pocket thanks to AI.

artigo.texto: A $410 million bet on Australia's biggest AI infrastructure IPO turned into a one-day stock rout for Maas Group, the industrial supplier caught holding Firmus equity nobody else wanted at the marketed price. Shares in Maas Group Holdings cracked as much as 30% in Sydney trading last Thursday. They closed down 22.4%, wiping out roughly A$517 million, or about US$340 million, in market value, then slid further on Friday and Monday. The trigger was the client it had quietly bet big on: Firmus, the Nvidia-backed AI data center operator, had just pulled its roughly A$7 billion ASX float. Investors refused to clear the offer even after the indicative price was cut from A$11 to A$8.25. StartupFortune covered the IPO withdrawal itself last week. What's new is who actually ate the loss, and it wasn't a hedge fund or a bank underwriter. It was a Dubbo-based construction and quarrying company that had piled A$410 million, including a A$300 million top-up in August, into a 3.2% stake in a business it also supplies through its JLE Group subsidiary. That's the uncomfortable mechanics of an AI infrastructure boom running years ahead of the capital markets built to fund it. Maas wasn't a passive financial investor chasing yield. It was a contractor who put real money into its own customer's growth story. Then it watched that customer's implied valuation collapse from almost A$44 billion to roughly A$33 billion in 48 hours of bookbuilding, before the whole deal got shelved entirely. The spark wasn't investor squeamishness about AI in the abstract. It was something far more specific: CDC Data Centres CEO Greg Boorer said on a podcast that CDC's partnership with Firmus on Project Southgate was no longer going ahead. The project had been announced just last October as a plan to build up to 1.6 gigawatts of AI factories across Australia, with a potential A$73.3 billion in investment behind it. Two people involved in the IPO transaction said institutional orders started pulling out the next day. Firmus co-CEOs Oliver Curtis and Tim Rosenfield pulled the $44 billion float on October 9 after bookbuilding stalled, with partner CDC Data Centres having already exited a $73 billion build-out only 2.5% complete. - nvidia backed AI data centre IPO withdrawn - Australian tech IPO cancelled after investor backlash The scale of the shortfall says everything. Project Southgate was supposed to scale toward 1.6 gigawatts by 2028. Firmus and CDC ended up deploying about 42 megawatts, about 2.6% of the original ambition, before calling it off. Boorer put it plainly: the two companies had made "other choices" about how to develop data centers that diverged from what CDC had envisaged. Layer that on top of Firmus's other problem and the IPO's failure looks less like bad timing and more like investors doing basic diligence. Only about 5% of the data center capacity Firmus has already sold to customers is actually built and running, well behind the roughly 25% completion rate at listed rival NextDC. Meanwhile Firmus is carrying close to $30 billion in debt against that unbuilt capacity. Two months before the float, a private funding round had priced the company at $10.5 billion. The IPO was asking the public market to pay more than three times that figure for a business that, by its own numbers, had delivered a fraction of what it had promised. Firmus says it will now chase private market capital instead, with a person involved in the process telling reporters a Nasdaq listing could follow down the line. The company declined to confirm that plan on record. Who's actually left holding the bag This is the part that should worry anyone watching the broader AI infrastructure trade, not just Firmus specifically. Banks and bond investors have spent recent months growing warier of data center debt generally, as the gap between promised AI compute capacity and physically delivered capacity widens across the sector. IREN is the AI data center firm serving a reported $9.7 billion Microsoft GPU cloud contract from its Childress, Texas campus. It raised $2.3 billion in convertible notes in December 2025 and arranged $3.6 billion of GPU financing in 2026 as it funded its buildout. Firmus's collapse is the clearest data point yet for what happens when that gap gets priced by a public market instead of a private one willing to take management's word for it. Maas Group's trading halt, imposed the morning after the IPO fell apart pending a "material announcement" about its contractual arrangements with Firmus, tells you how tangled supplier and investor relationships have become inside Australia's AI buildout. Maas isn't just exposed through its equity stake. JLE Group, its subsidiary, has construction and infrastructure contracts tied to the same Firmus campuses that are, by Firmus's own account, only 5% complete. A failed IPO doesn't just dent a balance sheet. It can slow or stall the actual construction pipeline that a supplier depends on for revenue. Frankly, the $340 million wiped off Maas in a single session is a cleaner measure of AI infrastructure risk than any valuation multiple Firmus or its bankers floated during the roadshow. Paper valuations can be marked up by a term sheet. A 22% single-day drop in a real, profitable industrial company's share price is money that doesn't come back just because the next funding round prices higher. artigo.texto: Meta has continued its PR blitz in support of its artificial intelligence push. On Oct. 8, the company published a new overview of data center myths as it works to counter negative sentiment around its massive infrastructure developments. In order to fuel its AI push, Meta needs to process increasing amounts of user data, which is why the company is spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build new data centers across the U.S. But the impacts on regions where these projects are being developed have been significant. Some regions have reported water contamination and impacted utilities, as well as damage to local infrastructure. Indeed, Time Magazine reported in July that only a third of Americans approve of the pace of data center development. Meanwhile, more than 300 cities, towns and counties have enacted bans or moratoriums on the construction of hyperscale data centers. Meta knows that this backlash could derail its AI push, which is why it’s been working to counter the negative reports about data center impacts with explainers from its own team about the main concerns with data center developments. In this latest iteration, creator Tom Shaw addressed three myths about data center development: - Regarding concerns about excess water usage and limiting water resources for local residents, Shaw said water usage for cooling Meta’s data centers is “permitted, metered, and counted in the local water plan, not carved out of it.” Shaw also said that many of Meta’s data center facilities use less water annually than an average U.S. golf course does in the same amount of time. - On power usage, Shaw said that Meta works with utility companies years before data center work begins in order to ensure that any new infrastructure is built and installed ahead of time with no impact to local supply. - Shaw also said that Meta’s data center developments create jobs in both the construction phase, and in the ongoing management phase. Shaw added that this often means Meta becomes the biggest employer in regions where data centers are installed. Meta is hoping that by addressing these concerns it can lessen community opposition and ensure that it can continue to build its massive data centers without facing negative public sentiment. Data center concerns have become a political issue, with some candidates using their support of, or opposition to, data centers in order to win support. U.S. President Donald Trump, however, has made his stance on data center development clear. As reported by ABC News, last month Trump said in a social media post: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign." Yet, even with the president’s backing, Meta knows the negative impacts of its developments could have longer-term impacts for its business, which is why the company is working hard to counter concerns.

artigo.texto: The Greek Ministry of Environment and Energy presented a bill of law setting detailed rules for the development of projects for data centers in the country. Greek authorities have witnessed a steep rise in interest in data centers. Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO or ADMIE) saw applications rise from 5 GW to 9 GW in just two months in the summer. The proposal for the new law is attempting to clarify the regulatory framework concerning the connections to the power network, as well as establish specific requirements. IPTO to handle requests above 10 MW When it comes to oversight, IPTO will have to include data centers in its ten-year development plan, separately from other large consumers. The operator is called to categorize availability at extra-high-voltage substations. They can be free, partially congested or fully congested. These estimations will be updated every two months to provide timely information to the market. As for the licensing process, IPTO will be responsible for data centers above 10 MW, with Hellenic Electricity Distribution Network Operator (HEDNO or DEDDIE) handling requests below that capacity. Projects won’t be allowed to be segmented into smaller parts for benefiting simpler regulations. Power must be 60% renewable Investors would be required to submit letters of guarantee for EUR 200,000 per MW, with a three-year duration. When ready, the operator would provide them with a three-year connection offer, at which point developers need to submit a report with the project’s technical features and a power supply agreement. Consumed electricity must be at least 60% renewable in origin. Data centers can connect directly to neighboring renewable electricity and energy storage facilities, or sign power purchase agreements (PPAs). Data centers above 200 MW would benefit from priority in their connection, although with certain caveats. The owner must establish that 80% of the electricity will come either from a distributed power producer, or from energy storage with a six-hour injection duration.

artigo.texto: Public backlash is rising against the construction of data centers, but Kalshi traders see a higher likelihood that the number of data centers planned or operating before the new year will top 5,000. Prediction market platform Kalshi shows a 75% chance that there will be more than 5,100 proposed and live data centers before 2027. In just two weeks, the likelihood has jumped from 60%. The contract's odds will be resolved and verified by Data Center Map, which plots out planned and running data centers on its website. So far, there are more than 4,700 operating and planned data centers in the U.S., according to Data Center Map. Among states, Virginia is in the lead with more than 670 planned and on-line facilities, followed by Texas with 537 and California with more than 200, Data Center Map found. Tech companies have been growing their data center footprint in states like Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. The buildout has faced backlash from communities and activists who argue such projects would raise utility costs for locals and consume significant amounts of water. Last month Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar, that Oracle sent its developer a "force majeure" notice tied to its New Mexico data center project in a bid to protect itself from higher expenses in the event the project doesn't come online in 2028 as anticipated. Oracle's proposed data center also hit snags this summer after New Mexico regulators turned down applications for a gas pipeline project to fuel it, Bloomberg reported. Às 4h24, um drone foi detectado na cidade. O centro de dados da Yandex em Vladimir é uma das maiores instalações da rede da empresa, com uma capacidade estimada em cerca de 56 MW. Em março de 2026, a empresa inaugurou outro centro de dados em Vladimir. A instalação tem uma capacidade declarada de 40 MW e uma capacidade projetada para 2.800 servidores. Você também pode gostar Esta subestação está equipada com dois transformadores de 25 MVA e duas linhas de energia de 110 kV, que conectam a subestação Yandex à subestação Vladimirskaya com uma tensão de 750 kV. Este centro de dados permite a operação da plataforma de computação em nuvem da Yandex, por meio da qual as empresas alugam espaço em servidores para executar seus próprios aplicativos, armazenar arquivos e processar dados. A infraestrutura das instalações também pode suportar os serviços próprios da Yandex, incluindo seu mecanismo de busca e muitos outros produtos. Esta não é a primeira vez que drones ucranianos atacam centros de dados da empresa. Em 9 de outubro, drones suicidas ucranianos alvejaram o maior centro de dados da Yandex na região de Kaluga, na Federação Russa. Segundo a empresa, este centro de dados é o maior das instalações da Yandex em termos de capacidade total de servidores e um dos maiores da Rússia. Você também pode gostar O projeto envolve a instalação de mais de 3.800 servidores com capacidade de até 15 kW cada. As instalações ocupam uma área de 130.000 m² e têm uma capacidade projetada de 63 MW. No dia 8 de outubro, o centro de dados Yandex DC Sasovo, localizado na cidade de Sasovo, região de Ryazan, Rússia, foi atacado. A capacidade de energia declarada do centro é de 12 MW.

artigo.texto: Three brothers wanted to use some land for solar, batteries, and cattle grazing. First they had to convince local officials — and the community — to allow batteries. The soil in northwest Iowa is so fertile it’s referred to as “black gold.” “It’s incredibly rich, wonderful topsoil from thousands of years of silty deposits from the Missouri River,” said Luke Seaberg, a researcher at Iowa State University’s extension program. So rich that some counties restrict development on land that scores especially high on the state’s official Corn Suitability Rating. The Smith family has been farming that soil for six generations in Cherokee County, population 11,000. But the corn market has been depressed lately, prompting the three Smith brothers to consider other uses for a 160-acre parcel, 10% of their farmland. Looking at rising beef prices and the region’s ballooning energy demand, they landed on an idea: Graze cows amid rows of solar panels. “We’re trying to diversify into another revenue stream. The cattle business is really good right now, and grain has been not as good,” Mark Smith told me over the phone, as he drove across the state for his son’s high school football game. “With solar, we can put cornfields back to pasture. Solar revenue plus cattle revenue makes it work.” But to loft the solar panels up above the butting heads of grazing cattle costs more than a regular solar installation; indeed, this type of agrivoltaics only recently entered commercial-scale use, at a 40-acre, 3-megawatt site in Tennessee developed by Silicon Ranch. To mitigate the extra cost, the Smiths want to pair 30 megawatts of cattle-friendly solar capacity with a 25-megawatt/100-megawatt-hour battery composed of modular containerized units covering about an acre and a half. The Smith brothers’ desire to install batteries on their land, though, set them on a collision course with local authorities. When the county supervisors heard of the plan, they approved an indefinite moratorium on March 24, blocking any battery projects in the county. Similar bans are popping up around the country as communities grapple with the real and perceived risks of lithium-ion batteries, which rose from obscurity over the last decade and now constitute the largest source of on-demand power getting built in the U.S. In many counties, this story ends with the battery moratorium, stymieing new emissions-free power capacity at a time when everyone from climate advocates to AI giants to the Trump administration wants to see more batteries get built. But the Smiths found an ally in Supervisor Shane Bellefy, the lone vote against the moratorium. Together, they set out to flip the county back to a place that lets landowners decide what to do on their acreage. Within just five months, they succeeded. The rise of the wind and solar moratorium Iowa subscribes to the “home rule” philosophy, whereby the state constitution leaves many decisions up to city or county governments, Seaberg said. But even those local authorities typically take a hands-off approach. The state’s “right to farm” law blocks local governments from regulating what landowners choose to grow or raise on their farmland. Some rural counties don’t even have a zoning code. “Your nearest neighbor might be 5 or 10 miles down the road,” Seaberg explained. “The general policy of county supervisors was, folks can do what they want to do with their land.” That attitude started to shift after the onshore wind boom came to Iowa in the early 2000s. The state has since added 13 gigawatts and remains the nation’s top state for share of wind energy produced. But in some rural counties, the nonexistent zoning code enabled a frenzy of development that “left a bad taste in their mouths,” Seaberg said. Now some counties have added land use regulations — but only for wind and solar. In Cherokee County, an earlier proposed 900-acre solar project prompted the supervisors to throw up a solar moratorium last year. But they subsequently worked through their concerns with the technology and adopted an ordinance allowing large-scale solar, with some restrictions. The March 2026 battery moratorium, though, would block the Smiths’ project, jeopardizing tens of millions of dollars in financing that the developers had lined up from investment banks. The Smiths might have had a case to challenge the moratorium on procedural grounds, since it passed without the usual multiple readings and lacked a specified time frame. But instead, they opted for persuasion. Opening up battery development After the moratorium was approved, it fell to the county zoning board to compose a long-term ordinance to govern battery development. That body held a public meeting in May where the Smiths testified about their plans. The family also invited Seaberg to answer the community’s questions about battery technology based on Iowa State University’s independent research. The Smiths explained what they wanted to build on their land in partnership with energy developer Nomad Infrastructure. The Indiana-based firm has considerable experience constructing solar and battery projects, and one brother, Thomas Smith, works there as an engineer. They had gotten permission from the local rural electric cooperative, Mark Smith noted, to transmit the generation over the wires and sell it in the broader regional grid, run by the Midcontinent Independent System Operator. The MISO grid has very high rates of wind and solar production, but batteries are just starting to proliferate there. Meanwhile, data center expansion is driving up electricity demand in the region to never-before-seen heights, making for auspicious conditions to sell on-demand power from a battery. Bellefy, who works as a banker, pitched his fellow supervisors on the economic potential of allowing the project to move forward. The Smith installation would involve investing upwards of $80 million, which could generate $60,000 to $80,000 in new county tax revenue annually, Bellefy

artigo.texto: Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) are two of the biggest spenders in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. Each has a sprawling cloud computing business with far more demand than capacity, so they're spending unprecedented amounts of money to expand their data center footprints. For 2026, Amazon plans to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures, while Alphabet expects to lay out about $200 billion. Nearly all of that will go toward building out data centers. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » While I think both stocks are strong investments, I believe Amazon has far more to gain. But don't sleep on Alphabet, as it's growing at an incredibly fast rate. AWS is a major part of Amazon's overall picture The reason why I think Amazon has more to gain from its cloud computing investment is the position of Amazon Web Services (AWS) within Amazon as a whole. In Q2, AWS accounted for about 21% of Amazon's total revenue. However, AWS produced 60% of Amazon's operating profits. That's a natural result of the fact that e-commerce and retail generally are relatively low-margin businesses; AWS' operating margin is far higher. This magnifies the effect that revenue growth from AWS has on the overall company's profitability. So its net sales rose 20 year over year in Q2, but its operating income increased by 43%. As Amazon continues to invest big time in AWS, its added capacity will translate directly into impressive revenue growth and even larger profit growth. Likewise, Alphabet is benefiting from Google Cloud's growth, but not to the same degree. The company's core business is advertising from its Google family of products, and that already has a pretty strong operating margin. Companywide, Alphabet had an operating margin of 34% in Q2. Google Cloud did slightly better, with a 36% operating margin, but since it's already pretty close to the company's overall margin, it doesn't have the outsized effect on profits that AWS has on Amazon. But don't disregard Google Cloud, either. Google Cloud's revenue growth in Q2 was 82% year over year, while AWS's was 37%. That mismatch shows how Alphabet is rapidly expanding its cloud segment. However, it's doing so off a much smaller base. Amazon is the world's largest cloud infrastructure provider, with a 28% market share as of Q2. While No. 3 Alphabet is slowly cutting into that lead, it still accounts for just 15% of the market. Google Cloud booked $24.8 billion in revenue in Q2, while AWS booked $42.2 billion.

artigo.texto: The Luxembourg meeting will test the bloc’s unity on climate policy and biodiversity goals as ministers prepare to negotiate on implementing global environmental commitments. Environment Council meets in Luxembourg on Monday as Europe prepares for key UN climate and biodiversity talks. European Union environment and climate ministers will gather in Luxembourg on Monday to debate the proposed overhaul of the bloc’s emissions trading system (ETS) and seek agreement on the EU’s negotiating positions ahead of two major United Nations summits on climate and biodiversity. The Environment Council meeting, scheduled for October 12, will open with a policy debate on the ETS review. The package was proposed by the European Commission on July 17, 2026, as part of efforts to implement the EU’s 2040 climate target. It is currently being examined by the Council’s preparatory bodies, and ministers will outline their views and priorities on key aspects of the proposal. The review also forms part of the “One Europe, One Market” roadmap. Ministers will then be invited to approve conclusions on preparations for COP31, the UN climate change conference scheduled for November 9-20 in Antalya, Türkiye, under the joint leadership of Türkiye and Australia. The EU’s main focus will be on implementing the Paris Agreement and delivering on commitments already made. They will also seek to adopt conclusions ahead of the UN biodiversity conference, COP17, to be held from October 19-30 in Yerevan, Armenia. The Yerevan summit will mark the first global review of collective progress towards the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and its 2030 targets. Under other business, the Irish presidency and the Commission will brief ministers on the outcome of the UN desertification conference (UNCCD COP17), held this summer in Mongolia. The meeting comes as governments worldwide face growing pressure to turn climate and nature pledges into concrete action. How united the EU’s 27 member states appear in Luxembourg is likely to shape the bloc’s influence in the negotiating rooms in Yerevan and Antalya, where developing countries are expected to press for stronger finance and implementation support. The next Environment Council meeting is scheduled for December 11.

artigo.texto: Volkswagen e chinesa Gotion aprofundam parceria em baterias Acordos preveem 3 joint ventures na Espanha, na Eslováquia e no Marrocos para ampliar a produção de baterias A unidade de baterias do Grupo Volkswagen, PowerCo SE, e a fabricante chinesa de baterias Gotion High-tech Co. Ltd. vão estabelecer 3 joint ventures na Espanha, na Eslováquia e no Marrocos para ampliar a produção de baterias. As empresas anunciaram os acordos em 28 de setembro. Em Valência, na Espanha, a megafábrica da PowerCo, atualmente em construção, será transferida para uma joint venture, na qual a PowerCo terá participação de 51% e a Gotion, de 49%. A unidade deverá se tornar o centro europeu de produção de baterias de LFP (fosfato de ferro-lítio) da Volkswagen, uma tecnologia de menor custo amplamente utilizada em veículos elétricos. Na Eslováquia, a fábrica de células de bateria da Gotion em Šurany será transferida para uma joint venture na qual a empresa chinesa terá participação de 51% e a PowerCo, de 49%. A parceria produzirá células LFP para veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. No Marrocos, as empresas estabelecerão uma joint venture para produzir materiais catódicos de LFP, com participação de 51% da Gotion e de 49% da PowerCo. A parceria é realizada enquanto a União Europeia avalia novas condições para investimentos estrangeiros em setores como o de baterias. De acordo com a proposta apresentada pela Comissão Europeia em março, investidores estrangeiros precisariam cumprir pelo menos 4 de 6 condições, incluindo limites à participação acionária estrangeira e exigências mínimas de pesquisa e desenvolvimento na UE e de aquisição de insumos localmente. A proposta continua em análise e ainda não tem um cronograma específico para implementação. Este texto foi publicado originalmente pela Caixin em 2 de outubro de 2026. Foi traduzida e republicada pelo Poder360 sob acordo mútuo de compartilhamento de conteúdo.

artigo.texto: Sodium-ion batteries have long been touted as the workhorse technology for grid-scale energy storage, promising abundant raw materials, low cost, and safety characteristics that lithium-ion chemistry struggles to match. Yet one stubborn problem has kept hard carbon—the leading anode material for these batteries—from reaching its full potential: the interface between the electrode and the electrolyte behaves in ways engineers cannot fully control. Now, a research team at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences reports a surface chemistry strategy that directly tackles this instability at the molecular level, steering the movement of anions in the electrolyte to build a tougher, more protective interface. The work, published in Nano-Micro Letters, could reshape how scientists design anode materials for next-generation sodium-ion cells. The core of the challenge lies in what happens during the very first charge of a sodium-ion battery. As sodium ions migrate into the hard carbon anode, the electrolyte—the liquid medium carrying those ions—also begins to decompose on the electrode surface. Some of this decomposition is desirable: it forms the solid electrolyte interphase, or SEI, a thin protective film that allows ions to pass while blocking further electrolyte breakdown. But when this process runs uncontrolled, too much electrolyte is consumed irreversibly, draining sodium from the cathode side and lowering the initial Coulombic efficiency, a key measure of how much charge put into a cell can be recovered. A poorly formed SEI also continues to thicken and crack over repeated cycles, accelerating capacity fade and shortening battery life. Existing approaches to taming this interface—electrolyte additives, pre-sodiation, or elaborate carbon coatings—offer only limited control over the fundamental processes at play: which ions arrive at the electrode surface first, and how they decompose. The Hefei team took a different route. Rather than treating the electrolyte, they redesigned the surface of the hard carbon itself, introducing two types of functional sites in a synergistic arrangement: pyridinic nitrogen atoms and carbonyl groups. Together, these sites create what the researchers describe as a capture-repel microenvironment, a molecular-scale gatekeeper that discriminates between the different species dissolved in the electrolyte. The selectivity works like this: the functional sites preferentially adsorb the hexafluorophosphate anion, PF6−, the salt species that carries negative charge in the most common sodium battery electrolytes, while repelling solvent molecules. Theoretical simulations performed by the team showed that this preferential adsorption establishes an anion concentration gradient near the electrode surface, effectively driving anions toward the interface in a directed, bottom-up flux. Instead of ions arriving in a random, diffusion-limited jumble, the surface chemistry actively orchestrates which species reaches the reaction zone first. That directed transport has a profound consequence. With anions concentrated at the interface, the decomposition barrier of PF6− is lowered, favoring an anion-dominated decomposition pathway. In practical terms, the SEI that forms is built primarily from inorganic compounds derived from the salt—species such as sodium fluoride and related inorganic phases—rather than from organic solvent breakdown products. Inorganic-rich SEIs are widely regarded as superior in sodium and lithium systems alike: they tend to be denser, more thermally stable, and better at suppressing continued electrolyte consumption. By controlling the chemistry of decomposition before it happens, the team effectively programmed the interface to build itself well. The electrochemical results bore this out. The modified hard carbon anode delivered improved initial Coulombic efficiency, meaning less charge was wasted in parasitic side reactions during the first cycle—a critical metric for full-cell energy density, since sodium inventory is finite. The anode also showed enhanced rate capability, sustaining fast charging and discharging better than untreated hard carbon, and maintained stable performance over extended cycling. For a material whose commercial viability depends on surviving tens of thousands of shallow cycles in grid applications, that combination of first-cycle efficiency and long-term stability is exactly what the field has been seeking. Direct analysis of the interface confirmed the mechanism. Interfacial characterization revealed that the SEI formed on the functionalized hard carbon was thinner, more uniform, and mechanically stronger than the layer on pristine material. A thin, uniform film minimizes impedance and ensures that current flows evenly across the electrode, while mechanical robustness helps the SEI withstand the volume changes hard carbon undergoes as sodium ions enter and leave its disordered structure. The team also validated the strategy beyond laboratory half-cells, demonstrating its potential in pouch-type full cells—a format much closer to commercial reality, where electrode loading, electrolyte volume, and pairing with a cathode all impose additional demands. What makes the study conceptually significant is its reframing of interface engineering. Much of battery research treats the SEI as something that happens to an electrode—a byproduct to be managed after the fact. This work treats it as something an electrode can actively direct, using surface functional groups as molecular levers to control ion transport and decomposition chemistry. The idea of an anionic bottom-up flux, in which the surface recruits the right species from the electrolyte rather than passively accepting whatever arrives, could extend beyond hard carbon to other electrode materials and battery chemistries where interfacial stability limits performance. artigo.texto: Equinix, a digital infrastructure and data center provider, has told w.media that it is finalizing a full incident response report in an effort to prevent a recurrence of a fuel leak that occurred at its NY2 data center facility in Secaucus, New Jersey, in September 2026. Equinix said it detected a leak from a storage tank outside the facility on September 11, 2026. It added that the leak was stopped and that it immediately engaged Clean Harbors, an environmental and industrial services provider, to begin remediation efforts. The company also notified the Secaucus Fire Department, New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP), and other agencies. “Our investigation found that a mechanical failure of two valves used as part of a routine filtration process for stored fuel caused the leak. We regret that this occurred and the concern it has caused the community. We are finalizing a full incident response report to prevent recurrence,” Equinix said in a statement to w.media. The company added that it has been a part of the Secaucus community since 2001 and is committed to rectifying the incident and maintaining the trust of its neighbors and local officials. Last week w.media reported that Congresswoman Nellie Pou, who represents the Ninth District of New Jersey, put pressure on NJDEP to provide answers about the fuel spill that had allegedly contaminated local waterways. According to Pou, this incident was the largest data center fuel spill on record in the state of New Jersey with as much as 5,500 gallons of fuel spilled during the incident. “I appreciate that NJDEP is working to investigate and address the spill. But NJDEP must provide a clear account of exactly what happened and what is being done to prevent another spill to ensure transparency and accountability,” the congresswoman said. NJDEP was given until October 9, 2026, to respond, but at the time of publication neither Pou’s office nor NJDEP had publicly confirmed that the deadline was met or that a report was submitted.

artigo.texto: A Yandex, empresa russa de tecnologia e inteligência artificial, informou neste domingo, 11 de outubro de 2026, que seu data center na região de Vladimir foi completamente desativado após um ataque com drones. A companhia garantiu que nenhuma pessoa ficou ferida, mas reconheceu que alguns de seus serviços ficaram indisponíveis para os usuários em decorrência do incidente. Essa instalação em Vladimir é a terceira a ter sua operação afetada em um intervalo de quatro dias. De acordo com a agência Reuters, a sequência de ataques compromete a infraestrutura digital da Yandex, que desempenha papel fundamental no avanço de projetos de inteligência artificial na Rússia. Na sexta-feira, 9 de outubro de 2026, drones ucranianos atingiram o data center localizado na região de Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou, provocando paralisações parciais em sua operação. A companhia relatou que parte de sua capacidade de processar dados ficou suspensa temporariamente, gerando indisponibilidade de alguns sistemas. Um dia antes, na quinta-feira, 8 de outubro de 2026, outro ataque ucraniano desativou totalmente o data center da Yandex em Sasovo, ao sudeste de Moscou. Essa instalação abriga dois dos três supercomputadores utilizados para treinar e aprimorar os modelos de inteligência artificial da empresa, o que representa um golpe significativo à sua infraestrutura de pesquisa. A empresa alertou que a perda de capacidade em seus data centers pode prejudicar o funcionamento de serviços essenciais e atrasar o desenvolvimento de novos sistemas de IA. Até o momento, a Yandex não apresentou um cronograma para o restabelecimento completo das operações nas unidades atingidas. A série de ataques tem levantado dúvidas sobre a segurança dos demais data centers da companhia, espalhados por várias regiões do país. A Yandex ainda não detalhou quais contramedidas de proteção serão adotadas nem ofereceu uma previsão de quando as atividades poderão ser normalizadas em todas as suas instalações. Conhecida informalmente como “o Google da Rússia”, a Yandex oferece uma variedade de serviços digitais e lidera iniciativas de inteligência artificial no país. A empresa monitora atentamente o impacto desses incidentes para avaliar as consequências em sua operação diária e em seus projetos de pesquisa tecnológica.

artigo.texto: ULSAN — Korean researchers have developed an electrolyte technology that can triple the cycle life of next-generation lithium metal batteries by harnessing interactions between inexpensive commercial solvents. The approach addresses the rapid degradation that occurs during high-voltage charging without relying on costly specialty solvents or high-concentration salts. A joint research team led by Professor Song Hyun-kon of the Department of Energy and Chemical Engineering at the Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology (UNIST) and Professor Seo Dong-hwa of the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) said on the 12th that it had developed an electrolyte that extends lithium metal battery life by exploiting the attraction between two commercial solvents. Lithium metal batteries are regarded as a next-generation high-energy-density option because they can deliver far greater capacity than commercial lithium-ion batteries that use graphite anodes. But their cycle life falls off sharply because lithium metal triggers unwanted side reactions with the electrolyte during charging and discharging, and the capacity loss becomes more severe under high-voltage charging conditions. The team solved the problem by mixing two solvents, ethylene carbonate (EC) and sulfolane (SL), at a weight ratio of 3 to 7 and adding a small amount of an additive that stabilizes the protective film. Both solvents had previously been excluded from lithium metal battery design because they bind lithium ions too strongly, hindering deposition on the electrode surface. When the two were combined, however, strong intermolecular attractions including hydrogen bonding formed between the hydrogen in EC and the oxygen in SL, which instead weakened the solvents' grip on lithium ions. The team identified this phenomenon — in which the two solvents influence each other to regulate lithium-ion binding and the interfacial accessibility of anions — as "cooperative solvation." In performance testing, the new electrolyte recorded an initial Coulombic efficiency of 98.24% and an average Coulombic efficiency of 99.35%. A battery with a high-nickel (NCM811) cathode retained about 80% of its initial capacity after 150 charge-discharge cycles in a 4.5-volt high-voltage environment. That is three times the cycle life of conventional carbonate-based electrolytes, which fell below 80% after about 50 cycles. Gas generation from electrolyte decomposition and nickel leaching from the cathode material were also suppressed. "We improved electrolyte performance using only commercial solvents, without depending on expensive fluorinated solvents or high-concentration salts," Song said. "This should help extend the service life of high-capacity lithium metal batteries for use in energy storage systems (ESS) and electric vehicles." Hong Jin-ki, the researcher who is first author of the paper, said the work represents "a new design principle in which solvents with strong binding forces are mixed to weaken their bonding with lithium ions." He added that it "can be extended not only to lithium metal batteries but also to commercial lithium-ion batteries and next-generation battery systems." The research was supported by the Korea Evaluation Institute of Industrial Technology (KEIT) under the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy and by the National Research Council of Science and Technology (NST), and was published in ACS Nano, an international journal in the field of nanoscience.

artigo.texto: The Real Footprint of Trump’s Data Center Boom What the sprawling buildout means for energy, water, and land. Weeks ahead of high-stakes midterm elections, many Americans are revolting against the data centers being developed in their communities to power President Donald Trump’s artificial intelligence ambitions. About two-thirds of Americans oppose local data center construction, according to polls, and that resistance has been reflected in sweeping protests. In addition to concerns about the impact a new data center may have on jobs, local residents commonly cite the amounts of water, electricity, and land data centers consume and what that could mean for energy bills and the environment. Weeks ahead of high-stakes midterm elections, many Americans are revolting against the data centers being developed in their communities to power President Donald Trump’s artificial intelligence ambitions. About two-thirds of Americans oppose local data center construction, according to polls, and that resistance has been reflected in sweeping protests. In addition to concerns about the impact a new data center may have on jobs, local residents commonly cite the amounts of water, electricity, and land data centers consume and what that could mean for energy bills and the environment. Most controversial are the “hyperscale” data centers used by companies such as Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, which can dwarf the size of other facilities and have taken off amid the AI boom. Opposition has grown so fierce that at least 15 states are weighing moratoriums, while lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have aligned themselves with outraged locals. “We’ve finally found something that can unite the left and the right,” quipped Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin. Yet that backlash has done little to deter the Trump administration, which has championed data centers in its bid for global AI dominance. More than 1,500 data centers are now under development, adding to the 3,000 already operating in the country, according to the Pew Research Center. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump declared in a post on Truth Social in August. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.” As tensions threaten to reach a fever pitch ahead of midterms, here’s what we know about data centers’ actual resource footprint. Power At a time of surging energy costs, national attention has focused on data centers’ power consumption, with half of Americans saying that they spell trouble for energy bills, according to Pew. Data centers accounted for 4.7 percent of total U.S. electricity consumption in 2024, up from 4.4 percent the year before, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. That share is set to surge in the coming years, though estimates range. Data centers could consume nearly 12 percent of U.S. electricity by 2030, according to Lawrence Berkeley. And by 2035, data centers could suck up so much energy that they make up about one-fifth of U.S. electricity consumption, according to BloombergNEF. So far, the data center construction frenzy has been largely concentrated in a handful of hot spots, with the biggest in Virginia, Texas, and California. But that is poised to spread as even more data centers are planned, including in Illinois, Georgia, Ohio, and Arizona. All of those forecasts point to a buildout unfolding at a speed and scale that states are ill-equipped for. “We’re looking at very rapid growth, and what’s been happening in recent years is very flat demand in the power sector,” said Lori Bird, an energy expert at the World Resources Institute. “So this is quite a reversal.” Texas offers a window into how such an expansion can strain local infrastructure—and ignite a political firestorm. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott once vowed to make the state the “epicenter of AI development,” and at least 248 new data center projects are planned, adding to the state’s existing 335. “There’s almost no muscle memory in the system to meet those growth rates,” said Ashish Sethia, the global head of commodities at BloombergNEF, citing a scarcity of technicians, transformers, and transmission lines. “Therefore, you’re seeing this kind of scramble to try and get hands on as much power capacity to support your data center.” Demand has been relentless. Over the summer, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which operates the state’s grid, said it was considering about 474 gigawatts (GW) of interconnection requests—or over five times the state’s record peak electricity demand for the operator, according to the state officials; 90 percent of those new power requests are from data centers, ERCOT said. In August, Abbott directed state regulators to stop data center connections and ordered audits. “It’s insane,” said Rhodes, who said that the entire Houston area sees about 17 GW at peak demand. “Houston is about 17 gigawatts, and we’re seeing multiple Houstons’ [worth of] data centers trying to connect to the ERCOT system at a time.” The big question looming over the buildout, in Texas and beyond, is what this all means for consumers’ electric bills. The answer is, unsurprisingly, somewhat complicated. “It really depends on how much are you doing [and] does the system have the capacity to manage it,” said Bird, who said that it can be a benefit if you have a power system with excess generation available. “But what we’re seeing is that in a lot of these regions there’s not enough, and that they’re trying to move so quickly.” Gas turbine prices, for example, have spiked nearly 200 percent as a result of the data center expansion. artigo.texto: Three European Parliament groups oppose weakening ETS — Politico Europe In Brussels, Belgium, three major political groups in the European Parliament said they would oppose the European Commission’s proposal to weaken carbon emissions pricing rules. The Socialists and Democrats, Renew Europe and the Greens seek to preserve a more ambitious path toward net-zero emissions within the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), Politico reports. Dispute over the pace of reductions The position of these groups runs counter to the approach of the largest parliamentary group, the center-right European People’s Party, which generally supports the European Commission’s proposal. The main differences concern the linear reduction factor, a mechanism that determines the pace of the annual decrease in the number of emissions allowances. Under the current trajectory, the overall emissions cap for sectors covered by the ETS is to fall to zero around 2039–2040. The system covers, among others, electricity producers, steelworks and chemical plants. The proposal by Member of the European Parliament Peter Liese envisages moving this date into the 2040s, in line with the European Commission’s summer initiative. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. The Socialists and Democrats, Renew Europe and the Greens have submitted nearly identical amendments that provide for maintaining a higher reduction rate until the end of the next decade. According to Politico’s assessment, this would mean faster decarbonization of industry in Europe. Possible votes from right-wing groups Liese, who is leading Parliament’s work on the ETS revision, said he seeks to create the “broadest possible coalition,” which could include the European Conservatives and Reformists, the Greens and the Left. At the same time, Czech MEP Alexandr Vondra of the European Conservatives and Reformists group proposed cooperation with the EPP on condition of support for a more industry-friendly course, including slower progress toward net-zero emissions. According to the outlet, Polish, Spanish and Italian EPP representatives are dissatisfied with what they consider Liese’s proposal to be too favorable to climate goals. The Europe of Sovereign Nations group, which includes members of Germany’s Alternative for Germany, is seeking the complete abolition of the ETS. Patriots for Europe generally advocates a substantial slowdown of this policy, especially the planned ETS2 system. Their votes could potentially become one option for the EPP to support the reform.
