artigo.texto: Cientistas dos EUA criam a primeira bateria inspirada no metabolismo humano: ela funciona com vitamina B2 e glicose Livre de metais pesados e totalmente biodegradável, a nova bateria de fluxo utiliza reações do nosso próprio organismo para armazenar energia renovável Pesquisadores da Universidade de Utah criaram uma inovadora bateria de fluxo inspirada no metabolismo humano para o armazenamento de energia limpa em larga escala. O dispositivo substitui metais pesados e compostos tóxicos por biomoléculas orgânicas e biodegradáveis: usa derivados de glicose no polo negativo e vitamina B2 no polo positivo para gerar eletricidade, reproduzindo a respiração celular e oferecendo uma alternativa sustentável às baterias convencionais de íon de lítio. Uma equipe da Universidade de Utah desenvolveu uma bateria de fluxo bioinspirada que utiliza biomoléculas totalmente orgânicas e biodegradáveis para armazenar energia limpa sem depender de metais pesados. O armazenamento de energia em grande escala é um dos maiores gargalos da transição energética. Baterias de íon de lítio convencionais são eficientes para eletrônicos e veículos elétricos, mas envolvem mineração tóxica e alto impacto ambiental. Para resolver isso, a resposta veio da própria biologia. Pesquisadores da Universidade de Utah, nos Estados Unidos, criaram uma bateria de fluxo bioinspirada que imita o metabolismo do corpo humano, utilizando vitamina B2 (riboflavina) e glicose para armazenar e liberar eletricidade de forma limpa e sustentável. Como funciona a bateria "metabólica"? As baterias de fluxo armazenam energia em eletrólitos líquidos contidos em tanques externos que passam por uma célula central onde ocorrem as reações eletroquímicas. No protótipo desenvolvido pela equipe, o processo é diretamente espelhado nas rotas metabólicas que as nossas células usam para extrair energia dos alimentos: - Anólito (polo negativo): Utiliza derivados de glicose, atuando como o "combustível" primário. - Católito (polo positivo): Utiliza flavinas modificadas com base na vitamina B2, que atuam como aceitadores de elétrons — um papel idêntico ao que desempenham no nosso organismo durante a respiração celular. artigo.texto: Ultium Cells LLC, a joint venture between Detroit-based General Motors (GM) and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution, has announced a plan to produce lithium manganese-rich (LMR) prismatic battery cells at the GM manufacturing complex in Spring Hill, Tennessee. The Ultium partnership and EV battery production in the United States overall attracted investment momentum in the early 2020s as the administration of President Joe Biden offered incentives tied to EV sales and production. That momentum stalled significantly as the administration of President Donald J. Trump discontinued support measures for EVs and demonstrated a preference for fossil fuels and fossil fuel-consuming industry sectors. The shift in priorities also may have stalled momentum in the scaling up of U.S. EV battery recycling, including agreements reached by Ultium with battery materials recyclers and suppliers. Now, GM says it is “blazing a new trail in battery technology” at its Spring Hill complex near Nashville. The investment is “expected to make Ultium Cells the first manufacturer globally to commercially produce this next-generation technology, positioning GM at the forefront of bringing the technology to market in future electric vehicles.” GM says LMR prismatic battery cells mark a major step forward for the future of its EV sector, adding the technology is designed to offer energy density 33 percent greater compared with lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry but at a comparable cost. “Establishing LMR prismatic cell production at Ultium Cells in Spring Hill is a key step in our strategy to match the right battery technology to customer needs and strengthen our leadership in domestic battery manufacturing and innovation,” states GM. The automaker says high-nickel batteries will continue to give customers the highest range in its EV portfolio, while adding LMR positions the company to “leapfrog today’s more affordable chemistries and deliver lower costs with better performance.” According to GM, the manufacturing capabilities of Ultium Cells offers flexibility, with a planned ability to produce battery cells in multiple chemistries and form factors, helping tailor battery technology to the needs of different vehicles and applications. “Bringing this new battery cell to market first is a milestone moment for keeping America competitive globally in EV and battery technology leadership,” states GM. General Motors says construction and facility upgrades in Spring Hill will begin later this year and are expected to be completed in 2028. The expansion is projected to create 500 new jobs, joining the current workforce of 1,200 people.

artigo.texto: Bulgaria Raises Net Electricity Exports 62% on Solar Power and Battery Storage Net electricity exports have reached 3.5 TWh since January, driven by photovoltaics and storage. Industry group APSTE points to the lack of new wind capacity, as solar output declines in winter. Bulgaria's net electricity exports rose 62% from the start of the year to early October, reaching 3.5 TWh, compared with 2.16 TWh a year earlier. Renewable energy sources, supported by storage systems, are the main driver of the increase in output. According to grid operator ESO, the country is producing 12.24% more electricity, while consumption has risen 8.45%. Renewables drive the rise in output ESO data show renewable generation reaching 11.5 TWh, nearly 34% more than a year earlier. Renewable sources therefore account for almost 80% of the growth in the country's electricity output. In the region, Renalfa and Eurowind have inaugurated Tenevo, a 242 MWp solar complex with batteries, while Vojvodina has launched the environmental scoping phase for the Baranda solar plant. Storage deployment is advancing sharply. From the start of the year to 4 October, batteries delivered 1,720 GWh to the power system, compared with 190 GWh a year earlier, an increase of more than nine times. This storage allows cheap electricity produced during the day to be used in hours of high consumption and higher prices. A summer marked by heat and low Danube levels Prolonged heat and low Danube levels limited nuclear and hydropower generation in the region. Bulgaria nonetheless remained a net exporter and, during key periods, kept prices below those of neighboring markets. Industry group APSTE attributes this result to the combination of solar plants, batteries and the Kozloduy nuclear plant. On 8 October, the sixth reactor at Kozloduy was in planned maintenance and the fifth was running at reduced output because of the low Danube level. In the early afternoon, photovoltaic plants nonetheless produced close to 4,300 MW, more than national consumption of 4,100 MW. Batteries were charging at the same time at more than 4,000 MW to supply energy in the evening. Wind power remains stalled According to APSTE, solar output declines in winter while consumption rises. Since 2020, photovoltaic capacity has grown by about 600%, to nearly 7 GW, and storage systems are approaching 6 GW / 17 GWh. The association estimates investment in photovoltaics, batteries and related infrastructure at roughly â¬7 billion since 2020. Wind development, by contrast, has practically stopped. Bulgaria has only 716 MW of wind capacity and no new large wind farm has been built since 2013. By comparison, Romania has more than 3.5 GW and Greece more than 6 GW. Wind has a different daily and seasonal profile from solar and can deliver significant output in winter. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 % APSTE calls for easing administrative constraints Nikola Gazdov, chairman of APSTE, says solar power and batteries have significantly strengthened the country's energy security, but that this is not enough. He argues for attracting investment in wind power and says new capacity does not require subsidies, but clear rules and genuine easing of procedures. APSTE says Bulgaria could attract more than â¬4 billion in additional private investment in wind plants and storage systems by 2030. This outlook assumes that institutions provide predictable rules and remove administrative restrictions deemed unnecessary, including for projects located outside renewable acceleration zones.

artigo.texto: Chinese challengers are flexing hard with cheap tech, big screens and ever-faster charging across a dizzying array of new EVs. But there’s one thing they can’t engineer, import or undercut, and that’s heritage. The French know it and that’s why Citroen brought back the 2CV name as a cut-price supermini, and now Peugeot is digging into its own sports car back catalogue. This one isn’t about cheap thrills, though. Revealed at the Paris motor show, the Peugeot RCZ Vision revives the cult RCZ coupe that was built between 2009 and 2015. It revives the name with a potent 368kW electric powertrain, a solid-state battery and a 1000-volt architecture. The French have come out firing at the 2026 Paris motor show, seemingly doubling their efforts in the new car space and the headline numbers for Peugeot’s reborn sports coupe, the RCZ, are serious. Peugeot claims 500 horsepower, which is about 368kW. It also claims up to 600km of driving range and a target energy consumption of 11.5kWh/100km on the WLTP cycle. The efficiency figure is still to be confirmed but that’s a frugal number for something this quick and powerful. Peugeot hasn’t given a battery capacity but something around the 70kWh realm appears to line up with the maths. The solid-state cells were developed with Factorial Energy, an American energy technology company based in Massachusetts. It’s currently developing next-gen solid-state battery technology for EVs, aerospace and even defence. The battery cell pack is claimed to be just 110mm thick and that thin pack is the main reason the roofline sits so low. The Peugeot RCZ Vision rides on a platform based on Stellantis’ new STLA One architecture, which goes into production under the next E-208 in 2027. Stellantis had previously talked about 800-volt electrics and LFP batteries for STLA One but the RCZ Vision steps that up to 1000 volts, which is what allows the 10-minute fast-charge claim. The tech gets even more interesting inside. Peugeot calls its approach ‘X-by-Wire’. The steering wheel has no mechanical connection to the front wheels and the steering ratio changes with speed. The Hypersquare control looks like a tray-table with cupholders turned on its side, and Peugeot reckons it turns slightly less than one full rotation from lock to lock, making it super direct. Conventional steering wheels takes about three turns lock to lock, give or take. Brake-by-wire also replaces the hydraulic link between the pedal and the brakes, which Peugeot says makes regenerative braking smoother. Level 2++ hands-free driving is also on board. Peugeot has bucked the screen-count arms race by fitting transparent Micro LED displays and the central screen can be switched off completely so it virtually disappears from view. “With Peugeot RCZ Vision, we are setting out our vision with a car firmly focused on the future, dedicated to delivering the ultimate driving pleasure,” said Peugeot CEO Alain Favey. There are plenty of nods to the original car too. The ‘double-bubble’ glass roof and the active rear spoiler both return and the forged wheels measure 21 inches at the front and 22 inches at the rear. Unlike the original, the RCZ Vision has a four-seat cabin that Peugeot says can carry two adults comfortably in the back. Peugeot hasn’t committed to building the RCZ and two-door coupes are a niche segment these days. The original RCZ’s old rival, the Audi TT, is reportedly due for an electric comeback, though, so you shouldn’t rule out a production version just yet. Even if this exact car never reaches showrooms, much of what’s underneath it will. Peugeot is one of four Stellantis brands sharing 70 per cent of the group’s future investment. The STLA One hardware, steer-by-wire and L2++ tech will spread across the wider Stellantis line-up, starting with the next Peugeot E-208.

artigo.texto: O evento ocorre em um contexto de forte crescimento contínuo da demanda por eletricidade no Vietnã, impulsionado pelo crescimento industrial e por uma onda de investimentos em centros de dados de inteligência artificial (AIDCs). A Trinasolar lança o sistema de painéis solares e armazenamento de energia Vertex N G3 TOPCon 3.0. A Trinasolar, uma das empresas líderes mundiais em energia solar e soluções inteligentes de armazenamento de energia, lançou recentemente o painel solar Vertex N G3 TOPCon 3.0 (até 760W) e o sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) Elementa 3 de 6,25MWh em um evento realizado na cidade de Ho Chi Minh. O Vertex N G3 foi desenvolvido na plataforma de tecnologia de células fotovoltaicas TOPCon 3.0 da Trinasolar, apresentando quatro avanços tecnológicos principais. A tecnologia da plataforma de células fotovoltaicas Ultra aumenta a potência e a eficiência bifacial. As tecnologias de corte múltiplo e passivação de borda reduzem as perdas de corrente, ao mesmo tempo que melhoram a eficiência sob sombreamento parcial e minimizam o fenômeno de pontos quentes. A tecnologia de encapsulamento de ultra-alta densidade aumenta a eficiência e a potência de saída do módulo. O coeficiente de bifacialidade atinge 85% ± 5%, permitindo que o módulo utilize radiação adicional da face posterior em condições adequadas. O coeficiente de temperatura de potência de -0,26%/°C ajuda a limitar a degradação de potência quando operando em altas temperaturas, sendo adequado para o clima quente do Vietnã. A degradação máxima de potência é de 0,35% ao ano a partir do segundo ano e é garantida por 30 anos, proporcionando aos desenvolvedores de projetos uma base mais sólida para estimar a produção de eletricidade e a eficiência do projeto a longo prazo. A Trina Storage também apresentou o Elementa 3, um sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) de grande escala com capacidade de 6,25 MWh, utilizando células de bateria de 587 Ah desenvolvidas pela Trinasolar. O Elementa 3 apoia a integração de fontes de energia renováveis e aumenta a flexibilidade na operação do sistema elétrico, incluindo projetos conectados à rede, à medida que o Vietnã continua a expandir a energia solar para atender à crescente demanda das indústrias e centros de dados. O armazenamento de energia também está recebendo crescente atenção no planejamento de desenvolvimento energético do Vietnã. De acordo com o Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético VIII revisado, o Vietnã pretende desenvolver de 10.000 a 16.300 MW de capacidade de armazenamento de energia em baterias até 2030, o equivalente a aproximadamente 5,5% a 6,9% da capacidade total de geração de energia do país. O plano também orienta a implantação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em áreas próximas a fontes de energia renovável ou grandes centros de consumo para dar suporte à operação do sistema elétrico. O projeto integrado de energia solar e armazenamento de energia da Trinasolar no Corona Resort em Phu Quoc é um exemplo da aplicação prática de soluções fotovoltaicas e de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) no Vietnã.

artigo.texto: “Kerthi Bhumi Satwika is not merely a place name, but a reflection of a broader shift in Bali’s development approach,” he said in a statement on Saturday (October 10). Koster said the six designated low-emission areas are Ubud, the Nusa Penida Islands, Nusa Dua, Kuta, Sanur, and the Gajah Mada Cultural Heritage Area in Denpasar. Each area has its own characteristics and priorities, he said. Ubud focuses on cultural and environmental tourism, while Nusa Penida emphasizes preserving the island's ecosystem. Meanwhile, Nusa Dua, Kuta, and Sanur are expected to promote the consistent adoption of environmentally friendly tourism practices. The Gajah Mada Cultural Heritage Area in Denpasar, meanwhile, aims to integrate historical preservation with sustainable urban development. Koster said the designation aims to align spatial planning policies with efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and accelerate the adoption of clean energy across sectors. “We must ensure that economic and tourism development go hand in hand with environmental protection and the long-term sustainability of local communities,” he said. The low-emission area policy was also developed in response to Bali's increasingly complex development challenges, ranging from transportation and mobility to climate change, the governor added. The program is built around five strategic pillars: Green Energy, Green Transportation, Green Ecosystems, Green Tourism Industry, and Green Society. Through these pillars, the Bali provincial government seeks to reduce emissions from the energy, transportation, and tourism sectors, as well as through waste management at the source. Koster emphasized that the program's success depends on consistent implementation and strong cross-sectoral coordination. The initiative also calls for active collaboration among various tourism businesses, traditional villages, local communities, research institutions, and the wider public. He added that the program aligns with Bali's development vision, Nangun Sat Kerthi Loka Bali, and the principles of local wisdom embodied in Sad Kerthi. It is also consistent with the Future Bali Development Guidelines and the 100-Year Bali New Era roadmap for 2025–2125. artigo.texto: Renewable energy producer R.Power is nearing completion of its first utility-scale BESS project in Romania, the 127MW / 254 MWh Scornicesti BESS. EPC contractor Parapet, working with R.Power’s in-house EPC management team, commenced construction in spring 2026. It has, over the past three months, laid foundations and deployed all 46 battery units and 23 containerised medium-voltage transformer stations. Scornicesti BESS will be one of the first assets of its kind in Romania, and one of the largest BESS assets to enter operation in Central & Eastern Europe (CEE). Connecting Scornicesti directly to the high-voltage national transmission grid, operated by Transelectrica, is a major undertaking that goes well beyond a standard project and has required extensive design works. Once connected, expected in late 2026/early 2027, the project will become a strategic energy asset for Romania’s national energy system. R.Power secured a €46 million financing package for the project in June 2026. Under the terms of the deal, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) provided €44 million in investment and bridge financing, while Polish development bank Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego (BGK) issued a €2.3 million bank guarantee to secure the long-term optimisation contract in place with regional trading partner GEN-I. The project, located in Olt County, is co-owned through a JV with France’s Eiffel Investment Group. “As a utility-scale asset connected to the national transmission grid, Scornicesti BESS will actively support the stabilisation of Romania’s energy system.” said Florin Federenciuc, R.Power Country Head for Romania. “By integrating BESS at the heart of its energy transition, Romania is strengthening its grid resilience and supporting the roll-out of renewable energy generation. Having contracted our first Romanian PV assets just two years ago, we are proud to now be playing this vital role in one of Europe’s fastest growth energy transition markets. “Together with EBRD, BGK, Eiffel Investment Group and GEN-I, we look forward to completing the final phase of construction and commissioning and getting this strategic asset to work”. Scornicesti BESS forms part of one of Central and Eastern Europe’s largest utility-scale energy storage pipelines. R.Power’s BESS portfolio in operations and under construction in CEE currently stands at 0.9 GW / 3 GWh, with an additional 0.7 GW / 2.8 GWh of commercialised, ready-to-build projects.

artigo.texto: Peugeot RCZ Vision previews a solid-state battery and 1000V charging Peugeot RCZ Vision is a 500 hp concept with a 110 mm solid-state battery, up to 600 km of range and 10–80% charging in 10 minutes. A 110 mm-thick solid-state battery, 500 hp and a 10–80% charge in ten minutes: Peugeot has presented an unusual continuation of the RCZ story. The RCZ Vision remains a concept and brand manifesto, but it showcases design and technologies Peugeot links to its future models. The key feature is a 1000V electrical architecture and solid-state battery cells developed with Factorial Energy. The concept uses an architecture based on the STLA One platform. Peugeot quotes up to 600 km of range and a target combined WLTP energy consumption of 11.5 kWh/100 km. The company explicitly says that consumption figure still has to be confirmed. The original RCZ is referenced by the sports-coupe format and its distinctive double-bubble roof. The new car is far more futuristic, with a low silhouette, pronounced fenders, a transparent upper body section and an active rear spoiler that deploys while driving. Inside, there is a Hypersquare control and Steer-by-Wire with no mechanical steering connection to the wheels. RCZ Vision is also Peugeot’s first model to demonstrate Brake-by-Wire electronic brake control. The concept differs from the former coupe by much more than the absence of a petrol engine. Peugeot presents RCZ Vision as a showcase for solid-state batteries, a 1000V architecture, X-by-Wire technologies and a new generation of the i-Cockpit driver interface. Peugeot has not announced a production date, a final production specification or a price. It is therefore too early to call RCZ Vision a confirmed return of the RCZ to showrooms: for now, the company has revived the idea of the coupe as a concept and shown technologies that could reach future Peugeot models.

artigo.texto: A corrida pela IA está a transformar o mercado global de energia. De acordo com um relatório da Wood Mackenzie, avançado pelo TechCrunch, o uso de baterias tornou-se uma opção mais barata do que as tradicionais turbinas a gás natural para alimentar grandes data centers. O estudo analisou 43 mercados em todo o mundo e confirmou a vantagem financeira das baterias em todos os continentes. A principal causa desta inversão reside na enorme procura por processamento na cloud, que esgotou os stocks de turbinas a gás disponíveis e inflacionou os preços destes equipamentos. Atrasos logísticos e a expansão solar Atualmente, a compra de uma turbina a gás simples implica um tempo de espera de dois a quatro anos. Nos modelos mais eficientes, as listas prolongam-se até à década de 2030. Com este estrangulamento logístico, a consultora projeta que a energia fornecida por baterias continuará a baixar de preço, enquanto a geração a gás tenderá a ficar cada vez mais cara. A energia solar surge como o complemento desta transição, assumindo-se como a forma mais barata de nova geração elétrica em todas as regiões analisadas. No mercado dos EUA, os grandes projetos solares conseguem evitar taxas de importação através de benefícios fiscais em vigor até ao final de 2027. Na Ásia, a China destaca-se com custos de armazenamento significativamente inferiores aos dos países vizinhos. Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, analista principal da Wood Mackenzie, resume o panorama atual ao afirmar que "esta mudança económica é decisiva e cada vez maior", sublinhando a perda de predominância do gás natural perante as novas tecnologias.

artigo.texto: Volkswagen Group, its battery subsidiary PowerCo SE, and Chinese battery manufacturer Gotion High-tech are expanding their strategic partnership with plans to establish three joint ventures focused on lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery production in Europe and North Africa. The agreement covers battery cell manufacturing in Valencia, Spain, and Šurany, Slovakia, alongside a new LFP cathode material production facility in Kenitra, Morocco. The initiative aims to strengthen Europe’s battery supply chain, reduce dependence on external suppliers, and support the growing demand for more affordable electric vehicles. The companies have worked together since 2020, with Gotion serving as both a battery cell supplier to Volkswagen Group and a strategic partner of PowerCo. The expanded cooperation will extend their relationship into industrial production, joint procurement, and sales activities across Europe. Why Volkswagen Is Expanding LFP Battery Production LFP batteries are becoming increasingly important to the electric vehicle industry because of their competitive production costs, long service life, and robust performance. Compared with some other lithium-ion battery chemistries, they offer a cost-effective solution for mass-market electric cars. According to forecasts cited by the companies, LFP batteries could increase their share of the European battery market from approximately 10% today to between 40% and 60% by 2030. Despite the expected growth, Europe currently lacks significant dedicated LFP battery production capacity. Expanding manufacturing in the region could help automakers secure battery supplies, improve cost competitiveness, and reduce exposure to supply chain disruptions. The Volkswagen-PowerCo-Gotion partnership is designed to address this gap by establishing a more integrated regional supply chain, spanning cathode materials and battery cell production. Thomas Schmall, Volkswagen Group’s Board Member for Technology and Chairman of PowerCo’s Supervisory Board, said the expanded partnership represents an important step toward strengthening Europe’s battery industry. He also highlighted Volkswagen’s ambition to cover the battery value chain, from development and cathode materials to manufacturing. PowerCo CEO Frank Blome described the agreement as another milestone in building Europe’s battery industry, emphasizing the importance of supply chain resilience and faster industrialization. Three Joint Ventures Across Three Locations The planned joint ventures will divide production responsibilities between Spain, Slovakia, and Morocco, with each location playing a specific role in the emerging battery supply chain. Valencia, Spain: LFP Battery Cell Production Volkswagen’s PowerCo battery factory under construction in Valencia is expected to be transferred to a joint venture between PowerCo and Gotion. PowerCo will hold a 51% majority stake, while Gotion will own the remaining 49%. Both companies intend to manage the operation jointly. One of the facility’s main objectives is to establish Valencia as a European production hub for Volkswagen’s Unified Cells using LFP technology. These batteries are expected to support more cost-effective electric vehicles, particularly in the high-volume market segment. The previously announced investment and job creation plans for the Valencia facility are expected to remain unchanged. Šurany, Slovakia: Batteries for EVs and Energy Storage The second joint venture will focus on LFP battery cell production at Gotion’s planned factory in Šurany, Slovakia. Under the proposed ownership structure, Gotion will hold a 51% majority stake, with PowerCo owning 49%. The companies intend to manage the operation together. The facility is expected to manufacture LFP cells for electric vehicles as well as energy storage systems. This broader focus could help meet demand from both the automotive industry and the growing market for stationary battery storage. The Slovakian project will also give PowerCo a direct stake in another regional battery manufacturing operation, complementing its activities in Spain. Kenitra, Morocco: LFP Cathode Materials The third joint venture will establish a new production facility in Kenitra, Morocco, dedicated to cathode materials used in LFP batteries. Gotion will hold a 51% majority stake, while PowerCo will own the remaining 49%. Both companies will jointly manage the venture. Cathode materials are essential components of lithium-ion batteries, and securing their supply is an important part of building a resilient battery industry. By adding production capacity in Morocco, the partners aim to diversify their sources of key materials, strengthen supply security, and expand the regional value chain supporting European battery manufacturing. Together, the three locations are intended to create a more integrated industrial network for LFP batteries, connecting materials production with battery cell manufacturing. Volkswagen and PowerCo Outline Their Investment Commitments The agreement includes substantial financial commitments from both companies, reflecting the scale of their planned industrial cooperation. PowerCo is expected to contribute approximately €470 million by 2030 to acquire its 49% stakes in the Šurany and Kenitra joint ventures. In return, Gotion plans to invest approximately €1.1 billion to acquire a 49% stake in the Valencia joint venture, where PowerCo will retain majority ownership. The investments are intended to distribute financial commitments and industrial responsibilities across the three facilities while supporting the partners’ long-term production plans. However, the agreements remain subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions. Approval from Gotion’s shareholders is also required. artigo.texto: The News Despite increasingly critical media coverage of AI and the spread of data centers across the US, one news network has been painting a more positive picture. More than half of the references to data centers on Fox News over the last two years would have left viewers with a favorable impression, compared to less than 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW, according to a new Semafor analysis of mentions of data centers on each network. The mentions were pulled from closed captions preserved by the Internet Archive, which keeps a digital, searchable library of recorded TV news. A pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI scored each reference on its content, with the networkâs name removed. Mentions of data centers have, predictably, shot up across all three networks in recent months as political backlash against AI swells and the data centers themselves have become a salient issue ahead of the midterms. But Foxâs opinion and morning shows, including My View with Lara Trump, Fox & Friends, and Life, Liberty & Levin, leaned on the promise of AI, economic investment and the race with China, skewing Foxâs coverage more favorably, the analysis showed. The networkâs news shows were more measured. In an Aug. 23 monologue that at one point featured a chyron reading âThe case for data centers,â Fox host Brian Kilmeade acknowledged âreal concerns,â but argued that âsaying no to data centers nationwide also means saying no to the tax dollars that can flow into a community. â¦ If Americans donât build the infrastructure to meet the demand, somebody else will.â On CNN and MS NOW, the criticism focused as much on the facilitiesâ political toxicity as on harms like power bills or water use, casting them as unpopular with voters and a liability for politicians who back them heading into the midterms. Data centers âare driving up energy costs, sucking up water supplies, wiping out rather than creating jobs,â MS NOWâs Katy Tur said in May. âPoliticians beware.â Polling shows that across demographic groups, Americans hold increasingly negative views of data centers: More than half of Americans say data centers are mostly bad for the environment, Pew Research Center found last month, compared with 39% in January. Fox News did not comment for this story. In this article: Maxâs view The pro-data center programming on Fox News comes as the right tries to define its positions in an AI-fueled, post-Donald Trump future. Foxâs favorable data center coverage mirrors Trumpâs position on their growth and the need for AI companies to help fuel the US economy. âThe only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,â Trump wrote on Truth Social in August. âIf we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.â But anger about data centers and the rapid advancement of AI represents a faultline within the MAGA coalition that swept Trump back into office. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., have questioned some data centers in their states, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott seems to have flipped from supporting data centers to looking to slow their growth in his state amid a tougher-than-expected reelection campaign. Some on the right I have talked to in the last several months worry that Fox News, which Trump watches religiously, and other pro-data center voices are encouraging the president to take positions that are broadly unpopular with his rural and suburban base. âThe Big Tech oligarchs, the guys driving AI, did a terrible job,â Steve Bannon, a staunchly anti-AI Trump ally, told the Daily Signal in September. âThey came in to try to muscle local communities, and particularly since President Trumpâs strongest base is in exurban and rural communities, thatâs where they were really the ugliest, and they havenât made their case, and they particularly havenât made their case at the local level about the economics of this, and the energy of this, and the water of this, and the manifestation of what these things are going to be used for.â Room for Disagreement Not all of Foxâs data center coverage has been rosy; its tenor grew slightly less favorable in 2026 compared to last year. âItâs taxing our system way too much on water, agriculture land, or electricity. Weâre gonna implode,â the Texas agriculture commissioner said in an interview on a weekend Fox show in August. âWe just canât do it. Thereâs not enough.

artigo.texto: Key Points - The makeup of the next Congress could set the policy trajectory for the future of the AI buildout. - At stake is $5 trillion in capital spending through 2030, as public opposition to data centers gains strength. - Wall Street is paying close attention to the election but feels reassured by the prospect of a presidential veto on any bold legislation that comes from Capitol Hill. Public opposition to data center construction and negative sentiment about artificial intelligence in general are growing, setting up AI as one of the defining political issues of the 2026 midterm elections, set for Nov. 3. Wall Street has gone all-in betting on AI, with total capital expenditures expected in excess of $5 trillion by 2030 . That spending is accelerating even as the technology remains largely unproven in terms of profitability and productivity . With electoral and financial forces at odds, equity markets and national politics could be on a collision course in November over the fate of the AI buildout, and some analysts say the fallout could persist well beyond the election. "What I consistently hear from investors is that the opposition to data centers is really about the political backlash and that after the midterms things get a lot better. But I think that after the midterms, things get worse," Ed Mills, a political analyst at Raymond James, told CNBC. "That is a huge blind spot for the market." Others take a more measured view while admitting to the possibility of a market dip if Democrats win big, since Democrats are generally viewed to be more critical of the AI buildout than Republicans. "[We see the] midterms themselves producing muted results across the broader market, although we see a potential knee jerk near-term reaction if Democrats outperform expectations," analyst Ariana Salvatore at JPMorgan wrote in a report last month. Legislative prospects Some kind of AI law is expected to come out of the next Congress, though it's not clear yet what it will look like, how it will be delivered, or whether it would clear the president's desk. AI companies have already opened themselves up for the possibility of regulation, calling for a collective slowdown due to product safety concerns. Many on Wall Street think the appeal is less about safety and more about establishing anti-competitive protections that will steer the industry toward a duopoly comprising the leading proprietary model makers, Anthropic and OpenAI. Legislation could take many different forms, including utility bill protections for consumers, a measure that already made it through the House before getting spiked by Democrats in the Senate on the grounds that it was " toothless ." A federal moratorium on data center construction, similar to the one enacted by New York , is another proposal that analysts are discussing. An AI tax has also been proposed, with advocates saying it would allow for partial public ownership of the technology while reducing any harmful effect on the tax base. That issue has attracted international attention as AI threatens to redistribute national income toward profit and away from wages, potentially eroding labor income as a source of tax revenue. "So much of the AI future is about these multinational companies trying to attribute their earnings to their [intellectual property] rather than to the productivity of their workers, and that's going to mean huge tax base erosion," Jeremy Bearer-Friend, a George Washington University tax professor whose work became the basis for the AI tax proposal, told CNBC. Other proposals include a measure that would hold AI developers legally liable for harms committed by their software, and a " governance framework " from the Senate Commerce Committee that builds on a 2017 legislative plan . Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., who backed the original plan and has since pursued AI policy including safety standards, independent testing and consumer protection, has called for an "AI-era workforce initiative modeled on the GI Bill." Gridlock scenario "Democrats are more opposed [to data center construction] than Republicans," Mills, at Raymond James, said, adding that "it looks to be a good year for Democrats." If Democrats take even one chamber of Congress, that will translate into gridlock in Washington, where a Republican White House wields veto power over any assertive legislation, which would reassure the tech industry. President Donald Trump is closely allied with Big Tech. He has received hundreds of millions of dollars in political donations from Silicon Valley, which has been described as a dedicated donor class for the administration. Trump featured tech moguls prominently at his inauguration and received a 24-karat gold and glass statue from Apple CEO Tim Cook. The Trump administration claims to already have something of an AI framework , but has declined to share it publicly. This has drawn criticism from two Democratic senators , who say it's been "shaped in secret by a handful of executives at self-interested trillion-dollar companies." What's been released concerning the draft framework is heavily redacted . "What we want to learn is, how is the White House [deciding] which frontier AI models get released to the public and which don't? Under what terms or conditions?" Deana El-Mallawany, an attorney with nonpartisan advocacy group Protect Democracy, told CNBC. The group filed a Freedom of Information Act request for the release of the policy document. In terms of potential legislation, the White House veto means that any new AI law may get tacked onto a higher priority, bipartisan piece of legislation, such as an appropriations bill, a bill to raise the debt ceiling, a defense authorization or a tax extension package. But despite the assumed protection from the White House, anti-AI public sentiment could still force an atypical level of agreement in Congress on the subject of AI. "Could we see 67-plus senators vote in favor of [a data center moratorium]?

artigo.texto: Indiana utility regulators unanimously approved a plan for utility AES Indiana to build the solar, battery storage and electric line project needed to power a 390-megawatt Google data center project in Monrovia. At the Oct. 7 meeting, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission said the proposed project meets a 2025 state law that requires data centers and other large electricity users to cover 80% of costs reasonably assigned to it. The law also requires the plan to protect existing and future customers. The Monrovia project is the first data center filed under the new law. AES estimates the infrastructure investment at $1.3 billion. AES Indiana says Google will pay all of the costs. But the order says it is reasonable for existing customers to be assigned a share of the cost upgrades. The Citizens Action Coalition objected to this. AES Indiana says Google’s payments to the utility system will make up for customers’ costs. The Monrovia project, southwest of Indianapolis in Morgan County, will include two battery energy storage systems and a solar facility. The total project cost is $737.3 million. Commissioner Joby Jerrells said AES Indiana had testified that Google would pay for at least 100% of the costs under the requirement. “Not only does this agreement satisfy the statutory requirement, it exceeds it substantially,” Jerrells said. Regulators put their approval in a written order. It explains the energy project is designed to mainly serve large electricity customers, like the Google data center, while protecting current AES customers. Several groups joined the case, including the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor, a consumer watchdog; Citizens Action Coalition, a nonprofit consumer advocate; the AES Indiana Industrial Group; and several residents of Morgan County. Brian A. Wright, an electric utility analyst with the consumer counselor’s office, testified that power line transmission upgrades wouldn’t be necessary without the data center’s energy needs. The office did not oppose the plan. “What we’re concerned about is a $74 million set of transmission upgrades that AES Indiana identified that it had to make specifically because this Google data center is being added to the grid,” Ben Inskeep, program director at Citizens Action Coalition, said. AES US Utilities CEO Gustavo Garaviglia said in testimony that Google will pay $32.3 million for direct connection facilities, while $73.8 million in network upgrades will be included in AES’s transmission rate base and recovered in future retail rates. Bickey Rimal, vice president of consulting firm Concentric Energy Advisors, testified for AES that it wouldn’t be reasonable to assign all transmission upgrades to Google because the utility hadn’t done that with a customer in the past, and the upgrades would benefit all customers. The commission agreed. Inskeep said the data center, not the customer, should foot the upgrade costs. “We already have high bills here in Indianapolis,” he said. “We don’t need more rate increases caused by data centers to be added on top.” In a statement, AES Indiana President Brandi Davis-Handy called the approval “an important milestone.” The company has said that the partnership with Google protects existing customers. “None of those costs are shifted to existing AES Indiana customers,” it said. Google’s head of data centers in the Americas, Will Conkling, said that the company is paying for 100% of its electricity and any new infrastructure required to serve them. AES said the agreement will benefit customers by spreading fixed costs to more users and bring the cost per customer down, and that its modeling estimated about $770 million in savings during the term of the project. The contract with Google lasts at least 15 years, according to AES, and includes assurances that customers won’t get stuck paying for upgrades if Google scales back or leaves the project. AES also requested to keep certain information confidential, including portions of temporary, electric and construction service agreements and testimony. The Citizens Action Coalition raised concerns about that. The commission approved the request for confidentiality because the information includes trade secrets exempt from public disclosure under state law. A spokesperson for AES Indiana, Claire Rice, said in response to emailed questions seeking details about the agreements and what customer protections exist, that the company’s filings could be found in the case. “I want to clarify that the agreements are filed publicly with only certain competitively sensitive and confidential information redacted. The terms and details of the customer protection provisions and customer benefits have not been redacted,” she said. The electric, construction and temporary service agreements are filed as exhibits, but they include many redactions, including dollar amounts, rate schedules and timelines. The utility commission recently agreed to reconsider its June approval of a rate increase for AES Indiana. It will consider evidence related to the Monrovia data center project and the announced acquisition of AES’s parent company by BlackRock and other investors. The review will continue into 2027. artigo.texto: Segundo a CNBC, Wall Street vem tentando vender a investidores a infraestrutura de inteligência artificial como uma aposta imobiliária capaz de diversificar carteiras, mesmo diante da crescente rejeição de parte da população americana à construção de data centers. Os fundos que prometem participação na estrutura física da economia de IA ainda são, em sua maioria, restritos a investidores institucionais, como fundos de pensão, mas a tendência já chegou de forma limitada ao mercado de varejo. A Blackstone está à frente desse movimento. A gestora criou neste ano o Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust, um fundo imobiliário — REIT, na sigla em inglês — negociado na NYSE. Em entrevista à CNBC, o CEO Nick Pell afirmou que a empresa viu ali a oportunidade de capturar o mercado de data centers já estabilizados e criar um veículo no mercado público para esse tipo de ativo. Procurada, a Blackstone não quis comentar. O fundo prioriza data centers em mercados já maduros, como o norte da Virgínia e Dallas, onde a presença desse tipo de instalação é anterior ao boom da IA. Pell disse que essa é a forma de menor risco de se posicionar no setor e que a Blackstone pode escolher a dedo ativos dentro de um mercado que ela avalia em US$ 300 bilhões. A empresa vendeu 87,5 milhões de ações a US$ 20 cada na estreia, em meados de maio. Desde então, porém, o fundo acumula queda de cerca de 16%, com os papéis fechando abaixo de US$ 17 na quinta-feira. A Blackstone não é a única. A Blue Owl, que já administra um fundo privado de infraestrutura digital, estuda lançar um REIT público que pode chegar a US$ 6,5 bilhões, incorporando investimentos já existentes em data centers. A empresa afirma ter mais de 130 data centers em 32 mercados globais, com mais de US$ 18 bilhões em ativos. O co-CEO Marc Lipschultz defendeu o setor em publicação no LinkedIn, citando um dos melhores perfis de retorno de longo prazo das últimas décadas. A Blue Owl não comentou com a CNBC. O REIT da Blackstone, por sua vez, ainda não aplicou capital em nenhum investimento. Nem todo papel do setor vai bem. A Brookfield listou na NYSE em julho a Csquare, sua prestadora de serviços de data center, cujas ações caem quase 16% desde a estreia. Equinix e Digital Realty Trust, desenvolvedoras que também negociam como REITs, têm bom desempenho no longo prazo, mas os papéis estagnaram desde o lançamento do fundo da Blackstone. Já o setor de REITs como um todo teve desempenho melhor neste ano do que o habitual em períodos de juros e rendimentos de títulos em alta, mas a maior parte dos ganhos veio antes da intensificação do estresse no mercado de títulos, e muitos fundos sofreram correções desde agosto. Rejeição política e riscos A aposta esbarra em uma resistência política que era menor quando a Blackstone lançou seu fundo. Pesquisa da Gallup mostrou que 70% dos americanos se opõem à construção de um data center em sua região, rejeição que é bipartidária: levantamento do New York Times/Siena deste outono apontou cerca de dois terços de oposição independentemente do partido. Nova York foi o primeiro estado a aprovar uma moratória para novas aprovações de data centers de grande porte, em julho, seguido pelo Texas em agosto, quando o governador Greg Abbott ordenou a suspensão de novas autorizações. Os riscos também aparecem em projetos específicos. As ações da Oracle caíram 4% no fim de setembro depois que a companhia enviou um aviso de força maior relacionado ao Project Jupiter, campus de data centers no Novo México que faz parte da expansão Stargate, desenvolvida pela Blue Owl. A Oracle busca adiar pagamentos caso o projeto não esteja operacional até 2028, citando entraves regulatórios e oposição local, mas afirma que o empreendimento segue no prazo. Fora dos EUA, uma empresa australiana de data centers com apoio da Nvidia e da Blackstone retirou seu IPO do mercado por falta de interesse dos investidores. Há ainda a volatilidade do próprio mercado de IA. Na quinta-feira, papéis ligados ao tema recuaram após a informação de que uma projeção de receita da OpenAI ficou cerca de US$ 20 bilhões abaixo de estimativa anterior. Sabur Mollah, professor de finanças do Gettysburg College, disse que data centers podem ser investimentos atraentes no longo prazo pela demanda por nuvem, IA e armazenamento de dados, com contratos longos gerando receita de aluguel relativamente estável. Ele ressalta, porém, que o setor consome muito capital, depende de energia, refrigeração e conectividade e está sujeito a riscos como avaliação exagerada pelo entusiasmo com IA, dependência de poucos locatários, restrições de energia, obsolescência tecnológica e atrasos de obra.

artigo.texto: Solid-state lithium-metal batteries have long been heralded as the successor to the lithium-ion cells that have dominated the market since 1991. By replacing the flammable organic liquid electrolyte with a solid polymer electrolyte, these batteries promise improved safety, the possibility of using a lithium metal anode with a theoretical capacity of 3860 mAh per gram compared to 372 mAh per gram for graphite, and consequently higher gravimetric and volumetric energy density. Yet a stubborn obstacle has kept them out of commercial devices: the relatively low ionic conductivity of polymer electrolytes, which is typically addressed by incorporating highly dissociated lithium salts such as LiTFSI into a poly(ethylene oxide) host. Now, a team of researchers led by L. Fernandez-Diaz and M.C. Morant-Miñana, publishing in Results in Engineering, has shown that one of the most decisive factors in solid-state battery performance is not the chemistry of the materials at all, but something far more mundane: how long and how fast the electrode slurry is mixed. The composite cathode of a solid-state battery is a dense, non-porous blend of active material, conductive additive and a portion of solid electrolyte known as the catholyte. Unlike conventional lithium-ion cells, where a liquid electrolyte seeps into every pore, the solid-state version has no pore-filling liquid to rescue poor contacts. Every particle must touch its neighbour intimately, and both ions and electrons need homogeneous, percolating pathways through the electrode. The conductive additive in this study is Super C65, a carbon black from Imerys, which must form an unbroken electronic network threading through the cathode. The active material is carbon-coated lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, whose own carbon coating enhances intrinsic electronic conductivity and interfacial lithium transfer. The researchers were careful to distinguish between these two carbons: the factory-applied coating on the LFP particles and the C65 introduced during electrode processing behave very differently under the forces of mixing. To isolate the effects of processing, the team prepared slurries under dry-room conditions with a dew point below minus 60 degrees Celsius, using a bead mill to first dissolve LiTFSI in acetonitrile and then mix in high molecular weight PEO to form the catholyte. The LFP and C65 powders were dry-mixed in a planetary vacuum mixer at 200, 750 or 1500 revolutions per minute, and the resulting powder blend was then wet-mixed into the catholyte for 60, 120 or 180 minutes. Five slurries were produced in total, each cast onto carbon-coated aluminium current collectors and dried under vacuum. Crucially, the researchers deliberately skipped calendering, the mechanical compaction step common in electrode manufacturing, so that the morphological fingerprints left by the mixing process itself would remain visible in the finished electrodes. One of the study’s most elegant methodological contributions is the introduction of a relative viscosity parameter. Batch-to-batch variability in the PEO raw material, stemming from differences in molecular weight distribution, meant that absolute viscosity measurements could not be compared reliably across samples. By normalizing the slurry viscosity to the viscosity of the corresponding catholyte at the end of its own mixing, the team could decouple the true effects of mixing time and speed from uncontrolled fluctuations in the polymer feedstock. Validation experiments with four separate preparations, including three different PEO batches, confirmed that this normalization substantially reduced variability, offering a practical tool that other laboratories can adopt to make their slurry comparisons meaningful. The rheological results revealed a counterintuitive trend. Longer wet mixing times and higher dry mixing speeds both reduced slurry viscosity, and the researchers traced this not to further polymer degradation but to the progressive deagglomeration of the carbon black. Gel permeation chromatography showed that the PEO molecular weight decreased exponentially toward a plateau, with an apparent scission-rate constant of 7.49 times ten to the minus seven per minute, but since total mixing times stayed below the point where degradation becomes negligible, the viscosity drop had to come from elsewhere. As C65 agglomerates break apart, the number of carbon particles rises, promoting immobilization of polymer chains and reducing chain entanglement, a mechanism previously described by Hoffman and colleagues. More effective deagglomeration also increases interparticle volume, allowing more solvent molecules to occupy the spaces between carbon particles and thereby lowering the suspension viscosity. These rheological differences translated directly into electrode microstructure. Scanning electron microscopy of surfaces and argon ion-milled cross-sections, analysed with ImageJ, showed that longer wet mixing produced electrodes with lower porosity, higher active material loading and fewer surface lumps, because lower viscosity allows better particle rearrangement and compaction during drying. In the dry mixing series, the sample processed at 1500 rpm displayed the most homogeneous morphology, while the 200 rpm sample exhibited a highly cracked surface, suggesting that large C65 agglomerates weaken the mechanical integrity of the composite cathode and hinder uniform polymer distribution. Porosity values ranged from about 1.65 percent for the longest wet mixing time to nearly 3 percent for the mildest conditions, differences that proved consequential for transport properties. Electronic and ionic conductivity measurements told a more nuanced story. Reference pellets containing as little as 5 weight percent C65 achieved electronic conductivities of roughly ten to the minus two siemens per centimetre, confirming that this modest carbon fraction is sufficient for percolation. artigo.texto: Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca Bellan: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco, which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony Ha: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York. I believe it’s a one year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried. It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step. Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc. And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant. artigo.texto: A data center moratorium could once again be moving forward in Michigan City, but who controls the language is a topic of debate. The city council introduced, then tabled, an ordinance last month, to give the city’s planning department a chance to weigh in. But this week, council members announced a new ordinance, similar to the last one. It would suspend the approval of new data center developments, until the city adds regulations to its zoning ordinance or until July 31, 2028. It explicitly excludes both phases of Google’s current development. Council member Bryant Dabney said the pause would let city officials evaluate the Google project, before allowing more. “Not something that we heard happened in Texas or in Tennessee or wherever it may be. We’ll be able to get real data regarding noise, water usage, energy and so forth, from a data center right here in Michigan City,” Dabney said. But the sponsors of the original ordinance complained that they weren’t consulted about the new one. Council member Joseph Nelson called it disingenuous. "I worked my butt off for this, me and Nancy [Moldenhauer] and a lot of good people," Nelson said. "So, for you to come in and swoop and do this and not speak to me or Nancy about this, I do not appreciate that." Reaction from residents was mixed. While they want a moratorium, they had concerns with the way the ordinance was written and presented. Just Transition Northwest Indiana Executive Director Ashley Williams opposed letting the moratorium end as soon as new regulations are adopted. “It pauses just long enough to create an illusion of action while the planning department skates in an M-3 Data Center zoning district that we know it’s been working on behind the scenes, without public knowledge or input up until this point,” Williams told council members. Residents also voiced concerns about Google’s data center, including potential emissions from diesel generators and the storage of diesel fuel. Since the ordinance wasn’t filed in time for the council to take official action Tuesday, a formal first reading is scheduled for the next meeting.

(WAFF) - Doug Jones held a rally in Huntsville Sunday as he seeks to become Alabama’s first Democratic governor since 2003, with 23 days remaining until the Nov. 3 midterm election. The former senator discussed issues he said are important to Alabama communities, including expanding Medicaid to help rural areas where hospitals have closed or are at risk of closing. Jones also called for stronger regulations on data centers, including limits on tax incentives and requirements to address their power and water use. Jones points to consistency Jones said his consistency in office should speak to voters. Voters in attendance said they are ready for the change Jones is talking about. Congressional candidate speaks at rally Andrew Sneed, the Democratic candidate for Alabama’s 5th Congressional District, also spoke at the rally. Sneed is facing incumbent Dale Strong in the Nov. 3 election. Sneed said people at the event were given the space to be heard. Jones and Sneed will both be on the Nov. 3 ballot. Tuberville rally set for Thursday Jones’ opponent in the governor’s race, Sen. Tommy Tuberville, will hold a rally Thursday. The Marshall County Republican Club is hosting the event, called “Liberty on the Lake.” Organizers say the event is free and open to anyone in the community who wants to hear from Tuberville. It will run from 4:30 to 6 p.m. Thursday at the Marshall County RSVP building on Highway 431. Strong has not advertised any upcoming campaign events on his social media pages or campaign website. artigo.texto: Um estudo publicado na revista científica Cambridge Prisms: Water estimou em 16,1 bilhões de litros por ano a pegada hídrica da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial (IA) na região metropolitana de São Paulo. O número soma água de refrigeração e de geração de eletricidade. O estudo, assinado pelo pesquisador Guangda Liang, analisou um conjunto de data centers com carga operacional de cerca de 550 megawatts na região. Mais de 46% da pegada hídrica é "água virtual" indireta, consumida na geração hidrelétrica que alimenta essas instalações, não na refrigeração direta dos servidores. Uma pergunta feita a uma IA, uma busca na internet ou um arquivo guardado na nuvem dependem de data centers, instalações que abrigam servidores e consomem recursos naturais para funcionar. Além de eletricidade, essas estruturas podem gastar água para controlar a temperatura dos equipamentos. Por que um data center precisa de água? Os servidores produzem calor durante o funcionamento, e as instalações usam sistemas de refrigeração que podem empregar água, ar ou outras tecnologias para evitar o superaquecimento. "Um data center utiliza água principalmente para resfriar os equipamentos, que geram muito calor durante a operação. Quanto maior o data center, mais calor ele vai gerar e mais água vai consumir", explica Diego Mota Siqueira, do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (INPE). Siqueira chefia o Serviço de Supercomputação (SESUP) do instituto. Publicidade O resultado do estudo veio de modelagem científica, com base em dados de infraestrutura, consumo energético e características dos sistemas hídricos da região. Não é uma medição direta da água consumida pelas instalações, e o próprio pesquisador pede cautela na leitura do número. "Essa resposta é muito relativa. De que tamanho de data center estamos falando? E de que tamanho de cidade? Isso vai determinar diretamente o impacto", afirma Siqueira. O debate ambiental soma-se a outro, econômico. Um data center de IA no Brasil pode valer R$ 25 bilhões e gerar 37 mil empregos, segundo levantamento recente. A fatura de energia também preocupa o setor. A energia necessária para alimentar data centers de IA já é um teste para a infraestrutura elétrica brasileira. O impacto de data centers sobre recursos naturais não é exclusividade brasileira. O boom desses empreendimentos já provocou protesto de moradores na Índia, em caso parecido. O que acontece agora Mesmo com a preocupação ambiental, o Brasil segue incentivando a instalação de data centers. O Senado isentou o setor de impostos por cinco anos, abrindo mão de R$ 5,2 bilhões em arrecadação como estímulo aos investimentos no país.

artigo.texto: QuantumScape Announces QS PowerBlock for In-Rack Energy Storage in AI Data Centers SAN JOSE, Calif., Oct. 08, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — QuantumScape Corporation (NASDAQ: QS), a global leader in solid-state lithium-metal battery technology, today introduced the QS PowerBlock for AI data centers. The modular system can deliver four times the power density and five times the runtime of current data center industry standards. The QS PowerBlock brings QS solid-state lithium-metal battery technology into AI data centers, supporting safer, higher-performing energy storage and 800VDC architecture. An adaptable reference design, QS PowerBlock can fit a variety of module, shelf, and rack formats, and is designed for deployment in industry-standard power rack configurations. Paired with advanced power system components, it can provide AI data center customers with a compelling combination of power, runtime, and safety to power the 1 MW racks of next-generation data centers. In a demonstration using an expected data center training workload, the QS PowerBlock exceeded key specifications set by the Open Compute Project (OCP), the industry consortium that defines open hardware standards for data centers: - 4x the power density, allowing power-hungry AI systems to integrate into compact and cost-effective data center designs. - 5x longer runtime, giving data center operators more margin to smooth out power fluctuations and improve hardware productivity. - Better safety compared to conventional lithium-ion batteries, helping protect billion-dollar infrastructure investments. QS battery cells have demonstrated thermal stability well over 300 °C in third-party and customer safety testing, compared to conventional lithium-ion cells, which typically go into catastrophic thermal runaway at ~180 °C. Dr. Siva Sivaram, CEO and president of QS, said: QS solid-state battery technology offers an unmatched combination of energy, power, and safety for many different applications, from electric vehicles to AI data centers and beyond, “With the QS PowerBlock, we are bringing this value proposition to AI data center customers, to enable the 800VDC designs that will power the next phase of AI growth.” The QS PowerBlock design will be on display at the 2026 OCP Global Summit, October 12–15 at the San Jose Convention Center, at booth C19, hosted by Megmeet, an official partner and power system component provider for the NVIDIA MGX™ Ecosystem. QS also announced that it has joined the OCP as a member. As AI workloads push data centers toward unprecedented power density, QS is joining industry leaders to build the open standards that infrastructure providers depend on. The QS PowerBlock performance results were achieved through prototype testing and modeled system configurations under controlled conditions, with comparisons benchmarked against the OCP Open Rack V3 (ORV3) specification. Final QS PowerBlock performance will depend on product design, system configuration and real-world operating conditions. artigo.texto: Água, calor e baterias gigantes dividem o papel de guardar energia limpa para abastecer cidades inteiras quando a produção cai. A transição global para fontes limpas enfrenta o desafio da intermitência, exigindo megaestruturas capazes de estocar gigawatts de eletricidade quando o sol se põe ou o vento cessa. Por que estocar energia em grande escala exige estruturas tão diferentes? Você já percebeu como a bateria do celular descarrega rápido sob uso intenso? Na rede elétrica de uma metrópole ocorre algo parecido, onde a oferta de eletricidade precisa corresponder exatamente ao consumo em cada segundo para evitar apagões. Quando usinas solares e eólicas geram mais energia do que a cidade precisa, o excesso precisa ser retido em megaestruturas de retenção. Isso se chama armazenamento de energia em escala de rede. A física por trás dessas soluções varia entre reação eletroquímica, acúmulo térmico e energia potencial gravitacional. Enquanto baterias de lítio entregam resposta instantânea em milissegundos, sistemas de hidrelétrica reversível bombeiam milhões de litros de água para reservatórios superiores a 800 metros de altura, obtendo eficiência de ciclo de até 80% ao retransformar esse volume em eletricidade. Quais são as dimensões e capacidades das maiores estruturas de armazenamento do mundo? A dimensão física das maiores obras de armazenamento do planeta impressiona pelo volume de material escavado, pela tolerância a pressões elevadas e pela capacidade de suprir milhões de pessoas continuamente. Capacidade da usina reversível Snowy 2.0 na Austrália: entrega 2.200 MW de potência contínua e 350 GWh de energia acumulada, o suficiente para abastecer 3 milhões de residências por sete dias consecutivos. - Volume de armazenamento térmico no MBR Solar Park em Dubai: acumula 5.907 MWh de energia térmica em sais fundidos mantidos a 565°C dentro de torres e tanques isolados. - Capacidade da maior bateria de rede em Abu Dhabi: complexo BESS com 19 GWh (19.000 MWh) de armazenamento combinado a 5,2 GW de painéis solares para fornecimento constante de 1 GW. - Profundidade e extensão de tunelamento subterrâneo: escavação de 27 quilômetros de túneis por tuneladoras TBM com cavernas de máquinas instaladas a 800 metros abaixo da superfície. - Pressão hidráulica e sistemas de revestimento FACS: anéis de concreto pré-moldado com juntas elásticas projetados para suportar pressões internas brutas de até 60 bar. Como a água e o sal fundido geram eletricidade nos momentos de maior consumo? Durante o meio-dia, quando os painéis solares operam em capacidade máxima e produzem sobra de energia, motores elétricos acionam bombas hidráulicas de alta pressão para erguer a água até um reservatório superior. Paralelamente, em usinas solares concentradas, milhares de espelhos direcionam a luz solar para o topo de uma torre, aquecendo sais líquidos que retêm o calor sem evaporar. Quando a noite chega e a demanda por eletricidade atinge o pico, o processo é invertido sem perder o controle do fluxo. A água retida na montanha desce em alta velocidade por túneis de concreto acionando turbinas Francis reversíveis, enquanto o sal aquecido passa por trocadores de calor que geram vapor para mover geradores convencionais, garantindo energia estável 24 horas por dia. Como é construída uma usina de armazenamento de energia dentro de uma montanha? A engenharia de usinas subterrâneas exige escavações de altíssima precisão em rocha dura para criar cavernas capazes de abrigar geradores do tamanho de prédios de dez andares. O controle do maciço rochoso é feito com tirantes pré-tensionados e concreto projetado para evitar desabamentos durante a operação. O transporte e a montagem de turbinas e rotores que pesam mais de 450 toneladas a centenas de metros abaixo do solo exigem rotas logísticas reforçadas e pontes rolantes de alta capacidade instaladas dentro do próprio complexo subterrâneo. Abaixo, um vídeo do canal oficial Snowy Hydro que mostra a chegada de grandes componentes hidráulicos na obra: Quais normas de engenharia regem a segurança de cavernas e reservatórios de alta pressão? A concepção de estruturas subterrâneas e reservatórios pressurizados obedece a diretrizes internacionais rígidas, como a norma ASCE 56 para instalações subterrâneas e a norma brasileira ABNT NBR 6118 para projeto de estruturas de concreto. Essas especificações definem as margens de segurança contra fadiga do material e fissuração por variação de pressão. A aplicação rigorosa dessas normas assegura que as juntas do revestimento dos túneis e as paredes de retenção suportem ciclos contínuos de enchimento e esvaziamento por mais de um século, impedindo infiltrações no maciço rochoso e mantendo a estabilidade estrutural permanente. Quando é necessário contratar um engenheiro geotécnico para obras de contenção e reservatórios? A execução de reservatórios, contenções de grande porte ou escavações profundas exige obrigatoriamente a consultoria e o projeto assinado por um engenheiro geotécnico e um engenheiro estrutural. Apenas profissionais habilitados possuem conhecimento para analisar a resistência do solo e o comportamento de cargas do terreno. A tentativa de realizar obras de retenção de água ou escavação sem estudos de sondagem e modelagem geotécnica pode resultar em colapsos estruturais, erosões severas e vazamentos catastróficos. Esse tipo de intervenção não é um trabalho artesanal e exige cálculo estrutural rigoroso. Contexto importante: Este artigo é informativo. Para projetos estruturais locais similares, recomenda-se avaliação de engenheiro geotécnico e engenheiro estrutural, especialmente em contextos de risco de escavação, estabilidade de taludes, infiltração ou comprometimento estrutural.

artigo.texto: SACRAMENTO, Calif. — There are many issues Sacramento retiree Laureen Anderson said she is driven to speak out on, like reminding people to get out and vote early. Another she said are data center’s impacts on communities and the environment. “I’m very passionate about; I do not want data centers in our area,” Anderson said. “We don’t have enough water. It takes gallons and gallons of water every day to maintain it [a data center].” Anderson isn’t alone in her opposition. Several California communities have moved to temporarily pause or restrict new data center development. And beyond water consumption, there’s another concern, said Anderson. “Also, the electricity, that’s an issue too,” she said. The potential impact on electricity rates and who should pay for major grid upgrades are at the center of a California Public Utilities Commission review of an agreement between utility company PG&E and Google to connect a massive 250-megawatt data center in San Jose. The power needed for the center, sizeable to say the least, said assistant attorney at The Utility Reform Network, a utility watchdog organization, Elise Torres. “At 250 megawatts, it’s approximately the entire load of Marin County,” Torres said. “So that gives you a sense of the scale of just this one facility.” The commission has repeatedly postponed a vote on the agreement. One possible sticking point is a proposed requirement for Google to pay an additional upfront advance toward infrastructure costs, a first for data centers, said Torres. “My speculation is that Google and PG&A are both unhappy about the current provision in the draft resolution that requires Google to pay $600,000 per megawatt,” Torres said. That would amount to as much as $150 million, intended to protect other electricity customers from potentially being left with the costs of major grid upgrades. PG&E argues the upgrades were already planned, would move forward without Google, and would benefit thousands of homes and businesses. Google said the site will feature research and development facilities as well, and reports have noted the company said it will mainly use recycled water. The commission’s eventual decision could have implications well beyond this project, said Torres. “I personally think whatever they decide here, you know, will give us a big indicator of what they’re going to do in Rule 30,” Torres said. “And, will probably be the same standard they apply to exceptional case filings going forward.” Rule 30 is a broader set of proposed standards that the commission is considering for connecting large electricity customers to the transmission grid. Other environmental impacts Torres said he worries about are their potential to produce a large amount of e-waste, and also because they need so much energy, it may make it harder for the state to move away sooner from fossil-fueled power plants. As for Anderson, she said she’s not entirely opposed to data centers, but wants stronger oversight. “It really does need to be regulated, totally, totally regulated by the feds, by the state, by local [governments],” Anderson said. “They need to get together and regulate.” So, as she said, they truly can benefit every community that encounters them.
