artigo.texto: How to Secure Data Centers During the Construction Phase Before operations begin, layered defenses at the site and in the supply chain help prevent theft, vandalism, counterfeit gear, and covert endpoints. As data center build-outs accelerate, most conversations about physical security focus on operational facilities, with threats ranging from mundane events, such as break-ins, to novel threats like drone attacks. Yet the period of greatest exposure is often earlier: during construction. Sites are porous, contractor populations are large and fluid, and high-value materials and preinstalled equipment can be targeted or tampered with. Protecting the build phase should be a core pillar of any data center’s broader physical security strategy. Construction-Phase Risks to Data Centers Physical intrusions during construction come in many forms: Material theft. Theft of construction materials is common on open or lightly controlled construction sites. Copper, cabling, generators, and networking gear are all attractive targets, leading to financial losses and construction delays. Vandalism and sabotage. In some markets, community opposition to data center expansion can increase the likelihood of on-site disruption or damage. Deployment of spy devices. More covertly, malicious actors may attempt to plant devices – such as rogue wireless access points, small network switches, or hidden sensors – during construction to enable remote backdoor access once the facility is operational. Supply chain tampering. Risks also extend into supply chains: tampering with shipments, swapping components, or introducing counterfeit or compromised gear can create backdoors or degrade reliability before the facility ever goes live. Aerial reconnaissance or nuisance activity. Hobbyist drones can expose site layouts and procedures or create safety hazards. Practical Strategies to Secure Data Center Construction Sites While the overarching goal is simple – prevent unauthorized access to construction sites and their supply chains – executing this amid complex projects and large contractor populations is challenging. The following layered controls help reduce risk while maintaining construction speed. Establish a strong perimeter and active monitoring. Build robust physical barriers, ensure all ingress/egress routes are controlled, and funnel all foot and vehicle traffic through staffed gates. Pair this with temporary but professional-grade surveillance cameras covering the perimeter, material laydown yards, and sensitive areas; lighting designed with Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design principles; and motion or thermal sensors where feasible. Verify and control who enters the construction site. Vet contractors and delivery personnel before granting access, consistent with local laws and company policy. Require visible badges and use zoned access so workers can enter only the areas relevant to their tasks. This is no guarantee that bad actors won’t find their way in, but it’s one way to reduce risk. Grant access in phases. Bringing contractors on-site in smaller groups (e.g., having electricians complete their work before allowing HVAC workers to begin) reduces crowding and makes anomalous activity more visible. The trade-off is that this may slow construction by reducing the amount of work contractors can perform in parallel. Rope off construction areas. In addition to establishing a strong perimeter around the data center site, roping off or caging high-value storage (e.g., copper, cabling, generators, and networking equipment) provides another layer of defense against theft and sabotage. Harden the supply chain and track custody. Vet vendors for chain-of-custody controls, tamper-evident packaging, and secure transit practices. Upon receipt, record serial numbers and MAC addresses of networked devices, use barcodes or RFID to track movement, and keep sensitive equipment in controlled cages until deployment. Prepare for drone threats. Use drone detection where appropriate for visibility into potential aerial activity. Many forms of active drone interdiction are illegal, so coordinate with local authorities and legal teams, emphasizing deterrence, detection, and evidence capture rather than unlawful countermeasures. Validate what’s installed before commissioning. Another way to detect supply chain abuse is to compare installed assets against purchase orders and approved bills of materials. Conduct technical sweeps for unauthorized wireless signals or unexpected network endpoints to identify situations where someone installed a device that isn’t supposed to be included. Balancing Speed and Security Complete eradication of construction-phase physical security risks isn’t realistic, just as fully preventing cyberattacks isn’t. However, a multilayered defense strategy based on practices like those described above goes a long way toward reducing the likelihood and impact of intrusions, while improving your chances of detecting and remediating those that do occur.

artigo.texto: Demand for data center labor is up, but can Indiana’s workforce growth match the pace? (Inside INdiana Business) - With large technology companies offering hefty wages and enticing incentives as a wave of data center developments washes across the state, now seems a good time to be a skilled tradesman in Indiana. But it’s a different story for contractors focused on wrapping up other projects. For them, the unprecedented number of data center projects and the benefits that come with them are becoming a hard-to-beat competitor. READ ORIGINAL REPORT HERE: Demand for data center labor is up, but can Indiana’s workforce growth match the pace? Several area industry leaders IBJ spoke with said Indiana’s current workforce might not be able to keep up with the rapidly rising demand for skilled electricians, pipe fitters and builders — even though national statistics show that labor numbers are growing steadily. Over the past decade, the number of construction workers in Indiana has increased by 37%, from 132,300 in August 2016 to 181,300 in August 2026, according to the latest federal labor statistics. And across the state, data center projects already under construction are employing thousands, with Google alone expected to employ about 5,000 workers daily across three sites. And they’re paying well — at least one data center project is reported to be paying workers $5,000-$6,000 a week. Major opportunities With the increased media and public attention on data centers over the past year or so, some might think they are a fresh concept, but that’s not necessarily the case. Data centers have existed for years. They are typically large facilities that support cloud computing and infrastructure for everyday internet uses. Advocates compare them to power plants or water treatment facilities. But in recent years, they have become more prominent and more controversial, likely because of the artificial intelligence boom. While supporters say data centers mean more economic development for communities and workers, opponents say the facilities’ staggering energy and water usage will strain local resources. According to the International Energy Agency, a conventional data center might have the capacity for 10 to 25 megawatts of power — which is equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of 10,000 to 25,000 homes. But a hyperscale, AI-focused data center can have the capacity of 100 megawatts or more, equivalent to about 100,000 households. Several large data center projects are already under construction in Indiana. For example, Meta is building a massive $10 billion, 1,500-acre data center campus at the LEAP Research and Innovation District in Lebanon. And Google is working on three data centers in the state: one in Fort Wayne, one in Morgan County and another in Michigan City. And three other projects were approved in Indianapolis before the City-County Council put a moratorium in place through the end of next year. While some of these facilities might only establish several dozen permanent jobs once complete, the size of the projects means building them will take years — and require lots of workers. Google’s projects, for example, are expected to support thousands of trade jobs daily, according to a spokesperson. In Fort Wayne, where Google is investing $847 million to build a 900-acre campus, about 3,000 workers are on site every day. The Morgan County project, which recently saw the topping out of its first building, has over 750 daily workers — 80% of whom are local and regional hires — and the company’s Michigan City data center is projected to have about 1,500 workers daily during “major construction phases.” (For reference, about 1,500 are still working on Indiana University Health’s new downtown hospital, according to recent IBJ reports.) In Lebanon, Meta’s project is expected to employ 4,000 skilled workers on site during peak construction. Once complete, there will be about 300 operational jobs. In Decatur Township in Marion County, Sabey Corp. was able to get a $4.3 billion, 1-million-square-foot data center project approved before Indianapolis put a moratorium in place. Economic development officials have called the project the largest private capital investment in the city’s history. The Indianapolis project would be the company’s largest data center development. Sabey Corp. CEO John Sabey told IBJ he expects the project to break ground in spring 2027, but that depends on when the company can get through the permitting process and resolve an ongoing legal challenge from several Decatur Township residents. Sabey said the company does not have exact figures, but he estimated the number of workers on site could reach 500 to 1,000, if not more, depending on when the project gets underway. David Peterson, the CEO and president of Indianapolis-based electrical contractor ERMCO, said data center projects have created a “tremendous” opportunity for the trades. Peterson said ERMCO now has 1,200 electricians on site at a data center in Fort Wayne he would not name. He did not disclose specifics of the other projects the company is working on, other than saying that another two are in Indianapolis. Intense competition Data center development not only creates tons of jobs for skilled tradespeople. The pay and incentives are also significant. “We have electricians on some of our work sites, with the amount of time that they’re working in overtime, they’re making, you know, $250- to $300,000 a year in some cases,” Sabey, the data center developer, said. According to Jon Hooker, president and executive director of the Central Indiana Building Trades Council, Meta is paying electricians about $10 above the union pay scale to work on its Lebanon site — which is equivalent to about $5,000 to $6,000 a week. It is “just almost unheard of,” Hooker said. artigo.texto: O Brasil está criando condições para acelerar a instalação de Data Centers, estruturas responsáveis por armazenar e processar os Dados utilizados por serviços digitais, sistemas de Inteligência Artificial e Computação em Nuvem. Sancionada em setembro, a Lei nº 15.504/2026 criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (ReData), que prevê incentivos fiscais para estimular investimentos no setor. Para o advogado especialista em LGPD e professor de Direito Constitucional Newton Moraes, os incentivos previstos na legislação contribuem para fortalecer a soberania tecnológica brasileira. “Sem Data Centers no Brasil, o armazenamento de Dados e a própria operação de sistemas de IA teriam de ser realizados em outros países. Isso significa que uma infraestrutura que será cada vez mais estratégica para a economia e para a sociedade ficaria fora do nosso território”, afirma. Panorama no Brasil Segundo o Ministério de Minas e Energia, o Brasil possui 205 data centers em operação, enquanto os projetos em construção representam mais de R$ 114 bilhões em investimentos. Os pedidos de conexão de novos empreendimentos cresceram 330% entre 2024 e 2025. Apesar desse avanço, o país ainda tem participação reduzida no mercado mundial, ocupando a 10ª posição em participação relativa, atrás de países como Japão e Holanda. O Ministério da Fazenda também aponta uma elevada dependência nacional de serviços digitais prestados no exterior, que atendem cerca de 60% das cargas digitais brasileiras. A expectativa é que a nova legislação contribua para ampliar a infraestrutura instalada no País e, consequentemente, reduzir a dependência de estruturas localizadas no exterior. O avanço, no entanto, traz também desafios relacionados à segurança das informações processadas e armazenadas nesses ambientes. Newton chama atenção para a necessidade de que a expansão ocorra acompanhada de mecanismos adequados de proteção. “Quanto maior a quantidade de informações concentradas nesses centros, maior também é a responsabilidade em relação à segurança e à proteção de dados pessoais”, explica. As contrapartidas Os incentivos previstos pelo ReData estão vinculados ao cumprimento de uma série de requisitos. Poderão se habilitar ao regime pessoas jurídicas que implementem projetos de instalação, modernização ou ampliação de serviços de data center no Brasil. Os serviços abrangidos serão estabelecidos em ato do Poder Executivo federal, de acordo com a Nomenclatura Brasileira de Serviços (NBS). A habilitação ao ReData exige compromissos relacionados à sustentabilidade, ao desenvolvimento tecnológico e à oferta de capacidade ao mercado brasileiro. Entre as exigências estão: disponibilizar ao mercado interno, no mínimo, 10% do fornecimento efetivo de capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados a ser instalada com os benefícios do ReData; cumprir critérios de sustentabilidade a serem definidos em regulamento; atender à totalidade da demanda de energia elétrica por meio de contratos de Suprimento ou Autoprodução provenientes de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, conforme disposto em regulamento; apresentar Índice de Eficiência Hídrica (WUE) igual ou inferior a 0,05 L/kWh, com aferição anual; investir no País 2% do valor dos bens adquiridos com os benefícios do ReData em projetos de pesquisa e desenvolvimento (P&D), em parceria com instituições científicas, tecnológicas e de inovação (ICTs), universidades, empresas públicas ou organizações sociais.

artigo.texto: The construction workers building Meta's largest-ever data center are arriving in a tiny Louisiana town with more than specialized skills and manpower. They've also got cash to spend. It's a fact that local entrepreneurs are leveraging to build new businesses. "It's been a good opportunity for everybody," David Rodgers, the cofounder of Ice Queen, a local business, told Business Insider. "I tell people, you can't stop it unless you have $50 billion. You might as well get on board and go with the flow." Meta said the data center, dubbed Hyperion, will span nearly 10 million square feet in rural Holly Ridge and will support more than 7,500 jobs at peak construction. That's a workforce larger than the population of Aspen, Colorado. While the influx of workers is straining the local housing market and disrupting aspects of daily life, their presence has also boosted the region's economy. Spinning straw into gold Holly Ridge is a very small sliver of the nearly 19,600 residents in Richland Parish, where agriculture has been the main industry for decades. Before Meta arrived, the smattering of towns, villages, and unincorporated areas that make up Richland Parish hadn't seen significant economic growth in years. Tim Allen, a Richland Parish restaurant owner, lived through that stagnation in the nearby town of Rayville. "Rayville has been a small community my whole life, and it's been in decline over the last several years. We have a lot of people whose children are moving out, and they usually don't come back," Allen said. "Growing up, downtown Rayville had multiple businesses, hardware stores, and clothing stores. One by one, they shut down until only a couple of stores were left." When Meta announced its project in 2024, Allen and his family were among those who saw an opportunity to turn things around. "Since Meta's announcement, we've seen old businesses revitalize and new ones open, including ours," Allen said. Holy Tacos opened in April 2025. TJ and Kaycie Weed, also based in Rayville, said the new demographic created by Meta's project has boosted their sales. They first opened their café, HeBrews Coffee & Eats, near the end of 2021. "When we first started, we thought 30 tickets was a good day," TJ said. "Now, we're hitting 30 tickets before the first hour and a half through the drive-thru alone. We're probably hitting 130 tickets now." The café in Rayville is a brick-and-mortar, but the couple has two franchise locations, including a food truck that opened in 2025 directly across the street from the construction site in Holly Ridge. They said the Holly Ridge location opened specifically because of Meta. "Holly Ridge does most of the catering. If it's any of the businesses under the umbrella of Meta, I send it to Holly Ridge," TJ said. The wave of construction workers inspired Rodgers and his former business partner, Linda Edwards, to cofound Ice Queen in 2025. The business sells $3 bags of ice to subcontractors and companies working on the Meta project. The parish has weathered several heat waves this summer, making ice a necessity for outdoor trade workers. Since July, residents have seen temperatures reach 100 degrees Fahrenheit more than two dozen times. The pair keeps the ice bags in a large tractor-trailer parked near the construction site and has a separate ice truck available to make deliveries. Ice was only the beginning, though, and soon Ice Queen transformed into a one-stop shop of sorts for the work crews. Coffee machines. Cups. Sugar packets. Fridges. Microwaves. Straws. You name it, Ice Queen tries to supply it. Robert Cleveland, president and CEO of the local economic development authority, Grow NELA, said the economic growth happening in Richland Parish is undeniable. Data collected by Grow NELA shows that Richland Parish's annual sales tax revenue jumped from $21 million in 2024 to $39 million in 2025. At the end of 2026, Grow NELA expects the parish will see $92 million in annual sales tax revenue. Richland Parish has gained more annual sales tax revenue in 2025 alone than in the last 20 years combined, Grow NELA says. "We have a number of small businesses that have propped up and have grown significantly because of the project," Cleveland said. Supply and demand Part of the business growth in Richland Parish is supplying construction workers with what they need while they are away from home: lodging, food, and basic necessities. Angel and Bryan Crawford, for example, chose to address the housing market gap with their rental company, Parish Line Properties. The couple owns a mobile home park called Antley Pines that opened in 2025. "We added two homes last December, four this May, and our last four in July. All the homes were secured by deposits from Meta workers before we even got them into the park," Angel said. A fully-furnished four-bedroom, two-bathroom mobile home that's eight miles from the construction site costs an average of $3,000. The couple previously worked in the nursing field, but decided to dive into real estate and property management after becoming empty nesters. "In 2024, we started buying older houses that had been on the market for a long time or needed a lot of work. We had a vision to create a mobile home park and already purchased some land when we heard about Meta's data center," Angel said. The company now owns 18 rental properties, 14 of which the owners have set aside as workforce housing. "Location is very important to Meta's workers because they work six to seven days a week and 12-plus hours a day. They leave around 4:30 in the morning, and they don't come home until 7 at night," she said. Those long days can be taxing, making places like HeBrews Coffee & Eats popular with workers. Shelbie Stephenson, owner of the Holly Ridge location, said they deliver 450 lunch plates to the Meta work site twice a month. artigo.texto: EU ministers have signed off new rules to adjust the market stability reserve for the EU’s second emissions trading system, ETS2, ahead of its planned launch in 2028. The market stability reserve is designed to balance supply and demand in ETS2 by automatically changing the number of emission allowances available, the Council of the European Union announced on Friday. The amended rules extend the reserve beyond 2030. They also double the number of allowances that can be released when the carbon price rises above €45 per tonne of CO2 equivalent (in 2020 prices) — from 20 million to 40 million allowances. A further change introduces a more gradual release of allowances when the number in circulation falls below 260 million, to avoid sudden shifts linked to a fixed threshold. What ETS2 covers ETS2 is the EU’s emissions trading system for buildings, road transport and additional sectors, created under the EU’s “Fit for 55” package in 2023, the Council said. It is intended to cut emissions from those sectors by 42% by 2030 compared with 2005 levels. Unlike the EU’s existing emissions trading system, ETS1 — which covers areas such as heavy industry and aviation — ETS2 applies “upstream” to fuel distributors, meaning companies that sell fuels must monitor and report the emissions linked to those fuels and surrender allowances to match them. The new rules will be signed and published in the Official Journal of the EU and take effect 20 days after publication.

artigo.texto: Com restrições na rede elétrica e parte da produção renovável sem aproveitamento, estado busca atrair grandes consumidores, ampliar o armazenamento energético e transformar sua capacidade de geração em oportunidades para a indústria O Rio Grande do Norte tem capacidade de gerar até dez vezes mais energia do que consome, segundo a Federação das Indústrias do Estado (FIERN). Essa vantagem coloca o estado na disputa por investimentos em data centers, infraestrutura digital e indústrias que demandam grandes volumes de eletricidade. Apesar desse potencial, parte da geração renovável enfrenta restrições de escoamento na rede elétrica. O desafio agora é aproximar a produção dos grandes consumidores e desenvolver soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias BESS. O assunto será discutido em Natal durante dois eventos promovidos pelo Grupo FRG Mídias & Eventos. O Energy Storage Brasil ocorrerá nos dias 21 e 22 de outubro de 2026, enquanto o Data Center Conference 2026 será realizado no dia 23. - Energia renovável perde ritmo no Brasil com cortes de geração e incerteza para investidores - Áustria teve 43.300 tickets em 10 minutos para disputar R$ 215 milhões de subsídio solar que paga R$ 838 por kWp, enquanto no Brasil painel novo já paga 60% do Fio B - Usina solar de Indiana instalou 20 mil painéis por dia com 1.800 operários em 18 meses e está prestes a operar - Agricultor de Illinois tem 10 torres eólicas na fazenda e recebe cerca de R$ 600 mil por ano, mas no Nordeste os relatos vão de R$ 600 a R$ 2 mil por mês por torre Abundância de energia renovável pode impulsionar a instalação de grandes centros de processamento de dados O presidente da FIERN, Roberto Serquiz, considera que a capacidade de geração energética já representa uma vantagem competitiva para o Rio Grande do Norte. Entretanto, o estado precisa transformar essa disponibilidade em consumo efetivo, criando condições para receber novos empreendimentos. Entre os principais interessados estão os data centers, instalações que exigem fornecimento contínuo de eletricidade para manter servidores e equipamentos em funcionamento. A proximidade das estruturas de comunicação que chegam pelo Nordeste também favorece o estado, segundo Serquiz. O dirigente avalia que o Rio Grande do Norte reúne condições para disputar esses investimentos no mercado brasileiro. Contudo, ressalta a importância de ampliar a segurança jurídica e avançar na regulamentação necessária à instalação dos empreendimentos. A chegada desses grandes consumidores poderia aumentar a demanda local por eletricidade e estimular novas atividades econômicas. Para isso, será necessário alinhar os projetos industriais à infraestrutura energética disponível. Cortes na geração de eletricidade expõem desafio da rede e ampliam interesse por sistemas de armazenamento Embora tenha elevada capacidade de geração renovável, o Rio Grande do Norte enfrenta o chamado curtailment, fenômeno associado às restrições operacionais que impedem o aproveitamento integral da produção de eletricidade. O presidente do Conselho Regional de Engenharia e Agronomia do Rio Grande do Norte (Crea-RN), Roberto Wagner, explica que existe um descompasso entre geração e consumo. Dessa forma, parte da capacidade energética disponível encontra limitações para chegar aos consumidores. Uma das alternativas envolve os sistemas BESS (Battery Energy Storage Systems). Essas estruturas armazenam eletricidade em baterias durante períodos de maior disponibilidade e podem fornecê-la quando a demanda aumenta. A instalação de data centers também pode contribuir para ampliar o consumo de energia no estado. No entanto, Wagner destaca que esses projetos exigem planejamento da transmissão, subtransmissão, subestações e pontos de conexão. O avanço dessas tecnologias também cria oportunidades para profissionais especializados em sistemas elétricos, automação, proteção, gerenciamento térmico e prevenção de incêndios. Segundo o presidente do Crea-RN, será necessário ampliar a qualificação de engenheiros e técnicos. O objetivo é permitir que profissionais locais participem das oportunidades geradas pelos novos investimentos. Natal receberá dois eventos sobre baterias, inteligência artificial e expansão da infraestrutura digital A discussão sobre o aproveitamento da energia renovável ganhará espaço na sede da FIERN, em Natal, durante três dias de programação voltada ao setor energético e tecnológico. Nos dias 21 e 22 de outubro, a sétima edição do Energy Storage Brasil reunirá fabricantes, investidores, desenvolvedores de projetos, especialistas e representantes do poder público. O encontro abordará tecnologias de armazenamento, incluindo baterias de íon-lítio, sódio, fluxo, estado sólido e ferro-ar. Também haverá discussões sobre hidrogênio, armazenamento térmico, regulamentação e modelos de negócios. Já no dia 23 de outubro, o Data Center Conference 2026 terá como foco a expansão dos centros de processamento de dados, conectividade e inteligência artificial. O diretor do Grupo FRG Mídias & Eventos, Tiago Fraga, destaca que a proposta é aproximar os setores de geração energética, armazenamento e infraestrutura digital. A organização espera receber entre 650 e 1.000 participantes qualificados. A programação pretende aproximar investidores e empresas interessados em aproveitar a disponibilidade energética do Rio Grande do Norte. Com isso, o estado busca transformar sua capacidade de geração renovável em demanda, investimentos e novas oportunidades econômicas, sem perder de vista as limitações da infraestrutura elétrica existente.

artigo.texto: News Brief Arjun Brij Oct 11, 2026 | Updated 11:58 AM GMT+5:30 Save & read from anywhere! Bookmark stories for easy access on any device or the Swarajya app. Nine new electric buses equipped with Blade Battery technology arrived at Mumbai’s Magathane depot on Saturday (10 October), with another 49 expected within a week, taking the city’s bus fleet closer to 2,900. Another 49 buses are expected to arrive within a week, according to a senior official, taking the city’s bus fleet closer to 2,900. Manufactured by Olectra Greentech Limited, the new buses use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries fitted directly into the chassis. The technology is designed to improve safety, increase energy storage and reduce operating costs. As per news reports, the new vehicles are expected to cover between 325 km and 500 km on a single charge, compared with approximately 250 km for existing electric buses The stated minimum range of 325 km in congested urban conditions could allow the buses to operate for up to two days without returning to the depot for recharging. The battery system offers at least 30 per cent more energy storage than batteries currently used in electric air-conditioned buses. Its compact and lightweight design is also intended to improve vehicle stability and make more efficient use of space. Charging times are another feature of the new fleet. A full charge typically takes one to two hours. Blade Battery technology is also designed to limit heat generation and improve thermal safety under demanding conditions. With a reported lifespan of more than 5,000 charge cycles, the batteries could help lower replacement and maintenance costs over the vehicles’ operating lives. artigo.texto: A Amazon.com (AMZN) está novamente sob escrutínio na Índia após novas reportagens publicadas em 9 de outubro destacarem a oposição local ao seu planejado campus de data center em Thane, nos arredores de Mumbai. Moradores próximos ao local de aproximadamente 22 hectares em Balkum e Majiwada afirmam que a instalação trará ruído, emissões e pressão sobre os recursos locais. A resposta da Amazon não mudou. A empresa diz que o local em Thane não usará água para resfriamento e não consumirá energia da rede que atende residências e comércios próximos. (Este é um projeto existente, não um novo investimento.) O que os Moradores de Thane Estão Combatendo - Água: Os moradores temem que o campus sobrecarregue uma cidade já com escassez de abastecimento. A Amazon diz que o local não usará água para resfriamento. - Energia: Moradores estimam que o campus precisará de cerca de 422 MW. A Amazon diz que não consumirá da rede que atende residências e comércios próximos. - Ruído e emissões: O plano inclui aproximadamente 190 geradores de backup a diesel, com cinco escolas e três hospitais dentro de um quilômetro. - Política: O deputado de Thane, Naresh Mhaske, pediu a suspensão da construção em 7 de julho, e a cidade disse que encaminhará as preocupações dos moradores ao governo estadual. Contextualizando o Investimento da AWS em Maharashtra Os gastos de capital da Amazon aumentaram de US$ 52,73 bilhões em 2023 para US$ 83,00 bilhões em 2024 e US$ 131,82 bilhões em 2025. Nos últimos doze meses, atingiram US$ 173,03 bilhões. A AWS anunciou um plano de investimento de US$ 8,3 bilhões em Maharashtra em janeiro de 2025, como parte de seu compromisso anterior de US$ 12,7 bilhões com a Índia. A Amazon desde então expandiu seu planejado investimento indiano em nuvem e IA para mais de US$ 21 bilhões para 2026–2030. Para dimensionar, todo o compromisso de US$ 8,3 bilhões em Maharashtra equivale a cerca de 4,8% dos US$ 173,03 bilhões em gastos de capital da Amazon nos últimos doze meses. Isso compara um compromisso de investimento regional plurianual com um ano de capex em toda a empresa; não estabelece o custo do projeto de Thane ou o gasto anual. Onde um Atraso Prejudicaria a AWS Atrasos são uma questão diferente. A receita da AWS atingiu US$ 42,23 bilhões no 2º trimestre de 2026, um aumento de 37% em relação aos US$ 30,87 bilhões de um ano antes. O crescimento acelerou em cada um dos últimos três trimestres, a partir de 20% no 3º trimestre de 2025, e apenas o segundo trimestre adicionou US$ 4,64 bilhões de receita em relação ao primeiro. Quando a demanda supera a capacidade, um data center que abre com atraso significa receita adiada. A AWS abriu sua primeira região indiana em Mumbai em 2016. Um atraso em Thane poderia restringir a expansão da capacidade local, embora as divulgações citadas não quantifiquem a contribuição do campus para o crescimento da AWS. O que Thane Significa para Alphabet e Microsoft Thane não é o único ponto de tensão. A Alphabet (GOOGL) tem a exposição mais próxima: seu hub de IA de US$ 15 bilhões em Visakhapatnam, construído com a Adani, enfrenta protestos organizados sobre água e energia, entre os primeiros na Índia ao lado de Thane. A Microsoft (MSFT) anunciou um investimento de US$ 17,5 bilhões para 2026–2029 cobrindo infraestrutura de nuvem e IA, capacitação e operações contínuas, construindo sobre um compromisso anterior de US$ 3 bilhões. Thane é um teste para saber se a expansão em hiperescala da Índia mantém sua licença social local. Condições adicionais poderiam aumentar os custos ou atrasar o desenvolvimento de Thane. Uma suspensão da construção também poderia encorajar opositores de outros projetos, incluindo o hub de Visakhapatnam do Google, onde ambientalistas já estão protestando contra o desenvolvimento. artigo.texto: CATL surpasses LG Energy Solution to claim top spot in global battery patents According to data released on October 6 by the IP consulting firm PatSnap’s global patent database, battery giant CATL has officially surpassed LG Energy Solution to become the global leader in battery patent holdings, as reported by ChinaNews. The statistics, covering the period from October 2016 to September 2026, show that CATL holds 26,574 simple patent families, leading LG Energy Solution (22,597) by approximately 3,900 patents. This milestone marks a shift in the global battery industry, as the centre of innovation moves from Japan and South Korea to China after a decade of rapid development. “Simple patent families” consolidate identical core inventions filed in different countries or regions into a single count, providing a more accurate reflection of a company’s true technological innovation volume. Key patent statistics (2016–2026) For decades, the global battery patent landscape was dominated by Japanese and Korean firms. However, the latest rankings show a clear transition: LG Energy Solution has slipped to second place, while Panasonic has fallen out of the top ten with only 4,994 patents. Toyota remains the only Japanese company in the top ten. According to CATL, it has spent over 100 billion yuan (14.9 billion USD) in cumulative R&D investment. CATL’s innovation pace is accelerating. PatSnap data indicates that CATL holds a total of 27,402 battery patents, with 16,722 of those filed in the last three years alone. This represents 61.0% of its historical total, the highest three-year growth ratio among leading domestic companies. Specifically, 61.8% of its power battery patents and 78.1% of its solid-state battery patents were filed within the last three years, both ranking first in China. In the power battery sector – the industry’s primary battlefield – CATL holds 19,539 total patents, 2.2 times that of the second-ranked domestic competitor. When looking at the last three years, CATL filed 12,084 patents compared to 4,384 by the runner-up. The 12,084 power battery patents nearly equal the combined total of 14,500 patents from the second through fifth-ranked domestic companies. Solid-state batteries are widely considered the key to next-generation technology. In this field, CATL holds 3,538 patents, more than double the second-ranked domestic competitor. CATL has maintained the top position across all time windows, with 3,511 patents over the last decade and 2,763 in the last three years. In the last three years, CATL’s 2,763 patents nearly match the combined total of 2,891 patents from the second- through tenth-ranked domestic companies.

artigo.texto: Who Should Coordinate the Heavy Lift? A general contractor can have a detailed master schedule, clearly defined scopes, and an experienced team of subcontractors, yet still run into problems when a major piece of equipment needs to move. The crane is available. The rigging plan is complete. The truck is scheduled. But the site is not ready. The access route is blocked. Another trade is still working in the area. The equipment is arriving before the installation team is ready. The crane scheduled for one lift is now needed somewhere else, and the next available window is already tied to another activity. The lift itself may not be the problem. The breakdown in coordination leading up to it may be. On a typical data center project, crane, rigging, and heavy-haul work may sit beneath an electrical or mechanical contractor: GC → EC / MC → Crane, Rigging & Heavy Haul That structure has a clear purpose. The trade contractor manages its scope and brings in the specialty expertise required to execute it. But data center construction is increasingly difficult to divide into completely separate scopes. The equipment may belong to one trade. Its transportation may involve another. The crane may be supporting several scopes, each with its own schedule and priorities. When those activities overlap, a change in one area can disrupt work happening across the site. That raises a question worth considering: When specialty work crosses trade boundaries, who is coordinating it at the project level? The Scope Is Not Always as Contained as the Contract A crane may be supporting an electrical installation, but the crane does not know that it is an electrical crane. The same equipment may be used to set mechanical equipment the next day. A heavy-haul provider may deliver equipment for both scopes. A rigging crew may be working around several different installation sequences during the same phase of construction. The contract may define where the work sits. The construction schedule does not always work that way. A major lift depends on more than the equipment being ready. The haul path needs to be available. The crane needs a suitable setup location. The receiving area needs to be ready. Other trades may need to clear the work area. The installation team needs to be prepared for the equipment once it is set. A change in one part of that sequence can affect several others. That is where the distinction between trade coordination and project coordination becomes important. When the Lift Becomes a Project-Level Activity The more interconnected the project becomes, the more difficult it is to manage critical movement entirely within one trade's schedule. Consider a major generator delivery. The electrical contractor may own the generator installation. The heavy-haul contractor may be responsible for transportation. The crane and rigging contractor may handle the final set. But the generator still has to arrive when the site is ready for it. If the delivery slips, the crane schedule may have to shift. That can push another installation out of its planned window. If access changes in the meantime, the haul plan may need to be revised. And if the installation sequence changes, the original lift plan may no longer reflect the conditions in the field. None of those decisions necessarily belong to one contractor. They belong to the project. That does not mean the GC needs to take over the technical work. It means there can be value in having a direct relationship with the specialty contractor responsible for it. Direct Does Not Mean Bypassing the Trade There is an important distinction here. A GC contracting directly with a crane, rigging, and heavy-haul company does not have to mean removing the EC or MC from the process. The electrical contractor still owns its electrical scope. The mechanical contractor still owns its mechanical scope. The crane and rigging contractor remains responsible for its specialized work. What changes is the line of communication. Rather than having issues involving crane, rigging, or transportation pass through another trade before reaching the GC, the GC has a direct relationship with the company performing that work. That can matter when a specialty contractor identifies a constraint that affects more than one scope. It can also give the GC direct access to the people who understand the technical and logistical implications of a proposed change. The GC does not need to become the rigging expert. It needs direct access to one. The Master Schedule Does Not Coordinate the Lift by Itself A schedule can show when a generator is supposed to be set. It cannot guarantee that the access route will still be clear that morning, especially when other trades are working against their own deadlines. It can show when a crane is needed. It may not account for another lift competing for the same crane, setup area, or crew when schedules shift, and previously available resources are committed elsewhere. It can show when equipment should arrive. It does not guarantee that the site will be ready to receive it. This is where specialty planning has to connect back to the project schedule. The crane selection, haul route, equipment arrival, site access, rigging configuration, and installation sequence all have to work together. artigo.texto: Battery storage is scaling faster than almost any other grid resource in the U.S. As transmission and distribution networks accommodate increasing shares of solar and wind power, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are emerging as one of the most effective technologies to enhance grid flexibility, stability, and resilience. What was once considered a niche solution is now becoming strategic infrastructure. But deployment is outpacing the industry's confidence in how these systems will perform on the grid, under stress, and over decades of service. Closing that gap requires connecting independent testing, grid modeling, and owner oversight across the full project lifecycle. Today's BESS installations play a far broader role than simply storing surplus electricity. Modern battery systems support frequency regulation, voltage control, peak shaving, congestion management, renewable integration, and ancillary services. Their fast response times allow them to react within seconds to grid disturbances, making them valuable assets for balancing increasingly dynamic energy systems. At the distribution level, utilities are evaluating BESS solutions to postpone costly network reinforcements, increase renewable hosting capacity, and improve power quality. Energy storage can support local grids by reducing transformer overloads, mitigating voltage deviations, and managing demand peaks driven by electric vehicle charging and growing electrification. At KEMA Labs, battery research is complemented by the multidisciplinary expertise of the Digital Lab, which combines battery testing with Electromagnetic Compatibility (EMC) testing and Accelerated Life Testing (ALT). This integrated approach clarifies how batteries, power electronics, control systems, and communication devices interact within BESS architectures. Its expertise also extends to plant controllers and IEC 61850 testing, helping assess communication between grid-connected assets, including BESS, and network operators. Beyond operational benefits, the business case for energy storage is evolving rapidly. BESS operators can stack multiple revenue streams, combining ancillary services, energy arbitrage, capacity or resource adequacy contracts, and congestion management. This evolution is encouraging larger-scale deployment and attracting investment across global markets. However, growth also brings technical and operational challenges. A modern BESS comprises battery cells, racks, Battery Management Systems (BMS), energy management systems, power conversion systems, transformers, cooling systems, and fire protection solutions. Each component influences efficiency, safety, and lifetime. Owners also need confidence in grid interaction, as inverter-based resources respond to disturbances differently from conventional generators. That confidence starts before a project is energized. Grid integration studies, including system impact, harmonic and power quality, temporary overvoltage, insulation coordination, and ride-through assessments, determine whether a BESS will support the grid or introduce new risks. Detailed Electromagnetic Transient (EMT) models capture inverter and plant controller behavior, helping identify control interactions and compliance issues early. Models, however, are only as good as the data behind them. Independent testing laboratories such as KEMA Labs, the testing Division of CESI Group, evaluate batteries under realistic operating conditions. Dedicated facilities can reproduce environmental and electrical stress, including extreme temperatures, humidity, charging and discharging cycles, and accelerated aging scenarios. These tests provide insight into battery performance, reliability, degradation, and expected service life. Recent KEMA Labs’ research on Lithium Iron Phosphate (LPF) batteries demonstrates the value of testing and modeling. Laboratory aging campaigns supported semi-empirical and thermal models for predicting capacity fade, State of Health, and battery lifetime under real-world operating conditions. The study highlighted temperature and State of Charge as key factors affecting degradation, providing insights for battery operation and long-term asset management. The greatest value comes when these disciplines are connected. Laboratory results can validate simulation models so planning studies reflect equipment behavior rather than relying solely on vendor data. Owner's engineering carries that discipline through procurement, factory acceptance testing, commissioning, and performance verification. Within CESI Group, KEMA Labs and EnerNex, the Group’s U.S. grid innovation company, link what is proven in the laboratory with how a system performs on the grid. Once a system is in service, combining laboratory test data with BMS information enables aging models to predict capacity fade, State of Health, and Remaining Useful Life. These capabilities support optimized maintenance, improved operational efficiency, and better-informed investment decisions. As energy storage moves from pilot projects to mainstream infrastructure, utilities and developers should require validated models early, confirm them against test and commissioning data, treat testing and performance verification as core project requirements, and use owner's engineering services to ensure that installed systems match what was studied and contracted. The future power system will require unprecedented flexibility, and battery storage is uniquely positioned to provide it. Realizing that potential will depend on robust testing, accurate modeling, and technical oversight working together across the full lifecycle of every project.

artigo.texto: Ataques de drones desativam centros de dados de empresa russa de IA Empresa russa de tecnologia perdeu total ou parcialmente a operação de unidades em 3 regiões do país em 3 dias consecutivos A Yandex, empresa russa de tecnologia e IA (inteligência artificial), informou neste domingo (11.out.2026) que seu centro de dados na região de Vladimir foi totalmente desativado depois de um ataque de drones. Ninguém ficou ferido, mas alguns serviços da companhia estão indisponíveis para os usuários. A unidade de Vladimir é a 3ª instalação da empresa a perder total ou parcialmente a operação em 4 dias, segundo a Reuters. A sequência de ataques afeta a infraestrutura digital da companhia, que tem papel central no desenvolvimento de inteligência artificial na Rússia. Ataques em 4 dias Na 6ª feira (9.out.2026), drones ucranianos atingiram um centro de dados da Yandex na região de Kaluga, a sudoeste de Moscou. Segundo a empresa, a unidade ficou parcialmente fora de operação. Na 5ª feira (8.out.2026), um ataque ucraniano desativou o centro de dados da companhia em Sasovo, a sudeste de Moscou. A instalação abriga 2 dos 3 supercomputadores usados no desenvolvimento dos modelos de IA da Yandex. Conhecida informalmente como “o Google da Rússia”, a empresa oferece serviços digitais e desenvolve tecnologias de IA no país. A perda de capacidade em seus centros de dados pode afetar o funcionamento de seus serviços e o desenvolvimento desses sistemas.

artigo.texto: The two candidates running for Wisconsin's 7th Congressional District met Wednesday for what could be their only debate before the November election. Republican Michael Alfonso and Democrat Fred Clark met in Duluth, Minnesota, for the debate hosted by WDIO-TV. Among the issues discussed was Enbridge's Line 5 pipeline, which has faced renewed scrutiny following a major natural gas liquids spill in Iron County and environmental concerns surrounding construction of its reroute around the Bad River Reservation. When asked about Line 5, Alfonso expressed support for the pipeline. He also said protecting northern Wisconsin's lakes, forests and farmland doesn't have to come at the expense of building energy infrastructure. “Line 5 is one of these things that brings costs down for every single family in Northern Wisconsin. I really look at this issue and say, if you truly want prices to come down, how can you not support it.” Alfonso had earlier said Clark opposed Line 5. Clark disputed that claim and said his concerns were with Enbridge's environmental record. “I have put out a statement calling on the Wisconsin DNR to hold the Enbridge company accountable for the set of environmental problems they've had. This company has not operated in good faith and until they're willing to do that, we need the state to hold them accountable and stop work until there are reforms.” The candidates were also asked about data centers, which have become a growing concern in Wisconsin over their potential impact on water supplies and electricity costs. Clark called for state and federal regulations to protect communities from the environmental and financial risks of data center development. “We need that badly to protect our water resources, absolutely, to make sure that consumers of energy are held harmless by the huge power demand these things generate, absolutely,” Clark said. Alfonso agreed that water use and electricity costs need to be addressed, but said local communities should decide whether to allow data centers. “If you were to ask me, do I want a data center in Hayward, Wisconsin, where I live? Absolutely not,” Alfonso said. “But I'll tell you what, the federal government does not have a role in stepping in and telling local municipalities what they can and cannot do.” Clark then questioned Alfonso about President Donald Trump's efforts to limit state regulation of artificial intelligence. "So are you willing to tell the president that he's wrong to want to preempt states from having regulations around artificial intelligence and that he's wrong to let Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos basically run the table the way they want to with AI and data centers?” Clark asked. Alfonso responded that Trump supports local control. “President Trump was actually very clear with this. He said, if you're a local municipality and you don't want one, you don't need one. President Trump truly listens to the people,” Alfonso said. “I mean, when we look at issues like the data center issue, it's very clear. People in northern Wisconsin don't want it. But I can't say the same for Kansas. I've never been there. If they want one, it's not the federal government's job to step in and say, no, it's the state or local government.” The full debate is available to watch on WDIO-TV's website.

artigo.texto: JAMES CITY — The James City County Planning Commission is recommending going forward with a 650-megawatt battery energy storage plant, substation and switchyard project off Pocahontas Trail. The commission voted 5-2 on Wednesday to send a favorable recommendation for the project to the Board of Supervisors, which will make the final decision. Commission member Crystal Haskins and chair Kira Allman voted no. The project has already raised some concerns from people who live near the proposed 220-acre industrial waterfront location in the county’s Grove community. On Wednesday, residents told the Planning Commission they were worried the battery storage facility could pose a fire risk and that construction could cause disruptions to the community. The site is an abandoned industrial area with past environmental contamination issues. In 1958, the Dow Chemical Co. developed the properties close to the James River to manufacture acrylic fibers. BASF Corp. acquired the site in 1978 to continue making acrylic products until 1989, when Mann Industries bought the industrial portion of the facility. In 1993, Mann Industries filed for bankruptcy, and the facility has been inactive since. BASF reacquired the Mann Industries portions of the property. In 2021, the property was declared remediated by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality. Planner Allison Jackura said the proposed use “provides a low-impact industrial use in an area planned for such use.” The site is not expected to generate much traffic or noise and would adhere to national fire safety standards. The county’s planning staff recommended approval of a special use permit on the site. The storage plant would provide about 150 construction jobs over two years. Keith Latham of Tenasca, an energy company based in Nebraska, spoke in favor of the storage facility, which is a partnership with Pelican Energy Storage. The lithium-ion batteries would hold energy that power plants generate and that can be fed back into the power grid when demand is highest. The battery site would connect to Dominion Energy’s 500-kilovolt Surry-Skiffes Creek transmission line, which crosses the property. “They’re banks of batteries that are connected to the grid,” Latham said. “Ultimately, they are there to provide reliability and resilience to the grid in case there’s any challenges.” Latham called the project a great reuse of the BASF facility that has been inactive for many years. He said the location is ideal, especiallybecause it’s almost a mile to the nearest residential neighbor. Suzanne Berthier, who lives on Pocahontas Trail, said she was concerned about the safety of Grove residents because of the potential of fires caused by something called “thermal runaway,” when a fire in a battery could trigger other batteries to explode. “Once they fail, there are dangerous toxic chemicals released into the air that are life-threatening,” Berthier said. Christopher Balser, an apprentice with the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, spoke in favor of the application. “I encourage you to support this project and help provide people like me a pathway into the middle class while working near home,” he said. Another resident, Cathy Reynolds, said she felt as though opinions from Grove residents were being “disregarded in lieu of revenue.” Pelican Energy hosted a public informational meeting on Sept. 29, during which a spokesperson said the company wanted “to ensure that they’re a good neighbor.” Planning commissioner Jack Haldeman moved for the approval of the project. “The proposal will provide economic development,” he said. “It provides a significant boost to the county’s increasingly strained treasury, easing pressure on taxpayers.” David Macaulay, davidmacaulayva@gmail.com

artigo.texto: O Ministério de Minas e Energia e a EPE abriram na quinta-feira (8) a consulta pública do PDE 2036. O plano decenal mostra quanto o Brasil deve gastar, onde o consumo de eletricidade cresce e quanto vem do sol e do vento. O PDE 2036, o plano decenal do setor elétrico e de combustíveis, ficou aberto a críticas na quinta-feira (8). O Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) e a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) publicaram o Relatório Síntese e marcaram o fim da consulta pública para 6 de novembro, segundo o comunicado do MME. O número que abre o documento é grande: cerca de R$ 3,3 trilhões em investimentos entre 2027 e 2036, de acordo com a nota da EPE. Quanto o consumo de eletricidade deve crescer no PDE 2036? O consumo de eletricidade deve subir 3,4% ao ano e chegar a 979 TWh em 2036. Hoje ele é de cerca de 702 TWh, número que o Eixos trouxe do plano decenal. - Energia renovável perde ritmo no Brasil com cortes de geração e incerteza para investidores - Áustria teve 43.300 tickets em 10 minutos para disputar R$ 215 milhões de subsídio solar que paga R$ 838 por kWp, enquanto no Brasil painel novo já paga 60% do Fio B - Usina solar de Indiana instalou 20 mil painéis por dia com 1.800 operários em 18 meses e está prestes a operar - Agricultor de Illinois tem 10 torres eólicas na fazenda e recebe cerca de R$ 600 mil por ano, mas no Nordeste os relatos vão de R$ 600 a R$ 2 mil por mês por torre A conta é simples: 979 dividido por 702 dá 1,39. É um consumo de eletricidade cerca de 39% maior em uma década. No PDE 2036, a geração acompanha. Vai de 829 TWh em 2026 para 1.133 TWh em 2036, um salto de 304 TWh de geração a mais por ano. Quanto da energia vem do sol e do vento? Solar e eólica juntas respondem por cerca de um terço da geração elétrica em 2036. Em 2026, a fatia é de 28,1%, segundo a EPE. A matriz elétrica continua perto de 90% renovável. Na matriz total, que inclui transporte, indústria e casas, a parcela renovável sobe pouco: de 50,2% para 51,2%. A explicação está no petróleo, que segue forte no PDE 2036. O plano projeta 4,9 milhões de barris por dia em 2036 e 135 milhões de metros cúbicos diários de gás natural, 85% a mais que hoje. Quem puxa a demanda: data centers, carro elétrico e hidrogênio O consumo dos data centers passa de 3 TWh para 30 TWh. É dez vezes mais, e os data centers sozinhos somam 27 TWh por ano a mais na conta do sistema. A eletromobilidade vai de 1 TWh para 15 TWh. Pelo Eixos, os carros leves ficam com 9,4 TWh, os ônibus urbanos com 4,6 TWh e os caminhões com 0,7 TWh. O hidrogênio só entra no consumo de eletricidade a partir de 2031, com 3 TWh em 2036. Quanta bateria e quantos quilômetros de linha o plano prevê? O armazenamento aparece como peça central no PDE 2036. O plano prevê 7,2 GW em baterias, 4,0 GW de resposta da demanda e, pela primeira vez, 2,0 GW em usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis. Somando baterias e reversíveis, são 9,2 GW. Na rede, o PDE 2036 prevê 31,9 mil quilômetros de novas linhas de transmissão e 99,6 mil MVA de capacidade de transformação, de 2026 a 2036. Fora do plano decenal, mas ligado a ele, os primeiros leilões de baterias estão marcados para dezembro, com suprimento a partir de agosto de 2028, informa o Eixos. O motivo, segundo o próprio plano, é ter excesso de energia de dia e falta de potência no começo da noite. E o telhado de casa? A geração distribuída quase dobra A micro e minigeração distribuída, que inclui a solar em telhado, deve passar de cerca de 50 GW para 92 GW. É um aumento de 42 GW, ou 84%, e os data centers e os carros elétricos entram na mesma conta da rede. O Eixos registra que armazenar essa energia em casa pode atrair até R$ 417 bilhões em investimentos até 2036. Como mandar sugestão na consulta pública do PDE 2036 Qualquer pessoa pode contribuir com a consulta pública, do cidadão a empresas. Os caminhos são o portal de consultas públicas do MME e a plataforma Brasil Participativo. O Capítulo 4, “Questões para o Futuro do Setor Energético Brasileiro”, é o espaço aberto para sugerir temas. O MME diz que o conteúdo será consolidado na versão final do plano decenal, depois da avaliação técnica do ministério e da EPE. A consulta pública terá o apoio de dez cadernos temáticos, entre eles Transmissão, Eletromobilidade e Geração de Energia Elétrica, que saem nas próximas semanas, informa o MME. O que o plano ainda não responde é quanto disso vai parar na conta de luz. O PDE 2036 traz projeções de quantidade, não de tarifa, e por isso o consumidor não deve ler os R$ 3,3 trilhões como aumento direto.

artigo.texto: New Peugeot RCZ Vision: solid state battery, 493bhp, and a mad steering wheel A warm welcome back for Peugeot's stylish small coupe. But that wheel? Yeesh... Peugeot is feeling funky. In fact, its new design language is feeling feline, so much so that it’s actually called ‘feline future’. Peugeot wants to be the left-field, extrovert French brand, without being self-consciously wacky. The RCZ Vision showcases the direction of travel. A crisply resolved coupe with echoes of its forebear – which ran from 2009 until ’15 and shifted a healthy 68,000 units – there’s plenty to like on the surface. But actually the bigger stories here are within and beneath, because this car introduces us to two significant developments – both of which are actually coming down the pipe. Core to the RCZ is the STLA architecture, a modular mega-platform that will underpin in excess of 30 new cars across the Stellantis constellation, to the tune of two million vehicles per year by 2035. Coupled to it is a new software and control system called STLA Brain, fast-tracking the company’s ability to deliver autonomous driving capability and innovations such as steer-by-wire. That’s also key to the RCZ Vision. Peugeot was one of the first to genuinely reimagine the car interior, with its odd but also oddly effective i-Cockpit. This new concept car develops the theme in various ways: highlights include ‘mobile’ air vents that can disappear when not in use, an aluminium centre console topped with frosted glass, and a transparent micro LED display screen above the wheel, which can be configured to show as much or as little as the driver wants to see. You might like Well, we say wheel. The dominant innovation inside the RCZ is clearly the so-called Hypersquare, which groups switchgear into four rings. That’ll take some getting used to, but we suspect the ergonomics are sound. Another head-spinner is the arrival of steer-by-wire; yep, there’s no mechanical linkage here, everything is 100 per cent electronic. And fast: the maximum wheel rotation is a little less than one turn compared to the three turns lock-to-lock that we’re used to. A variable steering ratio means that you’re not all at sea at motorway speeds, and vibrations and torque steer are now relics of a different era. The RCZ – and indeed all future Peugeots – will brake-by-wire too. What of the propulsion? The STLA One platform can accommodate ICE, but not here. On the RCZ Vision, we’re talking about a solid-state battery built on a 1,000 volt architecture so that it can charge from 10 to 80 per cent in 10 minutes. Most of the big players are exploring solid state, whose primary benefit is a superior energy density in a more compact configuration. Peugeot is collaborating with a company called Factorial Energy in order to deliver this (Stellantis has a 9.5 per cent equity stake). The company says the RCZ has a power output of 491bhp, is targeting a range of 375 miles, and can deliver 5.4mpkWh overall. Back to the new design language. Peugeot’s design director Matthias Hossann says it’s predicated on five key principles: freedom, courage, elegance, instinct and inner force. Answers on a postcard – if anyone remembers those – as to the meaning of the last one. The RCZ is an undeniably pretty thing, if not as outré as some of its previous concepts (it’s worth looking those up – as far back as you care to go). The horizontal light ‘claws’ are present and correct at the front and rear, and there’s a micro-perforated RCZ graphic across the bumper. The original’s glass bubble roof treatment reappears, and the slinky silhouette is made possible thanks to a battery that’s just 110mm thick. Forged aluminium wheels help reduce weight; they’re 21in upfront, 22in at the rear. Top Gear Newsletter Get all the latest news, reviews and exclusives, direct to your inbox. Note the triangular motifs, another callback to the original. Inside, there’s a dashboard clock from French specialist Serica, enough physical switchgear to satisfy analogue ideologues, and Pelinova recycled leather that uses offcuts that would otherwise be heading to the bin. No word yet on whether the RCZ is destined for production. But a whole heap of the tech and thinking it contains is 100 per cent happening. Good news.

artigo.texto: GEORGE TOWN: A 31-year-old man was injured while trying to put out a fire at an electric vehicle (EV) battery storage room in Jalan Jelutong yesterday. The Penang Fire and Rescue Department received an emergency call at 3.42pm. Its assistant operations director, John Sagun Francis, said the fire involved a battery storage room measuring about 10sq ft. An estimated 85 per cent of the premises was damaged. "The victim was injured while attempting to put out the fire. "He received initial treatment from the Emergency Medical Rescue Services (EMRS) team before being taken to Penang Hospital for further treatment," he said in a statement. Firefighters from the Jalan Perak station, assisted by teams from the Lebuh Pantai and Paya Terubong stations, were deployed to the scene. John said the team used two water lines fitted with two 60-metre jets and a hose reel to extinguish the blaze. "The fire was brought under control at 4pm and fully extinguished at 4.10pm. "Firefighters then carried out overhaul operations to ensure there were no further hazards," he added. The operation ended at 5.57pm, after which the case was handed over to the Fire Investigation Unit for further action.

artigo.texto: A capital paulista receberá, nos dias 4 e 5 de novembro de 2026, a conferência executiva DCD Connect | Brasil 2026, encontro corporativo voltado à cadeia de infraestrutura digital e processamento de dados. A realização foi anunciada pela DatacenterDynamics, organização internacional especializada em inteligência de mercado e eventos para o setor de data centers. As atividades ocorrerão nas instalações do Sheraton São Paulo WTC Hotel, reunindo lideranças empresariais, fornecedores de tecnologia e operadores de ativos digitais. Segundo informações divulgadas pela entidade organizadora, a agenda terá como eixos centrais a expansão física e operacional das instalações de missão crítica no país, a escalabilidade de cargas de trabalho impulsionadas por inteligência artificial (IA) e os requisitos de sustentabilidade operacional. O evento busca congregar gestores de engenharia, tomadores de decisão de operadoras de telecomunicações, investidores institucionais e formuladores de políticas para analisar os gargalos regulatórios e as oportunidades comerciais associadas à crescente digitalização da economia nacional. Conforme informou a equipe de comunicação da empresa promotora, a iniciativa foi estruturada para detalhar o avanço de novos modelos arquiteturais de instalações de processamento, além de promover rodadas técnicas sobre eficiência energética e gestão de recursos hídricos em ambientes computacionais densificados. Cenário regional e capacidade instalada no mercado brasileiro De acordo com a entidade promotora, o território brasileiro concentra a maior fatia da capacidade computacional instalada na América Latina, sustentado por investimentos contínuos em conexões submarinas, anéis de fibra óptica metropolitanos e proximidade com grandes centros financeiros e industriais. O estado de São Paulo, em particular a Região Metropolitana e o interior paulista, atua como polo primário de atração de aportes de capitais privados voltados a infraestruturas de hiperescala (hyperscale) e instalações de colocation. Paralelamente ao crescimento da demanda por armazenamento em nuvem e aplicações corporativas complexas, o setor enfrenta restrições estruturais severas. Entre os principais entraves mapeados por analistas da indústria figuram a disponibilidade de conexão em alta tensão junto às concessionárias de energia elétrica, o tempo de licenciamento ambiental para empreendimentos de grande porte e a necessidade de ampliação das malhas de transmissão regional. Transformação técnica da infraestrutura sob a demanda de inteligência artificial A ascensão de aplicações avançadas de aprendizagem de máquina (machine learning) e processamento neural impõe uma reconfiguração na engenharia básica dos data centers. A organização do evento assinala que os modelos computacionais contemporâneos demandam densidades de potência por bastidor muito superiores às médias históricas do setor corporativo tradicional, desafiando os sistemas convencionais de distribuição de energia e resfriamento por ar forçado. Para atender a essa nova classe de cargas de trabalho de alta densidade, a cadeia de fornecedores vem acelerando a oferta de soluções integradas de resfriamento direto no chip (direct-to-chip) e sistemas por imersão líquida. Essa transformação técnica altera a cadeia de valor dos projetos de engenharia civil e eletromecânica, exigindo revisões contratuais em acordos de nível de serviço (SLA) e novos investimentos em equipamentos modulares de precisão. A pauta submetida pela entidade organizadora também contempla a resposta das operadoras de telecomunicações e provedores neutros diante da descentralização das arquiteturas de processamento. Observa-se um movimento de expansão de ativos de borda (edge computing), projetados para executar inferências algorítmicas próximas aos usuários finais em capitais regionais e polos industriais fora do eixo primário paulista. - Elevação da densidade energética: aumento da potência requerida em racks dedicados a processamento gráfico (GPU); - Adoção de refrigeração líquida: substituição gradual dos sistemas legados de ar condicionado para contenção de calor; - Resiliência de rede e redundância: integração direta com múltiplas rotas de fibra para mitigação de latência; - Sustentabilidade e conformidade: utilização prioritária de energia de fontes eólicas, solares e biomassa. Projeções setoriais e perspectivas de investimento Estimativas compiladas por consultorias do segmento apontam que os investimentos privados em data centers na América Latina deverão manter taxas expressivas de expansão nos próximos ciclos plurianuais, tendo o Brasil como principal receptor de aportes financeiros. A realização do encontro em São Paulo visa catalisar debates estratégicos entre desenvolvedores imobiliários industriais, fabricantes de hardware e operadoras de serviços de rede. Segundo o cronograma técnico indicado pela DatacenterDynamics, os painéis e grupos de trabalho abordarão as expectativas operacionais para os anos subsequentes, incluindo o papel das parcerias público-privadas na desregulamentação setorial e o fomento a polos de inovação digital. Representantes de diferentes elos da cadeia de suprimentos avaliarão formas de equalizar custos de importação de equipamentos críticos e mitigar riscos cambiais em contratos de implantação. As conclusões técnicas e propostas operacionais discutidas ao longo dos dois dias de conferência deverão orientar futuras tomadas de decisão de operadoras que planejam novas fases de expansão de capacidade para o final desta década. Análise Brasil Inovador A convergência entre a demanda massiva por processamento algorítmico e a infraestrutura física representa o teste definitivo para a competitividade industrial nos próximos anos. Data centers deixaram de ser tratados como meros ativos imobiliários corporativos e assumiram o papel de infraestrutura crítica para a soberania econômica e a eficiência das cadeias produtivas. artigo.texto: At 5 a.m. in Northern Virginia, chefs are already preparing chicken and chile roja enchiladas, fried shrimp tacos, and big batches of rice and beans to feed thousands of data center construction workers. By late morning, a crew brings the food from the off-site kitchen to a break tent where workers can pick up lunch without leaving the worksite. They don't pay: The Big Tech companies spending billions on AI infrastructure foot the bill. On an average day, National Jobsite Catering serves about 1,500 meals at each of its dozen data center construction sites across Northern Virginia, Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Nevada, and Georgia, founder Scott Kaplan tells me. The busiest sites serve twice as many. After one to three years, the crews wrap up and move on. Kaplan, whose business used to consist of a fleet of food trucks catering one-off events along the East Coast, designed a venture that can follow them. If you build it, they will cook. National Jobsite Catering is part of the economic ecosystem being generated by America's data center boom. The tech giants leading the AI buildout are expected to spend more than $5 trillion on technology and data centers through 2030, with more than 1,500 data centers already in the works in the US. The room where a worker sleeps, the gym he hits before his shift, his parking spot, his lunch — these are all provided by a growing network of businesses. Local firms in the suburban and rural areas where the bulk of data centers are being built can get a windfall from a single project, but a more lasting proposition is the opportunity to serve site-to-site as construction crews move around. Whether that translates into lasting benefits for host towns is at the heart of growing pushback against the wave of data centers popping up across the country. Kaplan recognized the new opportunity a few years ago when a hyperscaler hired him to bring trucks to a site outside Philadelphia to feed 2,500 workers. "Literally the town that it was in had one restaurant — and it was in a strip club," he says. To avoid a lunch-hour bottleneck, Kaplan proposed preparing meals in a temporary kitchen and bringing them to the site. After replicating this model for other projects, his company now has 20 full-time employees and partners with established local vendors, helping them add equipment and plan production. He estimates a project can employ about 15 local people in kitchen, delivery, and distribution roles. "They know what they're doing," Kaplan says of the local partners. "But they've never cooked for 1,000 to 3,000 people." Since pivoting to data centers exclusively four years ago, revenue has gone up 10X, Kaplan says. Before thousands of construction workers can arrive on-site, they need somewhere to leave their cars — a logistical challenge that's creating a new market. WhereiPark began as a marketplace for city parking spots, but its fastest-growing business now comes from leasing lots near data center construction sites. General contractors have asked WhereiPark to find as many as 2,000 spaces for a project. A church lot used mainly on Sundays might work, as might a struggling shopping center or a nearby fairground or casino. In more remote locations, a contractor may need to grade and stripe land. Local landowners, meanwhile, earn temporary income from unused space without selling the farm. "If there's nowhere for the construction workers to park, the thing doesn't get built," says Joshua Eisen, WhereiPark's chief revenue officer. A team in Toronto does much of the search via property data, calls, and emails; a partner or the general contractor then inspects a prospective lot locally. The company also partners with shuttle operators to ferry workers between the lots and construction sites. For a builder juggling several projects, that means one contact and billing relationship instead of a new search and lease negotiation in every town. A completed facility the size of a Walmart might have just 50 spaces, so most lots return to their previous use. WhereiPark can repeat the search around another project without owning land. With global AI investment expected to exceed a trillion dollars in 2026 alone, companies of all sizes are getting in on the gold rush. Food services and facilities management giant Aramark launched a new division called Nexus earlier this year, which offers hotel-like amenities, fitness centers, and recreation to help attract skilled workers. The company noted that Nexus contracts carry higher-than-average profit margins. Executives projected that three initial data center sites could each generate Aramark about $150 million in annualized revenue once fully running. The data center housing business has a precedent in the oil patch, where companies have long followed temporary crews from project to project. Target Hospitality, a $1.8 billion company that has housed oilfield workers and operated two Texas detention centers for ICE, is building and operating accommodations for data center construction crews, including a $550 million deal for a 4,000-bed facility in North Texas. The company advertises furnished bedrooms equipped with small fridges and microwaves, as well as communal dining, gyms, and WiFi. Its modular assets can be redeployed elsewhere. In August, the company said it has secured contracts representing more than 9,000 beds and $1.4 billion since January. Facing growing opposition, hyperscalers have pitched the AI buildout as an engine of economic development, promising spillover benefits for local areas. Microsoft's "community-first" promise cited its experience in Washington state to estimate that for every direct construction job created, another is generated in sectors including security, maintenance, retail, and food service. While spillovers certainly occur, the exact level varies project to project. artigo.texto: Hoymiles HiOne All-in-One BESS Powers Thai Homes with More Resilient, Flexible Energy Systems By PR Newswire BANGKOK, Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Thailand’s hot and humid climate, growing household electricity demand and the need for greater power reliability are driving more homeowners to look beyond solar generation alone. Hoymiles’ HiOne all-in-one BESS system, paired with HiBox gateway, is helping households in Bangkok make better use of solar power, manage electricity consumption and maintain power availability during grid interruptions. Meeting Thailand’s Growing Residential Energy Needs For Thai households, hot climate drives heavy air-conditioning use, while high electricity costs and power interruptions create demand for systems that offer more than daytime solar generation. The market is also moving toward wider residential solar adoption. According to the Department of Alternative Energy Development and Efficiency (DEDE), Thailand had 3,310 MWp of cumulative rooftop solar capacity by the end of 2024. In 2026, the government also introduced a residential solar feed-in program targeting up to 500 MW of capacity nationwide, allowing eligible households to sell surplus solar electricity to utilities at THB 2.20/kWh under 10-year power purchase agreements. In this context, local installer COMSYS SOLAR has deployed Hoymiles HiOne systems with HiBox gateway across multiple residential properties in Bangkok. Configurations include 10kW or 12kW of solar capacity with 8kWh or 16kWh of storage, allowing each system to be matched to the household’s energy needs. Flexible Solar-plus-Storage for Greater Energy Resilience Hoymiles’ HiOne BESS integrates the inverter, battery and energy management system (EMS) into a minimalist, space-saving design. With maximum efficiency of 98.5% and more than 8,000 battery life cycles, HiOne combines efficient energy conversion with long-term performance. New and existing batteries can be mixed through built-in DC-DC technology, with storage capacity expandable from 8 to 64kWh. Its AI-powered time-of-use (TOU) optimization adjusts charging strategies based on electricity prices and household consumption patterns to maximize self-consumption and reduce electricity costs. The HiBox gateway serves as a central hub for whole-home backup, providing seamless off-grid switching to help keep household appliances running during grid outages. It also supports system expansion through an additional inverter, compatible third-party generators and PV inverters, as well as smart load management through its Smart Port. Hoymiles’ HiOne helps Thai households make better use of locally generated solar power while adapting to changing electricity demand. The multiple installations by COMSYS SOLAR in Bangkok demonstrate how flexible system configurations can meet diverse household energy needs and support more resilient residential energy use.
